Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 1:

Surat al-Kahf 18

It is also said: it is the Surah of the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf), as in a hadith narrated by Ibn Mardawayh. Al-Bayhaqi related from a hadith of Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is called in the Torah "the Protector" (al-Ha'ilah), because it shields its reciter from the Fire. However, he said: "It is munkar (a rejected narration)." It is entirely Meccan according to the well-known view, and al-Dani chose this view. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both. Some scholars counted it among the surahs that were revealed all at once, based on what al-Daylami related in Musnad al-Firdaws from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Surat al-Kahf was revealed all at once, and with it seventy thousand angels."

In another narration from Ibn Abbas, it is Meccan except for the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾, and so on, which is Medinan. This is also reported from Qatadah. Muqatil said: it is Meccan except for its beginning up to ﴿barren land (juruzan)﴾, and the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾ to its end, which are Medinan. Its number of verses is one hundred and eleven according to the Basrans, one hundred and ten according to the Kufans, one hundred and six according to the Syrians, and one hundred and five according to the Hijazis.

The reason for its placement after the Night Journey (al-Isra'), as it has been said, is that the former opens with glorification (tasbih) and this one opens with praise (tahmid), and the two are paired in the Balance and in the rest of speech, as in: ﴿So glorify the praise of your Lord﴾, and "Glory be to Allah and with His praise." Also, the close of the former is similar to the opening of this one, since each contains praise. Yes, a distinction has been made between them: the first praise is evident as essential praise (al-hamd al-dhati), while the praise with which this one opens indicates praise by a non-essential entitlement (al-istihqaq al-ghayr al-dhati).

Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti said about this: The Jews instructed the polytheists to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about three things: the Spirit, the story of the People of the Cave, and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. The answer to the first question was mentioned at the end of the first surah, and the answers to the other two are in this one, so their connection is appropriate. The three answers were not gathered in one surah, because the answer to the first was not given with clarification, so it was fitting that it be mentioned alone in a surah. The Surat al-Isra' was chosen because there is a shared feature between the Spirit and the Night Journey: each is something that the intellects can scarcely reach in its reality. It has also been said: the Spirit was mentioned there because the Night Journey includes an ascent (ur'uj) to the loftier station, and the Spirit is characterized by descent from that station. For this reason Ibn Sina said about it:

She descended to you from the highest abode,
a bird of dignity and inaccessibility.

Then he said: "Another aspect has appeared to me, which is that when He, the Exalted, said in that surah: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾, with the address being to the Jews, He reinforced this with the story of Musa, the prophet of the Children of Israel, with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. Its cause was the mention of knowledge and the more knowledgeable, and what it indicates of the multitude of the known things of Allah, the Exalted, which cannot be counted. So this surah is like establishing proof for the ruling mentioned in that surah."

It is narrated in a hadith that when ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ was revealed, the Jews said: "We have been given the Torah, in which is the knowledge of everything." Then this was revealed: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾, and so on. Thus this surah, from this aspect, is an answer to the doubt of the opponents regarding what was established in that one. Also, when He, glorified be He, said there: ﴿Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth in a mass﴾, He explained that here and elaborated it with His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Then when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level﴾, up to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And the Horn is blown, and We gather them in a gathering﴾ ﴿And We present Hell that Day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾. End quote. There are other aspects of connection that become apparent with slight reflection. As for its virtues, they are well known.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Kahf on Friday, a light will shine for him from beneath his foot up to the clouds of the sky, illuminating for him until the Day of Resurrection, and what is between the two Fridays will be forgiven for him."

Many narrators related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "Whoever recites Surat al-Kahf on Friday, there will be lit for him, from the light, what lies between him and the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-Atiq)."

Al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to recite it every night, as Abu Ubayd and al-Bayhaqi related from Umm Musa.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The house in which Surat al-Kahf is recited, a devil will not enter it that night." The recitation of it on Friday being a sunnah (sunniyyah), and likewise its night, many of the Imams held, and they said that repeating its recitation is recommended (mandub).

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and a group related from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever memorizes ten verses from the beginning of Surat al-Kahf will be protected from the trial (fitnah) of the Dajjal."

In another narration from him, related by Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Hibban as well, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the last ten of Surat al-Kahf will be protected from the trial of the Dajjal."

al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sahih, from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, whoever recites three verses from the beginning of al-Kahf will be protected." Etc.

A hadith related by Ibn Mardawayh from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), has come: "Whoever recites the last five of it when he sleeps, Allah, the Exalted, will raise him at whatever part of the night he wills." I have tested this many times, so let it be memorized. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Granter of success.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down upon His servant﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿the Book﴾, the perfect one, free of the need to be described with the perfection known among all other books, deserving that the name "Book" be exclusively attributed to it. It is either a reference to the whole of the Qur'an, in which case the existing is given precedence over what is awaited, or it is a reference to the whole that was sent down at that time, in which case the matter is clear. In describing Him, the Exalted, by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), there is an indication that what is within the sphere of the relative clause is the cause for entitlement to praise, which is indicated by the lam (of praise), as Ibn Hisham and others explicitly stated. It is also a notice of the great status of this glorious revelation, for how could it not be, when it is the guide to the perfection attainable in both knowledge and action? And in referring to the Messenger (ﷺ) as "servant," with his pronoun attributed to Him, the Exalted, there is an allusion to his exaltation, upon him be prayer and peace, and likewise the exaltation of what was sent down to him. There is also in it an indication that it is the nature of the Messenger to be a servant of the One who sent him, not as the Christians claimed concerning Isa, peace be upon him.

The postponement of the explicit object (al-maf'ul al-sarih) after the prepositional phrase, although its proper place is to precede it, is so that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and has not made for it﴾ may be connected to it. That is, for the Book ﴿any crookedness (iwaja)﴾, meaning any part of crookedness, whether by a defect in the wording from the standpoint of grammar (i'rab, grammatical case inflection), a violation of eloquence, a contradiction in meaning, or its containing what is not true, or calling to other than Allah, the Exalted.

Al-iwaj and likewise al-awaj both mean deviation and inclination away from straightness. However, it has been said: the one with a kasra on the ayn (iwaj) is what is perceived by the inner sight, and the one with a fatha on the ayn (awaj) is what is perceived by the eye. So the first is deviation from the immaterial straightness perceived by insight, like the crookedness of religion or speech, and the second is deviation from the sensory straightness perceived by sight, like the crookedness of a wall or a stick. It was objected to this with His saying, the Exalted, concerning the earth: ﴿You see in it no crookedness (iwaja) or unevenness (amt)﴾, for the earth is perceptible, and its crookedness and likewise its straightness are things perceived by sight, so according to what was mentioned it should have been with a fatha on the ayn. It was answered that since what is meant here is what is hidden of crookedness, to the point that establishing it requires geometric measurements that need the employment of true insight into what is purely intellectual, it was therefore named that. This was countered by the objection that "you do not see" (la tara) apparently indicates that what is negated is what is perceived by sight, so it needs to be understood that perception is intended. And from Ibn al-Sikkit: the kasra form is more general than the fatha form.

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on al-Fasih, chose that there is no difference between them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 2:

﴿Qayyiman﴾ means: upright (mustaqiman), as Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak, and it is also related from Ibn Abbas. What is meant by what has been said is that there is no flaw in its wording or in its meaning. What is meant by this is that it is balanced, with no excess in the obligations it contains such that they would burden the servants, and no deficiency in neglecting what is needed such that another book would be required, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. For this reason it was the last of the Books sent down upon the Seal of the Messengers, peace be upon him. It has also been said: what is meant by it is what was meant by the previous word, and it was mentioned for emphasis.

Al-Farra' said: what is meant is qayyiman over all the other heavenly Books, bearing witness to their soundness. Abu Muslim said: what is meant is qayyiman over the interests of the servants, taking charge of them and of their explanation for them, since it contains what orders both livelihood and the Hereafter. According to these two opinions, it is also a new affirmation (ta'sis) and not an emphasis (ta'kid). It is as if it were said: a Book that is truthful in itself and confirms others, or a Book free from defects and adorned with virtues. It has been said that, according to the latter, what is meant is that it is perfect in itself and perfects others. Its accusative is governed by a hidden verb, meaning He made it qayyiman, with the sentence being a fresh clause (mustet'nafah), or He made it qayyiman with the sentence being conjoined to what precedes it. However, it has been said that omitting the conjunction together with the conjoined element is forced. Hafs used to pause briefly on ﴿'iwajan﴾, then say ﴿qayyiman﴾.

Many have chosen that it is a circumstantial (hal) state from the pronoun in "lahu", meaning: He did not make for it any crookedness, while being upright, and with no crookedness in it, according to what you heard first regarding the meaning of upright, since its essence is that He, exalted is He, protected it from flaw in wording and meaning while being free from excess and deficiency. The same applies according to the last two opinions. Indeed, it has been said that making it a state from the pronoun, together with interpreting "upright" as "free from crookedness," is weak (rakik).

Some have responded that the weakness is removed by taking it as an emphatic circumstantial state, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾. In this there is room for discussion. It is also permitted that it be a state of the Book. It is objected that then the conjunction would come before the completion of the relative clause, since the state is like a part of it. It is answered that ﴿and He did not make﴾ etc. may be considered a continuation of the first relative clause, as an explanatory conjunction (ʿatf bayani), where He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He sent down to His servant the Book﴾, the complete one in its kind, and then followed it with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and He did not make for it any crookedness﴾. In that case there is no separation before the completion of the relative clause. This is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and hindering from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾, according to one opinion. Also, the waw in ﴿and He did not make﴾ may be a waw of circumstance, and the clause after it is a state of (the Book), like "qayyiman." This was chosen by al-Isfahani.

Abu Hayyan said: that is according to the view of those who permit two states from one state-bearer without a conjunction, while many of our companions prohibit it. Another said: the analogy of al-Farisi's view regarding the predicate, that it is not multiplied when differing between singular and clausal form, would apply to the state as well.

It was answered that this is not relevant, since what al-Farisi mentioned contradicts the view of the majority, and moreover it is an analogy with a difference (qiyas ma'a al-fariq), so it is not heeded. Likewise, what Abu Hayyan mentioned from the many is contrary to what is relied upon by most. Yet, to escape idle talk, some made the waw parenthetical (li'tirad) and the sentence a parenthetical clause, and there is inversion in the speech. The original would be: "All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book, qayyiman, and did not make for it any crookedness." This inverted order was related from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Samin mentioned that Ibn Abbas, wherever a parenthetical clause occurs within the arrangement of the verse, takes it as a delayed-moved (muqaddamah min ta'khir). He justified this by saying that it occurs between two linked words, so it is in effect outside the space between them. Since ﴿qayyiman﴾ indicates an inherent or established uprightness, being an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) and an intensive form, and there is nothing like that without some slight crookedness being imagined in it, He mentioned His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He did not make﴾ etc. as a safeguard, and it was placed first for emphasis, as in the saying of the poet:

"Ala ya islami ya dara Mayya ʿala al-bila / wa la zala munhallan bi-jaraʾika al-qatru"

From here it is known that interpreting qayyim as "upright" in its obvious sense, and al-Zamakhshari's statement that the purpose of combining it with the negation of crookedness is emphasis, since many an upright thing is attested to be upright, yet is not free of slight crookedness upon close examination and scrutiny, and that the statement of the Imam is not refuted, that His saying, exalted is He: ("He did not make for it any crookedness") indicates its being perfect in itself, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿qayyiman﴾ indicates its being perfecting of others, so by rational proof it is established that the correct order is as Allah, exalted is He, mentioned, and that what they mentioned of inversion and delay is corrupt, which reason refuses to accept. End.

By my life, this statement should not come from the Imam if it was sound to him that the said view is related from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, for the first is the interpreter of the Qur'an, and enough is it for him in eminence and knowledge of the subtleties of the tongue, and it has been said of the second: "If the tafsir comes to you from Mujahid, that is sufficient for you." The author of Hall al-'Aqd said: it is possible that qayyiman is a substitute (badal) for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He did not make for it any crookedness﴾. Abu Hayyan said: then it would be a substitution of a single word for a clause, as they said in "I knew Zayd, who is he?" that it is a substitution of a clause from a single word, and there is disagreement regarding the permissibility of that. Moreover, some claimed that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to "his servant," and then not all the previously mentioned grammatical analyses would be possible.

Aban ibn Tha'lab read "qiyaman" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the lightened ya'. In some of the Companions' codices: "and He did not make for it any crookedness, but He made it qayyiman," and this is taken as an explanation, not a recitation.

﴿Li-yundhira﴾ is connected to "anzala" (He sent down), and the lam is for causation (ta'lil). It was used as evidence by those who hold that God's acts are explained by purposes, like the Salaf and the Maturidiyya, while those who deny this make it a lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). Al-Hufi claimed that it is connected to "qayyiman," but it is not a qayyim, and the agent is the pronoun of the Divine Name; likewise in the two verbs conjoined to it. It is permitted that the agent in all of them be the pronoun of the Book or his pronoun, peace be upon him. "Andhara" takes two objects, as He said: ﴿We have warned you of a near punishment﴾. Here the first object is omitted and only the second is mentioned, which is His saying: ﴿a severe might﴾, indicating that what the speech is directed toward is the second object, and that the first is evident and needs no mention, namely those who disbelieved, by the indication of what follows. The intended are those who disbelieved in the Book. The apparent meaning of "severe might" is the punishment of the Hereafter alone. It has been said that it may include the punishment of this world too.

﴿From Him﴾ means: proceeding from His presence, exalted is He, sent down from His side, in return for their disbelief. The prepositional phrase is connected to a deleted verb, falling as a second attribute of "might." "Ladun" here means "ʿinda" (with/at), as related from Qatada. Al-Raghib mentioned that it is more specific than it, since it indicates the beginning of an end, as in "I stayed with him from the rising of the sun until its setting." It may be placed in the position of "ʿinda."

Some said: "ladun" is more emphatic and more specific than "ʿinda," and it has dialects. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read with ishmam of the dal, meaning the lightening of the voice by the vowel that separates the two letters, so it becomes a concealing of it; and with a kasra on the nun because of the meeting of two sukuns, and a kasra on the ha' for assimilation. It is understood from some statements that he read with sukun together with ishmam, meaning indicating the vowel by pressing the lips with a slight opening between them, and this was found problematic in al-Durr al-Masun and elsewhere, because this ishmam is only realized in pause at the end, and its occurrence in the middle, as here, is not conceivable. For this reason it was said that it is pronounced here after pausing on the ha'. The objection was answered by saying that it then does not indicate the vowel of the dal, though it was given as a reason that it is determined, since there is nothing in the word that could suit indicating its vowel other than it. What we have mentioned settles the matter of the problem. The majority read with a damma on the dal and the ha' and sukun on the nun, except that Ibn Kathir joins the ha' with a waw, and others do not join.

﴿And gives good news﴾ is in the accusative, conjoined to "li-yundhira." It was read irregularly in the nominative.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yabshuru" with lightening. ﴿The believers﴾, that is, those who affirm the Book, as indicated by it and by what preceded; this is mentioned after the favour of sending down the Book. ﴿Who do righteous deeds﴾, that is, the righteous works explained within it. The use of the future form in the relative clause indicates the renewal and continuity of the action, and placing the relative pronoun in agreement with its mentioned antecedent is because the basis of the acceptance of deeds is faith. ﴿That for them﴾, that is, that for them, in return for their faith and their aforementioned deeds, ﴿is a good reward﴾, which, as al-Suddi and others said, is Paradise, with its enduring bliss and great reward and what is in it. The apparent meaning supports that what is meant by it is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 3–4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning: remaining in the reward ﴿forever﴾, without any end to the duration of their staying.

﴿Abiding﴾ (mākithīna) is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾ (lahum), and the two adverbials (al-ẓarfān) are connected to it. The placing of the warning (indhār) before the good news (tabshīr) serves to show the utmost concern with restraining the disbelievers from what they are upon, while observing the precedence of clearing away (takhliyah) over adorning (taḥliyah). The repetition of the warning in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾, is connected to a specific group from among those whom the previous warning covered, of those deserving severe punishment, to indicate the complete horribleness of their state and the extreme ugliness of their disbelief and error, as what follows indicates. That is: and to warn, from among these disbelievers who utter such a monstrous thing, specifically, namely the Arabs who say "the angels are the daughters of Allah, Exalted is He," and the Jews who say "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, glory be to Him," and the Christians who say "the Messiah is the son of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He." Leaving the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) unconnected to its antecedent (al-mawṣūf), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and to give good news to the believers﴾, etc., serves to indicate that what is in the relative clause (ḥayyiz al-ṣilah) is sufficient as disbelief in the most hideous manner. The choice of the past tense form in the relative clause serves to indicate the certainty of the utterance of that ugly word from them in the past. Some have made the omitted object in what preceded a reference to this group.

In the verse there is the figure of speech called iḥtibāk (interlocking omission), where it omits from the first part what is mentioned in the latter part, which is the one warned, and omits from the latter part what is mentioned in the first, which is the one warned against. It has been objected that this leads to the exclusion of all other categories of disbelievers from warning and threat.

It has been answered that the warning of all other categories and their inclusion in the threat is known a fortiori (min bāb al-awlā), because saying "adoption" (tabannī), though grave as a word, is less than associating partners (ishrāk); and in this there is room for consideration. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah supposed the omitted object to be "the world" (al-ʿālam), and Abu al-Baqāʾ "the servants" (al-ʿibād), so that it would encompass the believers as well. It has been objected that generalization requires taking the warning in the sense of mere informing of a harmful matter without considering the befalling of what is warned against upon the warner, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you warn the people and give good news to those who believe﴾; and this leads to the noble text being devoid of indication of the befalling of severe punishment upon anyone other than this group. So reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 18, verse 5:**

﴿What do they have of it﴾, that is, of their taking Him, glory be to Him and exalted, to have a son, ﴿of knowledge﴾. The word *min* ("of") is in the nominative position, either as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) or as the agent (*fa'il*, the doer of a verb), because the adverbial phrase precedes it and depends on it. The *min* is an emphatic addition (*za'idah*) that strengthens the negation. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) or a resumptive new sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), explaining their state in what they say. The meaning is: they have no knowledge of this whatsoever, not because they are unable to attain knowledge while the object of knowledge is real or possible, but because it is impossible in itself, and with its impossibility the existence of knowledge of it cannot hold.

It has been favored that the pronoun in *bihi* ("of it") refers to the son and to the absence of knowledge, and likewise the status of the clause, as you have heard. Al-Mahdawi claimed that the clause, on this reading, is a qualifier (*sifah*) of *waladan* ("a son"), but this is not valid. It has been permitted that the pronoun refers to the implied statement drawn from *qalu* ("they said"), meaning: their saying this does not arise from knowledge, reflection, and consideration of what is permissible for God and what is impossible for Him. Al-Tabari said that the pronoun refers to God, exalted be He, with the sense: they have no knowledge of what is permissible for Him and what is impossible for Him.

﴿Nor of their fathers﴾, who said the like of this, ascribing adoption to Him, mighty and majestic be He. The explicit mention of the negation of knowledge concerning them is because they are the model (*qudwah*) for these people.

﴿Great is the word﴾, that is, their statement is great in disbelief and fabrication, because in it is the attribution to Him, exalted be He, of what scarcely befits His majesty, glory be to Him and exalted. The verb *kabura* ("it is great") and likewise every form on the pattern *fa'ula* (with the vowel *u* on the middle radical, as in *zarufa*), or transformed from *fa'ila* or *fa'ula*, al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad held, is to be attached to the category of exclamation (*ta'ajjub*). Thus the agent here is a pronoun referring to the phrase, ﴿He has taken﴾ and so on, with the interpretation of "the saying." The word *kalimah* ("word") is in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies the sense of a verb or adjective). It is as if it were said: how great is it as a word! The statement of God, exalted be He, ﴿that comes out of their mouths﴾ is a qualifier of *kalimah*, conveying the magnitude of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths. For much of what Satan whispers and the self speaks of cannot be uttered; rather, thought turns away from it. How then with such a reprehensible matter?

Al-Farisi and most grammarians held that it belongs to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (the verbs of praise and blame). Thus all their rulings apply to it, such as the agent being defined by *al-* ("the") or being a noun annexed to a definite noun, or a pronoun explained by the specifier. From here it has been permitted that the agent here is the pronoun of *kalimah*, and this is also a specifier, and the clause is its qualifier. There is no harm in describing the specifier in the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa*. Abu Hayyan and others permitted that it be a qualifier of an omitted word, which is the object of the blame, meaning: "a great word has become great, a word coming out of their mouths." The apparent sense of al-Akhfash's words is that the two positions differ.

In *al-Tashil* it is stated that it is of the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa*, and it contains the sense of exclamation, and the purpose here is the magnification of the matter in the hearts of the listeners. This is clearly indicative that there is no difference between them, and the words of some of the imams incline toward this. It was said that it is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), but its state is not hidden. Calling that *kalimah* is in the manner of calling a poem by the same name (*qasidah*, a long ode, is called a word in the sense of a complete utterance).

It was read *kabrat* with the *ba'* vowelless, and this is the dialect of Tamim. In verbs of this type the middle vowel may be *damma*, may be silent, and the vowel may be transferred to the first radical. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read *kalimatun* with *raf'* (nominative), as the agent. The accusative is more eloquent and more emphatic.

Al-Nazzam used this verse as evidence that speech is a body, since it describes it here with coming out, which is one of the properties of bodies. It was answered that what actually comes out is the air carrying it, and attributing it to speech, which is a quality, is metaphorical. It was objected that al-Nazzam, who holds that speech is a body, says it is the air qualified in a particular way, not the quality, and his argument for this is based on the principle that the literal meaning is primary. Nonetheless the dispute is verbal, with no practical consequence.

﴿They say nothing but a lie﴾, that is, what they say concerning that matter is only a statement of falsehood, which scarcely enters under the possibility of truth at all. The two pronouns refer to them and to their fathers.

[p. 204]

[Page 205]

*Fa-la'allaka bakhi'un* (﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ﴾): that is, "killing" (﴿qatilun﴾) ﴿yourself﴾ (﴿nafsaka﴾). Its meaning also includes what is in *Sahih al-Bukhari*: "destroying" (*muhlik*). The first meaning is related from Mujahid, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn 'Abbas. He cited the line of Ibn al-Azraq, when he asked him about the verse of Labid ibn Rabi'a:

*La'allaka yawman in faqadta mazaraha* ∗ *'ala bu'dihi yawman li-nafsika bakhi'u*
(Perhaps one day, if you lose its visit, despite its distance, you will one day be destroying yourself.)

In *al-Bahr* (from al-Layth): *bakha'a al-rajulu nafsahu bakhan wa-bukhuan*, meaning he killed himself out of intense grief (*al-wajd*). He cited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*Ala ayyuha dha al-bakhi'u al-wajdu nafsahu* ∗∗∗ *li-shay'in nahathathu 'an yadayhi al-maqadiru*
(Oh you, whom grief has driven to destroy himself, over a thing that the decrees have carved out of his hands.)

It is from *bakha'a al-ard bi-l-zira'a*, meaning he made the land weak by continuous cultivation, as al-Kisa'i said. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that *al-bakh'* is for the slaughtering to reach the *bikhaa'* (with a *ba'*), which is a vein lying along the nape. Ibn al-Athir and others rejected this, on the grounds that it is not found in the books of lexicography and anatomy. However, al-Zamakhshari is a trustworthy authority in this field, with wide knowledge.

It was also read as *bakhi'u nafsika* (with idafa, i.e., the genitive construction). According to al-Zamakhshari, this is contrary to the original rule for the active participle when it fulfills the conditions for governing (*'amal*), and Sibawayh alluded to it in *al-Kitab*.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Governing (*'amal*) and idafa are equivalent." Abu Hayyan claimed that idafa is better than governing.

﴿'ala athariham﴾: that is, ﴿after them﴾ (*min ba'dihim*), meaning after their turning away from faith and their distancing from it. Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and Abu al-Bukhturi, along with a group of Quraysh, gathered, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been greatly pained by what he saw of his people's opposition to him and their denial of what he had brought of sincere counsel. This grieved him intensely, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿fa-la'allaka bakhi'un﴾, etc. From this it is known that what we have mentioned is more appropriate to the occasion of revelation than the view that the meaning is "after their death upon disbelief."

﴿in lam yu'minu bi-hadha al-hadith﴾: that is, "this discourse," of great standing, which is the Qur'an, referred to at the beginning of the surah as "the Book." Describing it as such, even if its indication of being created (*hudush*) is granted, does not harm the Ash'arites (*al-Ash'ariyya*) and their like, who say that the utterances (*al-alfaz*) are created. "In" (*in*) is conditional, the clause after it is the protasis (*fi'l al-shart*), and the apodosis is omitted, relying on what preceded it, according to the majority (*al-jumhur*). It was said that the apodosis is the aforementioned ﴿fa-la'allaka﴾, etc., which is fronted in wording but delayed in meaning, and the *fa'* in it is the *fa'* of the apodosis.

It was read as *an lam yu'minu* with the hamza of *an* open, on the assumption of a preposition, i.e., *li-'anna* ("because"), and it is related to *bakhi'un* as its cause. Some have claimed that it is not permissible to govern it in this way, since it is an active participle whose governing is conditioned on its referring to the present or future, and it does not govern when referring to the past. *In* (conditional) turns the past into the future through *lam*, unlike *an* (verbal, meaning "that"), which enters upon the past that remains in its past sense, unless it is taken as a narration of a past state to evoke the image for its strangeness.

Some eminent scholars objected to this: it does not follow that when that which was the cause of something has passed, its effect has passed. How many a grief arises in the future over a past matter, whether it continues or not? And if it continues, it is more fitting, since it is more painful. So there is no need to take it as narrating a state. In *al-Kashf* this was justified on the basis that if the cause of the destruction is the non-belief, then if the cause has been completed, the effect is likewise, by necessity of the effect's realization when the complete cause is present; and if it is still ongoing, then it is similar, by necessity that it is not realized without its completion. This was challenged: it is not accepted, because this is not a true complete cause such that what was mentioned would follow. Rather, it is a source and motive, so its preceding does no harm. It was also said that the hyperbole in describing his grief over their turning away is then lost, since the destruction would not be immediately after it, but after some time. This is unlike the case where it is a narration. It was also challenged: there is no basis for this, rather the hyperbole in this is stronger, since if it issued from him over a past matter, how much more so if it continued or renewed itself? Perhaps there is in the verse what favors retaining the future sense, so reflect.

The accusative of Allah's words ﴿asafan﴾ depends on *bakhi'un*, as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*).

It was permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in it, with the interpretation "grieving" (*mut'asifan*), because the original in the circumstantial clause is derivation. It was also permitted that it be in the accusative as the verbal noun (*masdar*) of an implied verb, i.e., *ta'assafa asafan* ("he grieved with grief"). According to what is related from al-Zajjaj, *al-asaf* is intensity in grief and anger.

Al-Raghib said: *al-asaf* is grief and anger together, and it may be said of each of them separately. Its reality is the boiling of the heart's blood with the desire for vengeance. When it is directed at one who is below, it spreads and becomes anger; when it is directed at one who is above, it contracts and becomes grief. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was asked about grief and anger, and he said: "Their source is one, and the wording differs. Whoever contends with one he can overpower shows it as rage and anger, and whoever contends with one he cannot overpower shows it as grief and lamentation." With this view the poet said:

*Fa-huznu kulli akhi huznin akhu al-ghadabi*
(So the grief of every brother of grief is a brother of anger.)

Mundhir ibn Sa'd went to the view that *al-asaf* is more general than grief and anger, and that grief is over one who is not under one's control and is not under the hand of the one who grieves, whereas anger is over one who is in his grasp and possession. Here *al-asaf* is interpreted as grief, unlike its use in Allah's words ﴿fa-lamma asafuna intaqamna minhum﴾ ("when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them"). When *al-asaf* is used together with anger, what is intended by it is grief over what was said in Allah's words ﴿wa-lamma raja'a Musa ila qawmihi ghadban asifan﴾ ("when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved"), and each of them is attributed to some of the people in relation to one another.

It is related from Qatada that *al-asaf* here is interpreted as anger, and in another narration as grief. In *Sahih al-Bukhari* it is interpreted as regret (*al-nadam*).

It is related from Mujahid that it is interpreted as distress (*al-jaza'*), and those who interpret it as grief are more numerous.

Perhaps *la'alla* here is for expectation (*al-tarajji*), which is hope of occurrence or apprehension of it. Here it is a metaphor, meaning: you have reached a state in which people expect this from you, because of what is witnessed of your grief over their non-belief.

Al-'Askari said: *la'alla* here is placed in the position of a prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not destroy yourself." It was also said: it is placed in the position of interrogation. Ibn 'Atiyya made it a rebuke (*inkari*), meaning: "Do not be like that." The view that *la'alla* comes for interrogation is a Kufan view. What appears is that here it is for solicitude (*al-ishfaq*), which is intended to console and to urge abandoning grief and sorrow. It is possible that this is what al-'Askari meant.

In the verse, according to more than one scholar, there is a metaphor of representation (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*): his state, may blessings and peace be upon him, in the intensity of grief over the people's disregard and their turning away from belief in the Qur'an, and the completeness of his sorrow over them, is like the state of one from whom one expects the destruction of his own self upon the loss of what he loves, when parting from his beloved ones, out of regret for their separation and longing for their emigration. Then what was said was said. This is preferable to considering it a singular subordinate metaphor across its parts.

It was permitted that it be of the type of simile (*tashbih*), by mentioning its two sides, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and *bakhi'un*, by likening the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the intensity of his eagerness for the matter to one who wants to kill himself over the loss of a thing. And this, as you see, is weak.

[Page 207]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 18, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth﴾. The apparent meaning of *ma* (what) is its generality, encompassing all that does not have intellect, whether it is an animal, a plant, or a mineral. That is, We have made everything upon it, of those who lack intellect, ﴿an adornment for it﴾, that it may adorn itself with it and be beautified by it. This also includes the adornment of its inhabitants, and the adornment of everything that a person supposes to be such, though in reality it is an adornment only for its inhabitants. It has been said that what contains harm from animals and plants is not included in this. Whoever holds the view of generality says: there is nothing on the earth that does not have some aspect of benefit, and at the least it serves as evidence for the Maker and His oneness. Some scholars restricted *ma* to trees and rivers, others to plants because of their flowers of varied colours and their benefits, others to animals because of their varied forms, benefits and actions, and others to gold, silver, lead, copper, rubies, emeralds, pearls, coral, diamonds, and what is similar to these of precious stones.

A group said: what is meant is greenery, water, blessings, garments, and fruits. By my life, this is a restriction that the elite would not accept as general. It has also been said that *ma* here refers to rational beings, and what is meant by this, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan, and what came in a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, is men; according to what Abu Nasr al-Sijzi related in *al-Ibana* from Ibn 'Abbas, scholars; and according to what 'Ikrima related, caliphs, scholars and rulers. You know that making *ma* refer to rational beings together with the intention of what has been mentioned is very far-fetched. Perhaps those eminent authorities intended by *ma* rational beings and others together, giving precedence (*taghlib*) to the majority over the rest. What is on the earth, in this sense, is only some of the four elements and the three kinds of generated beings. The most noble of these generated beings is the human species, and it varies in nobility according to its categories. So it is possible that what they mentioned is a case of restricting to some of the categories of this most noble species for a reason that pertains to those categories. It may also be said: what is meant by *ma* is the generality of what lacks intellect and of rational beings, so that it includes those to whom the obligation (*taklif*) is addressed and others. There is no harm in this, for the accountable person has two aspects: an aspect by which he falls under the adornment, and an aspect by which he falls under the trial (*ibtila'*) indicated by God's saying: ﴿that We may test them﴾. Glorified is He, He has explicitly named some accountable persons as an adornment in His saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾. From here one knows what is in the words of al-Qadi: "It is better that the accountable person not be included, because what is on the earth is not in reality an adornment for it, but is an adornment for its inhabitants for the purpose of the trial; so the one for whom there is adornment will be outside the adornment."

*Zinatan* (as an adornment) is in the accusative as a second object of *ja'ala* (made), if it is taken in the sense of "rendered," or as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), as Abu al-Baqa' and Abu Hayyan said, if it is taken in the sense of "originating" (*ibda'*). The first *li-* (for) is either connected to it, or connected to a deleted element which functions as a qualifier of it, that is: an adornment that exists for it. The second *li-* is connected to *ja'alna* (We made), and the sentence on this basis is as follows. *Zinatan* may be taken as an object of purpose, like your saying: "I stood in honour (*ijlal*) of you so that you would respond to me with the same." The plural pronoun refers to the inhabitants of the earth among the accountable persons, which is understood from the context.

It is also permitted that the pronoun refers back to *ma*, on the supposition that it refers to rational beings. Trial (*ibtila'*) in its original sense is testing. Hisham ibn al-Hakam permitted this attribution to God, Glorified is He, on the basis of his ignorance and his claim that He, Mighty and Majestic, does not know events until after they exist, lest it entail the negation of His power over doing or not doing. Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni orthodox) refuted him in its proper place, and they said: Exalted is He, He knows the universals and particulars from eternity. They interpreted this verse to mean that He treats them as one who tests them, ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾, so that We reward each according to what befits him and what wisdom and the goodness of deed require: asceticism regarding the adornment of this world, not being deceived by it, spending it in the right manner, reflecting on its state, making it a means to knowing its Creator, enjoying it within what the Law permits, fulfilling its rights, and giving thanks for what one is given of it, not taking it as a means to desires and corrupt aims as the disbelievers and the followers of whims do. The degrees of goodness vary, and the more asceticism is strengthened, for example, the better it is. Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, asked the Prophet ﷺ about the best in deed, as Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim in *al-Tarikh* related. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The best of you in intellect, the most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God Most High, and the quickest of you in obedience to Him, glory be to Him."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: "The best of them in deed is the one most abstaining from this world." He related something similar from Sufyan al-Thawri. Some mentioned that the best is one who renounces and is content with this world with the provision of a traveller, and beyond that is good, namely one who acquires much of its lawful things and spends it in its proper channels; and the worst is one who gathers its lawful and unlawful things and spends them on his desires. The words of the Prophet ﷺ in explaining the best are the best. ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾. The use of the superlative form, although the trial includes both groups in terms of their deeds, which are divided into good and bad, and not only into good and better, is to indicate that the primary purpose of the mentioned creation is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers.

As for *ayyu* (which): if it is interrogative, then it is in the nominative as the subject, and *ahsanu* (best) is its predicate, and the sentence is in the place of an accusative object of the verb of trial, and because of what it contains of the meaning of knowledge in view of its outcome, like questioning and looking. The place of the interrogative is suspended from the action (*ta'liq*). If it is relative, in the sense of *alladhi* (the one who), then it is built on the vowel *damma*, its place is the accusative, being a substitute (*badal*) for the accusative pronoun in ﴿that We may test them﴾, and *ahsanu* is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the sentence is its relative clause. The estimated meaning is: that We may test the one who is best in deed. It is understood from *al-Bahr* that the view of Sibawayh regarding *ayyu* when it is annexed and its first part of the relative clause is deleted, as here, is that building is permitted, not obligatory. The detailed investigation of his view is not free from difficulty. The elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) remains, according to the correct view, in its literal meaning, as we have indicated, and the one being preferred over is deleted. The estimate, as Abu Hayyan said, is: that He may test them, which of them is best in deed, over the one who is not best in deed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 18, verse 8:**

﴿And indeed, We will surely make﴾ (in what will come, when the life of the world reaches its end) ﴿what is upon it﴾ of what We made an adornment. The explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun for the sake of emphasis. Many have allowed that this may be more general than what was made an adornment, and for this reason the pronoun was not used. The verb *ja'l* here means *taşyir* (making), that is, ﴿We will make﴾ that into ﴿ṣa'īdan﴾, meaning dust, ﴿jurzan﴾, meaning without vegetation. This is what Qatadah said. Al-Raghib said: *al-ṣa'īd* is the surface of the earth. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the level part of the earth, and this was also narrated from al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the road on which there is no vegetation.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported that *al-juruz* means ruin. The apparent sense is that this is not the literal meaning, and the literal meaning is what we have mentioned. Many of the imams of the language have also mentioned it. In *al-Bahr* it is said: *jaraza al-ard* (the land became *jarazah*) when its vegetation has gone due to drought or locusts, and *ardun ajrāz* means lands without vegetation. It is also said: *sanatun juruz* and *sinūn ajrāz* (a year, years) without rain. The *juruz* of the land is locusts, sheep and camels when they eat what is upon it. A man who is *jarūz* is a great eater or quick to eat, and likewise the female. The poet said:

*Indeed the old woman is a glutton, a devourer,*
*Eating a qafīz every night.*

In *al-Qamus*: *ardun juruzun* and *jarzun*, *jirzun*, *juzun*: it does not produce vegetation, or its vegetation has been eaten, or it has not been reached by rain. In the proverb: "The hater is not satisfied except with *jurazah*," meaning with uprooting. The intended meaning is making what is upon the earth into plain dust after it had been a source of wonder to the beholders and a delight to the eyes. The apparent meaning of the verse is making what is upon it, in all its parts, into such dust. This would only occur by converting all the elements of the generated beings into the element of earth, and there is no impossibility in this, since the transformation of some elements into others occurs today. It may be said that this is according to common usage, for people say: "So-and-so has become dust" when his body has disintegrated and no trace of him remains except dust. The idea of the transformation of the elements hardly occurs to them, and likewise the claim of the verifying philosophers (*muḥaqqiqī al-falāsifah*) that the forms of the elements remain in generated beings. It is very likely that the composition of generated beings from the elements is also of this kind. This matter you will hardly hear from the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*). And God Most High knows best.

The connection of these two verses with what precedes them, according to what some of the verifiers said: the words of God Most High, ﴿Indeed We have made﴾ and so on, are a justification for the sense of concern (*al-ishfāq*) contained in *la'alla* (perhaps). His words, glorified is He, ﴿And indeed We will surely make﴾ and so on, complete the justification. The sum of the meaning is: do not grieve over what you witnessed from the people of denying what We sent down to you of the Book, for We have made what is upon the earth of all kinds of things an adornment for it, in order to test their deeds, so that We may repay them according to them, and indeed We will annihilate that soon and repay them according to their deeds. In the same sense it has been said that it is a consolation to him (peace and blessings be upon him), as if it were said: do not grieve, for We will take vengeance on them for you. The apparent sense of some of their statements is to make what is understood from the beginning of the surah a justification for the concern, where he said: the meaning is: let not your grief become great because of their disbelief, for We have sent you as a warner and a bringer of good news, and as for producing faith in their hearts, you have no power over it. It has been said: there is no harm in making what was mentioned a justification for that too, because causes are not real causes. It has also been said regarding the connection: what came before contained his (ﷺ) prohibition from grief, and this contains guidance to him to adopt some of God's characteristics, as if it were said: I created the earth and adorned it as a trial for creation through obligations; then they rebel and disbelieve, and yet I do not cut off My blessings from them. So you too, O Muhammad, do not cease occupying yourself with calling them, after not regretting them. The second sentence is merely to discourage inclination toward the adornment of the earth. This connection is not hidden from you, indeed the mind hardly inclines toward it, so reflect.

[page 208]

[p. 209]

﴿Or do you think﴾: an address to the chief of those addressed (ﷺ), though the intended meaning is someone else, as many have held. The "am" here is a *munqati'ah* (disconnecting "am," which takes the sense of a shift from one statement to another), understood as if it were *bal* (rather). It indicates a transition from one topic to another, not a negation. According to the majority, the interrogative hamza is also present, while according to some scholars *bal* alone is present. It has also been said that here it has the meaning of the hamza alone, but the first view is the correct one. The meaning is: "Rather, did you think that the companions of the Cave and the Inscription were, ﴿among Our signs﴾, i.e., among the clear proofs of Our power and divinity, ﴿a wonder﴾, i.e., a sign of wonder, with the word placed in the position of an annexed noun, or described by the verbal noun for emphasis. It is the predicate of "were," and ﴿among Our signs﴾ is a circumstantial phrase relating to it, as is the rule for a indefinite noun qualified when it precedes it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿a wonder﴾ and ﴿among Our signs﴾ be two predicates, and that ﴿a wonder﴾ be a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, but this is not so. The meaning is that their story, although it breaks the customary order, is not wonderful in comparison with the other signs, of which the earlier ones are part. From here the connection becomes clear. In al-Kashf it is said that He, exalted is He, mentioned universal signs, even though it was to console Him (ﷺ), and that his soul should not be consumed with grief over their traces. The one seeking guidance is satisfied with the slightest hint, while the one who has strayed is not benefited by the signs of warning and good news, which include the principal wonders. And He, glorified is He, followed this with His saying: ﴿Or do you think﴾, etc. That is, that matter is greater than this, so whoever is not amazed at that should not be amazed at this. The address is intended for someone other than him (ﷺ), because he knew of God's power what none of the first or the second could magnify. So He denied their disagreement about their condition, out of astonishment, and their turning away from such clear signs. As for the objection to this, that turning away from the first statement is only good if the second is more strange, so that progression occurs; and the preference that the hamza is for affirmation, which is another opinion regarding this verse, is not detrimental to it, because their astonishment at this, rather than the first, is what is rejected, and it is the stranger; so understand. And [there is the objection] that what is rejected should be established and known to the hearer, whereas this is the beginning of information from Him, exalted is He, according to what is known of the occasion of revelation. That is so, because the denial of their astonishment is sufficient, and knowing it in general suffices, and it was already present. How so, when you know that it refers to another, namely the People of the Book who ordered the Quraysh to ask, and they were knowledgeable? Then, it is a shared implication, because affirmation also requires knowledge, rather even more so." End quote.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is a denial of that supposition on his part (ﷺ), in the sense: "Let that not seem great to you according to what the disbelieving questioners made great for you, for all of God's other signs are greater than their story." It is claimed that this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq, but there is something troubling in the heart about it. It has also been said: the meaning of the interrogative is the affirmation that they are a wonder, as if it were said: "Know that they are a wonder," just as you say: "I was informed that so-and-so did such-and-such," meaning: he has done it, its doer.

The address is also intended for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but this is not correct. Al-Tibi claimed that the proper reading is that the speech proceeds as consolation and the interrogative as alerting. It is said that when he (ﷺ) was overcome with grief and sorrow at the people's refusal to believe, what was overcome him, so it was said to him what was said, and it is justified by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have made…﴾ up to the end, meaning: "Indeed, We have made that so that We may test them, and when Our will was not connected to their belief, they occupied themselves with it instead of Our signs, and were distracted from gratitude, and exchanged faith for disbelief, so We did not care for them. And indeed, We will make their bodies dust for your swords, just as We will make what is upon them a barren ground. Do you not see those youths, how they were guided, fled to God, exalted is He, left the adornment and glitter of this world, and took refuge in the cave, saying: ﴿Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair﴾? Just as the will was connected to their guidance and they were guided, so it is connected to guiding a people of your community whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers." End of al-Tibi's words.

It is almost more wonderful than the story of the People of the Cave, so reflect. The word *husban* (supposition) may mean either ẓann (opinion) or 'ilm (knowledge), and it has been used in both senses. *Al-Kahf* is the wide hollow in a mountain; if it is not wide, it is a *ghar* (cave). Ibn Abi Hatim related that it is a cave of a valley. From Mujahid: it is an opening between two mountains. From Anas: it is the mountain itself, which is not well known in the language. *Al-Raqim* is the name of their dog, according to what is reported from Anas and al-Sha'bi, and this is found in a narration from Ibn Jubayr, and it is supported by the verse of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"There is none in it but al-Raqim, a neighbor, and their hunting dog, while the people in the cave lie sleeping."

[p. 210]

Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn Jubayr that it is a slab of stone on which they wrote the story of the People of the Cave and their affair, and which was then placed at the entrance of the cave. It has also been said: a slab of stone on which their names were written and which was placed on the city wall; this is reported from al-Suddi.

It has also been said: a slab of lead on which their condition was written, placed in a copper coffin at the mouth of the cave. It has also been said: a slab of gold on which this was written, and it was beneath the wall that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) built. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it was a book they had, containing the law to which they adhered from the religion of Jesus (peace be upon him). It has been said: from a religion before Jesus (peace be upon him). Thus it is an Arabic word, *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn 'Abbas, that it is a valley below Filastin, near Ayla, and the cave is, as has been said, in that valley, so it is from the *raqmat al-wadi*, that is, its side. Ibn Jarir and others related through another chain from him, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I do not know what al-Raqim is. I asked Ka'b, and he said: it is the name of the town from which they came out." According to all these views, the People of the Cave and the Raqim are a reference to one group. It has been said that the People of the Raqim are other than the People of the Cave, and their story is in the two Sahihs and elsewhere.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "While three men from among those before you were walking, rain fell on them, so they took refuge in a cave, and it closed upon them. Some of them said to others: 'By God, O people, nothing will save you except truthfulness. Let each one of you call upon God with what he knows he was truthful in.' One of them said: 'O God, if You know that I had a worker who worked for a faraq of rice and left and abandoned it, and I took that faraq and sowed it, and its outcome was that I bought with it cattle. Then he came to me seeking his wage, and I said: "Go to those cattle and drive them." He said to me: "I only have a faraq of rice with you." I said: "Go to those cattle, for they are from that faraq." So he drove them. If You know that I did that out of fear of You, then relieve us.' So the rock was moved away from them. The other said: 'O God, if You know that I had two elderly parents, and I used to bring them milk from my goats every night. One night I was late to them, and I came and they had fallen asleep, and my family and children were crying from hunger. I would not give them to drink until my parents drank. I disliked waking them, and I disliked leaving them, lest they be deprived of their drink. I kept waiting until dawn broke. If You know that I did that out of fear of You, then relieve us.' So the rock was moved away from them until they could see the sky. The other said: 'O God, if You know that I had a cousin who was among the dearest people to me, and I sought her, but she refused except that I bring her a hundred dinars. So I sought until I was able, and I brought them to her, and gave them to her, and she let me have her. When I sat between her legs, she said: "Fear God, and do not break the seal except by right." So I got up and left the hundred dinars. If You know that I did that out of fear of You, then relieve us.' So God relieved them, and they came out."

Similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, and al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, each raising it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

On this view, *al-Raqim* means a place in the mountain. It has also been said: the rock. It has also been said: the mountain. The mention of that would then be an allusion to their story and an indication that God, exalted is He, does not waste the deed of anyone, whether good or bad. But it is not the intended object in itself. It is not hidden that this is far from the context, and there is nothing in the authentic reports that compels us to adopt it, so reflect.

﴿إذْ أوى﴾ (when they took refuge) is governed by (ma'mul, the governed element) ﴿عَجَبًا﴾ (a wonder), or by ﴿كانُوا﴾ (they were), or by a supposed verb "udhkur" (remember). It cannot be an adverb of time (zarf) of ﴿حَسِبْتَ﴾ (you thought), because your thinking them to be such did not occur at that time. That is, at the time when ﴿الفِتْيَةُ﴾ (the youths) sought refuge in ﴿الكَهْفِ﴾ (the cave) and took it as a shelter (ma'wa) and a place for themselves. ﴿الفِتْيَةُ﴾ is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah) of fata, which, as al-Raghib and others said, means a young man in the prime of youth. It is also pluralized as fityan. Ibn al-Sarraj said it is a collective noun (ism jam'). Others said it is the plural of fata, like sabiyy and sibyah, and this is preferred because its like is more common. The intended meaning is the People of the Cave. The use of the explicit noun instead of a pronoun is to confirm the youthfulness they had in themselves.

It has been narrated that they were young men from the sons of the nobles and leaders of the Romans, adorned with collars and bracelets of gold, with locks of hair. It is said that because the companion of the cave is a consequence of their taking refuge in the cave, it is not appropriate to consider her with them before her explanation. The apparent meaning with the pronoun is to consider her, but the matter is not like that with this apparent noun, even though the article (al) in it is for definiteness (al-'ahd).

﴿فَقالُوا رَبَّنا آتِنا مِن لَدُنْكَ﴾ (So they said: Our Lord, grant us from Yourself), that is, from Your presence, ﴿رَحْمَةً﴾ (mercy), great mercy or a kind of mercy. The tanwin is for magnification or for kind. "Min" is for origin and is connected to "atina." It is permissible for it to be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of "rahmah," placed before it because it is indefinite; if it were placed after, it would be a qualifier of it. Mercy has been explained as forgiveness, provision, and security, but the better explanation is by what includes those and other things. In mentioning ﴿مِن لَدُنْكَ﴾ (from Yourself) there is an indication that this is by way of favor (tafaddul) and not obligation. So it is as if they said: Our Lord, favor us with mercy. ﴿وهَيِّئْ لَنا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ (and prepare for us from our affair) which we are in, of emigrating from the disbelievers and persevering in Your obedience. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and al-Zuhri read "wa-hiyyi" with two yas without hamza, meaning that they substituted the quiescent hamza with ya. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr from Asim: "wa-hi" without hamza. End.

It may be that he substituted the hamza with ya, or that he deleted it. The first is a regular substitution (ibdal qiyasi), and the second is disputed: is deletion of the letter substituted for hamza in the imperative and the jussive present analogically valid or not? The root of "tahiyah" is producing a form (hay'ah), which is the state in which a thing is, whether perceptible or intelligible. Then it was used for bringing a thing and making it easy, that is: make easy for us from our affair ﴿رَشَدًا﴾ (right guidance), reaching the path that leads to the desired goal and being guided to it. Abu Raja' read "rushdan" with a damma on the ra and sukun on the shin. The meaning is one, except that the recitation of the majority fits better with the verse endings. Al-Raghib adopted the unity of meaning, saying: al-rashad with two fathas is the opposite of error, and is used in the sense of guidance, as is al-rushd with damma and sukun.

Some said: al-rashad (with two fathas, as in some vocalized copies) is more specific than al-rushd, because al-rushd with damma is used for worldly and otherworldly matters, while al-rashad is used only for otherworldly matters. There is disagreement here with what Ibn 'Atiyya said, for he said: this supplication from them was about the affairs of their worldly life, and its wording requires that, and they were confident of the rectitude of the Hereafter and its mercy. Every believer should make his supplication about his worldly affairs according to this verse, for it is sufficient.

It may be that by mercy is meant the mercy of the Hereafter. End. Indeed, there is scrutiny in what he said, and the better course is to make the supplication general, covering the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, although its following context appears to restrict it to the affairs of the first. The lam and min are both connected to "hayyi'." If their meanings differ, such that the first is for purpose (li-l-ajal) and the second is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), there is no problem. If both are for purpose, the validity of the connection requires the well-known answer.

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases before the direct object is to show concern for them and to highlight the desire for what is postponed. The same applies to fronting ﴿مِن لَدُنْكَ﴾ before "rahmah" if it is connected to "atina." Fronting the first prepositional phrase before the second is to indicate from the outset that what is asked for is desired by them. It has been said that the expression is by way of abstraction (tajrid), which is to derive from a thing with a quality another like it, as hyperbole, as if it had reached such a level of perfection that another like it can be derived from it, as in "I saw from you a lion," meaning: make our whole affair right guidance.

[Page 212]

﴿So We struck over their ears﴾, meaning: We placed over them a veil that prevents hearing. The object is omitted, as in their saying: بَنى عَلى امْرَأتِهِ (he built upon his wife).

The intended meaning is that We put them to a deep sleep, one in which no sound could rouse them. The striking over the ears is taken as a metonymy (kinayah) for deep sleep. It is apt as a metonymy because sound and waking are among the means of removing sleep, so blocking that means indicates how firmly the sleep has taken hold. Striking over the eye, although it is more closely connected to sleep, is not suitable as a metonymy, since seeing things is not one of the means of removing sleep, so that blocking the sight would signify it. And even if it were suitable, it would signify the onset of sleep, not a heavy slumber.

Al-Qutb (al-Qutb al-Shirazi) objected to taking it as a metonymy for what was mentioned, with an objection whose refutation is not hidden. He construed the verse as an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah): the heavy sleep is likened to the placing of a veil over the ears, and then the phrase "We struck" is mentioned while "We put to sleep" is meant. This is one possible reading. It has also been permitted that it is an explicit representative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), and some verifiers (muhaqqiqin) chose this reading.

Some people took the striking over the ears to mean rendering them inactive, as in their saying ضَرَبَ الأمِيرُ عَلى يَدِ الرَّعِيَّةِ (the ruler struck upon the hand of the subjects), meaning he prevented them from acting freely. It has been objected that, apart from not fitting what will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, concerning the resurrection, this does not indicate that sleep is meant, although sleep is certainly the intended meaning. It has been answered that the one who holds this view may intend, by this, to arrive at the meaning of putting to sleep. Understand this.

The striking (al-darb) is either from ضَرَبْتُ القُفْلَ عَلى البابِ (I struck the lock upon the door) or from ضَرَبْتُ الخِباءَ عَلى ساكِنِهِ (I struck the tent upon its occupant). The fa' here is like its use in His saying the Exalted: ﴿So We answered him﴾, after His saying: ﴿when he called out﴾. For the mentioned striking and what follows from it, namely turning them to the right and to the left, the resurrection, and other things, are effects of the answering of their earlier supplication.

﴿in the cave﴾ is an adverbial complement of ﴿We struck﴾, and likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿years﴾. There is no barrier to this, especially since the two differ in place and time.

﴿a number﴾ means possessing a number. It is a verbal noun described by the common interpretation (al-ta'wil al-shai'), i.e., as if it were an adjective. It has been said that it is an adjective meaning "counted". It has also been said that it is a verbal noun of an implied verb, meaning "count a count". The 'adad (number), according to al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) and others, may be used to indicate abundance, because a small amount generally does not need counting. It may also be used to indicate a small quantity in contrast to what cannot be counted for its abundance, as when one says: بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ (without reckoning). Here it can bear both meanings. The first is more suitable for demonstrating the completeness of power, while the second is more fitting to the context of denying that the story is a wonder among the other wondrous signs, for although the length of their stay was great in itself, it is like part of a day in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that abundance suits the perspective of the addressees, while fewness suits the perspective of the one addressed. End of quotation. Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam was unaware of the nature of this description and supposed that it cannot indicate abundance and that fewness is impossible here. This is strange given his high rank, and he has similar things in his Amali (dictations). Al-'Allamah Ibn Hajar has a discussion on this in his al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyyah, which I do not think amounts to anything.

[Page 213]

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We woke them and raised them from their sleep. ﴿So that We might know which of the two parties﴾, i.e., of them, were those who said, "We have remained a day or part of a day," and those who said, ﴿"Your Lord knows best how long you have remained"﴾. It has been said that one of the two parties was the youths who thought the time they had stayed was short, and the second was the people of the city among whom the youths were raised, who knew the date of their disappearance. Ibn Atiyya claimed that this is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that one of the two parties was the youths and the other was the kings who ruled the city one after another. It is reported from Mujahid that the two parties were people of the cave's own community: one group of them were believers and another group were disbelievers. Al-Farra' said: the two parties were two believers who lived in their time, and they disagreed about the length of their stay. Al-Suddi said: the two parties were two disbelieving groups, meaning the Jews and the Christians, who taught the Quraysh to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the People of the Cave. Ibn Harb said: the two parties are Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and creation, as in His saying, ﴿"Are you more knowing or is Allah?"﴾.

[Page 214]

The apparent meaning is the first, because the definite article (lam al-'ahd, the article of prior reference) points back to something already known, and there is no prior reference to anyone other than those you have heard of. ﴿Ahsa﴾, i.e., counted or kept precise account: it is a past-tense verb, and its subject is the pronoun referring back to ﴿ayyu﴾ ("which"). This is the view preferred by al-Farisi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya. The ﴿ma﴾ in His saying ﴿for what they stayed﴾ is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya, one that turns the following clause into a verbal noun), and the preposition with its object is a fronted circumstantial phrase (ḥal muqaddam) relating to His saying ﴿a term﴾, which is the direct object (mafʿul bihi) of ﴿ahsa﴾. According to al-Raghib, ﴿amad﴾ (term, span) means a duration that has a limit. The difference between it and ﴿zaman﴾ (time) is that amad is used with reference to the end-point, unlike zaman, which is general with respect to both beginning and end. For this reason some have said: "al-mada and al-amad are close in meaning, and amad is not a name for the end-point, so that using it for duration would be a metaphor, as the end-point is used for duration in their saying: 'the beginning and end of the end-point.'" That is, so that it might be known which of them counted the duration of their stay most precisely. What is meant by counting it is keeping precise account of its discrete quantity, which is attached to it by its division into years, and its reaching, in that respect, the levels of numbers, as the fact that the duration is an expression for the years that have passed indicates. The intended meaning is not keeping account of its continuous, intrinsic quantity, since that is not called counting. It has also been said that using amad for duration is a metaphor, and its literal meaning is the end-point of a duration.

It is also permissible to intend this by supposing an omitted genitive (taqdir al-muḍaf): i.e., "so that We may know which of them kept account of the end-point of the time of their stay." It is also permissible without that supposition, since staying (al-lubth) is an expression for a continuous state corresponding to the stated time. Because of the extension that attaches to it through this, it necessarily has a term and an end-point. However, what is meant is not the end-point of that continuous state with respect to its continuous quantity attached to it by its correspondence to time that extends intrinsically, namely the moment of their rising from sleep. Knowing that is not hidden from anyone, and it is not called counting either. Rather, what is meant is its discrete quantity, attached to it by the attachment of that quantity to the time to which it corresponds, in respect of its division into years and its arriving at a particular level in the scale of numbers. The difference between this and what preceded is that in the earlier case, what counting was applied to was the duration itself, divided into years, which is the sum of three hundred and nine years; while in the later case, what counting was applied to is the end-point of that duration, namely the ninth year after the three hundred. The attachment of counting to the term in the first sense is evident; its attachment to it in the second sense is in respect of the term's arrangement of the levels of numbers beneath it and its containing them. End of quotation.

[Page 214, continued]

You know that the apparent meaning of al-Raghib's words, regarding the lexical sense, requires that amad is literally a duration and that its use for end-point is metaphorical; and that the attribution of the meaning of end-point here, through what was mentioned, is a forced interpretation that is not needed if ﴿ma﴾ is verbal-source. Yes, it is needed if ﴿ma﴾ is taken as a relative pronoun (ism mawṣul), with the omission of its returning pronoun from the relative clause; i.e., "so that We may know which of them counted the term that they stayed," that is, the time in which they stayed. It has also been said that ﴿ma labithu﴾ is in the position of an object of purpose (mafʿul lahu), and the purpose particle (lam al-taʿlil) is used because it is not a clear verbal noun and is also not concurrent. But this is not right. It has also been said that the ﴿lam﴾ is superfluous, ﴿ma﴾ is a relative pronoun, and it is the direct object, with its returning pronoun omitted; i.e., ﴿ahsa﴾ (counted) what they stayed, and what is meant is the time in which they stayed, and ﴿amad﴾, on this view, is a specifier of the relation (tamyīz li-l-nisba), which clarifies the vagueness in the relation of the direct object, transferred from the direct object; its original form being: "counted the term of the time in which they stayed."

It has been claimed that it cannot be a specifier of the relation, because it must be transferred from the subject, and that is not possible here. This is not valid, since the matter is open to dispute. What has been established in the authoritative works, such as the commentaries on al-Tashil and others, is that it may be transferred from the direct object, as in ﴿We caused the earth to gush forth springs﴾, and it may also be transferred from the subject, as in "Zayd sweated sweat." If it were made a specifier, it would not be a specifier for a single noun, and no one has stipulated that it must be transferred at all.

It has been permitted, on this supposition, that ﴿ma﴾ be verbal-source, but this is remote. The view that ﴿lam﴾ is superfluous here has been judged weak, on the ground that it is not superfluous in such a construction.

[Page 215]

Al-Zajjaj and al-Tibrizi preferred that ﴿ahsa﴾ be an elative (ism tafḍīl, comparative/superlative form), because it corresponds to what occurs in the other noble verses, such as ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾ and ﴿which of them is nearest to you in benefit﴾, and to countless other instances. Also, because its being a past-tense verb suggests that the goal of the raising was knowledge of a counting that preceded the raising, not a counting that came after it, and this is not the case.
