It has been objected, first, that forming an elative from a form other than the bare triliteral is not regular, and what has come from it is irregular, like ﴿a'dā min al-jarab﴾ ("more hostile than mange") and ﴿aflasu min Ibn al-Mudliq﴾ ("more penniless than Ibn al-Mudliq"). This is answered: there are three positions on forming an elative from such forms. The first is permissibility without restriction, which is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words. The second is prohibition without restriction, and what has come is irregular and may not be used as a model; this is the view of Abu Ali. The third is a distinction: if the hamza (the prefix) indicates transitivity, it is not permitted; otherwise, as in ﴿ashkala al-amr﴾ ("the matter became confused") and ﴿aẓlama al-layl﴾ ("the night became dark"), it is permitted. This is the preference of Ibn Usfur. Perhaps those two (al-Zajjaj and al-Tibrizi) hold permissibility without restriction, like Sibawayh, or the distinction, like Ibn Usfur. The hamza in ﴿ahsa﴾ does not indicate transitivity.

Second, ﴿amad﴾, in this case, if it is put in the accusative as a direct object, then if the verb governing it is a suppressed one, as in the words of al-Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"I have not seen a folk like our folk when we met in the morning, nor like us, when we met, as horsemen
more fierce and more protective of the truth than they are, and more striking with swords on helmets than we are."

— this entails falling into what they fled from, since they did not make the stated word a verb and then supply a suppressed one. If the governing word is the elative itself, it is not suitable for this. If ﴿yalbathu﴾ ("they stayed") is taken as governing it, the meaning is not sound, since the counting is of the duration of their stay and its term, not of their staying within the term. It cannot be said: "let it be like your saying: 'Which of you is most careful about his fasting in the month?', meaning, 'about the days of his fasting'; and the meaning is: 'Which of them is most careful about the days of their staying or its hours within the term', intending by it the entire duration." This is because, on that reading, the indefiniteness of ﴿amad﴾ becomes problematic. The excuse that they did not know its specification as a day, a month or a year, so it was left indefinite, is also not sound. The question, whether about hours and days or about months, is known to be the term of the duration of their stay, so it should be made definite either by an annexation (iḍāfa) or by prior reference ('ahd), and the possibility remains as it was.

Abu Hayyan justified its accusative status as follows: it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, and the meaning of the term is duration, and the original form is "for what they stayed of a term", and ﴿min amad﴾ ("of a term") explains what was left vague in the word ﴿ma﴾, as in His saying ﴿whatever sign We abrogate of a verse﴾ and ﴿whatever mercy Allah opens to the people﴾. When the preposition was removed, the verb reached it directly. This is, as you see, not convincing. The claim that the elative cannot govern a direct object was countered by saying that this is the view of the Basrans, not the Kufans; so perhaps the two imams (al-Zamakhshari and al-Farisi) followed the way of the Kufans, making ﴿ahsa﴾ an elative and ﴿amad﴾ an object of purpose. The truth is that whoever holds ﴿ahsa﴾ to be an elative makes ﴿amad﴾ a specifier, and that governs the specifier according to the correct view. The claim that a specifier must be transferred from the subject has already been addressed.

Third: the notion that the goal of the raising is knowledge of a counting that precedes it is rejected, because the past-tense form is used according to the standpoint of narration, and it is hardly conceivable that this implication could be understood from it.

Fourth: it would follow then that the basic counting would be realized in both parties, except that some of them would be more excellent and others less, yet this is not the case.

In al-Kashf it is stated that al-Zajjaj's view is not subject to that rejection; however, what al-Zamakhshari preferred is more deserving of preference, both in wording and in meaning. As for the first, it is evident. As for the second, it is because God related their questioning among themselves, and that is addressed to one who knows, not to one more knowing than they are, and others than them are more fitting for this. End of quotation. So understand.

﴿Ayyu﴾ is an interrogative and is the subject of the nominal sentence, and what follows it is its predicate. ﴿Naʿlama﴾ ("We might know") has been suspended from operating (ʿamal mu'allaq), as is the usual case for interrogative particles in this position. This applies whether ﴿ahsa﴾ is a past-tense verb or an elative. It has also been permitted to take ﴿ayyu﴾ as a relative pronoun. In al-Bahr it is stated: if we say that ﴿ahsa﴾ is an elative, it is permissible for ﴿ayyu﴾ to be a relative, built according to the view of Sibawayh, since the condition for its being built is present in it, namely that ﴿ayyu﴾ is annexed and the beginning of its relative clause is omitted. The meaning would be: "so that We may know the party which is most careful in counting, for what they stayed as a term, among those who did not count." When it is a past-tense verb, this is impossible, because then the beginning of its relative clause is not omitted, since the verb occurs together with its subject as a relative clause, and so it may not be built, as the completion of the condition, which is the omission of the beginning of the relative clause, is lacking. End of quotation.

[Page 215, continued]

Al-Zuhri read ﴿liyaʿlama﴾ ("that He might know") with the yā' (third person masculine), attributing the verb to God, the Exalted, by way of iltifat (a shift of grammatical person). Whatever the reading, knowledge is the goal of the raising. This is not to be taken literally, for otherwise the verse would be evidence for Hisham's view, which Allah, exalted be He, is far above saying. It has been said that it is a goal, by taking it as a metaphor for manifestation and differentiation. It has also been said that what is meant is that Our knowledge should attach to it in a present, actual manner, corresponding to its prior attachment in a future manner, as in His saying ﴿that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾. Some eminent scholars objected to this: the raising of this group did not result in their division into those who counted and others, such that knowledge could attach to them in a present manner, or manifestation and differentiation could attach to them, nor could any of that be placed in the category of goal, as occurred when the direction of prayer was changed, which resulted in mankind being divided into those who followed and those who turned back, so that present knowledge and manifestation could both attach to each of the two categories. What resulted from that raising was only their division into those who speculated, who were in error, and those who left knowledge to God, the Mighty and Majestic; and neither of these involves counting at all. He then said: if that is made a goal, by reading the noble verse as a parable based on taking knowledge as a metaphor for testing, by attributing the effect to the cause (ism al-musabbab for al-sabab), it is certain that testing does not necessarily entail that the act tested is performed by the one tested; rather, it may be intended to manifest his inability to do it, in the manner of impossible commands, such as His saying ﴿so bring it from the west﴾. This is what is meant here. The meaning then is: "We raised them to treat them as one who tests them, to see which of them counted the term of their stay most precisely; so that their inability would become apparent to them, and they would leave that to the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, and would come to know their own condition and what Allah, exalted be He, did for them by preserving their bodies; and so they would increase in certainty about the perfection of His power and knowledge, and would take insight from it regarding the matter of resurrection; and that would be a kindness to the believers of their time and a clear sign to their unbelievers."

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 18, verse 12 (part 2 of 2):

Here he has confined these lofty purposes to their origin, which proceeds from Him, glorified is He, while in what will come, God willing, he (confines them) to what proceeded from them of questioning that leads to them. This is better than depicting the simile by saying: "We raised them as one raises someone who wishes to know," since it may be imagined from it that the wish entails the realization of what is wished, so the objection returns, and one resorts to making the wish to know an expression for testing. So test and choose. End of quote.

Al-Khafaji (d. 1069 AH) critiqued him, saying: what he mentioned, along with its contrivance and its scant benefit, is not sound, because genuine choosing cannot be conceived of one who encompasses everything in knowledge. Therefore, wherever it occurs, they made it a metaphor for knowledge or what follows from it, and so he is ultimately obliged to return to what he denied. He chose to make knowledge a kinaya (metonymy) for the manifestation of their affair, so that the hearts of the believers may be reassured by the increase of faith and the proof of the deniers may be cut off. The knowledge of God, Exalted is He, when its true meaning cannot be intended in His Book, is made a kinaya for some of its necessary implications suited to its context, and the suitable one here is what has been mentioned. Then he said: The knowledge was attached to the disagreement about their term, that is, which of the two parties understood, "for how long they remained," because that is more apt to make it manifest and more effective in its spread. In al-Kashf, there is a clarification of what is in al-Kashshaf: he intended that "the knowing" is a metaphor for distinguishing and making manifest, as if it were said: that We may make it manifest and distinguish for them the one who knows the term they remained, and that it may be seen who this knower is, for it is not permissible that he be any of them, since they were between one who delegates and one who estimates incorrectly. The difference between what is in al-Kashf and what al-Khafaji mentioned is not hidden from the discerning, and what is in al-Kashf is less burdensome than his.

The depiction of the simile by saying "We raised them as one raises someone who wishes to know" is better in my view than the first depiction, and the mentioned imagining is something hardly to be heeded, so reflect deeply. It was also read: "li-yu'lima" (with the verb in the active voice, from i'lam, "to inform"). This was construed as: its subject is His pronoun, Exalted is He, and the first object is omitted, being indicated by the meaning. And "ayyu al-hizbayn" etc., from the subject and predicate, stands in the position of the second and third objects of nu'lim, and the estimate is: "that God may inform the people which of the two parties etc." When the knowing is taken as cognitive (irfani), the sentence stands in the position of the second object of nu'lim only, which is clear. It was also read: "li-yu'lama" (in the passive voice), and it was construed as: the deputy subject is omitted, i.e., "that the people may be made to know."

Then the sentence is either in the position of the two objects or of the single object, as you have heard. Some of them said: the sentence itself is the deputy of the subject, and this is a Kufan doctrine. In al-Bahr: The Basrans do not permit the sentence to be a subject or a deputy of it. The Kufans have two doctrines: one, that attribution to a sentence is permitted absolutely; the other, that it is permitted only when the predicate is something that can be suspended (ta'liq). The verification of this belongs in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 13:

﴿We narrate to you their account⁠﴾ This begins the detailing of what was summarized earlier. That is, We inform you of the detailed account of them, which is of great significance and importance. ﴿In truth⁠﴾ is either an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿We narrate⁠﴾, or from ﴿their account⁠﴾, or an adjective of it according to the view of those who permit deleting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause. That is: We narrate a narrative connected with truth, or We narrate it while connected with it, or We narrate their account connected with it, or their account that is connected with it. Perhaps in the restriction ﴿with truth⁠﴾ there is an indication that in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) there were those who narrated their account, but not with truth.

In al-Kashf, after quoting the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt mentioned earlier, there is the following text: This indicates that the story of the People of the Cave was among the knowledge of the Arabs, even if they were not fully aware of it in its exact form. Their account, as mentioned by Ibn Ishaq and others, is that the people of the Gospel (Injil) became corrupt, their sins grew great, and their kings transgressed. They worshipped idols and sacrificed to the tyrants (taghut), though among them there remained remnants upon the religion of the Messiah, peace be upon him, holding fast to the worship of Allah the Exalted and His Oneness. Among their kings who did this and became exceedingly arrogant was Diqyanus, and in another narration Diqyus. He went to extremes of excess, roamed through the lands and cities, spread much corruption in them, and killed whoever opposed him among those who held fast to the religion of the Messiah, peace be upon him. He would seek out people and give them the choice between being killed and worshipping idols. Whoever desired the life of this world submitted to his command and obeyed it, and whoever preferred the eternal life over it did not care what kind of killing he was subjected to. So he would kill the people of faith, cut their bodies into pieces, and place them on the walls and gates of the city. When the youths saw this, and they were among the notables of their city, whose name according to some narrations was Ephesus (Afsus) and in others Tarsus (Tarsus), and it was said that they were among the close companions of the king, they stood, humbled themselves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and devoted themselves to prayer and supplication. While they were in this state, the police (shurta) entered upon them, seized them, their eyes flowing with tears and their faces covered with dust, and brought them before the tyrant. They said to them: What prevented you from attending the sacrifice to our gods? He gave them the choice between being killed and worshipping idols. They said: We have a God who has filled the heavens and the earth with His greatness and majesty. We will never call upon anyone besides Him, and we will never acknowledge what you call us to, ever. Decide what you will decide. The first to say this was the eldest of them, Maksilmina. The tyrant then ordered that the fine garments upon them be stripped off, and he expelled them from his presence. He himself went out to another city, said to be Nineveh, for some matter of his, and gave them respite until his return. He said: What prevents me from hastening your punishment is only that I see you as youths. I do not wish to destroy you until I give you a term in which you may reflect and return to your senses. If you do so, well and good; otherwise I will destroy you. When they saw him leave, they consulted among themselves and agreed that each of them should take some money from his father's house, give some of it in charity, and take provision with the rest, and that they should set off to a cave near the city called Bankilus. They did what they did, and took refuge in the cave. They remained there with no occupation except prayer, fasting, glorifying and praising (Allah). They entrusted the matter of their provision to a youth among them named Yamlikha. Each morning he would disguise himself, enter the city, buy what they needed, gather news of what was happening there, and return to them. They continued in this state until the tyrant came to their city and searched for them, and summoned their fathers. The fathers excused themselves by saying that the youths had disobeyed them, plundered their wealth, squandered it in the markets, and fled to the mountain. Yamlikha at that time was in the city. He returned to his companions weeping, with a little food, and informed them of the terror he had witnessed. They turned to Allah the Exalted in fear, and fell down prostrate before Him. Then they raised their heads and sat talking about their affair. While they were in this state, Allah the Exalted struck upon their ears (sleep), and they slept, with their provision beside their heads, and their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold (wasid), and it was struck by what had struck them. The tyrant went out in pursuit of them with his cavalry and infantry, and found that they had entered the cave. He ordered that they be brought out, but no one could bring himself to enter it. When he was at his wits' end, one of them said: Did you not say that if you had power over them you would kill them? He said: Yes. He said: Then build over them the door of the cave, and leave them to die of hunger and thirst, and let their cave be their tomb. He did so. Then there came about concerning them what Allah the Exalted related.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they were in the kingdom of a king among the tyrants who called people to worship idols. When they saw this, they left that city, and Allah gathered them without prior appointment. Some of them began to say to others: Where do you want to go? Where are you going? Some of them concealed from others, because each did not know why this one had set out, and why that one had set out. So they took covenants and pledges that whoever of them had something to tell would inform the others. If they agreed upon something, well and good; otherwise each would conceal from the others. They then agreed upon one word, and said: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth⁠﴾ - to - ﴿a means of ease⁠﴾.

Then they set off until they entered the cave, and Allah struck upon their ears, and they slept. They were missed by their families, who began to search for them but did not find them. The matter was reported to the king, who said: These people will surely have a matter after today. People who left, and we do not know where they went, without any crime or anything known. He called for a lead tablet, wrote their names on it, and placed it in his treasury. Then there came about concerning them what Allah, glorified and exalted, related.

According to what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Ja'far, they were money-changers (sayarifa). Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: A man from the disciples (hawariyyun) of Jesus, peace be upon him, came to the city of the People of the Cave, wanting to enter it. It was said to him: At its gate there is an idol, and no one enters without prostrating to it. He disliked to enter, so he went to a bathhouse (hammam) near the city and hired himself out to its owner. He worked there, and the owner of the bathhouse saw the blessing and provision (that came with him), and began to rely upon him. Some youths of the city became attached to him, and he began to tell them about the news of the heavens and the news of the Hereafter, until they believed. They were of similar appearance and good bearing to him. He stipulated with the owner of the bathhouse that the night was his, and that nothing should come between him and his prayer when it was time. Then the son of the king came with a woman, to enter the bathhouse with her. The disciple reproached him, saying: You are the son of the king, and you enter with this woman, whose description is such and such! He was ashamed and left, but returned a second time, and he insulted him and rebuked him, yet he paid no attention until he entered, and she entered with him. They both spent the night in the bathhouse, and both died there. The king was informed, and it was said to him: The owner of the bathhouse has killed your son. He sought him but could not find him, and whoever was with him fled. He then sought the youths, and they left the city. They passed by a companion of theirs who was in his field, and he was in the same condition as they were. They told him that they were being sought, so he went with them until night overtook them at a cave. They entered it, and said: We will spend the night here, and in the morning, if Allah the Exalted wills, we will see what we decide. Then (sleep) was struck upon their ears. The king went out with his companions following them until they found that they had entered the cave. Whenever any man among them tried to enter it, he was terrified and could not bring himself to enter. One of those present said to the king: Did you not say that if you had power over them you would kill them? He said: Yes. He said: Then build over them the door of the cave, and leave them to die of thirst and hunger. He did so, and then what happened happened. Other accounts have been narrated, and the reports concerning the details of their affair differ.

In al-Bahr: There has come no sound hadith describing how they gathered and set out, and there is no reliance except on what Allah has related of their story.

﴿Indeed they were youths⁠﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), built upon a question from the one being addressed. The discussion of the youths has already preceded. ﴿who believed in their Lord⁠﴾: that is, in their Master and the one who looks after their interests. Here there is a shift (iltifat) from the first person (speaking) to the third person (absence), and it is chosen to indicate that the attribute of lordship is the reason for their faith, and for the statement that came from them, as will be related about them.

﴿And We increased them in guidance⁠﴾ by strengthening them in faith, granting them success in righteous deeds, devotion to Allah the Exalted, and asceticism regarding this world.

In al-Tahrir: The meaning is: We increased them in fruits of guidance, or in certainty; there are two views. What brought about the increase was the carrying out of what was commanded and the abandoning of what was forbidden, or the making of the dog speak to them, telling them that it was upon what they were upon of faith, or the sending down of an angel upon them to give them good news and strengthen them, and to inform them of the emergence of a Prophet from the Arabs through whom the religion will belong entirely to Allah the Exalted, so they believed in him (ﷺ) before his mission. End of quote.

It does not follow from the statement that an angel was sent down upon them with that message that they were prophets, as is not hidden. In ﴿We increased them⁠﴾ there is a shift from the third person (absence) to the first person (speaking), upon which the composition of the noble verse is built both in its context and in its sequence, and in it there is what there is of magnifying the matter of the increase.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 14:

﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾ We made them firm through patience, so that the violent winds of separation from their homeland, of leaving behind their families, their comforts and their brothers did not uproot them, and fear of their tyrannical king did not disturb them, nor did the multitude of the disbelievers alarm them. The original meaning of *rabt* (binding) is tying firmly, a well-known sense, and its use for what has been mentioned is figurative (*majaz*), as more than one scholar has said. In al-Asas (*Asas al-Balagha*): "I bound the animal (*rabatta al-dabba*): I tightened it with a tether (*ribat*), and the *marbat* is the rope." Among the figurative usages: "God Most High bound upon his heart," meaning He made him patient, and *rabit al-ja'sh* (one whose heart is steady).

In al-Kashf (*al-Kashshaf*): Since fear and attachment disturb hearts from their places of rest, do you not see the words of God Most High: ﴿and the hearts reached the throats﴾ (33:10). It has been said that the opposite of this is "his heart was bound" when it became firmly established and steady, and this is an illustration (*tamthil*).

Some have permitted that the statement contains a implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya takhyiliyya*, a metaphor in which the comparandum is concealed and only an imaginative feature is indicated), and the verb was followed by *'ala* although it is transitive by itself, because it has been treated as intransitive, as in his saying: "his blade wounds in their hamstrings."

﴿when they stood up﴾ is connected to *rabatna* (We strengthened). Their "standing" means their rising with resolve to turn to God Most High and to separate themselves from the people, as in the saying "So-and-so stood up to such-and-such" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness. Close to this is what has been said: that it means their taking a stand to proclaim the religion.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related that they went out of the city and gathered behind it without prior arrangement. One man among them said: "He is more like them. I find in myself something that I do not think anyone else finds." They said: "What do you find?" He said: "I find in myself that my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said also: "We are like that," and they all stood up, ﴿and they said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. It has already been mentioned just above, from Ibn Abbas, the report that they gathered without prior arrangement too, except that he said that some of them concealed their condition from others until they made a covenant with one another and gathered upon one word, and so they said that.

The author of *al-Ghaniyan* said: What is meant is their standing before the tyrant Daqyanus. They stood before him when he invited them to worship idols, and he threatened them with what he threatened. While they were before him, a cat (*hirra*), and it is said a mouse (*fa'ra*), moved, and the tyrant was frightened of it. Some of them looked at others, and they could not restrain themselves from saying that, without caring about him. It has also been said: what is meant is their standing to call the people secretly to faith. Ata said: what is meant is their rising from sleep, and this is nothing. Similar to it is what has been said: that what is meant is their standing upon faith. How excellent is what they said! For His Lordship over the heavens and the earth requires His Lordship over what is in them, and they are among that whole, that is, by implication. They followed their claim with disavowal of any god other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, and they said: ﴿We shall never call upon any god besides Him﴾. They used *lan* (never) because negation with it is more emphatic than negation with other particles, to the point that it has been said that it conveys the continuation of time, so the meaning becomes: we shall never worship, besides Him, any god, that is, any other object of worship, either independently or in partnership. It has been said: they changed from saying "lord" (*rabban*) to saying "god" (*ilahan*) to make explicit the refutation of the opponents, who used to call their idols gods, and to indicate that the basis of worship is the attribute of divinity, and to make known that His Lordship, Exalted is He, is by way of divinity and not by way of figurative ownership.

It may be said: they indicated by the first clause the Oneness of Lordship (*tawhid al-rububiyya*), and by the second clause the Oneness of Divinity (*tawhid al-uluhiyya*), and these are two distinct matters. The idol-worshippers do not hold this, and they hold the first, ﴿and if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God﴾ (31:25). God, Glorified is He, related about them that they say: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us nearer to God in position﴾ (39:3). And it is authentically reported that they also say: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns." They placed the first clause, although the apparent story is that they were in the situation indicated by the second clause, namely the Oneness of Divinity, because the apparent meaning is that their people associated others with Him in it, and they were only called to that association. This is to show the perfection of faith. They began with what points to the Oneness of Lordship, because it is the first level of Oneness. And the Oneness that the souls acknowledged in the world of atoms (*'alam al-dharr*), on the day when He, Glorified is He, said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ (7:172). In mentioning that first and the other after it there is a gradual progression in opposing the idolaters, for the Oneness of Lordship points to the Oneness of Divinity, on the basis that the exclusiveness of Lordship to Him, Mighty and Majestic, is the cause of the exclusiveness of divinity and the entitlement to being worshipped to Him, Glorified and Exalted. God, Majestic and Exalted, has held the idolaters, who affirm the exclusiveness of Lordship to Him, to this in more than one place. And because the first clause, by pointing to the Oneness of Lordship, also points to the Oneness of Divinity, it has been said that the second clause in it is an emphasis upon it. So reflect, and do not hasten to object.

The prepositional phrase *min dunihi* is connected to an omitted element which occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the indefinite noun after it; had it been postponed, it would have been a qualifier: "We shall never call upon a god existing besides Him, Exalted is He." ﴿Indeed we would have uttered then an enormous lie﴾, that is, a statement containing excessive deviation, that is, a distance from the truth that is extreme, or a statement that is itself the very excess and extreme distance from the truth, with the verbal noun used as a qualifier for intensification, then limited to the qualifier for intensification upon intensification. Abu al-Baqa permitted that *shatatan* be an object of *qulna* (we said). Qatada explained it as "falsehood," Ibn Zayd as "error," and al-Suddi as "injustice." All these are explanations by necessary implication, and the original meaning is what we have pointed to, for it derives from *shatta* when someone goes to extreme distance. They cited the verse:

"The desire has gone far away at Hazwa, and hope has come to an end."

The sentence contains an implied oath, and the *lam* falls in its answer. *Idhan* is a particle of answer and of condition, so it indicates an implied condition, that is: "If we called upon and worshipped besides Him a god, by God, we would indeed have said," and so on. The implication of worship for speech is because worship does not lack acknowledgment of the divinity of the object of worship and supplication to Him. In this statement there is an indication that the youths were called to worship idols and were rebuked for abandoning it, and this is more consistent with their standing before the king

[p. 219]

﴿Hā'ulā'﴾ ("these") is the mubtada' (the subject of a nominal sentence), and the demonstrative carries a sense of belittling them. ﴿Qawmunā﴾ ("our people") is an 'atf bayan (explanatory apposition) to it, not its khabar (predicate), because it does not complete the meaning, nor a sifah (qualifying adjective), because the condition for that is not met. The khabar is His statement, exalted is His majesty: ﴿ittakhadhū min dūnihi﴾ ("they have taken besides Him") ﴿ālihah﴾ ("gods"), meaning: they made them, carved them for themselves.

Al-Khafaji said: This implies that they worshipped them, and there is no need to supply a further element as some have said, on the basis that mere making is not sufficient for the intended meaning. Interpreting ittikhādh as "making" is one of two possibilities mentioned by Abu Hayyan; the other is interpreting it as "rendering," in which case it takes two objects, the first being ﴿ālihah﴾ and the second being implied. It has also been permitted that ﴿ālihah﴾ is the first object and ﴿min dūnihi﴾ the second, but as you see, that is far-fetched. In any case, the statement is a report that carries the meaning of denunciation, not a pure report, as indicated by what follows it, and because the benefit of the report is already known. ﴿Lawlā ya'tūna﴾ ("why do they not bring") is an exhortation in the form of denunciation and challenge, since it is impossible for them to bring ﴿'alayhim﴾ ("upon them") — with an implied noun, that is, upon their divinity, or upon the validity of their taking them as gods — ﴿bisulṭānin bayyin﴾ ("a clear authority"), meaning a proof clearly indicating their claim, since religion is not to be taken except by it. It has been used as evidence that whatever has no proof, such as the examples mentioned, is rejected.

[p. 220]

﴿Faman aẓlamu mimmani iftarā 'alā Allāhi kadhibā﴾ ("Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God") — by attributing a partner to Him, exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. The meaning of this construction has already been verified. This statement may have been made by them in the presence of the tyrant, as a rebuke to him, a challenge to him, and an emphasis on "disavowal" of worshipping what he calls them to, in a fine manner. It may also be that they said it among themselves, concerning what they had resolved upon. The report of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, mentioned earlier, is explicit that this statement, and what precedes it and what follows it up to ﴿mirfaqā﴾ ("a means of support"), was said among themselves. The claim that, if the standing mentioned earlier refers to their standing before the tyrant, it necessarily follows that this statement was issued by them after leaving his presence, is not accepted, as is not hidden. Yes, it should be that

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وإذِ اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ إلا اللَّهَ﴾ ("And when you withdraw from them and from what they worship, except Allah"), as a saying that was spoken among themselves in general, one of them addressing another. In Majma' al-Bayan (a major Shi'i Qur'an commentary), it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (رضي الله عنهما) that its speaker was Yamlikha. I'tizal (withdrawing, keeping away from something) means avoiding a thing either physically or in the heart, and both meanings are possible here. Ta'azzul has the same meaning, and from this is the line:

*O house of 'Atika, from which I keep away for fear of enemies, while my heart is entrusted to it.*

The word *mā* (ما) may be a relative pronoun (meaning "what") or a verbal-source particle (meaning "that"). In both cases the conjunction connects to the object pronoun (in ﴿اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهم﴾). The apparent view is that the exception (istithna', exception from a general statement) is connected (muttasil) in both cases. On the second possibility, a noun must be supplied on the excepted side for the connection to work, meaning: "And when you have withdrawn from them, and have withdrawn from those who worship them, except Allah the Exalted"; or "when you have withdrawn from them and from their worship, except the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Supplying an excepted-from noun for this second possibility, such as "their worship of their objects of worship," is strained. It is also possible that the exception is disjunctive (munqati', where the excepted item is not of the same kind as what precedes). On the first view, the people worshipped Allah the Exalted and also worshipped others, as is reported in some narrations.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym transmitted from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that he said: "The people of the youths used to worship Allah the Exalted and worship with Him various other gods. So the youths withdrew from the worship of those gods, but they did not withdraw from the worship of Allah the Exalted."

On the second view, they worshipped none but other than Allah the Exalted. It has been said that this is more fitting with His words the Exalted at the beginning: ﴿هَؤُلاءِ قَوْمُنا اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ آلِهَةً﴾ ("These are our people; they have taken gods besides Him"). So reflect.

It is also permitted that *mā* be a negation, with the exception being "emptied" (mufarragh, where the excepted element is left without a stated antecedent), and the sentence is a report from Allah the Exalted about the youths concerning monotheism, placed parenthetically between *idh* (إذ) and its response, namely His words ﴿فَأْوُوا﴾ ("then take refuge"), meaning: "resort" ﴿إلى الكَهْفِ﴾ ("to the cave"). This parenthetical insertion has been objected to in al-Kashshaf (a major commentary by al-Zamakhshari), on the grounds that His words ﴿وإذِ اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ with ﴿فَأْوُوا﴾ mean: "And when you have withdrawn from them and from what they worship, then devote worship to Him in a place where you can be firm." Thus the parenthetical insertion indicates that they were truthful, and that they carried out what they had enjoined on one another, so it confirms the content of the sentence. As for ﴿فَأْوُوا﴾ being the response, al-Farra' held this view. It has been said that it is an indicator of the response, meaning: "And when you withdraw from them in an inward withdrawal (i'tiqadi), then withdraw from them in a bodily withdrawal (jismani); or if you intend bodily withdrawal, then do so." Both of these views have been objected to on the grounds that *idh* without *mā* is not used as a conditional particle. In Hama' al-Hawami', the view that it can be is a weak opinion of some grammarians, or a loose usage, because it has the meaning of the conditional. So here it is causal (ta'lilliyya) or temporal (zarfiyya). Its connection has been said to be to a deleted *fa'wū* (فأووا) that is indicated by the mentioned one, not to it, because of the presence of the *fa'* (ف); or to the mentioned one, and the adverbial element (zarf) admits extension that other elements do not. Abu al-Baqa' said: *idh* is an adverbial element attached to a deleted verb, meaning: "And some of them said to others." Its apparent meaning is that by the deleted verb he meant this. He said: "And I say: this is among the most astonishing of wonders."

In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada, the reading is: "and what they worship besides Allah." Harun said that in some of the codices it reads: "and what they worship besides us." This supports the parenthetical view. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, a major commentary by Abu Hayyan), it is said that what is in the two codices is an explanation and not a recitation, because it contradicts the black script of the Imam (the 'Uthmanic codex). He claimed that the widely transmitted (mutawatir) reading from Ibn Mas'ud is what appears in the text.

﴿يَنْشُرْ لَكُمْ﴾ ("your Lord will spread for you") means: will extend and widen for you ﴿رَبُّكُمْ﴾ ("your Lord"), the Master of your affair, who guided you to faith ﴿مِن رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ ("of His mercy") in both abodes ﴿ويُهَيِّئْ﴾ ("and will prepare") means: will facilitate ﴿لَكم مِن أمْرِكُمْ﴾ ("for you concerning your affair"), which you are facing, namely fleeing with your religion and turning wholly toward Allah the Exalted ﴿مِرْفَقًا﴾ ("a means of ease"), that by which you may gain benefit and advantage. It is the object of *yuhayyi'* (يُهَيِّئْ), and the object of *yanshur* (يَنْشُرْ) is deleted, meaning: the good and the like ﴿مِن أمْرِكُمْ﴾ ("concerning your affair"). According to some marginal notes, it is connected to *yuhayyi'*, and *min* (مِن) is either for the starting point of the action or for partiality. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is for substitution, and the meaning is: "He will prepare for you, in place of your difficult affair, a means of ease," as in His words the Exalted: ﴿أرَضِيتُمْ بِالحَياةِ الدُّنْيا مِنَ الآخِرَةِ﴾ ("Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?") and the line:

*So would that we had a drink of the water of Zamzam, chilled, that had spent the night on Tahayan.*

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial element (hal) of *mirfaqan* (مِرْفَقًا), in which case it is attached to a deleted element. The fronting of *lakum* (لَكم) is, as has been mentioned many times, a signal from the very beginning that what is delayed is among their benefits, and a stirring of anticipation for its arrival. The apparent view is that they said this out of confidence in the grace of Allah the Exalted, and strength in their hope, because of their reliance upon Him, glory be to Him, and the clarity of their certainty, for they were knowers of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Allah the Exalted never sent a prophet except while he was young, and no one was given knowledge except while he was young." And he recited: ﴿قالُوا سَمِعْنا فَتًى يَذْكُرُهم يُقالُ لَهُ إبْراهِيمُ﴾ ("They said: We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim"), ﴿وإذْ قالَ مُوسى لِفَتاهُ﴾ ("And when Musa said to his young companion"), and ﴿إنَّهم فِتْيَةٌ آمَنُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("Indeed they were youths who believed in their Lord").

It is also permitted that they said this on the report of a prophet in their era concerning it, or that one of them was a prophet to whom this was revealed, and so he said it. It is not hidden that what has been mentioned is merely a possibility without a reason.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Humayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr in the transmission of al-A'sha, al-Barjami, and al-Ju'fi from him, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of Harun, read: *mirfaqan* (مَرْفِقًا) with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'* (مَرْفِقًا). There is no difference in meaning between this and the form with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa'*, according to what al-Zajjaj and Tha'lab reported, because each of them is used both for the matter by which one gains benefit and for the limb (the elbow). Makki transmitted from al-Farra' that he said: "I know of no form for matter, for the hand, or for anything else except the kasra on the *mim*." Al-Kisa'i denied that *mirfaq* could refer to the limb except with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'*. Abu Hatim disagreed and said: "*mirfaq* with a fatha on the *mim* is a place, like *masjid* (mosque)." Abu Zayd said: "It is a verbal noun following the pattern *mafil*, like *marji'* (return-place)." It has been said that both are dialectal forms for that by which one gains benefit. As for the limb of the hand, it is with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa'* only. Al-Farra' also reported that the people of the Hijaz say *mirfaqan* with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'* for that by which you gain benefit, and they use a kasra for the human elbow. As for the Arabs in general, they may use a kasra on both *mim* and *fa'*, end of quote. Mu'adh permitted a fatha on both the *mim* and the *fa'*.

This verse has been cited as evidence for the excellence of emigrating (hijra) for the safety of one's religion, and for the reprehensibility of remaining in a land of disbelief when it is not possible to remain there without openly displaying the word of disbelief. And success is from Allah the Exalted.

[Page 221]

[Page 222]

﴿And you see the sun﴾: an explanation of their state after they had taken refuge in the cave. God, exalted is He, did not state it explicitly, relying on His earlier words: ﴿when the youths sought refuge in the cave﴾, and on what follows from the attribution of the cave to them and their being in a spacious part of it. It has also been permitted that this omission is a notice that explicit mention is unnecessary, because their conduct in accordance with the requirement of the matter is evident, since it proceeded from a correct judgement. God, exalted and glorified is He, has also omitted other clauses which are not hidden. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit for it, and it is for emphasis on the visibility of the matter. The intention is not to report that the seeing occurred, but to inform that, if you were to see the cave, you would see the sun ﴿when it rises, inclining﴾

[Page 223]

That is: it withdraws. Its original form is *tatazāru* with two *tā'*s, one of which was deleted for lightness. This is the reading of the Kufans: al-A'mash, Ṭalḥa, Ibn Abī Layla, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dān, Abū 'Ubayda, Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, and Muḥammad ibn 'Īsā al-Iṣbahānī. The two Ḥaramīs (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and Abū 'Amr read *tazzāwaru* with a fatḥa on the *tā'* and a shadda on the *zāy*. Its original form is also *tatazāru*, but the *tā'* was assimilated into the *zāy* after being converted into a *zāy*. Ibn Abī Ishāq, Ibn 'Āmir, Qatāda, Ḥumayd, and Ya'qūb (from al-'Umarī) read *tazwarru* like *taḥmarru* (*taḥmarru* being the pattern of verbs of defects and colours). This pattern occurs rarely outside those categories. Jābir, al-Jaḥdarī, Abū Rajā', al-Sikhtiyānī, Ibn Abī 'Abla, and Wardān, from Abū Ayyūb, read *tazwārru* like *taḥmārru*, which in form is like the previous reading. Ibn Mas'ūd and Abū al-Mutawakkil read *tazwa'irru*, with a hamza before the doubled *rā'*, like *taṭma'innu*. Perhaps the hamza was introduced to escape the meeting of two consonants (*sākinān*), although that is permissible in such cases where the first is a long vowel letter (*ḥarf madd*) and the second is assimilated into a similar letter. All of these are from *al-zawar* with two fatḥas and light pronunciation, meaning inclination. Some scholars restricted it to inclination of disposition, while most held it general. From it comes *al-azwar*, one who inclines his eye toward a side, and it may occur in other than the eye. Ibn Abī Rabī'a said:

*And my side, out of fear of the people, is inclined*

'Antara said:

*He inclined away from the impact of the spears upon his chest, and complained to me with a tear and a neigh*

Bishr ibn Abī Ḥāzim said:

*The guides aim with them for the waters of a palm grove, and in them is a turning away from the Abānīn*

From it also comes *zārahu*, when he inclined toward him. *Al-zūr* (falsehood) is so called because it inclines away from the reality and does not correspond to it. Likewise *al-zūr* in the sense of an idol, in the verse:

*They came with their idols, and we came with the deaf*

Al-Rāghib said: *al-zawar* with the *wāw* moved (*zawar*) is inclination, while *al-zawr* with the *wāw* still (*zawr*) is the upper chest. *Al-azwar* is one inclining in his chest. *Zurtu fulānan* means I met him with my chest, or I intended his chest, like *wajjahtuhu*, meaning I intended his face. What we have mentioned is the well-known meaning. It is related from Abū al-Ḥasan that he said: "There is no meaning to *tazwarru* in the verse, because *al-izwirār* is contraction." This is a criticism of the reading of Ibn 'Āmir and those with him, by something that would necessitate changing the *kunya*. In sum, the meaning is: when it rises, it turns away and inclines ﴿away from their cave﴾ in which they took refuge. The attribution is for the slightest connection. ﴿to the right﴾: that is, toward the side of the right of the cave as the one entering proceeds to its depth, that is, its side which faces the west. Or it means toward the right side of the youths, and its outcome is like the previous one. It is in the accusative by way of adverbial location. Al-Mubarrad said in *al-Muqtaḍab*: "*dhāt al-yamīn* and *dhāt al-shimāl* are among the variable adverbs, like *yamīnan* and *shimālan*."

﴿And when it sets﴾: that is, you see it at its setting. ﴿passes them by﴾: that is, it turns away from them. Al-Kisā'ī said: "It is said: *qaraḍtu al-makān* when you turned away from it and did not stay at it." ﴿to the left﴾: that is, toward the side of the left of the cave, that is, its side which faces the east. Many said: it is from *al-qarḍ* in the sense of cutting. The Arabs say: *qaraḍtu mawḍi' kadhā*, meaning I cut it. Dhū al-Rumma said:

*To litters which pass over the sand-hillocks of a height, to the left, and on their right are the horsemen*

The meaning is that it passes beyond them. ﴿while they were in a spacious part of it﴾: that is, in a wide space of the cave. It is, as is said, from *al-fajā*, which is the distance between the thighs. It is said: *rajulun afjā* (a man with wide thighs) and *imra'atun fajwā*. It is pluralised as *fijā'*, *fijan*, and *fajawāt*. The sum of the two clauses is that they were not touched by the sun at all, so that it would harm them, while they were in the middle of the cave in such a place that the breeze reaches them and the distress of the cave and the heat of the sun do not harm them. That is because the door of the cave, as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, was opposite the Dippers (*Banāt Na'sh*). The nearest of the risings and settings to its alignment are the rising and setting of the head of Cancer. When the sun's path is its path, it rises inclining away from it, facing its right side, which is the side toward the west, and sets aligned with its left side, so its rays fall on the side of it, dissolving its foulness and balancing its air. They do not fall upon them, which would harm their bodies and wear out their clothes. Perhaps the inclination of the door toward the west was greater, and for this reason *tazāwur* was applied to their cave and *qaraḍ* to themselves. Al-Zajjāj said: "It is not for what has been mentioned, but purely because God, exalted is He, turned the sun by the hand of His power away from striking them, as a departure from custom, as an honour for them." The phrase ﴿while they were in a spacious part of it﴾ was brought as a circumstantial clause showing that what was mentioned is a marvellous matter, as though it were said: "You see the sun inclining away from them to the right and left, and not circling around them, while they are in a spacious part of the cave exposed to its striking, were it not that the hand of decree held it from them." It is argued from this for that, by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾, where *dhālika* is made a reference to what was mentioned of the inclining and passing by in rising and setting, to the right and left. It does not appear that it is a sign according to the previous view, as clearly as it appears according to this view. For its being a sign indicating the perfection of God's power, the truth of monotheism, and the honour of its people with Him, exalted is He, is on this view more manifest than the sun at the height of the day.

It is said that this was before the door of the cave was sealed. Abū ʿAlī said: "The meaning of *taqriḍuhum* is that it gives them a portion of its light, then quickly departs and takes back its light, so it is like a loan which its owner takes back." The sum of the two clauses according to him is that the sun inclines in the morning away from their cave and touches them in the evening with a light touch. It was refuted that the verb *qaraḍa* in this sense is not heard as a triliteral, so that the *yā'* of the present tense would take a fatḥa. Some chose that the meaning is what was mentioned, except that he made *taqriḍuhum* from *al-qarḍ* (lending) to them, and the meaning is: "When it sets, it cuts off for them a portion of its light." The reason for choosing this is his supposition that if the sun did not touch their place at all, its air would become corrupt and what is in it would rot, and that would be a cause of their destruction. There is much in this. Most commentators hold that the sun did not touch them at all, although they differ about the origin of that.

A group chose that it was purely God's blocking the sun, contrary to what is customary. They said: "The indication supports that most fully, and the improbability is not to be considered, especially in what we are concerned with, for the whole matter of the people of the cave is contrary to custom."

Some who held that the origin is the door of the cave being opposite the Dippers made that an indication of their sheltering in a cave of this kind. Another made it an indication of God, exalted is He, preserving them in that cave for the long period. Another made it an indication of God, exalted is He, informing His Messenger (ﷺ) of their history. It is objected to the last two that the mention of that within the course of the narrative does not support them. Some made it an indication of their being guided to monotheism, opposing their people and fathers, and their disregard for them and their king despite their youth, and their taking refuge in a cave of this description. This is not without beauty, and to it I incline. And God knows best.

It was read *yaqriḍuhum* with the *yā'* (third person), and perhaps the pronoun refers to the setting of the sun.

Abū Ḥayyān said: "That is, the cave passes them by."

﴿Whom God guides﴾: whom He, exalted is He, directs by a guidance that reaches the truth and grants him success in what He loves and is pleased with. ﴿is the one rightly guided﴾: the one who attains the greatest portion in both abodes. What is intended is either praise of the people of the cave, and testimony for them that they attained the sought goal, and a report of the realisation of what they hoped for of the spreading of mercy and the providing of a place of ease; or an alert that such signs are many, but the one who is favoured by them is the one whom God, exalted is He, has enabled to reflect upon them and to be enlightened by them. So what is meant by *man* is either the youths or whoever includes them and others, and in this there is also praise of them, and it is as you see.

Some made it praise of God, exalted is He, to match His words ﴿and We increased them in guidance﴾ and to join it, and to harmonise with His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿and whomever He leaves astray﴾, meaning: He creates misguidance in him by diverting his choice toward it. ﴿you will never find for him﴾ ever, even if you search and investigate thoroughly, ﴿a protecting friend (walī)﴾ who helps, ﴿a guide (murshid)﴾ who directs him to the truth and rescues him from misguidance, because it is impossible for such to exist in itself, not that you do not find him though he exists or is possible. For if praise of them were intended, He would have sufficed with His words, exalted is He: "is the one rightly guided." In this there is an objection that it does not fit the context. The contrast does not negate praise but rather confirms it, so there is in it an implicit suggestion that they are people of protection and rightful guidance, because they have the protecting and guiding Friend. Perhaps in the verse there is the figure of speech called *iḥtibāk* (the rhetorical device of omitting from each of two parallel parts what is mentioned in the other).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And you would think them﴾ with a fatha on the sin.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sin, meaning "you would think them" (tazunnuhum). The address in it is as in what preceded. The apparent meaning is that this is a new statement (ikhbar mustanaf) and not dependent on any supposed element. It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "And if you saw them, you would think them ﴿awake﴾." The word ﴿ayqazan﴾ (awake) is the plural of yaqiz with a kasra on the qaf, like ankad and nakid, as in al-Kashshaf, and with a damma, like a'dad and 'adud, as in al-Durr al-Masun.

In al-Qamus: "A man is yaqiz, like nadis and katif," and it records both dialects, with a damma and with a kasra on the 'ayn. The yaqzan is the one who is awake. The basis of the supposition is that their eyes are open in the manner of one who looks, as more than one has said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that the observer would think that because of the intensity of the preservation that was upon them and the slightness of change. This is because what usually characterises sleepers is slackness and postures that sleep entails. So when a sleeper does not have these, the observer would think him awake, even if his eyes were closed. And if the opening of their eyes were established by a chain of transmission that cuts off excuse, it would be clearer in this supposition."

Al-Zajjaj said: "The basis of it is the abundance of their turning," and he took as evidence the mention of that afterwards. In it there is a problem: it does not fit with ﴿and they were sleeping﴾, where ﴿ruqud﴾ is the plural of raqid, meaning sleeper. What has been said, that it is a verbal noun (masdar) used for the agent and that it is equal in the few and the many, like rukui and qu'ud, is rejected, because fa'il is not pluralised as fa'ul. This has been stated by the grammarians, as clarified in al-Mufassal and al-Tashil. This is an explanation of what was not mentioned earlier, relying on the earlier mention of the striking upon their ears.

﴿And We turn them﴾ in their sleep, many times, ﴿to the right﴾, meaning towards a side that is on their right, ﴿and to the left﴾, meaning towards a side that is on their left, so that the earth would not consume what is on them of their bodies. This was reported by Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jubayr. Al-Imam found this strange and said: "He who was able to keep them alive for that long period is able to preserve their bodies too without turning them." It was answered that His wisdom required that the preservation of their bodies be by what is customary, even if we do not know the wisdom of that. A similar answer applies to what has been said about the ﴿turning away﴾ (tazawur) and its brother. It has also been said: "It is possible that their turning was a preservation of their habit in sleep of turning right and left, out of care for their state."

It has been said: "It is possible that this was a manifestation of the great power of God, the Exalted, concerning them, in that He combined concerning them the heavy sleep indicated by His saying ﴿so We struck upon their ears﴾ with the abundant turning. And it is customary that heavy sleep does not involve much turning." Its remoteness is not hidden.

The times of their turning have been disputed. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they were turned every six months once. More than one reported something similar from Abu 'Iyad. It has been said: they were turned every year once, and that was on the day of 'Ashura. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid that the turning was in the nine years added, and not in what was other than them. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada that this turning was in their first sleep, meaning the three hundred years, and they were turned every year once; and in the period of the second sleep, meaning the nine, there was no turning.

Al-Imam criticised this by saying: "These estimates have no path for the intellect to them, the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate them, and what came concerning them is not a sound report." End of quotation. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates abundance, because of the present tense, which indicates continuity and renewal, along with what it carries of emphasis. The apparent meaning is that ﴿and We turn them﴾ is a new statement. Al-Tibi, relying on what you have heard from al-Zajjaj, allowed that the clause could be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and that is, as you see, not right.

It was read: ﴿wa-yuqallibuhum﴾ with a ya' at the beginning and with the shadda, and the pronoun refers to God, the Exalted. It has been said it refers to the angel.

Al-Hasan read, as transmitted by al-Ahwazi in al-Iqna': ﴿wa-yaqlibuhum﴾ with an open ya', a silent qaf, and a light lam. He read, as transmitted by Ibn Jinni, ﴿wa-taqallubahum﴾ in the form of a verbal noun (masdar) in the accusative. Its explanation is that it is an object of a deleted verb indicated by ﴿wa-tahsabuhum﴾, meaning "and you see or witness their turning." It is also reported from him that he read likewise but in the nominative. It is then in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), as Abu Hatim said, and the predicate is what follows, or it is deleted, meaning: "a great sign," or "of the signs of God, the Exalted." Ibn Khalawayh transmitted this reading from al-Yamani, and mentioned that 'Ikrima read ﴿wa-taqlibuhum﴾ with the ta' as third-person, the present of qalaba unaugmented. It is explained as "as if you were turning them," and the clause is made a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿tahsabuhum﴾. In it is an indication of the strength of their resemblance to the awake, to the point that they are thought awake while the examination of their states and their turning right and left is going on. ﴿And their dog﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is the well-known barking animal. It has many names, and al-Jalal al-Suyuti devoted a treatise to them.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "It was a dog that passed by them and followed them. They drove it away, and it returned, and they did that many times. It said to them: 'What do you want from me? Do not fear my side. I love the beloved of God, the Exalted. So sleep, and I will guard you.'"

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it was the dog of a shepherd. They passed by him, and he followed their religion and went with them, and the dog followed them. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "It was the hunting dog of one of them." It has been said: "It was the dog of their flock." There is no harm in our law in keeping a dog for that purpose. As for other than that, and what is not attached to it, it is forbidden. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both: "Whoever keeps a dog that is not a hunting dog or a herding dog, his deeds are diminished by two qirats every day," and in another narration: "a qirat."

Its colour has been disputed. Ibn Abi Hatim reported by way of Sufyan, who said: a man in Kufa called 'Ubayd, who was not accused of lying, said to me: "I saw the dog of the People of the Cave, red, as if it were a Anbijani cloak." He reported from Kathir al-Nawa', who said: "The dog was yellow." It was said: "It was spotted (anmar)," and that was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Other things have been said.

Regarding its name: Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that it was Qitmir. He reported from Mujahid that it was Qatmura. It has been said Rayyan, and it has been said Thawr, and other things have been said. In its age, according to what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, it was above the qalati and below the kurdi.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ubayd that he said: "I saw it small, zayni." Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: "He means Chinese (sini)." In the Tafsir of al-Khazin, al-Qalati is explained as that.

Some claimed that by the dog here is meant the lion, and that is, according to al-Qamus, one of its meanings. It has come that the Prophet ﷺ prayed against an unbeliever, saying: "O God, set against him a dog from Your dogs," and a lion then seized him. This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "I said to a man from the people of knowledge: 'They claim their dog was a lion.' He said: 'By God's life, it was not a lion, but it was a red dog that they took out of their houses, called Qatmura.'" Further from this is the claim of one who went to the view that he was a cook of theirs who followed them, or one of them sat near the door as a watchman for them.

Yes, Abu 'Amr al-Zahidi, the freedman of Tha'lab, transmitted that it was read ﴿wa-kali'uhum﴾ with a hamza with a damma in place of the ba', and an alif after the kaf, from kala'a, meaning to guard. It is not far from this that the intended is the watchman (ruba'a). But the apparent meaning of the mutawatir reading requires the meaning of the well-known dog too, and applying that name to him is for his guarding what he was asked to guard and his protecting it. It has been said concerning this reading that it is an explanation or a distortion.

Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, read ﴿wa-kalibuhum﴾ with a ba' and the form of the active participle. The intended is the owner of their dog, as you say labin and tamir, meaning owner of milk and dates.

Concerning their dog it has come that it will enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection. From Khalid ibn Ma'dan: "There is no animal among the beasts in Paradise except the dog of the People of the Cave and the donkey of Balam." I have seen in some books that the she-camel of Salih and the ram of Isma'il are also in Paradise. I have also seen that the rest of the animals considered beautiful in this world, such as gazelles and peacocks, and what the believer benefits from, such as sheep, enter Paradise in a manner fitting that place and that creation. Nothing in what has been mentioned is a report to be relied upon, as far as I know. Yes, in Paradise there are animals created in it, and in a report that is understood from the words of al-Tirmidhi as sound, there is explicit mention of horses among them. And God knows best.

The saying that this dog enters Paradise has become well known, to the point that some of the Shi'a name their sons "Kalb 'Ali" (the dog of 'Ali), and whoever is named thus hopes for salvation by a fortiori analogy with what was mentioned, and recites:

"The youths of the Cave, their dog was saved; how should the dog of 'Ali not be saved tomorrow?"

By my life, if 'Ali, may God honour his face, accepted a dog, it would be saved; but I do not think he would accept it, because it is a biter.

﴿Stretching out his two forelegs﴾, meaning extending them. The forearm (dhira') is from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. ﴿Dhira'ayhi﴾ is in the accusative as the object of ﴿basit﴾. It operated although it has the meaning of the past, and the active participle does not operate when it is so, because the intent is the narration of a past state. Al-Kisa'i, Hisham and Abu Ja'far ibn Mada' went to the permissibility of the active participle operating in whatever form, so there is no question and no answer.

﴿At the threshold﴾, meaning at the place of the door and the place of passage from the cave. They recited:

"In an open land whose threshold is not closed against me, and my being known there is not disliked."

This is what is meant by the courtyard (fina') in the tafsir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata'. It has been said: "at the doorstep (ʿatabah)," and what is meant by it is what lies opposite that of the earth, not the customary sense. So it is not said that the cave has no door or doorstep. Moreover, there is no obstacle to that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ibn Jubayr that al-Wasid is al-Sa'id (the surface), and that is not right. They mentioned, in the wisdom of his being at the threshold, that the angels, peace be upon them, do not enter a house in which there is a dog. It may be said that this is because he was a guard, as what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj indicates, when he said: "Stretching his forelegs at the threshold, he keeps the door of the cave closed upon them." It was said that he would break his right ear and sleep upon it when they were turned to the right, and break his left ear and sleep upon it when they were turned to the left. The apparent meaning is that he slept as they slept, but Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Humayd al-Makki that his provision was placed in the licking of his forelegs. This apparently indicates that his sleep was not as deep as theirs.

﴿If you had looked upon them﴾, meaning if you had observed them and seen them. The root of ittila' is standing upon a thing by observation and witnessing. Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read ﴿lawu ittala'ta﴾ with a damma on the waw, likening it to the waw of the pronoun, for it is sometimes given a damma when a silent consonant follows it, as in ramu al-sihām (they threw the arrows). It is reported that this was from Shayba and Abu Ja'far.

﴿You would have turned from them in flight﴾, meaning you would have turned your face away from them and turned your side to them. ﴿Firaran﴾ is in the accusative either as a verbal noun for ﴿lawallayta﴾, since turning away and fleeing are from one valley, so it is like "I sat sitting," or as a deleted "faraḥta" (you would have fled). Or it is in the circumstantial position, by interpreting it as an active participle, or by making it of the type of "it is only turning towards and turning away." Or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning "you would have returned for the sake of fleeing."

﴿And you would have been filled with terror from them﴾, meaning fear that fills the breast. It is in the accusative as a second object. It may also be a specification (tamyiz), transferred from the subject. That fear fills is a metaphor for its greatness, as is well known, just as it is said of beauty that it fills the eyes.

[Page 225] [Page 226] [Page 227]

In Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), he says: "Far-fetched is the view of one who held that it is a *tamyiz* (a specifying accusative, i.e. a noun clarifying the sense of a verb) transferred from the object, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾. This is because if the verb were applied to it, it would not transitively reach it the way a direct object does, unlike what is in this verse." The reason for what was mentioned is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cast upon them the awe and majesty that He cast. It was also said that its cause was the length of their hair and nails, the paleness of their faces, and the change in their garments. And it was said that it was the darkness and desolation of the place.

Abu Hayyan criticised this by saying: "Neither of these two views is anything, for if they had been in that state they would not have failed to recognise their own condition, and they would not have said, ﴿We have stayed a day or part of a day﴾. Moreover, the one who was sent to the city only denied the landmarks and the buildings, not their own state. And moreover, they were in such a good condition that the beholder could not distinguish them from the awake, while they were in a cave described as it has passed. So how could their place be desolate?" End of quote.

It was answered: It is not unlikely that they were unaware of their state, for one who has just risen from sleep may be oblivious to many of his affairs. And it may be claimed that the continuation of heedlessness was in the messenger, and his denial of the landmarks does not contradict the people's denial of his state, and that he was in an objectionable state of which he was not aware. Also, it is possible that they did not at first perceive their condition, so they said, ﴿We have stayed a day or part of a day﴾, and then became aware of it and said, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed﴾. Also, it is possible that this address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and that condition only came about after their awakening, when they sent their messenger to the city. On this view, the messenger's not denying his own state does no harm, because nothing objectionable had yet happened to him. And the desolation of the place may also have occurred afterwards on this view, through its change over the passage of time. End of quote. Whoever is fair will not fail to see the weakness of these answers. What should be relied upon is that the cause of this is what Allah, Exalted, cast upon them of awe while they were in their cave; and that their hair and nails, if they had grown long, had not grown to a degree that would be denied by one who sees them. Some commentators chose that Allah, Exalted, did not change their state and appearance at all, so that this would be a clear sign. The address here is like the address in what preceded. And on the possibility that it is addressed to him ﷺ, it follows that they remained in that state which causes the one who looks upon them to flee and be greatly terrified, up to after the revelation of the verse. So whoever does not say this, let him not say it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "We campaigned with Mu'awiyah in the Battle of al-Madiq towards the Romans. We passed by the cave in which were the People of the Cave, whom Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an. Mu'awiyah said, 'If only they were uncovered for us so that we could look at them.' Ibn Abbas said to him, 'That is not for you. Allah, Exalted, has prevented that from one who is better than you.' He recited: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight and been filled with terror of them.﴾ Mu'awiyah said, 'I will not stop until I know their state.' So he sent men and said, 'Go, enter the cave and look.' They went, and when they entered it, Allah, Exalted, sent a wind upon them which drove them out."

It was said: It seems that Mu'awiyah did not act in accordance with the implication of Ibn Abbas's words, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because he supposed that their state had changed from what it had been, or he sought to know it as far as possible.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "I had a companion who was determined and strong-willed. He passed by the side of the cave and said, 'I will not stop until I look at them.' It was said to him, 'Do not do that. Do you not read: ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾, etc.?' But he refused except to look, so he went up to them, and his eyes turned white and his hair changed. He used to tell people that their number was seven." Such reports may perhaps be taken as support for their existence today, or even for their remaining in that state in which their condition cannot be observed. On this there is disagreement.

Al-Suhayli related the view of a group that they are still alive, and from Ibn Abbas its denial. For Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah that Ibn Abbas campaigned with Habib ibn Maslamah, and they passed by the cave, and there were bones in it. A man said, "These are the bones of the People of the Cave." Ibn Abbas said, "Their bones have decayed for more than three hundred years." And there is no hiding the contradiction between this report and the previous report from him, and indeed the other one as well. What the heart inclines to is that they do not exist today; and if they do exist, they are not in that state to which Allah, Exalted, pointed. And the address in the verse is to an unspecified person, and what is meant by it is the report that they were in that state at that time.

As for what Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The People of the Cave are helpers of the Mahdi," even if it is authentic, it does not indicate that they exist today in that state. And as for the view that the address is general, and not specific to a particular individual, it does not include the Prophet, peace be upon him, because he ﷺ was made to witness what is greater than them from the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And whoever held that he ﷺ is specified said: The meaning is, "If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight and been filled with terror of them," by the judgement of the customary course and human nature, and since the reward is not bound to his ﷺ looking upon what is greater than them, which is an extraordinary matter dependent on angelic power, or something beyond it. Or the meaning is, "If you had looked upon them yourself, without Us making you look upon them, you would have turned from them in flight," etc. And his ﷺ looking upon what he looked upon was by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, causing him to look, and there is a difference between the two kinds of looking.

It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, had a stomach ache, so he complained to his Lord, glorified is He, and He said to him, "Go to such-and-such plant in such-and-such a place and eat from it." He went and ate, and what he had been feeling went away. Then the ailment returned after years, so he went to that plant and ate from it, but he gained no benefit from it. He said, "My Lord, You know best. In such-and-such a year my stomach ached and You commanded me to go to such-and-such a plant, so I went and ate and I benefited. Then what I had been feeling returned, so I went to that and ate and I gained no benefit." He, glorified is He, said, "Do you know, O Musa, what the cause of that is?" He said, "No, my Lord." He said, "The cause is that the first time you went to the plant at Our command, and the second time you went to it of your own accord."

Among what is considered objectionable speech is what is related from some of the Sufis: that he heard a reciter reciting this verse, and he said, "If I had looked upon them, I would not have turned from them in flight, nor would I have been filled with terror of them."

And what has been reported from some of them as an answer, that the speaker's intention was to affirm for himself the rank of childhood, since a child does not fear a snake, for example, when he sees it, nor does he distinguish between it and a rope. Even if it is granted that this was his intention, it does not remove the objectionability. This is like the statement of one who said, "Glorified and exalted is He; He does not know the unseen," meaning that there is no unseen with respect to Him, Mighty and Majestic, for His knowledge to relate to it. And how well 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Speak to people in terms they can understand. Do you wish for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ to be denied?"

Furthermore, Ibn Abbas, the two Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿وَلَمُلِّئْتَ﴾ with a doubled lam and a hamza. Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a doubled lam and the hamza changed to a yaa'. Al-Zuhri read it with lightening and changing of the hamza. Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read ﴿رُعُبًا﴾ with a damma on the 'ayn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 19:

﴿And thus We raised them﴾: that is, just as We put them to sleep for this long slumber, which is understood from what came before, We woke them up. So the thing compared (al-mushabbah) is the waking, and the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) is the mentioned sleep. The point of similarity (wajh al-shabah) is that each of them is a sign indicating the perfection and overwhelming power of His might, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿so that they might question one another﴾: that is, so that some of them would ask others, and what is detailed of profound wisdoms would follow from this. It was made a cause of the raising, which is itself caused by what preceded it. It has been said: this is because it is one of its consequences that follow from it, and mention was limited to it because it entails all its other effects. Many have made the lam (of purpose) here a lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah).
