Al-Khafaji endorsed this and claimed that whoever did it was attentive to the fact that the purpose of His action, exalted is His majesty, was to show the perfection of His power, not the questioning that was mentioned. So reflect.

﴿A speaker among them said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their questioning. ﴿One of them said﴾: it has been said he was their eldest, Maksalmina, and it has been said he was the one in charge of their provisions, Yamlikha. ﴿How long have you remained?﴾: that is, how many days have you stayed asleep? It seems he said this because he saw that their condition contradicted what is customary in general. It has also been said that what they had missed of prayer alarmed them, so they said this.

﴿They said﴾: that is, some of them said: ﴿We have remained a day, or part of a day﴾. The "or" (aw) is for doubt, as many have said. The meaning is: we have not ascertained the measure of our stay; that is, we do not know whether that duration is the length of a day or the length of part of a day. The apparent meaning is that they said this because the dazedness of sleep had not left their sight and insight, so they did not look at the signs. This is something beyond dispute, whether their sleep and waking were both, or one of them, during the day or not. The well-known view is that they slept in the morning and woke at the end of the day. It has also been said that they did not know whether their waking was on the day they slept or on the day after, so they said what they said. It was objected that this would imply the hesitation is between part of a day, a day, and part of a day. From here it has been said that the "or" (aw) is for correction (idrab): when they woke at the end of the day, while they were inside the cave and the dazedness of sleep had not yet left them, they said before looking: ﴿We have remained a day﴾; then when they verified that the sun had not yet set, they said: ﴿or part of a day﴾. You know that the apparent meaning is that it is for you. The objection is dismissed by taking what you heard from it as the intended meaning. Yes, it is metaphorical in that. Abu Hayyan related that it is for distribution (tafsil), meaning: some of them said, "We have remained a day," and others said, "We have remained part of a day." The statement of each is based on predominant assumption, as it has been said, so it is not a lie. It is not hidden that the view that it is for distribution is something the mind hardly goes to, and there is no need to base the matter on predominant assumption to deny that it is a lie, based on what we mentioned, that the intended meaning is that they did not verify its measure, as the people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) mentioned regarding the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he gave the salam by mistake from a four-rak'ah prayer, and Dhu al-Yadayn said to him: "Was the prayer shortened, or have you forgotten, O Messenger of God?" He said: "All of that did not happen."

﴿They said﴾: that is, another of them said, by way of reasoning or inspiration: ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾: that is, you do not know the duration of your stay, and only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a rebuke from them to the first ones in the best manner of observing good manners, and by it, as has been said, the division into the two known parties mentioned before is realized. It has also been said that the speaker of both statements is one person, but the state was different.

It was criticized: the noble wording does not support this, for the resumptive clause in the narration and the address in what is narrated require that the speech be following the method of dialogue and reply; otherwise it would have said "then they said: Our Lord knows best how long we have remained."

﴿So send one of you﴾: that is, one of you. He did not say "your one" (wahidakum) because it would give the impression of intending your chief, for it is often said "the one of the people came," meaning their leader.

﴿with your silver﴾: that is, with your minted dirhams, as is well known among the lexicographers. It has been said that al-warq is silver, whether minted or unminted. This is supported by what occurred in the hadith of Arfajah, that when his nose was cut off he made a nose of silver, which became foul, so he made a nose of gold. The apparent meaning is that al-warq was used there for unminted silver. The saying of al-Asmai, as related from him by al-Qutaybi, that al-waraq in the hadith is with a fatha on the ra', and it means the paper on which one writes, because silver does not become foul, is not to be relied upon, and the claim of foulness that he mentioned has no soundness.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, al-Yazidi, and Ya'qub in one narration, and Khalaf, Abu Ubayd, and Ibn Sa'dan read ﴿بِوَرْقِكُمْ﴾ with a sukun on the ra'. Abu Raja' read with a kasra on the waw, a sukun on the ra', and assimilation of the qaf into the kaf; likewise Isma'il from Ibn Muhaysin. He also related from him that he read in the same way except that he gave the ra' a kasra, so as not to incur a meeting of two sukuns against its rule, as in the other narration. This was objected to, and it was answered that this is permissible and occurs in Arabic speech, but as an irregularity. It has also been read as ﴿نِعْمَّا﴾ with a sukun on the 'ayn and assimilation. As for the claim that it cannot be pronounced, it is said in reply that this is a mistake. Al-Zajjaj related that it was read with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the ra' without assimilation.

Ali, may God honor his face, read ﴿بَوارِقِكُمْ﴾ on the pattern fa'il.

He made it a collective noun like "baqir" and "hamil." The description of the silver by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿this﴾, indicates that the speaker brought it so that he could hand it to one of his companions. Its indication that he handed it to him is remote. In their carrying it there is evidence that preparing the means of livelihood for one who leaves his home by carrying provisions and the like does not contradict trust in God, exalted is He, as in the hadith: "Tie it and trust [in God]."

Yes, one of the eminent scholars said: the trust of Abu Waqqas and Abu Muslim al-Khawlani with the armies on the surface of the sea, and the entry of Tamim into the cave from which the fire of al-Harrah came out, to turn it back by the command of Umar, may God be pleased with him.

Imam Ahmad, Ishaq, and others among the imams explicitly stated the permissibility of entering deserts without provisions and abandoning earning a living and seeking medical treatment for one whose certainty and trust are strong. Imam Ahmad defined trust as cutting off the looking toward creatures by despairing of them, and he cited as evidence the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him on the day he was thrown into the fire and said to him: "Do you have a need?" He said: "As for you, no." Abandoning the means is not the path of trust exclusive to the elite of the Sufis only, as the words of some virtuous scholars suggest, but has come from others as well.

﴿to the city﴾: the well-known one, which is the city they had left. It has been said: it is now called Tarsus, and its name on the day they left it was Afsus. By this the two earlier reports can be reconciled. This statement came from them as turning away from delving deeply into research and turning to what concerns them according to the present situation, as the particle fa' indicates. Some have said that this is from the indirect style of address (al-uslub al-hakim), like the saying of the poet:

She came complaining to me of the burden of hospitality, and she had seen the guests heading toward my house.
So I said, as if I had not heard her words: "They are guests; hasten to their hospitality and be quick about it."

﴿then let him look at which is purest in food﴾: that is, which is most lawful, for the people of that city in their time used to slaughter for the idols (tawaghit), as Sa'id ibn Mansur and others related from Ibn Abbas. In another report, they used to slaughter pigs. al-Dahhak said most of their wealth was usurped. ﴿Purest (azka)﴾ comes from zakah, whose root is growth and increase, and it can be spiritual and otherworldly or physical and worldly. It is intended here in the first sense, because of the reward and good outcome in seeking what is lawful. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: that is, best (atyab). If it means "most lawful," since it is applied to that, it returns to the first. If it is in its well-known meaning, then the increase is said to be physical and worldly. Ikrima said: that is, most abundant. Yaman ibn Rayyan said: that is, cheapest. Qatada said: that is, best quality; and this is the best. On this, and likewise on the preceding ones, as has been said, the increase is also physical and worldly. Some claimed that they meant by "purest" rice, and it was said dates, and it was said raisins. Good assumption of the youths requires that they sought out what is lawful. The verb "look" may be a look of the heart or a look of the eye. ﴿Which﴾ is an interrogative, a subject, and ﴿purest﴾ is its predicate, and the clause is one whose verb is suspended by the interrogative.

It is permitted that ﴿which﴾ is a relative pronoun, built, as the object of "look," and ﴿purest﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is the beginning of the relative clause. The pronoun in ﴿ايها﴾ is either for the city, with the sentence being elliptical, meaning: which of its people; or for the city taken figuratively to mean its people; and in the sentence there is istikhdam (using one word in two senses) and no deletion; or it refers to what is understood from the context of the speech, as if it were said: let him look at which of the foods or eateries is purest in food. ﴿So let him bring you provision from it﴾: that is, from that which is purest in food. So "from" (min) is for the starting point of the action or for partitive meaning. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the silver, so "from" is for substitution. Furthermore, if the youths had not previously sought out what is lawful, then their intention with "provision" here should be what is lawful, even if it is not exclusively so according to us.

The verse was cited as evidence, and what will come, if God wills, from which what is in it can be known, for the validity of agency and representation (wikalah and niyabah). Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is the strongest verse on this, and in it, as al-Kiya said, is evidence for the permissibility of mixing the dirhams of a group, buying with them, and eating from the food that is shared among them by partnership, even if they differ in how much they eat. Yes, there is no harm in the big eater increasing his share of the dirhams.

﴿Let him be gentle﴾: that is, let him take pains to be gentle in dealing, so that no dispute arises that leads to their discovery; or let him take pains to be discreet in entering and leaving. It has been said: let him take pains in that so that he is not cheated; so His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾ means: let him not do anything that leads to anyone among the people of the city becoming aware of you, founded on this. On the first two views, it is an emphasis of the command to be gentle, and interpreting it as mentioned is of the category of metonymy (kinayah), like: "I will not see you here." al-Imam interpreted it as: let him not inform anyone about you, so it is on its literal sense. al-Hasan read ﴿وَلِيَتَلَطَّفْ﴾ with a kasra on the lam of the command. Qutayba al-Mayyal related ﴿وَلِيُتَلَطَّفْ﴾ with a damma on the ya', in the passive form. He and Abu Salih and Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿وَلَا يَشْعُرَنَّ بِكُمْ أَحَدٌ﴾ with the verb built in the active voice and ﴿أحد﴾ in the nominative as the subject.

Verse 20 is a reason for the preceding commands (al-amr wa'l-nahy). The pronoun in "innahum" refers either to the people (ahl) implied in "ayyuha" (the people of the cave), or to the disbelievers, whose meaning is implied by context; this is the view preferred by Abu Hayyan. It is also permitted that it refers back to "ahad" (anyone), since it is a general term, so its pronoun may be plural, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿So none of you could withhold him from Us﴾.

﴿If they gain power over you﴾ means: they come to know of you and learn your whereabouts, or they overcome you. The basic meaning of "zahara" is "to be on the surface of the earth." Since what is on the earth is seen and within one's reach, the verb is used sometimes for becoming aware (al-ittila') and sometimes for victory and dominance (al-zafar wa'l-ghalabah), and it is construed with "ʿala" (over). Zayd ibn ʿAli read "yuzhiru" with a damma on the yaʾ, in the passive voice. ﴿They will stone you﴾ if you do not do what they want from you and you remain upon what you are upon. The apparent meaning is that the intended punishment is death by stoning with stones, which was the custom in the past for one who opposed a great matter, since it is more satisfying to the hearts and the people share in it. Al-Hajjaj said: the intended meaning is stoning with words, that is, abuse (al-sabb), and this is greater for proud souls than killing. ﴿Or they will return you to their creed﴾ means: they will make you return to it and enter it under compulsion. The use of "al-ʿawd fi'l-shay'" (returning into something) in this sense does not require that one was previously engaged in it. This was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. It was also said that "al-ʿawd" is in its literal sense, namely a person's return to what he was upon, and the youths were indeed upon their people's creed at first. The choice of the word "fi" (in) over "ila" (to) was explained by some scholars of verification as indicating settled residence, which is more hateful. The mention of the possibility of stoning is placed before the possibility of return because the apparent state of them is steadfastness upon the religion that leads to it. The pronoun of address in the four places is for emphasis in driving the one sent toward what is intended from him, and the rest (the others) for care in advising, since sincere counsel that is wholly free of self-interest is more readily accepted, and a person's concern for his own affair is greater and more complete.

﴿And you will never prosper, then, ever﴾ means: if you truly enter into it, even under compulsion and coercion, you will never succeed in any good, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. The connection on this reading is that compulsion to disbelieve may be a cause for Satan to lead one gradually into finding it attractive and persisting in it. By what has been mentioned, the objection is dispelled that displaying disbelief under compulsion while inwardly holding faith is pardonable at all times, so how could the failure to prosper forever be made a consequence of it? There is no need to say that displaying disbelief in any form was impermissible for them, nor to interpret "yuʿidukum fi millatihim" as "they will incline you toward it by compulsion or otherwise." So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 21 (part 1 of 4):

Then the youths sent one of them, and he was, as many have said, Yamlikha, so there came to pass what God, exalted is He, indicated by His words: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾, that is: just as We put them to sleep and raised them, so the reference is to the sleep, the raising, and the singular form is in view of what has been mentioned and the like.

Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said in his Amali: The reference is to the particular raising, which is the raising after that long sleep. The root of ʿuthur (ʿuthūr), as al-Raghib said, is falling on the face. It is said: ʿathara ʿuthūran wa ʿithāran when he fell on his face. On this is their proverb: "The noble steed hardly ever stumbles," and their saying: "Whoever takes the well-trodden paths is safe from stumbling." Then it was extended metaphorically to coming upon a matter without seeking it.

Al-Imam al-Mutarrizi said: Since every one who stumbles looks at the place of his stumbling, al-ʿuthūr came to mean becoming aware and recognizing. In this sense it is a well-known metaphor through the relation of causality, even though the mention of it by the lexicographers may give the impression that it is literal in that sense. Al-Ghawri considered it literal in the sense of becoming aware of a matter that had been hidden, while the matter of metaphor remains as it is. The first object of ﴿We caused them to be found﴾ is omitted for the purpose of generality, that is: and thus We made the people aware of them.

Abu Hayyan said: [the people of] their city ﴿so that they might know﴾, that is, those whom We made aware of them through what they witnessed of their wondrous conditions ﴿that the promise of God﴾, that is, His promise, glorified and exalted is He, of the raising, [taking "promise" in its verbal-noun sense, with its object understood], or His promised thing, exalted is His majesty, which is the raising, [taking the verbal noun as interpreted by the passive participle, meaning His known promised thing]. It is also permissible that all His promise, or all His promised things, glorified is He, be intended, and what has been mentioned enters into that as a first instance ﴿is true﴾, truthful with no falsehood in it, or established and certain, it will surely occur without fail. It was said: because their long sleep, contrary to what is customary, and their waking, are like death and resurrection.

﴿And that the Hour﴾, that is, the Resurrection, which in the language of the Law is an expression for the time of raising all creatures for reckoning and recompense.

﴿There is no doubt concerning it﴾, that is: it is fitting that no one now doubt its possibility, for there remains in the hands of those who doubt it no far-sighted reflection or inquiry, except reliance on deeming it unlikely. And their knowledge of the occurrence of that strange matter and wondrous state, which, had they heard of it without verifying its occurrence, they would have deemed unlikely and doubted, breaks the edge of that deeming unlikely and demolishes that reliance; so then it is fitting that they not doubt.

Some of the verifiers said, in explaining the ordering of knowledge of what has been mentioned upon the becoming aware: whoever witnessed that He, majestic and exalted, took their souls and held them for three hundred years and more, preserving their bodies from dissolution and crumbling, then released them back to them, there remains with him no trace of doubt that His promise is true, and that He, exalted is He, raises those in the graves, returns their spirits to them, reckons with them and recompenses them according to their deeds. End.

You know that there is room for scrutiny in deriving knowledge of reckoning and recompense from becoming aware of the state of that people. It was objected that what is sought in resurrection is the restoration of bodies after their parts have scattered, whereas in the story there is only the long preservation of bodies; how is this related to that? The claim that "whenever the long preservation of bodies, which need food and drink, is valid, His power to restore them after their parts have scattered is valid a fortiori" is not granted. It was answered that the said long preservation indicates His power over what has been mentioned by way of conjecture, so let it be pondered.

Perhaps the more evident explanation of the ordering is what he mentioned first, and its clarification: the condition of the youths, in that they slept for that long period and many years, their souls were withheld from acting, their faculties and senses were idle without the rising of vapours of drink and food or the onset of illnesses and sicknesses, their bodies were preserved from dissolution and crumbling and kept in the freshness and youth they had in former years, until the senses and faculties returned to their state and the souls were released from their bonds and sent back to managing their bodies and acting upon their servants and helpers. They saw the matter as it had been, the helpers were the same helpers, and they did not deny anything they had known in their city, nor did they recall the long time of their being withheld from acting upon the throne of their kingdom. The condition of those who rise from their graves, after their faculties have been idle and their souls withheld, and then when they are released find ruins inhabited and dwellings as if they had never been standing, saying before the thorn of the sorrow bares its fangs: "Who has raised us from our resting place?" is strange in a single respect, and no one denies this except an ignorant or stubborn person. The occurrence of the first makes doubt about the possibility of the occurrence of the second disappear, since that doubt, in reality, rested on deeming it unlikely, as you heard earlier, because the proofs of those who deny bodily resurrection are void. Yes, in the ordering of knowledge that the raising will certainly occur upon the mere becoming aware of the state of the youths there is obscurity; for the apparent meaning is that the said knowledge follows from the report of the truthful one about its occurrence and from its possibility in itself. But since the said becoming aware was a cause for knowledge of possibility, and was like the final part of the cause with respect to the unbelievers to whom the report of the truthful one had reached, it was said that knowledge of that follows upon it. Likewise, in the ordering of knowledge that everything God promised is true upon the mere becoming aware, there is obscurity, and I have not seen any of the excellent scholars address its explanation, so ponder.

Furthermore, it is not hidden that the mention of His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that the Hour is not in doubt concerning it﴾ after His words, glorified is He, ﴿that the promise of God is true﴾, according to the interpretation you have heard, is free of any blemish, and it is not a mention of possibility after actuality so as to be superfluous, as whoever claimed it claimed.

Some of them said: the apparent meaning is that His words, exalted is He, ﴿that the promise of God is true﴾ be interpreted as: everything He promised, glorified is He, is realized; and His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that the Hour is not in doubt concerning it﴾ be taken as specification after generalization, in the sense that there is no doubt in its realization. This is a possible reading of the verse, but in the claim of its being the apparent meaning there is a dispute, so do not be heedless.

﴿When they disputed among themselves their affair﴾: [the phrase] is an adverbial clause of time governed by "We caused them to be found" (aʿtharnā), and the end-point was placed before it to show full concern for mentioning it. Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Baqa and others permitted it to be an adverbial clause governed by "so that they might know" (li-yaʿlamū), but this was criticized on the ground that it indicates that the dispute arose after the causing to be found, although it is not so; and because the dispute existed before the knowledge and was removed by it, so how can its time be its time? There is room for debate on this.

It was also permitted that it be an adverbial clause governed by "is true" (ḥaqq) or by "promise" (waʿd), and that is, as you see, [weak]. The root of tanāzuʿ is mutual pulling, and it is used to express quarrelling. In its basic meaning it takes its object directly, and in the sense of quarrelling it takes "fī" (about), as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And if you dispute concerning anything﴾. The pronoun of ﴿they disputed﴾, since it refers back to the pronoun of ﴿so that they might know﴾, means: and thus We caused the people, or the people of their city, to find the companions of the cave, at the time when they disputed ﴿among themselves their affair﴾ and quarrelled about it, so that the disagreement might be removed and the truth made clear. The pronoun of ﴿their affair﴾ is said to refer also to the object of ﴿We caused them to be found﴾, and the intended "affair" is the raising; and the meaning of its attribution to them is their concern with its matter and their standing upon the reality of its condition.

They differed about it: some affirmed it, some denied it, and one who said: the spirits alone are raised without the bodies, and another who said: both are raised together, as is the true doctrine among the Muslims.

It is narrated that after God, exalted is He, had struck upon the ears of the youths, and a long age had passed, none of their people who had withdrawn from them remained, and others came, and their king was a Muslim; the people of his kingdom differed about the matter of the raising in the manner detailed, and this grieved the king. He went, put on sackcloth, sat on ashes, then called upon God, mighty and majestic, and said: "O Lord, You see the disagreement of these people; send for them a sign that will make it clear to them." So God, exalted is He, appointed a shepherd whom rain overtook; he kept on working to close what Decius had sealed over the door of the cave until he opened it, and he brought in his flock. When the next day came, they were raised from their sleep, and they sent one of them to buy food for them. He entered the market, began to look at the faces and recognize the roads, and saw faith openly in the city. He went on, being cautious, until he came to a man from whom he wished to buy food. When the man looked at the silver coins, he disapproved of them since they were from the minting of Decius, as if they were the wings of a locust; so he suspected him of a hoard and said: "You will show me where it is, or I will take you up to the king!" He said: "They are from the minting of the king. Is your king not so-and-so?" The man said: "No; our king is so-and-so," and his name was Yandusis. People gathered and took him to the king, and he was frightened. The king asked him about his affair, and he related the story to him. The king had heard that some youths had gone out in the time of Decius; he summoned the elders of his city, and there was a man among them who had their names and lineages; he asked him, and he informed him of that, and the youth was asked, and he said: "He is right." Then the king said: "O people, this is a sign which God has sent to you." Then he went out, he and the people of the city, with the youth among them. When the king saw the youths, he embraced them and rejoiced in them, and saw them sitting with radiant faces, their clothes not worn; they spoke with him and informed him of what they had suffered from Decius. While they were before him, they said to him: "We commit you to God; peace be upon you and the mercy of God; may God keep you and keep your kingdom, and we seek refuge in God from the evil of men and jinn." Then they returned to their resting places, and God took their souls. The king stood up to them, placed his garments upon them, and ordered that each of them be placed in a coffin of gold. When night came and he slept, they came to him in a dream and said: "You wished to place each of us in a golden coffin; do not do so, but leave us in our cave, for from dust we were created and to it we return." So he placed them in coffins of teak, and built a mosque over the door of the cave.

It is also related that when the youth was brought to the king, the king said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am a man of this city," and he mentioned that he had gone out yesterday or some days ago, and mentioned his dwelling and people whom no one knew. The king had heard that some youths had disappeared in the former age, and that their names were written on a tablet in the treasury. He called for the tablet and looked at their names, and behold, he was one of those people. The youth said: "These are my companions." So the people rode out, with him among them. When they came to the cave door, the youth said: "Leave me until I go in to my companions and give them good news, for if they see you with me they will be terrified." He entered, gave them good news, and God took their souls; the king and those with him were blinded to their trace, and they did not find them. So they built a mosque over them. Their being made aware of their condition was through the report of the youth, and they relied on his truthfulness; and this is what is meant by the causing to be found upon them. Other accounts have been narrated. It is also said: the pronoun of ﴿their affair﴾ refers to the youths, and the "affair" means the matter and state that existed before the causing to be found, that is: and thus We caused the people to find the companions of the cave when they discussed among themselves their affair and what befell them in the time of the tyrant king of the calamities and terrors; perhaps they had received that from legends and the mouths of men, but they did not know whether they remained alive or death had overtaken them. The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So they said: Build﴾, on the first view, is without doubt a fa' of explanation, in the manner of

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 18, verse 21 (part 2 of 4):

It is as if it were said: And thus We made the people come upon the Companions of the Cave when they disputed about the matter of the Resurrection, so they became certain of it and knew that these were a sign from Our signs. Then God, exalted is He, caused them to die after the purpose of the discovery had been achieved. ﴿Then they said: Build﴾ and so on to the end. Likewise, on the second opinion, it is as if it were said: And thus We made the people come upon the Companions of the Cave when they discussed their affair and what had happened to them in the time of the tyrant king, while they had not known what state they were in. So they came to understand their circumstances to the extent that they understood, and what they had been ignorant of became clear to them. Then God, exalted is He, caused them to die after the purpose of the discovery had been achieved. ﴿Then they said: Build﴾ and so on to the end, that is, some of them said: ﴿Build over them﴾, that is, over the entrance of their cave, ﴿a building﴾. It is in the accusative as the direct object. It is, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, a singular noun with no plural. Abu al-Baqa' said it is the plural of *bunyanah*, like *sha'ir* and *sha'irah* (barley). It was also said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*). This statement by some of them, according to some, came from concern for the young men, because they were protective of their remains and asked for a building over the entrance of their cave so that people would not reach them.

They also allowed, after saying that it is a parenthetical clause, that the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾ could be part of the speech of the disputing discoverers. It is as if they discussed their affair, exchanged words about their lineage, their circumstances and the length of their stay, and when they could not arrive at the truth of that, they entrusted the knowledge to God, exalted is He, the Knower of the unseen. It could also be part of His speech, exalted is He, as a refutation of those who were engaged in discussion about their affair, either from among the discoverers or from among the People of the Book who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case there would be an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) according to one of the two views. It was also said that the pronoun in *amrahum* refers to the young men, and that by *al-amr* is meant the state and condition that obtained after the discovery. The meaning is: when they disputed among themselves about the management of their affair and their state, when they died, how they should treat them and by what means they should honour their status; or when they disputed among themselves about their affair of death and life, since this became unclear to them after the discovery, so they did not know whether they had died or slept as at first. On this view, *idh* is governed by an implied *udhkur* (remember), or is a time adverb for the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said: We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾.

The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿so they said﴾, are coordinated with ﴿they dispute﴾. The use of the past tense form is chosen to indicate that this saying is not something that continues and renews itself like the dispute. Some eminent scholars stated that the *fa'* (so) is for sequence (*ta'qib*) on the first of the two meanings, and on the second it is *fasihah* (an explanatory *fa'*). It is as if it were said: Remember when they dispute about whether they died or slept, then they finished the dispute over that and became concerned with honouring their status and making their affair known: ﴿so they said: Build﴾ and so on to the end.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned the possibility that the pronoun in *amrahum* refers to the discoverers, and that by their affair is meant the affair of their religion, which is the Resurrection. He also mentioned the possibility that the pronoun refers to the young men, and in that case the meaning is: when people discuss among themselves the matter of the Companions of the Cave, and speak about their story and about the sign God, exalted is He, made manifest concerning them. Or: when they dispute among themselves about the management of their affair when they died, how to conceal their place and how to block the path to them. He made *idh* in these aspects an adverb for *a'tharna* (We made them come upon). The author of *al-Kashf* (al-Zamakhshari) stated that the *fa'* on the first view is undoubtedly *fasihah*, while on the last two it is for sequence. On the second of these two, it is evident; on the first, it is because when they discussed their story, their state and what God, exalted is He, had made manifest concerning them, they said: Leave that and build over them a building; that is, take up what is more important, and so on to the end of what he said. The possibility of making the *fa'* explanatory on this first view is not far-fetched. The attachment of the time adverb to *a'tharna* on the last two views, and likewise on what we quoted just above, is worthless, because their discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute over what has been mentioned, but before it.

To make the time of the dispute extend, so that the discovery occurs during part of it and the dispute during part of it, is a forced interpretation that is evident, and moreover there is no specifier for its being linked to the dispute, which occurs later in time. It was reported in *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) that the pronoun in ﴿that they might know﴾ refers to the Companions of the Cave, and that the meaning is: We made them come upon them so that they might increase in knowledge that the promise of God is true, and so on to the end. This was made a purpose of the discovery through the intermediary of their coming to know, by means of it, the length of their stay through what they had verified of the changing of generations. ﴿When they dispute among themselves﴾ is made on this view the beginning of a report about the people who were raised up in their time, and the matter in dispute is specified as the matter of the building and the place of worship. The adverb is then best attached to *udhkur* (remember). It is not hidden that making that pronoun refer to the young men, even if it calls for the interpretation of *ya'lamu* (they know) in the way you have heard, is not far from the intended sense of the noble text when one sets aside external matters such as the traces. No one, as far as I know, has gone to the possibility that the pronouns in the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿when they dispute among themselves about their affair﴾ refer to the young men, like the pronoun in *ya'lamu*, with *idh* as the adverb for *a'tharna*, and with the disputed affair being the measure of the time of their stay and their dispute about it: the saying of some of them: ﴿We stayed a day or part of a day﴾, and the saying of another in reply to him: ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you stayed﴾. Since the situation was not clarified and no agreement was reached on a known amount, the dispute was in the position of what remained, so its time was extended, and it was correct for it to be an adverb for the discovery. The pronoun in *fa-qalu* (so they said) refers to the discoverers, and the *fa'* is explanatory; that is: thus We made the people come upon the young men at the time of their dispute over the length of their stay, so that they might increase in knowledge of the Resurrection. Then what happened happened, and they became, among the people, a matter of such great standing. ﴿So they said: Build﴾ and so on to the end.

It seems that this is because of the strain involved, together with the fact that the remains do not support it. Then what was mentioned of the possibility that ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾ is part of the speech of God, exalted is He, that it was sent down to refute the disputing discoverers, is not free from remoteness. As for the last possibility, it is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that it is a report from the discoverers, and this is most suitable to the dispute being about their affair of death and life. What the words of many of the commentators imply is that the purpose of the two groups, the one saying ﴿Build﴾ and so on to the end, and the one saying ﴿We will surely take﴾ and so on to the end, was to honour them and exalt their status. By ﴿those who prevailed over their affair﴾ is meant the rulers, as ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah. The verb ﴿we will surely take﴾ fits this, rather than the imperative form *ittakhidhu* (take), which is the form expressed by the first group, because such an action is ascribed by rulers to themselves. The pronoun in ﴿their affair﴾ here is said to refer to the relative pronoun, and the meaning is the rulers. Their prevailing over their affair means that whenever they wanted a matter, it was not difficult for them, and nothing stood between them and it, as was said concerning the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And God prevails over His affair﴾.

Some distinguished scholars mentioned that the pronoun refers to the Companions of the Cave, and that by ﴿those who prevailed﴾ is meant, it was said, the Muslim king; it was said, the guardians of the Companions of the Cave; and it was said, the leaders of the city, because whoever has the upper hand in this dispute must be one of these. What is mentioned in the story is that the king placed a place of worship over the entrance of the cave and established for it a great festival every year. It is reported from al-Zajjaj that this indicates that when their affair became manifest, those who believed in the Resurrection prevailed, because places of worship are only for those who believe in it. End of quotation.

The first view is made remote by the expression that indicates plurality, and the second, if by the guardians is meant guardians by kinship, as in the phrase "guardians of the slain," then no trace has been found that the Companions of the Cave, when they were raised, had such guardians. Many have explained the relative pronoun as referring to the king and the Muslims, and there is no difficulty in applying the term guardians to them, as in the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are guardians of one another﴾. This indicates that the first group was not like that. It has been reported that they were disbelievers, and that they wanted to build a church or a shrine for their unbelief, but the believers prevented them and built over them a place of worship. The apparent meaning of this report is that the place of worship is the counterpart of the church. But what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that the king built a church over them and wrote on its top: "The sons of the *arakinah*, the sons of the landowners," clearly shows that there is no counterpart, and perhaps this is the truth, because it is not correct to mean by the place of worship here what is called today the prayer place of the Muhammadans. Rather, what is meant is the house of worship of the believers of that community, and they were, as you heard at first, Christians. Although there is another view on the matter that you will hear shortly, God willing, their house of worship is called a church. The apparent meaning of what preceded is that the place of worship was taken so that God, exalted is He, might be worshipped in it by whomever He wills.

Abu Hatim reported from al-Suddi that the king said: "I will surely take a place of worship beside these righteous people, and I will worship God, exalted is He, in it until I die." It is reported from al-Hasan that it was taken so that the Companions of the Cave might pray in it when they awoke. This is based on the view that they did not die but slept as they had slept at first. Some have gone to this view, and it was even said that they will not die until the Mahdi appears and they become among his helpers. There is no reliance on that, and in my opinion it is most like superstitions.

Then it is not hidden that on the view that the first group, which asked for the building to be erected over them, was disbelieving, the full purpose of the discovery was not realised among all the discoverers, and it is not necessary that the words ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾ are intended to settle the affair of the Companions of the Cave. Perhaps that group did not ascertain their condition, or that they had slept that period and then been raised, so they asked for the cave to be sealed over them and referred their affair to their Lord, exalted is He. God, exalted is He, knows best the reality of the matter.

Al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read *ghulibu* (they were overcome) with a *dammah* on the *ghayn* and a *kasrah* on the *lam*, so that the verb is in the passive voice. It was explained on this basis that a group of the believing discoverers wanted nothing to be built over them and no place to be touched, while another group among them wanted a building and did not want the cave to be obliterated. The first group could not prevent them, and they found themselves overcome, so they said: If there must be a building, then we will surely take over them a place of worship.

This is all. The verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of building over the graves of the righteous, taking a place of worship over them, and praying in that place. Among those who mentioned this is al-Shihab al-Khafaji in his glosses on al-Baydawi. This is a false, worthless, corrupt and fallacious view.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, exalted is He, has cursed the women who visit graves, and those who take over them places of worship and lamps." Muslim reported: "Beware! Those before you used to take the graves of their prophets as places of worship. I forbid you from that." Ahmad reported from Usamah, and he, along with the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and al-Nasa'i, from ʿAisha, and Muslim from Abu Hurayrah: "God, exalted is He, has cursed the Jews and the Christians, who took the graves of their prophets as places of worship." Ahmad, the two Shaykhs and al-Nasa'i: "Those people, when there was among them a righteous man and he died, they built a place of worship over his grave and depicted in it those images. Those are the worst of creation on the Day of Resurrection." Ahmad and al-Tabarani: "Among the worst of people are those upon whom the Hour will come while they are alive, and those who take graves as places of worship." ʿAbd al-Razzaq: "Among the worst of my community are those who take graves as places of worship." And also: "The children of Israel took graves as places of worship, so God, exalted is He, cursed them."

And other sound reports and explicit traditions besides these.

Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Zawajir (*al-Zawajir 'an Iqtiraf al-Kaba'ir*) that some Shafi'i scholars' statements counted taking graves as places of worship, praying toward them, touching them (*istilam*, here meaning kissing or touching them as a mark of reverence), circumambulating them, and similar acts among the major sins (*kaba'ir*). It seems they derived this from the hadiths that have been cited. The reason why taking a grave as a place of worship is forbidden is clear: the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed those who did this at the graves of the prophets (peace be upon them), and he made those who did it at the graves of the righteous the most evil of creation before God on the Day of Resurrection. So there is a warning for us in this. Taking a grave as a place of worship means praying over it or toward it. In that case, his words "and praying toward them" would be repetitive, unless by taking them as places of worship what is meant is only praying over them. Indeed, this reasoning is only valid if the grave is that of a revered person, a prophet or a saint, as the narration "when there was among them a righteous man" indicates.

For this reason, our companions (the Shafi'is) said: praying toward the graves of the prophets and the saints is forbidden if done for blessing (*tabarruk*) and veneration (*i'zam*). They stipulated two conditions: that it be the grave of a revered person, and that prayer toward it be intended. Praying over it is equivalent to seeking blessing and veneration. That this act is a major sin is clear from the hadiths. It seems he (Ibn Hajar) analogized from this every form of veneration of the grave, such as lighting lamps on it out of veneration and seeking blessing from it, and circumambulating it in the same way. This is not an unlikely inference, especially since some of the mentioned hadiths explicitly state the curse on whoever places a lamp on a grave. Thus the statement of the companions about the reprehensibility (*karahah*) of this should be understood as applying when it is not intended as veneration and seeking blessing from the one buried there.

Some Hanbalis said: a man's intention to pray at a grave, seeking blessing from it, is the very essence of opposition (*muhadda*) to God and His Messenger (ﷺ), and an innovation in religion (*ibda' din*) that God, the Mighty and Majestic, has not permitted, because of the prohibition against it. Moreover, it is contrary to consensus (*ijma'*), for among the greatest prohibitions and causes of polytheism (*shirk*) is praying at graves, taking them as places of worship, or building over them. It is obligatory to hasten to demolish them, and to demolish the domes that are over the graves, for they are more harmful than the mosque of harm (*masjid al-dirar*), because they were founded on disobedience to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) forbade this and ordered the demolition of elevated graves. It is obligatory to remove every lamp and lantern placed on a grave, and its endowment (*waqf*) and vowing (*nadhr*) are not valid. End quote.

In al-Minhaj and its commentary by the aforementioned scholar (al-Adhra'i? / Ibn Hajar): It is reprehensible to plaster the grave (*tajsis*) and to build upon it, within its precincts (*harim*) and outside it, in a non-endowed (*ghayr al-musabbalah*) cemetery, unless there is fear of exhumation, the attack of a wild animal, or destruction by flood. Building in an endowed cemetery is forbidden. Likewise, writing upon it is reprehensible, because of the authentic prohibition regarding the three (plastering, building, and writing), whether it is the writing of his name or other text, on a tablet at his head or elsewhere. However, al-Adhra'i investigated the prohibition on writing the Qur'an on it, because it exposes it to desecration by trampling and to defilement by the discharge of the dead when graves are repeatedly reused and rain falls. It is recommended to write his name merely to identify him over the long years, especially the graves of the prophets and the righteous, since this is a means of the recommended informing. When al-Hakim narrated the prohibition, he said: "The practice is not in accordance with it now, for the imams of the Muslims from East and West have written upon their graves; thus it is a practice that later generations have inherited from earlier ones." It is answered by rejecting this universal claim, and even by granting it: building over their graves is more common than writing on them in public cemeteries, as is observed, especially in the two Holy Sanctuaries (Mecca and Medina), Egypt, and similar places, and they know of the prohibition against it, so the writing is likewise (forbidden). If you say: this is a practical consensus (*ijma' fi'li*), and it is authoritative, as they have stated, I say: this is disputed; rather, it is only a majority practice, since it has not been preserved even from the scholars who hold it to be forbidden. And even granting that it is a practical consensus, the scope of its authority, as is evident, applies only when the times are righteous, such that commanding good and forbidding evil is enforced; and that has been suspended for ages.

If the grave itself is built for a reason other than those mentioned, as is evident, or a fence or a dome is placed over it, in a public cemetery such as unclaimed land (*mawat*) which people have customarily used for burial, or in land endowed for that purpose, then it is even more obligatory to demolish it, out of respect for it (the grave), as in al-Majmu', because it causes constriction, and also because the building becomes permanent after the deceased has disappeared, so people will treat that plot as forbidden. Is what is customary, of placing four square stones around the grave, with each head of them joined to the head of the next with firm plaster, considered building? The first view is the more likely, because the reason for permanence exists here. Also, a group of scholars issued a ruling to demolish all the structures in the cemetery of Cairo, including the dome of Imam al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, which some kings built. Everyone should demolish these, provided no harm would result from it; in that case, raising the matter to the ruler is required, following the statement of Ibn al-Rif'ah in *al-Sulh*. End quote.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu al-Hayyaj al-Asadi, who said: "Ali, may God honor his face, said to me: 'Shall I send you on the same mission that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent me on: that you leave no image without obliterating it, and no elevated grave without leveling it.'"

Ibn al-Humam said in *Fath al-Qadir*: This is to be understood as referring to what they used to do of raising graves with fine, high construction. The hadiths and the statements of the fair-minded scholars who follow what has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from the righteous predecessors are more than can be counted. Do not say: the verse clearly indicates that what is mentioned is part of the laws of those before us, and it has been cited as evidence.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it..." (the hadith to its end). Then he recited God's words: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, which were spoken to Moses (peace be upon him), and its context is evidentiary.

Muhammad (al-Shaybani) argued for the permissibility of dividing water by rotation (*muhayaah*) with the words of God: ﴿For her is a drinking day﴾ and the verse following it, ﴿and inform them that the water is to be shared among them﴾.

Abu Yusuf argued for the application of retaliation (*qawad*) between male and female by the verse: ﴿And We prescribed for them﴾. Al-Karkhi argued for its application between free and slave and Muslim and dhimmi by that same verse, which concerns the Children of Israel, and so on. For we say:

Our view regarding the law of those before us is that, although it binds us on the basis that it is (also) our law, this is not absolutely so. Rather, it applies if God related it to us without rejection (*inkar*), and rejection by His Messenger (ﷺ) is like rejection by Him, the Mighty and Majestic. And I have heard that he (ﷺ) cursed those who take mosques over graves. Moreover, the claim that what is mentioned is part of the laws of those before us is disputed. How can taking mosques over graves be among the earlier laws, given what you have heard of the curse on the Jews and Christians for taking the graves of their prophets as mosques? The verse is not like the verses we mentioned just before, which the imams cited as evidence. It contains nothing beyond relating the speech of a group of people and their resolve to do that, and it is not presented in praise of them or as an exhortation to emulate them. Therefore, unless it is established that there was among them an infallible person (*ma'sum*), their action does not prove anything, let alone their resolve to do what they were intent upon as a legitimate practice. And what strengthens the lack of confidence in their action is the saying that the reference to them is to the rulers and sultans, as narrated from Qatadah.

On this basis, someone may say: the first group were believers who knew that taking mosques over graves was not legitimate. They suggested building over the entrance of the cave and sealing it, and leaving its inhabitants alone. The rulers did not accept this from them and were angered by it, to the point that they swore to take a mosque. The first group did not suggest burial, although the apparent ruling is that this is what is prescribed in that case for the dead, just as it is what is prescribed according to us regarding them, since their death was not established. What prevented them from establishing their death was that they were unable to do so, as Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, namely entering upon them because of the awe that was cast over them. For this reason they said: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them.﴾ And if you insist on a good opinion of the second group, you may say: their taking a mosque over them was not in the manner of taking mosques over graves, which is forbidden and whose doer is cursed. Rather, it was taking a mosque near them and close to their cave. The phrase "near them" appears explicitly in the narration of the story from al-Suddi and Wahb. Such taking is not prohibited, for the most that follows from it is that the relation of the mosque to the cave in which they are is like the relation of the Prophet's Mosque to his revered resting place (ﷺ). Their words "we will surely take [a mosque] over them" in this interpretation would be in parallel with the words of the first group: "build over them." And if you wish, you may say that this taking was upon the cave, above the mountain in which it is. In the report of Mujahid, the king left them in their cave and built a mosque over their cave, and this is closer to the apparent wording, as is not hidden. All of this is only needed on the view that the People of the Cave died after they were discovered. As for the view that they slept just as they had slept at first, it is not needed, according to what has been said. In sum, no one with even a little sense should go against what the authentic reports and explicit traditions have stated, relying on the argument from this verse. For such a course is the utmost in error and the utmost in lack of intellect. I have seen people who permit what the ignorant do at the graves of the righteous: raising them, building them with plaster and brick, hanging lamps upon them, praying toward them, circumambulating them, kissing them, gathering at them at specific times, and other such things, citing this noble verse as evidence, and what has come in some versions of the story about the king making for them a festival every year and placing them in coffins of teak, and analogizing some of this to the rest. All of that is opposition (*muhadda*) to God and His Messenger (ﷺ), and the innovation of a religion that God, the Mighty and Majestic, has not permitted.

For knowing the truth, it suffices for you to trace what the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did at his grave (peace be upon him), which is the most excellent grave on the face of the earth, indeed more excellent than the Throne, and to examine their actions when visiting it and greeting him, peace be upon him, so trace that and reflect on what is here and what is there. And God, glorified and exalted, is the One who guides you.

Then know that they differed over determining the location of the mosque and the cave, and some of the opinions have already passed before you. In *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*): In Syria there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, and its neighbors claim that they are the People of the Cave. Over them is a mosque and a building called al-Raqim. With them is a dog, a decayed (*rimmah*) one. In al-Andalus, in the direction of Granada, near a village called Lushah, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, and with them is a decayed dog. Most of them have had their flesh stripped away, and some of them are still intact. Many centuries have passed, and we have not found any knowledge of their affair. Some people claim that they are the People of the Cave. Ibn Atiyyah said: I entered upon them and saw them in the year 504 (AH), in this condition. Over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim, as if it were a carved palace, of which some walls remain, in a barren open field. On the high part of the fortress of Granada, on the side facing the qiblah, are the traces of an ancient city called the city of Diqyus, and in its traces we found wonders. End quote. When we were in al-Andalus, people used to visit this cave and say that they err in counting them if they count them, and that a dog is with them. People would travel to Lushah to visit them. As for what he mentioned about the ancient city, I have passed by it many times, uncountable, and I have seen large stones there. It is more likely that this is in al-Andalus, because Christianity was widespread there, to the extent that it was the land of their great kingdom. And because reporting about what is at the farthest point of the land of the Hijaz is stranger and less likely to be known except through revelation from God, the Exalted. End quote.

The earlier report from Ibn 'Abbas and Mu'awiya weakens what has been claimed as its preference, because Mu'awiya did not enter al-Andalus. And the Andalusians calling the Christians of al-Andalus "Rum" in their prose and verse, and in addressing their common folk, as is also in al-Bahr, is of no benefit either. Many have relied on the view that this (the cave) is in Tarsus. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 22 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They will say﴾ The pronoun in it, and in the two verbs after it, refers, as Ibn 'Atiyyah and some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have chosen, to the Jews contemporary with him ﷺ who were disputing about the story of the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf). This is supported by the saying of al-Hasan and others that they were before the sending of Musa (Moses) peace be upon him, since it indicates that they had some general knowledge of their circumstances, and this would entail that they had a mention in the Torah. And there is what there is in this.

The apparent meaning is that this is a report of something that had not yet occurred, as if it were said: They will say, when you narrate the story of the People of the Cave, or when they are asked about their number: ﴿Three﴾, that is, three persons, ﴿their fourth is their dog﴾, that is, the one who makes them four by his joining them. ﴿Their dog﴾: so "three" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "their fourth is their dog" is a subject and predicate. The active participle does not govern here because it is in the past sense, and the sentence is in the position of a qualifier (na't) for "three." The two pronouns refer to it (three), not to the subject. For this reason it was dispensed with by omission; otherwise the apparent expression would have been: "They are three and a dog." However, since the intention was to single them out with a judgment of wondrous importance, he turned to what was mentioned, so as to alert, by the qualifying phrase that indicates distinction and singling out, that those youths were not like every three who kept company. For this reason God, exalted is He, in His Mighty Book, joined the basest of animals to the blessing of their companionship with the group of those devoted to Him and secluded in His presence, glorified is He. The same is said of what follows. To this parsing went Abu al-Baqa', and al-'Allamah al-Tibi chose it, and it is what indicated the point mentioned, and he strung together with the verse the hadith: "What do you think of two whose third is God, exalted is He?"

Because of this, some eminent scholars censured him, to the point of attributing to him disbelief. By my life, he wronged him, and his intention remained hidden from him, so he did not understand it. Ibn al-Hajib did not permit the sentence to be in the position of a qualifier, as neither he nor others such as Abu al-Baqa' permitted making it a circumstantial clause (hal), or making it a second predicate after the omitted subject. The complete discussion of that will come, God willing, exalted is He.

Page 241

The specification of the numeral's specifier as "persons" (ashkhas) is preferable to specifying it as "men" (rijal), because three men do not become four with their dog, due to the difference of the two genera. The non-requirement of unity of genus in such a case is refused by common usage, and it is contrary to what the grammarians stated. The claim that the dog, by the honor of their companionship, was joined to the rational beings is a poetic fancy. Ibn Muhaysin read "thalath" with the assimilation of the thа' into the ta', saying: "ibʿath tilka" (send that), and this is good due to the closeness of their articulation points and their both being voiceless (mahmus).

﴿And they will say: Five, their sixth is their dog﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) on ﴿they will say﴾. Although the present tense is shared between the present and the future, the intended meaning here is the second, by the context of what precedes it; therefore the sin (future particle) was dispensed with in it. If you coordinate it on the complement of the sin, it enters with it under its rule and is restricted to the future through it. But it has been said that coordination on that is forced. Shibl ibn 'Abbad, from Ibn Kathir, read "khamasah" with a fatha on the mim, and it is, like the sukun, a dialect form of it, similar to the fatha and sukun in "'asharah." Ibn Muhaysin read with a kasra on the kha' and the mim, and with the assimilation of the ta' into the sin; and from him also the assimilation of the tanwin into the sin without nasalization.

﴿Conjecturing about the unseen﴾: that is, casting at an unseen matter, hidden from them, of which they have no knowledge, and bringing it forth, or supposing it to be so. On the first reading, "rajm" is used figuratively, being the throwing of stones that do not hit a target or aim for the speaker without knowledge or attention, after likening it to that. In the Kashshaf it is stated that he made the speech about what is hidden from them, their knowledge, like the stone-missile that is not aimed at a specific addressee, and if it were aimed, it would miss, since it is not built upon certainty, just as a stone rarely strikes the stoned on target, unlike an arrow and the like. For this reason they said "qadhfan bil-ghaib" (casting at the unseen) and "rajman bihi," and did not say "ramyan bihi." As for shooting in insult and the like, the consideration is its effect on the honor of the target, the effect of the arrow on the shot. End.

On the second reading, the mention of a matter without certain knowledge and tranquility of heart is likened to the hurling of a stone that serves no purpose in its hurling and does not hit its mark. Then the placing of "rajm" in the place of "zann" (supposition) was used figuratively for it, until it became a conventional literal meaning for it. In the Kashshaf also: when the usage of their saying "rajman bil-zann" (conjecture) became frequent, they understood from the verbal noun its meaning without regard to the complement, and so they said "rajman bil-ghaib," meaning "conjecturing about it." On this goes the verse of Zuhayr:

"And war is only what you know and have tasted, and he is not concerning it a speech of conjecture."

where he intended the supposed. The accusative of "rajman" here is on both readings: either as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the two verbs, meaning "casting," or as an absolute object from them both, since the casting and the saying are one.

In al-Bahr it is stated that he included in "saying" the meaning of "casting," or that it is from an omitted new sentence, or that it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the two verbs together, meaning: they cast, casting. Abu Hayyan permitted its being accusative as an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlih), meaning: they say that for their casting at the unseen, or for their conjecture about it; that is, what moves them to speak is the casting at the unseen. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿And they will say: Seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾: the intended meaning is also the future. The discussion of its coordination is like the discussion of the coordination of the preceding. The sentence after the number is in the position of a qualifier for it, like the two preceding sentences, as Zamakhshari expressly stated. He did not make the waw a barrier to that, but mentioned that it is the waw that enters a sentence serving as a qualifier of an indefinite noun, as it enters one serving as a circumstantial clause of a definite noun, in your saying: "A man came to me and with him another," and "I passed by Zayd and in his hand is a sword." Among this is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾. Its benefit is to confirm the adhesion of the qualifier to the qualified, and to indicate that his being characterized by it is a fixed, established matter. It is this that here indicates that those who said what was mentioned spoke from firm knowledge and tranquility of soul, and did not cast by conjecture as others cast. So it is the truth, not the two former sayings. The proof of that is that He, glorified and exalted, followed the two with His saying: ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾, and followed this with His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾, that is, more powerful and more ancient in knowledge of them, ﴿none knows them﴾, that is, none knows their number according to what comes to the mind in view of the context, ﴿except a few﴾. The waw's indication of what was mentioned is also shown by the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: it is related that he said: "When the waw came, the number was cut off," meaning no number remained after it to be turned to again. And it is established that they were seven, and their eighth their dog, with certainty and conclusiveness.

ʿAta' expressly stated that this few are of the People of the Book. It has been said: of mankind in general, and this is what is required by what al-Tabarani recorded in al-Awsat with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I am of those few." It was also recorded from him by more than one through various routes, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded something similar from Ibn Mas'ud.

Some claimed that the intended meaning of "except a few" is a few of the angels, peace be upon them, which no human approves. The affirmed element in this exception is knowledge, and that does not harm the fact that the superiority of knowledge belongs to Him, mighty and majestic. That, and the view that the waw is as Zamakhshari mentioned, was taken by Ibn al-Munayyir, who said after citing it: "This is the correct view, not the saying that it is the waw of eight, for that is a matter on which its proponent has no firm footing," and he refuted what they mentioned of that. It will come, God willing, exalted is He, in its place, that this is to be noted.

Abu al-Baqa' said: when the sentence falls as a qualifier of an indefinite noun, the waw may enter it, and this is the correct view regarding the entry of the waw in "their eighth." Many objected to this. Abu Hayyan said: that the waw enters a sentence serving as a qualifier, indicating the adhesion of the qualifier to the qualified and the establishment of its connection to it, is something the grammarians do not know. Rather they established that a qualifier that is not a sentence is not conjoined to another qualifier unless the meanings differ, so that the conjunction indicates difference; and if they do not differ, conjunction is not permitted. This is for single nouns; as for sentences that serve as qualifiers, they are further from permitting that.

They also refuted those who held that Sibawayh's saying, "And as for what comes in meaning and is neither noun nor verb," with his "and is not a noun, etc.," is a qualifier for a meaning, and that the waw entered the sentence on the basis that this is not of the speech of the Arabs: "I passed by a man and he eats," on the assumption of a qualifier. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except that it had a known decree﴾, the sentence in it is circumstantial, and it suffices as a refutation of Zamakhshari's saying: "We do not know of any grammarian who held it," end.

The author of al-Fara'id said: the entry of the waw between the qualifier and the qualified is not sound, since the qualifier and the qualified are unified in essence, judgment, and emphasis, while adhesion requires duality. However, we say: we do not concede that the waw indicates emphasis; the intensity of adhesion is at most that it indicates collectivity, and collectivity implies duality, while the conjunction of qualifier and qualified implies unity with respect to the essence. The author of al-Miftah mentioned that the saying of whoever says that the waw in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it has a known decree﴾, enters between the qualifier and the qualified is an error on his part, and that it is only the waw of the circumstantial clause, with the circumstantial referent being "a town," which is qualified, i.e., "And We did not destroy a town of the towns except that it had a known decree..." As for "A man came to me and with him another," there are two aspects: one is that they are two conjoined sentences, and the second is that "another" is conjoined on "a man," i.e., "A man came to me and another man with him." It was preferred over "Two men came to me" to make it understood that they came accompanying each other. As for the waw in "I passed by Zayd and in his hand is a sword," it entered between the circumstantial and its owner only because the circumstantial is in the rule of a sentence, unlike the qualifier in relation to the qualified: "Zayd came riding" is in the rule of "Zayd came while he was riding," unlike "Zayd the rider came." Understand this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 22 (part 2 of 3):

Let us grant that it [the waw] is inserted between the qualifier (sifah) and the qualified (mawsuf) to emphasise adherence, but the indication that their attribution of it [the qualifier to them] is a fixed, established matter is not granted. Where is the evidence for it? That the waw is what signals that the aforementioned statement comes from firm knowledge and tranquillity of soul is extremely far-fetched. As for the claim that the following (ittiba') indicates this: if what is meant is that it indicates the waw's signalling of what was mentioned, then its invalidity is obvious. If what is meant is that it indicates the truthfulness of those who said the last statement and the untruthfulness of those who said the first two statements, then it is granted that following the first two statements with "conjecturing about the unseen" (rajman bil-ghayb) indicates untruthfulness, an indication without any doubt. But we do not grant that not following the last statement with it, and following it with what was followed, indicates this; and even if we grant it, it indicates it only weakly. We also do not grant that the words of Ibn 'Abbas indicate what was mentioned. The apparent meaning is that he knew that the last statement is true, from the Truthful, the one whose word is believed (ﷺ), and that his intention in his saying, "When the waw came, the count ended," is that what the waw was placed upon is truth, and the count ended with it. Therefore the correct view is that the waw is a conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf), and the sentence after it is conjoined to the sentence before it.

The scholar al-Tibi defended al-Zamakhshari and answered what was raised against him. He said: "Know that before beginning the answer it is necessary to clarify the intended meaning, to set the discussion in order. The waw here is not used in its literal sense (haqiqah), and figurative usage (majaz) does not require the specific transfer (naql al-khususi) but requires the consideration of the type of relation (al-'alaqah). They mentioned that figurative usage, in the convention of rhetoric (balaghah), is preferable to literal usage and more eloquent, and that the basis of the science of figurative expression ('ilm al-bayan) is sound taste (al-dhawq al-salim), which is more beneficial than taught taste; it does not depend on fixed transmission (tawqif), and this is unlike the science of grammar (nahw). Figurative usage is not restricted to nouns and verbs but may also occur in particles."

The author of the commentary on al-Lubab (sharih al-Lubab) reported from Sibawayh that the waw in their saying, "I sold the sheep and a dirham" (bi'tu al-shatta wa-dirhaman), has the meaning of the bi (preposition "with"). Its verification is that the waw is for conjunction (al-jam') and the ba' is for attachment (al-ilsaq), and both are of one category, so the figure of metaphor (isti'arah) was adopted with it, and so on. Once this is known, let it be known that the meaning of his saying, "its benefit is to emphasise the adherence of the qualifier to the qualified," is that the qualifier has a kind of connection with the qualified. When the emphasis of adherence is intended, the waw is placed between them to signal that this qualifier is not separable from the qualified. To this the reference is made in what follows of his words, and that the circumstantial clause (hal) in reality is a qualifier; there is no difference except by consideration. Do you not see that the qualifier of an indefinite noun, when it is placed before it while being the very same thing, becomes a circumstantial clause, and if the two were not identical this would not be valid? Then, your saying, "A man came to me, and with him another," and your saying, "I passed by Zayd, and with him another," since they are equal in form except in regard to definiteness and indefiniteness, their rule is the same regarding the waw. This is what al-Zamakhshari intended by citing the two examples, not as some understood.

As for the statement of al-Farahidi in explaining the prohibition of inserting the waw between the qualifier and the qualified, because the two are unified in essence and in rule, and this contradicts what the insertion of the waw requires of difference: it is based on the premise that the waw is conjunctive, because it is the one that requires difference, as al-Sakkaki said. He has explained the aspect of its figurative usage merely as linking (al-rabt).

As for his statement regarding "Came to me a man, and with him another," that it is two sentences: it is as you see. As for his statement that "Zayd came riding" (ja'a Zaydun rakiban) is in the rule of "Zayd came and he is riding" (ja'a Zaydun wa-huwa rakib): this is from the reversed (al-ma'kus), for the original in the circumstantial clause is the singular form, as the words of Ibn al-Hajib and other eminent scholars indicate. As for his granting the insertion for emphasising adherence, and from it the indication that attribution is a fixed, established matter: this is among the strange things. How can the emphasis be granted while its benefit is not granted? What repels the remaining objections is that what al-Zamakhshari relied upon is not from the category of certain proofs but from the category of indicators, and these suffice in such contexts.

Ibn al-Hajib said: "It is not permissible for [they say] 'Their fourth is their dog' (rabi'uhum kalbuhum) and 'Their sixth is their dog' (sadisuhum kalbuhum) to be a qualifier of what precedes, nor a circumstantial clause, due to the absence of the governing element (al-'amil) together with the absence of the waw. It is permissible that each of them be a predicate after a predicate for the omitted subject (al-mubtada' al-mahdhuf). When predicates are multiple, it is permissible for the second of them to be connected with the waw or not." This holds if it is granted that the meaning in the sentences is one. But if it is said that His statement, "And their eighth is their dog" (wa-thamimuhum kalbuhum), is a new statement from Him, glorified is He, not a report about them, then it is understood that the speakers were seven and were correct, and it does not necessarily follow that it is a predicate after a predicate. This is strengthened by the mention of "conjecturing about the unseen" (rajman bil-ghayb) before the third, which indicates that it differs from what precedes it in conjecturing about the unseen, so it is certainly truth. However, this view is weakened in that God, exalted is He, said: "None knows them except a few" (ma ya'lamuhum illa qalil). If "And their eighth is their dog" were made a confirmation from Him, exalted is He, of those who said seven, then the one knowing that would have to be many, for the report of God, exalted is He, is true; this indicates that none of them was truthful. If that is so, then the whole sentence must be equal in meaning, and since it has become impossible for the last to be a qualifier, it is necessary that all be so. End of quotation. It is understood that the waw is what prevents the qualifying function, and the disease is the disease, so the cure is the cure.

His statement, "And if that is so, it is necessary, etc.," is a discourse far removed from the requirements of eloquence, because in every difference there are benefits, and the eloquent person is one who looks to those benefits, not one who reduces it to verbosity and superfluity in speech. Furthermore, there must be a true statement among the three statements, so that God's saying, "None knows them except a few," agrees with His saying, "conjecturing about the unseen," because the first two statements have been refuted by it, so the true one is this.

Its being followed by this is a sign of its truth, and that is absent according to what the questioner held. Despite this, where is the sweetness of the discourse, and where is the subtlety which minds find delightful?
