As for his claim that it follows that the one knowing that would be many, on the assumption that "And their eighth is their dog" is a new statement from God, exalted is He, because the report of God, exalted is He, is true: this is not free from scrutiny, because the one confirming in that case would be the Muslims, and they are few in relation to others. Also, there is no restriction of "few" to what is less than ten. Even if Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said, "Every 'few' in the Qur'an is less than ten," this falls within the realm of prohibition, and establishing it requires great effort. Moreover, it is possible to say that what is meant is the scarcity of those who knew that before God's confirmation of it, and it is not far-fetched that they were few in themselves among the Muslims, or among the People of the Book, or among both. Yes, the view that it is a new statement is something that should not be given attention, even though some exegetes held it.

Here, a group agreed with him in the defence, among them the leader of the verifiers (sayyid al-muhaqqiqin) and the pillar of the scrupulous (sanad al-mudaqqiqin), who said: "The apparent meaning is that God's saying, 'And their eighth is their dog,' is a qualifier of seven, as its two companions testify. Also, seven is not in the rule of a qualified noun, as it was said regarding 'town' in His saying: 'We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree,' so that the circumstantial clause interpretation would be valid by consensus. There is no doubt that the meaning of conjunction (al-jam') is appropriate to the meaning of adherence, and the door of figurative usage is open, so let this waw be interpreted accordingly, as an emphasis of the adherence of the qualifier to the qualified. Thus this also becomes a branch of the conjunctive waw, like the one that means 'with' (ma'a), the circumstantial, and the parenthetical waw."

This was also supported by what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It was raised against his reason for rejecting the circumstantial interpretation, namely that the indefinite noun is not in the rule of a qualified noun, that the justification for a circumstantial clause coming from an indefinite noun is not restricted to its being a qualified noun or in the rule of one, as in the verse he cited. Indeed, Ibn Hisham mentioned in al-Mughni that among the justifications is the circumstantial clause being connected with the waw. So let this be remembered.

Ibn Malik agreed with those who rejected it, and said in the commentary on al-Tashil: "What the author of al-Kashshaf held, regarding the placing of the waw between the qualifier and the qualified, is corrupt for five reasons. The first: he analogised the qualifier to the circumstantial clause, and between them there are many differences: the circumstantial clause may precede its referent, may differ from it in case-ending, definiteness and indefiniteness, and the circumstantial sentence may dispense with a pronoun by the waw, while this is impossible in a qualifying sentence. Just as the difference between the circumstantial clause and the qualifier is established in these matters, so their difference is established in connecting the circumstantial sentence with the waw, and its impossibility in a qualifying sentence. The second: his view on this question is not known among the Basrans and the Kufans, so it should not be given attention. The third: it is justified by something that is not appropriate, for the waw indicates the joining of what precedes it and what follows it, and that necessitates their difference, which is the opposite of what is intended by emphasis, so it cannot be said of an emphasising conjunctive. The fourth: the waw separates the first from the second, and were it not there they would be adjacent, so how can it be said that it emphasised their adherence? The fifth: if the waw were suitable for emphasising the adherence of the qualified to the qualifier, then the most appropriate place for it would be a position that is not suitable for the circumstantial clause, unlike a sentence that is suitable for the circumstantial clause in its position." End of quotation. What is wrong with it can be known by sincere reflection on what preceded.

What he mentioned in the fourth reason is strange: it is an assumption that would be considered odd even from children, let alone from the mature men. So reflect on that. And God, exalted is He, guides you.

Some of them said: the pronouns of the three verbs refer to those who disputed about the story of the People of the Cave during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), from the People of the Book and the Muslims, not in the sense that each verb is attributed to all of them, but to some of them. So the first statement is for the Jews, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi. It was also said: it is for a chief of the Christian Arabs of Najran, who was a Jacobite, and who had come as a delegation with a group of them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The People of the Cave were mentioned, and he mentioned their number as God, exalted is His glory, related. Perhaps the expression with the plural pronoun is to agree with those who were with him in this. The second statement is according to what was also reported from al-Suddi: the Christians, without specifying them. It was also said: al-'Aqib and those with him from the Christians of Najran, who were also delegates, and he was a Nestorian. The third statement is for some of the Muslims. It seems that when God, exalted is His name, related the statements before they were said, He guided them to the truth and directed them to it by not placing that statement in the string of "conjecturing about the unseen," as He did with the other two, and by changing its composition through the insertion of the waw, and by following it with what He followed it with, as you have heard, that this is a sign of its truth. What is meant by "few" in this view is the one whom God, exalted is He, caused to seek guidance through these signs, such as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It has passed, not far back, that he was counted among them and mentioned what apparently amounts to citing the waw.

It was also said: they knew that count from a revelation other than what has been mentioned, namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) had informed them of it through God's informing him of it.

This was countered by saying: if it were so, it would not have been hidden from the rabbi (al-habr), and he would not have needed to cite evidence, and the Muslims would have been his equals in knowing it.

It was answered: there is no obstacle to the rabbi's being aware of the report together with a small group of Muslims, and it does not necessarily follow that all the Companions were aware of what the Prophet (ﷺ) said. How many a report containing a legal ruling was transmitted from him (ﷺ) by one of them alone, may Allah be pleased with them all! So what do you think about what belongs to the category of narratives, which did not contain that? His citing of it explicitly, may Allah be pleased with him, does not contradict awareness; rather it may coexist with it, according to what you have just understood. So it is not an explicit text that he was unaware.

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 22 (part 3 of 3):

It has been objected to the view that the source of knowledge is learning from this revelation, because it contains indications, that it would follow from this that the Companions who heard the verse would be a model for Ibn 'Abbas in knowledge, as the one who raised this objection stated. Rather, they were Arabs who were nursed at the breast of eloquence in the cradle of fluency, and upon the horizons of their hearts and the pages of their minds, from the dawning points of their level faith, there shone the lights of prophethood emanating from the sun of the Unique Presence. Rarely did a verse descend without casting its staff into the quadrangles of their ears, owing to their great eagerness to listen and the Prophet's (ﷺ) excessive desire to make them hear it. And if al-Zamakhshari and his like understood from this verse what they understood, why did his Companions (ﷺ) not understand that, when they were the way they were? Would it occur to anyone with even a little intelligence that non-Arabs perceived it while most of those Arabs did not perceive it? Or how is it conceivable that the secrets of the eloquence of the Qur'an are disclosed to one who knows its inimitability only after hardship, and concealed from one who knows that merely through natural ability? This objection can hardly be repelled except by committing to the view that the hearers of this verse were few, because it was revealed in Makkah, where the Muslims were few, with the gathering with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not easily available to them, and likewise the gathering of some of them with others, unlike what was easy in Madinah; or by committing to the view that those who attended to the indications it contains were few. And this, as you see, is [unsatisfactory].

It is said: the pronouns refer to the Christians of Najran, who debated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the number of the People of the Cave. The Melkites said the first statement, the Jacobites the second, and the Nestorians the third. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is more preferable than the earlier view related from some of them.

Al-Mawardi, and Abu Hayyan endorsed it, said: the pronouns refer to those disputing in their discussion before their victory over them, so that Allah, glorified is He, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of what there was of disagreement among their people regarding their number. It is not hidden that this view is far-fetched given the narration of those sayings in the future tense, together with its being followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾. It has already been mentioned that when the people reached the entrance of the cave with the one sent to buy food, he said: "Let me enter to my companions before you," and he entered, and their trace was concealed from the people. In another narration, whenever any of them wanted to enter upon them, they were terrified and left alone, and a mosque was built over them. So if it is said on this basis that the pronouns refer to those who came upon them and differed about their number, because they were unable to see them and gather with them, then each group said what it said. Perhaps the last group asked the youth, and he informed them of that number, so they believed him and accepted his word, and this was reinforced by what they had of the reports of their predecessors, so they spoke that with certainty, while the two earlier groups were speaking by conjecture, since there was no established knowledge for them. Perhaps they were both disbelievers. What al-Mawardi reported is not far-fetched after this, so reflect.

Among the strange things said: the pronoun in (﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ "they say, seven") refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the plural is for glorification. Their names, according to what is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, are: Maksilmina, Yamlikha, Marutulus, Thibyunus, Dirdunus, Kafashitiyatus, and Mintanwasis, who is the shepherd. And the dog's name is Qitmir.

It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that their names are Yamlikha, Makshilinya, Mathilinya, who are the companions of the king's right, and Marnush, Dibarnush, and Shadhnush, who are the companions of his left. He used to consult the six, and the seventh was the shepherd. The name of the shepherd is not mentioned in this narration, and the name of their dog is mentioned in it as Qitmir.

There is discussion about the authenticity of attributing this narration to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. Al-Allama al-Suyuti in the margins of al-Baydawi mentioned that al-Tabarani narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas in his al-Mu'jam al-Awsat with a sound chain.

What is in al-Durr al-Manthur is al-Tabarani's narration in al-Awsat, with a sound chain, of what we have previously mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas. And Allah knows best.

They have been named in some narrations by other names than these. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in his commentary on al-Bukhari, mentioned that there is considerable disagreement in pronouncing their names, and reliable accuracy in their vocalization cannot be established. In al-Bahr: the names of the People of the Cave are non-Arabic, and cannot be fixed by vowel marks or dots, and the chain for knowing them is weak. They also mentioned properties for them. Al-Nisaburi said, from Ibn 'Abbas: the names of the People of the Cave are suitable for seeking and fleeing, and extinguishing fire; they are written on a cloth and thrown into the middle of the fire. For a child's crying, they are written and placed under his head in the cradle. For tilling, they are written on paper and raised on a wooden stick planted in the middle of the field. For palpitation, for the triple fever, for headache, for wealth, rank, and entering upon rulers, they are tied to the right thigh. For difficult childbirth, they are tied to the left thigh. For guarding wealth, riding the sea, and salvation from killing. End of quotation. This is not authentically attributed to Ibn 'Abbas or to anyone else of the righteous predecessors. Perhaps it is something invented by those who pretend to the garb of shaykhs to take money from women, and by foolish minds. As for me, I count this among the properties of their names, for it is sound and tested. [The reading] "wa thaminuhum kalibuhum" was also recited, meaning: their dog's companion.

Some used this reading as evidence that they were eight men, and interpreted the widely transmitted reading as having an elided noun, i.e., "and the companion of their dog," which, as you see, is [unsatisfactory].

﴿So do not argue﴾: the fa' introduces a consequence of the prohibition on what precedes it. Mira' (arguing), according to al-Raghib, is disputing about something doubtful (mirya, doubt, i.e., hesitation), and its root is from "maraytu al-naqah," when you stroke the udder of the she-camel for milking. Many have interpreted it as mujadala (disputation), which is argument in general. That is: since you have come to know that among those who dispute there is one who errs and one who is correct, do not dispute with them ﴿concerning them﴾, i.e., regarding the matter of the youths, ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, not delving deeply into it. This is by restricting yourself to what the clear revelation has addressed, without declaring all of them ignorant, for among them there is one who is correct, though few; and without disgracing or rebuking the ignorant among them, for that harms the noble characteristics for whose completion you were sent.

Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning of "apparent" is saying to them: "It is not as you know."

Al-Mawardi reported that apparent argument is that which is with clear proof. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the disputation of a scholar who is certain of the truth of the report. Ibn Bahr said: it is what people witness. Al-Tabrizi said: the intended meaning of "apparent" is that which removes the opponent's proof; it is said "zahara" when it means "dhahaba" (went away), and he recited:

"And that is a complaint whose shame has gone away from you,"

i.e., has departed.

﴿And do not seek a ruling﴾: do not seek a verdict ﴿concerning them﴾, regarding their matter, ﴿from any of them﴾, from the disputants, ﴿anyone﴾. For in what We have given you as a ruling there is sufficiency from seeking a fatwa. It is therefore interpreted as seeking to appease, which conflicts with noble characteristics, since the situation does not call for soothing hearts or the like. It was also said: the meaning is: do not return to them concerning the matter of the youths, and do not accept the third statement from the standpoint of its being uttered by them, but from the standpoint of its being received from the revelation. It was also said: the meaning is: since you have come to know the ignorance of the advocates of the two statements, do not dispute with them about their matter except with an apparent argument, to the extent that the revelation addressed of their description as those who guess at the unseen, and do not seek a ruling concerning them from those two groups, anyone, since you are sufficed by what you have been given, and they have no knowledge of this. And this is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

﴿وَلَا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَيْءٍ﴾ means: "And never say about anything" (that is, for the sake of anything you are resolved upon), ﴿إِنِّي فَاعِلٌ ذَلِكَ﴾ "I will do that" (the thing), ﴿غَدًا﴾ "tomorrow" (that is, in whatever time is yet to come, without restriction). The word "tomorrow" here is an emphasis on what the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the grammatical form of the doer) indicates, on the basis that it is literally about the future. It includes "al-ghad" in the sense of the day that follows your day, which is the most immediate meaning.

The verse was revealed when "Quraysh asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Spirit, the People of the Cave, and Dhu al-Qarnayn. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'Tomorrow I will tell you,' and did not add an exception (istithna', saying 'if God wills'). So the revelation was delayed from him (ﷺ) for fifteen days," according to what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq. It is also said: three days, and it is said: forty days. This distressed him, upon him be blessings and peace, and Quraysh denied him, far be it from him.

Many scholars allowed that the verse remains on its apparent meaning, and that what follows it is understood by way of indication of the text (dalalat al-nass).

It has been objected that what follows it does not have the same meaning in the basis of the prohibition (manat al-nahy), which is the possibility of an obstacle (ihtimal al-mani'). For when time is extended, obstacles may be removed or lessened. But this is not valid, because the obstacle includes death, and the possibility of it over a wide span of time is stronger.

[Page 248]

﴿Unless God wills﴾ is an exception (istithna', exception) connected to the prohibition, according to the view chosen by a group of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, deceived by al-Tabari's rejection, is that it is so corrupt that it should not even be related, a departure from fairness, and it is an exception from the most general of circumstances.

In the sentence there is an implied bā' of accompaniment (li-l-mulabasah) entering on "an," and the preposition with its object is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do not say that in any circumstance except while accompanied by the will of God, Mighty and Majestic, by mentioning it." In al-Kashf, it is said: The accompaniment of the statement with the reality of the will is impossible, so what remains is that it be by mentioning it, which is "if God wills," or something similar that indicates making matters dependent on the will of God, Exalted.

It has been refuted by what could serve as a confirmation rather than a refutation. It is also permitted that the excepted element be the most general of times, meaning: "Do not say that at any time except at the time when God, Exalted, wills that you say it." On this interpretation, the will is explained as permission, because the time of the will is not known except through God's informing of it and His permission for it. Thus the meaning returns to: "Do not say it except after you are given permission to say it." It is also permitted that the exception be disjunctive (munqati'), with the purpose being perpetuity (ta'bid), meaning: "And do not ever say that." In al-Kashf this is justified by saying that he was forbidden from saying it except at a time of God's will, which is unknown, so it is obligatory to refrain forever. It indicates that this is what al-Zamakhshari intends, not what might be imagined from equating it with the statement of God, Exalted: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾, that the perpetuity is due to God not willing for them to do that tomorrow because it is ugly, like returning to the religion of disbelief. This is because the ugliness in what we are discussing, in its absolute sense, is not accepted, and restricting it to what relates to revelation, in the sense of: "Do not say, regarding what relates to revelation, 'I inform you of it,' unless God, Exalted, wills," and God, Exalted, has not willed that you say it from yourself. Therefore, "do not ever say it" is required, which is contradicted by the indefinite noun in the context of a prohibition that includes negation and restriction to the future. And [the statement] ﴿I am one who does that tomorrow﴾, meaning: one who informs of a matter relating to revelation tomorrow, does not indicate that his statement tomorrow will be from himself and not from revelation. So the comparison lies in the fact that the exception by the will is used in the context of perpetuity, even if the direction of indication differs, taking from the object of the will at one time and from ignorance of it at another. It is not hidden that the apparent meaning in the verse is the first aspect, and that his community (ﷺ), in the address it contains, whether it is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) or not, is not what is intended. It is not permissible for the exception to relate to the statement of God, Exalted: ﴿Indeed I will do﴾, by it being a disjunctive exception from what is within its scope of the most general circumstances or times, because in that case either you consider the will to relate to the act, and the meaning becomes: "I will do it in every circumstance or every time except in the circumstance or time of God's will for the act," which is not sound; or its relation is considered to be to its non-occurrence, and the meaning becomes: "I will do it in every circumstance or every time except in the circumstance or time of God's will, [that is,] God's will for the non-performance of the act." There is no doubt about its lack of suitability to the prohibition; rather, it is a desirable matter.

Al-Khafaji said: If the exception relates to "I will do," and the will relates to non-occurrence, the meaning becomes: "I will do it in every circumstance except if God, Exalted, wills the non-performance of my act." This cannot be prohibited. As for the view of Ahl al-Sunna, it is clear. As for the view of the Mu'tazila, they do not doubt that God's will for the non-performance of a volitional act of the servant, when it arises against it by bringing about what prevents it, such as death or the like, prevents it, even if, in their view, it is not related to its bringing into being or its annihilation. Likewise, the prohibition is not valid if the will relates to the act in both views. Therefore, what has been said, that the connection of the exception to what was mentioned is correct and the meaning based on it is a prohibition against following the path of the Mu'tazila regarding the creation of actions, so that one attributes them to himself, saying: "If God's will is not joined to the act, then I am its doer independently, and if it is joined, then what is in it is not hidden from His Prophet"; so reflect.

The objection to the Mu'tazila has become widespread in their claim that sins occur without the will and volition of God, Exalted, and that He, Exalted, wills only acts of obedience. [This is refuted] by saying: If it were so, then whoever says to his creditor who has demanded payment from him: "By God, I will give you your right tomorrow, if God, Exalted, wills," would have to be a violator of his oath if he does not do it, because God, Exalted, has willed that, since it is an act of obedience. If it does not happen, then he is obliged to the expiation (kaffarah) for his oath, and the exception does not benefit him, just as if he said: "By God, I will give you if Zayd stands up," and then he stood up but he did not do it. In committing to violation in that case is a departure from consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). Al-Murtada has answered this by saying that the exception entering into speech has various aspects. It may enter into oaths, divorce, manumission, and all contracts and what is similar to them of reports, and this requires suspension of the completion of the speech and the prevention of the obligation of what is bound by it, so that the speech becomes as if it has no ruling. In this aspect, the exception is valid regarding the past, so one says: "I have entered the house, if God, Exalted, wills," so that it may be excluded from being a definite report or from obligating a ruling by it. It is not valid in sins, because in it there is a display of dependence on God, Exalted, and sins are not suitable for that. He said: This aspect is one of the possible meanings of the verse. It may also enter speech with the intention of facilitation, decree, leaving things alone, and remaining in the states one is in, and this is what is intended when it enters permissible matters, and it is possible in the verse. It may enter merely for the purpose of dependence on God, Exalted, and in this case it is not counted in determining whether the speech is true or false, and this is also possible in the verse. It may enter with the intention of kindness (lutf) and facilitation, and this is specific to acts of obedience, and it is not valid for the verse to be understood in this way, because it encompasses everything that is not ugly.

As for the aforementioned statement of the debtor, if he intended this meaning, then violation does not follow from it if he does not do it, and the debtor and others will be held to his intention if he claims he intended what does not obligate him in it. So the objections they raised are not valid. The truth is that the objection is nothing, and refuting them is far beyond such [discussion]. This is it. Then know that the application of "exception" (istithna') to restriction by "if God, Exalted, wills," or rather to restriction by a condition in general, is established in the language and usage, as al-Sirafi explicitly stated in his commentary on the Book (Sibawayh's Kitab).

Al-Raghib said: Exception (istithna') is the removal of what a previous general statement requires, as in His statement, Exalted: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion﴾, etc., or the removal of what the wording requires, like saying: "His wife is divorced, if God, Exalted, wills." End.

In a hadith: "Whoever swears an oath about something and then says, 'If God, Exalted, wills,' has made an exception."

Therefore, what has been said, that the phrase "if God, Exalted, wills" is called an exception because it is expressed here by His, glorified be He, statement: ﴿Unless God wills﴾, is not correct. Likewise, what has been said: that it resembles exception in restriction, so its name was applied to it, is also what al-Khafaji said. It is not hidden that the hadith shows some reluctance toward the claim that the application of "exception" to restriction by "if God, Exalted, wills" is linguistic, because he (ﷺ) was not sent to convey the linguistic meanings of words, but to convey the legal rulings of the Shari'ah. So reflect.

﴿And remember your Lord﴾, Exalted; that is, the will of your Lord. So the speech is with an omitted genitive (mudaf), and the mention of the will of God, Exalted, is what is indicated by what precedes it, that one says, "if God, Exalted, wills." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said this when the verse was revealed: ﴿When you forget﴾, meaning: when forgetting that has occurred from you, then you remember it, for as long as he is forgetful he is not commanded to remember, and it is a command to make up for it upon remembering, whether the interval is short or long. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others have related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he used to hold that the exception may be made even after a year, and he would recite the verse. This is also related from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may God be pleased with them, and it is a narration from Imam Ahmad, may God have mercy on him. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jubayr, concerning a man who swore and forgot to make an exception, that he said: "He has his exception (thunya) until a month." Ibn Abi Hatim related through the route of 'Amr ibn Dinar from 'Ata' that he said: "Whoever swears an oath, then the thunya is the milking of a she-camel." He said: Tawus used to say: "As long as he is in his gathering." Ibn Abi Hatim also related from Ibrahim that he said: "He makes the exception as long as he is in his speech." Most jurists hold that the exception must be connected in order to avoid violating the oath. Even if it were valid to separate it, and it did not affect rulings, especially up to the limit narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, because it is established that there is no acknowledgment, no divorce, and no manumission, and no truth or falsehood is known [in that case].

It is related that the news reached al-Mansur that Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, differed from Ibn 'Abbas on this issue, so he summoned him in order to rebuke him. Abu Hanifa said to him: "This returns to you: you take the pledge of allegiance by oaths. Would you be content that they leave from your presence and make an exception and then rebel against you?" So he approved of his speech.

Among the strange things related: a scholar from the Maghrib wanted to see the scholars of Baghdad and to verify the extent of their knowledge, so he set out to gather with them. He entered Baghdad through the Karkh Gate, and encountered two men walking in front of him, selling herbs (baql) in baskets on their heads. He heard one of them say to his companion: "O so-and-so, I am amazed at Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, how he permitted separating the exception and said that it has no effect on rulings. If the matter were as he says, God, Exalted, would have commanded His Prophet Ayyub, peace be upon him, to make an exception so that he would not violate his oath, for that is less burdensome than what He, glorified be He, guided him to by His statement, Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not violate your oath﴾; and there was no more than a year between his oath and his command with what he mentioned." That man returned to his city, content with what he had heard and seen. He was asked: "How did you find the scholars of Baghdad?" He said: "I saw one who sells herbs on his head in the streets of its people reach a level of knowledge by which he objects to Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. So what do you think of the people of the madrasas, dedicated to the service of knowledge and fairness?" This objection to a scholar so eminent is considered excessive from one who sells herbs. And God, Exalted, knows best the soundness of the transmission.

It may be said: The apparent meaning of the verse, as you have heard, agrees with what the rabbi (al-hibr, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) held. Otherwise, there would be no meaning to the making-up, and likewise what came in the report. For they said: The making-up regarding what relates to the commitment of the servant is achieved by mentioning it after awareness. But regarding the effect on the ruling so that it removes it from being definite, the verse was not sent for that, nor does it indicate it in any way.

Some said: This is among the special qualities of the Prophet (ﷺ), so for him, upon him be blessings and peace, it is permissible to make an exception even after a while, unlike others.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir related with a connected chain from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: "If you forget the exception, then make the exception when you remember." Then he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it is not for any of us to make an exception except in connection with an oath." It was also said: The verse and the report do not state that the exception which makes up for the preceding statement is from the speech itself, but from an implied element indicated by it. The implied meaning in the verse is: "Whenever you forget the remembrance of God, Exalted, remember Him at the time of remembrance, if God, Exalted, wills."

In the hadith: "I will not forget the exception (al-mashi'ah, saying 'if God wills') after today, and I will not leave it, if God Most High wills; or I say 'if God Most High wills' whenever I say that I will do something later." It is clearly contrary to the apparent meaning.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Remember your Lord with glorification (tasbih) and seeking forgiveness (istighfar) when you forget the exception." The purpose of this is to strongly urge the practice by implying that neglecting it is one of the sins for which repentance and seeking forgiveness are required. It has been said that the meaning is: "Remember your Lord and His punishment when you leave some of what He has commanded you, so that this prompts you to make up for it." Reading forgetting (nisyan) as leaving (tark) is a metaphor (majaz) based on the relation of cause and effect (ʿalaqah al-sababiyyah wa al-musabbabiyyah). Or it means: "Remember your Lord when forgetfulness overtakes you, so that what you have forgotten may remind you." On this reading, ﴿nasita﴾ ("you forget") is treated as intransitive. The connection of the verse with what precedes is clearly weak on these two meanings.

Qatadah understood the verse as referring to performing a forgotten prayer when one remembers it. If he meant that the verse means: "Make up the forgotten prayer when you remember it," then it is as you see, and the question of connection is as in the previous case. If he meant that it indicates the command to make up a forgotten prayer when it is remembered, because it indicates the command to mention the forgotten exception, and the command of prayer is more serious and its importance greater, then the command is easier. However, the apparent sense of their words is that he meant the first.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others transmitted from Ikrimah that he said about the verse: "That is, remember your Lord when you become angry." The reason for explaining forgetting as anger is that anger is a cause of forgetting. The matter of this statement is similar to what has passed.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾, that is, will grant me success (yuwaffiqani), ﴿to something nearer than this﴾, that is, to something nearer and more evident than the account of the People of the Cave, of the signs and proofs indicating my prophethood, ﴿to right guidance (rashadan)﴾, meaning guidance for people and a sign of that.

This is the view of al-Zajjaj. God the Mighty and Majestic has indeed done this, since He gave him clear signs greater than that and more manifest, such as the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, whose times were far apart, and the events that would occur in future ages until the Hour. It seems to be a belittling by God the Mighty and Majestic of the matter of the story of the People of the Cave, just as He belittled it at the beginning by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Or do you think...﴾ etc. This is connected to the whole story. Some eminent scholars connected it to the governing element in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾, as if it were said: "Remember when the youths took refuge in the cave etc., and say: 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is more evident than that, as a proof of my prophethood.'"

Al-Jubba'i said: it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse. The meaning according to him is: "Call upon your Lord, glorified and exalted is He, when you forget something, that He may remind you of it, and say: 'If He does not remind you, glorified is He, perhaps He will guide me to something nearer to the forgotten thing in goodness and benefit.'" Here ﴿this﴾ refers to the forgotten thing, rashad is goodness and benefit, and ﴿nearer﴾ is in its literal sense. It is not hidden that this is closer in terms of its connection, but further in other respects. It has also been said that it is connected to the preceding coordinated statements, and ﴿this﴾ refers to what they contain of good in command and prohibition, as if it were said: "Do this and do not do that, and hope from your Lord that He will guide you to something nearer, in what you have been directed to within what you have heard of command and prohibition, in goodness and benefit." The Prophet (ﷺ) was guided, within what was revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, after that, to commands and prohibitions that are nearer in benefit, and they cannot be counted. This is as you see, and perhaps with its faults it is closer than what was reported from al-Jubba'i.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is: "Perhaps my Lord will inform me of the answer to your questions before the time that I set for you, and will hasten for me right guidance from Him." This meaning is hardly derived from the verse, and even if it were derived, it would be like deriving the meanings intended from riddles, and the noble Book of God is exalted above that.

Al-Bayhaqi transmitted through the chain of al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman, who said: I heard my father narrate from a man from the people of Kufa that he used to say: "When a person forgets the exception, his repentance is that he should say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer than this in right guidance﴾." Abu Hayyan related it from Muhammad al-Kufi the exegete, and it seems that he is the man mentioned by al-Mu'tamir. This is an opinion for which there is no evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ as sleepers, their ears struck (so that they could not hear), ﴿for three hundred years and nine more﴾. This is a resumed clause (jumla mustaʾnafa) explaining what was left general in His words: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾. Mujahid said this, and more than one scholar chose it. Al-Taybi (in al-Kashf) said: According to this, His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ confirm that the period during which their ears were struck is this period, as if it were said: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," and He knows it, so it is the true and correct matter about which no doubt ever circles. The benefit of delaying the explanation is to alert that they also disputed about this, since it is mentioned right after their disagreement over the number of their persons; and so that the concluding phrase ﴿Say: Allah knows best﴾ parallels the concluding phrase of His words: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾; and to indicate that it is among the unseen matters that he, peace be upon him, was informed of, so that it would be a miracle for him. If it had been said: "So We struck upon their ears for a number of years," and the explanation had been given first, this indication would not be present at all. So these are several benefits, and the last is the principal one. End of quote.

On this view, it requires explaining why the expected wording was departed from, namely "three hundred and nine years," although that is shorter and clearer. It is said that it is an indication that they were three hundred by the reckoning of the People of the Book, using the solar year, and three hundred and nine by the reckoning of the Arabs, using the lunar year. So the nine is the measure of the difference. Some have transmitted this from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face.

It was objected that the indication of the wording to what has been mentioned is not evident, and that it does not agree with what calculation and the astrologers hold, as al-Imam (al-Razi) said: the solar year is three hundred and sixty-five days, five hours and forty-nine minutes according to the Ilkhanid observations, while the lunar year is three hundred and fifty-four days, eight hours and forty-eight minutes. The difference between them is ten days, twenty-one hours and one minute. If this is the difference of one year, the difference over three hundred years would be one hundred thousand, seven hundred and eighty-seven days, thirteen hours and four minutes, which is three years, twenty-four days, eleven hours and sixteen minutes. Thus the difference over three hundred years would be nine years, seventy-three days, nine hours and forty-eight minutes. For this reason it has been said that his transmission from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, is not established. Al-Khafaji examined this, arguing that the indication in it is clear, because the meaning is: they remained three hundred years by the reckoning of the People of the Book, who taught your people to ask about their condition, and nine more by the reckoning of your people, who asked you about that. The departure from the apparent wording suggests this. The claim that the difference of nine years is based on approximation, since the excess does not reach half a year, nor even one of its seasons, so it was not regarded, and that the difference being nine years by approximation follows all the other opinions about the measure of the solar and lunar years, since the difference in all of them barely reaches a quarter, let alone a half. Al-Taybi, in explaining the departure, said: It may be said that perhaps when they completed three hundred years they came close to waking, then something happened that caused them to remain asleep for nine years. It has been objected that this requires the meaning to be: "and they increased in sleep," i.e. their sleep grew stronger during nine years, and what is wrong with that is not hidden.

He also said: It is possible that the People of the Book disagreed about the duration of their stay, as they disagreed about their number, so His words ﴿And they remained﴾ etc. came to remove the disagreement and clarify the truth, and ﴿and they increased by nine﴾ serves as confirmation and as a removal of the possibility, similar to the exception in His words: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾, which will be explained, Allah willing. This is not without merit.

It was also said: They woke briefly and then were returned to their original state, so He mentioned the increase; and this is what is required by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And We turn them﴾ etc. This, in my view, is closer than what preceded about the solar and lunar years.

A group said: the clause is part of the speech of the People of the Book, so it is part of the saying ﴿They will say﴾ mentioned earlier, and what is between them is a parenthetical interjection. This is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: A man may explain the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between heaven and earth. Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾, the verse. Then he said: How long did the people remain? They said: Three hundred and nine years. He said: If they had remained so, Allah would not have said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾. Rather, He related the saying of the people, so He said: ﴿They will say, three,﴾ up to His words ﴿a guess at the unseen﴾. So He informed that they do not know. And he said: "They will say: they remained in their cave three hundred years and increased by nine." Perhaps this is not authentically reported from the Rabbi, may Allah be pleased with him; for it is authentically reported from him that the number of the People of the Cave was seven, and the eighth is their dog, though He followed that saying with His words: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾; and there is no difference between that and His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾. So why does the one indicate refutation while the other does not?

Indeed, Ibn Masʿud recited: "Qalu labithu kahfahum" (They said: they remained in their cave), and this requires that it be part of the speech of those disputing about their affair. However, the following of it with His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ is like the following of the third saying about the number with what you have heard, in not indicating refutation.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿and they increased﴾ on this view refers to the People of the Cave, just as it does on the preceding view. Al-Khafaji said: the pronoun on this view refers to the People of the Book, unlike the first view; and the reason for departing from "three hundred and nine years" appears in it, since some of them said: they remained three hundred, and some said it was nine more. End of quote. And what is wrong with that is not hidden.

On both views, the apparent reading is that ﴿how long they remained﴾ refers to the period previously mentioned. Some claimed that it refers to the period after their discovery until the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and that is, as you see, far-fetched. It was also said: When He said ﴿and they increased by nine﴾, the nine was undefined, not known whether it was years, months, days or hours, and the Children of Israel disagreed about it, so he, peace be upon him, was commanded to refer knowledge of the nine alone to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. End of quote. This is nothing; for when a specified number precedes and something unspecified is joined to it, its specification is taken to refer to what precedes. So: "I have a hundred dirhams and ten," is clearly "and ten dirhams," and is not ambiguous, as is not hidden.

Furthermore, ﴿nine﴾ is in the accusative as the object of (izdadu), which is transitive to one object. Abu al-Baqa said: zada is transitive to two objects, and when formed as iftaʿala it is transitive to one. The apparent statement of al-Raghib and others is that zada may be transitive to one object: one says "I increased him by such-and-such, so he increased, and he increased by such-and-such." The reason for this is clear, so do not be heedless.

The majority reading, with the tanwin on "mi'ati" (hundred), has "sinin" in the accusative. They differed about its analysis. Abu al-Baqa and Ibn al-Hajib said it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to "thalatha mi'a" (three hundred). Al-Zamakhshari said it is in the accusative as an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) to "thalath mi'a." Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr, objected that this is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans.

Some claimed that it is better than the apposition, because the apposition entails that the number is not intended; and this is supported by what Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years? So Allah revealed 'years'."

Ibn ʿAtiyya permitted both analyses. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This was objected to on the ground that it entails an irregularity from two aspects, and you will know its aspect shortly, Allah willing. It was also objected, citing what al-Zamakhshari transmitted in al-Mufassal from al-Zajjaj, that it would entail that they remained nine hundred years. Ibn al-Hajib said: its justification is that it is understood from their language that the specification of a hundred is a single one out of a hundred, as when you say "a hundred men": one man is one of the hundred. So if "years" were a specification, it would be one of three hundred, and the least number of years is three, so it would be as if it were said: "three hundred of three years," which makes nine hundred years. It is answered that what was mentioned applies only when the specification is singular. As for when it is plural, the intent in it is like the intent in the specification being plural in such as "three garments," although the original for all of them is the plural; and they only turned to the singular for a reason explained in its proper place. So when the specification is used in the plural, it is used according to the original. The objection would hold only if what is used in the plural were used as the singular is used; but when the plural is used in its original sense for what the number is applied to, it does not hold. End of quote. Al-Khafaji clearly stated that this is like the plural being opposed by the plural (taqabul al-jam' bi-l-jam'). Al-Zajjaj permitted "sinin" to be in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt) of "mi'a," and this in meaning refers back to the whole number, as in the verse of ʿAntara:

*Therein are forty-two milch camels, black like the feather of the glossy black crow,*

where "black" (sudan) is described as an adjective of "milch camels" (haluba), which in meaning is an adjective of the whole number. Abu ʿAli said: It is not impossible that the poet considered "haluba" a plural and made "sudan" a description of it; and when it is meant as a plural, it is not impossible that it serves as an explanation of this kind of number, since it is in the form of singulars, as one says "twenty men" and "thirty tribes."

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read "thalathi mi'ati sinin" with the mi'a construct-attached to sinin. What was transmitted from al-Zajjaj is objected to here as well, and the same answer given there applies. There is no reason to restrict the objection to the accusative of "sinin" as a specification, since the source of the implication, assuming it is granted, is that it is a specification; and this holds even if it is in the genitive, with the specification of the hundred being by annexation, one of the two well-known usages. The second is that it is singular; and because the singular is well known in usage, it is called the original, so it is the original in terms of usage. This does not conflict with Ibn al-Hajib's statement that the original for specification in general is the plural, as you heard just now; for he meant the original rejected analogically, considering that "mi'a" is a plural like three and four and the like, as stated in al-Kashf. Sometimes it departs from the well-known usage and comes singular in the accusative, as in his saying:

*When a youth lives two hundred years, pleasure and youth have surely gone.*

Sometimes it comes plural in the genitive by annexation, as in the verse according to the reading of al-Kisa'i, Hamza and those with them. But they say that the plural mentioned there has been treated as if it lacked the plural marker, because the marker in it is not purely for plurality, since it is like a substitute for the dropped lam of its singular, to the extent that some do not inflect it with the letters but treat it like hin (a period of time). I have not found in what I have of Arabic grammar books any evidence from Arab speech for the annexation of "mi'a" to a plural. Most grammarians cite the verse according to the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i as evidence for this, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is sufficient as evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 25–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ubayy read: "thalath mi'at sanatin" (three hundred years) with the idafa (construct) and the singular, as is the common usage; and likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Dahhak read: "thalatha mi'atin sunūna" with tanwin and the nominative on sunūn, taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., "they are sunūn (years)." Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of al-Lu'lu'i from him, read: "tis'an" with a fatha on the ta', and this is a dialectal form of it. So understand this, and God the Exalted knows best.

﴿His is the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, all that is hidden in them and concealed of the affairs of their inhabitants. Al-Ghayb is a verbal noun in the sense of the hidden thing, and "the hidden" (al-khafi) has been made its very essence for emphasis. The lam is for exclusive knowledge (al-ikhtisas al-'ilmi); i.e., to Him, exalted is He, belongs that knowledge. It necessarily follows from this that His knowledge of all created things is established, glorified is He; for whoever knows the hidden knows what is other than it by a fortiori reasoning.

﴿See Him and hear Him﴾: these are two forms of exclamation (ta'ajjub), and the pronoun "hi" refers to Him, exalted is He. The speech falls under the category of saying, so the exclamation is not from Him, glorified is He, such that it might be said: the intended meaning is not its literal sense, since that is impossible for Him, exalted is He. Rather, the intended meaning is that this is a great matter which is worthy of being marvelled at, as has been said. It is not impossible that the exclamation proceed literally from some of His attributes, glorified is He, and His acts, mighty and majestic is He, from other than Him, exalted is He.

And in a hadith: "How forbearing You are toward the one who disobeys You, how near You are to the one who calls upon You, and how compassionate You are toward the one who asks You."

They have a lengthy discussion on this question, so whoever wishes should return to it. Ibn Hisham also has a treatise on this. In any case, it contains an indication that the state of His sight and hearing, mighty and majestic is He—and they are two attributes not reducible to the attribute of knowledge—is beyond what the sight of seers and the hearing of hearers are characterized by. For the subtle and the dense, the small and the great, the manifest and the hidden, the secret and the public, are all alike in not being veiled from His sight and hearing, blessed and exalted is He. Indeed, some people have said that the non-existent and the existent are equal in this, and this is based on the thingness (shay'iyya) of the non-existent,

صفحة 255

and the disagreement on this is well known. Perhaps the reason for placing what indicates the greatness of His sight, mighty and majestic is He, first is that what we are concerned with belongs to the category of things seen. The original form is "abṣir wa-asmi'," and the hamza is for becoming (al-ṣayrūra), not for transitivity; i.e., "he became one possessing sight" and "he became one possessing hearing." This does not entail that they are not realized for Him, exalted is He far above that by a great elevation. In both there is a hidden pronoun referring to Him, glorified is He; then they were converted into the imperative form, and the subject pronoun was made explicit because the imperative form is not suited to bearing a third-person pronoun. It was made genitive by the superfluous ba', so it has two positions: genitive by virtue of the ba', and nominative by virtue of being the subject. Because it has become a complement in form, it is given the ruling of a complement, so its deletion from the second clause is permissible even though it is the subject, and the subject may not be deleted according to them. This ba' is hardly ever deleted in this position except when the thing marvelled at is an anna clause and its complement, such as: "aḥsin an taqūla" (How well it is that you say...). This verb, since it is past in meaning, is said to be built on an assumed fatha, which its appearance in the form of the imperative prevents from showing. This is the view of Sibawayh regarding this construction. Al-Radi said: this has been criticized on the grounds that the imperative with the meaning of the past is not something known; rather the past has come with the meaning of the imperative, as in the hadith: "Whoever does a good deed, let him fear God, and he will be rewarded for it."

And [it is criticized] on the grounds that "ṣāra dha kadhā" (he became one possessing such-and-such) is rare; and if what was mentioned were the case, it would be permissible to say "alḥim bi-Zayd" and "ashḥim bi-Zayd"; and on the grounds that the superfluous ba' with the subject is rare, while its use with the object is regular.

This has been answered: that the imperative's meaning of the past is not known is not conceded; do you not see that "kafā bihi" with the meaning of "iktafi bihi" (be content with him) is according to al-Zajjaj? He intended by this citation to show that it was intended for a performative meaning, namely marvelling, and that it was not intended from the past, because the performative is more fitting to the imperative form than to the past, since the past is mostly informative. And [it is answered] that the frequency of "af'ala" in the sense of "ṣāra dha kadhā" is not hidden from one who surveys the usage. The permissibility of "alḥim bi-Zayd" in the sense of marvelling is established and has no objection; and in another sense it is not established. Yes, what was mentioned about the rarity of the superfluous ba' with the subject is beyond dispute. The truth is that Sibawayh's view on this question is not free from artificiality.

The view of al-Akhfash, which al-Radi attributed to al-Farra', is that "af'il" in such constructions is an imperative both in form and meaning. So when you say "aḥsin bi-Zayd," you have commanded each one to make Zayd good, and the meaning of making him so is describing him with it; as if you said: describe him with beauty however you wish, for in him is every quality that can be in a person, as the poet said:

You have found the place of speech wide,
So if you find a tongue that speaks, then speak.

This meaning fits marvelling, unlike Sibawayh's reading. Also, the hamza of making (al-ja'l) is more common than the hamza of "ṣāra dha kadhā," though neither of them, as al-Radi said, is a consistently regular analogy. The subject is taken as the pronoun of the addressee, who is everyone, because the intended meaning is that, due to the manifestness of the matter, everyone is addressed without specification by the description mentioned. The verb "af'il" is not inflected on this view, so it is not attributed to a dual, plural or feminine, for the reason they mention: that the reason "fa'ala" for marvelling is not inflected is its resemblance to particles in being performative, and that each word of its words has become a proper name for one of the meanings. If there is a clause, the analogy is that it should not be inflected, as a precaution to secure comprehension, like proper names. Thus "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" are not inflected in proverbs. What made this easy here is that the meaning of the imperative has faded from it, just as the meaning of making has faded, and it has become purely the performance of marvelling, with no sense of address remaining in it. The ba' is superfluous with the object. Al-Zajjaj permitted that the hamza be for becoming, so that the ba' is for transitivity, i.e., "make him possessing beauty." Then he offered an excuse for "aḥsin" remaining in one form in all circumstances, because the address is to the verbal noun of the verb, i.e., "O beauty, be beautiful with Zayd." There is artificiality and awkwardness in this;

صفحة 256

moreover, we say "aḥsin bi-Zayd, O 'Amr," and two things are not addressed in one situation, unless one says that the meaning of addressing beauty has faded. The fruit of the disagreement between Sibawayh and others appears when the ba' must be deleted: on Sibawayh's view, its genitive complement must be made nominative; on the others' view, it must be made accusative.

Furthermore, Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "See by the religion of God the Exalted and hear by it"; i.e., he saw by the guidance of God the Exalted and heard by it; so the pronoun returns either to the guidance or to the glorious Name. This was transmitted from Ibn al-Anbari, but it is nothing.

Ibn 'Isa read: "abṣara bihi wa-asma'a," in the past form in both. Abu Hayyan explained this as meaning the informative and not the exclamatory, and the pronoun in the genitive refers to God the Exalted; i.e., He made His servants see by knowledge of Him, glorified is He, and made them hear. It is also permitted that "abṣar" be an elative form, and likewise "asma'," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state from the pronoun in "lahu" and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the unseen. The intended meaning is not the literal elative, but the greatness of the status of His sight and hearing, mighty and majestic is He. Perhaps this is closer than what Abu Hayyan mentioned. The resulting meaning on this reading is that He, glorious is His majesty, knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, seeing it and hearing it in the most perfect and greatest manner.

﴿What they have﴾: that is, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, indicated by mentioning them, ﴿besides Him﴾, exalted is He, ﴿of any guardian﴾, one who manages their affairs. ﴿And He does not make anyone a partner in His judgment﴾, in His decree, exalted is He, ﴿anyone whoever he may be﴾, and does not give him any part in it. It was said: the pronoun may refer to the People of the Cave; the idafa of "ḥukm" is to the known, in the sense: they have no one besides God, glorified is He, who manages their affair and protects them, and He does not make any of the creation a partner in His judgment which became manifest concerning them.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it refer to the contemporaries of the Messenger of God ﷺ among the unbelievers who opposed him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he took the verse as a parenthetical threat. It was said: it may refer to the meaning of the believers among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the intended meaning is that they will not take any guardian besides Him, exalted is He. It was said: it refers to those who differed concerning the duration of the sojourn of the People of the Cave; i.e., no one other than God, exalted is He, manages their affair, for they cannot have power without His empowerment, glorified is He, so how could they know without His informing, mighty and majestic is He? All of these, as you see. Then, it is not hidden from you that what is in the noble composition is more eloquent in negating a partner than saying "no guardian and no partner."

Mujahid read: "wa-lā yushrik" with the yā' of the third person and the jazm; Ya'qub said: I do not know the reason for this; some explained it as the sukun being for the intention of pause. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, Zayd, Humayd ibn al-Wazir from Ya'qub, al-Ja'fi, and al-Lu'lu'i from Abu Bakr read: "wa-lā tushrik" with the tā' of the third person and the jazm, on the ground that it is a prohibition to everyone against associating partners, not a prohibition directed at him, peace and blessings be upon him. Had it been directed at him, peace and blessings be upon him, it would be an allusion to someone else, like the saying: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour." So its ultimate import returns to that. It was also permitted that the address be to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and that it be conjoined to "lā taqūlanna" (do not say), and the meaning would be: do not ask anyone about what you do not know of the story of the People of the Cave and their sojourn, and be content with what comes to you about it of revelation; or: do not ask anyone about what God the Exalted has informed you of the report of the duration of their sojourn, and be content with His explanation, glorified is He. The great deviation from the apparent sense in this is not hidden, though it is more suitable to His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ as sleepers, their ears struck (so that they could not hear), ﴿for three hundred years and nine more﴾. This is a resumed clause (jumla mustaʾnafa) explaining what was left general in His words: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾. Mujahid said this, and more than one scholar chose it. Al-Taybi (in al-Kashf) said: According to this, His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ confirm that the period during which their ears were struck is this period, as if it were said: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," and He knows it, so it is the true and correct matter about which no doubt ever circles. The benefit of delaying the explanation is to alert that they also disputed about this, since it is mentioned right after their disagreement over the number of their persons; and so that the concluding phrase ﴿Say: Allah knows best﴾ parallels the concluding phrase of His words: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾; and to indicate that it is among the unseen matters that he, peace be upon him, was informed of, so that it would be a miracle for him. If it had been said: "So We struck upon their ears for a number of years," and the explanation had been given first, this indication would not be present at all. So these are several benefits, and the last is the principal one. End of quote.

On this view, it requires explaining why the expected wording was departed from, namely "three hundred and nine years," although that is shorter and clearer. It is said that it is an indication that they were three hundred by the reckoning of the People of the Book, using the solar year, and three hundred and nine by the reckoning of the Arabs, using the lunar year. So the nine is the measure of the difference. Some have transmitted this from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face.

It was objected that the indication of the wording to what has been mentioned is not evident, and that it does not agree with what calculation and the astrologers hold, as al-Imam (al-Razi) said: the solar year is three hundred and sixty-five days, five hours and forty-nine minutes according to the Ilkhanid observations, while the lunar year is three hundred and fifty-four days, eight hours and forty-eight minutes. The difference between them is ten days, twenty-one hours and one minute. If this is the difference of one year, the difference over three hundred years would be one hundred thousand, seven hundred and eighty-seven days, thirteen hours and four minutes, which is three years, twenty-four days, eleven hours and sixteen minutes. Thus the difference over three hundred years would be nine years, seventy-three days, nine hours and forty-eight minutes. For this reason it has been said that his transmission from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, is not established. Al-Khafaji examined this, arguing that the indication in it is clear, because the meaning is: they remained three hundred years by the reckoning of the People of the Book, who taught your people to ask about their condition, and nine more by the reckoning of your people, who asked you about that. The departure from the apparent wording suggests this. The claim that the difference of nine years is based on approximation, since the excess does not reach half a year, nor even one of its seasons, so it was not regarded, and that the difference being nine years by approximation follows all the other opinions about the measure of the solar and lunar years, since the difference in all of them barely reaches a quarter, let alone a half. Al-Taybi, in explaining the departure, said: It may be said that perhaps when they completed three hundred years they came close to waking, then something happened that caused them to remain asleep for nine years. It has been objected that this requires the meaning to be: "and they increased in sleep," i.e. their sleep grew stronger during nine years, and what is wrong with that is not hidden.

He also said: It is possible that the People of the Book disagreed about the duration of their stay, as they disagreed about their number, so His words ﴿And they remained﴾ etc. came to remove the disagreement and clarify the truth, and ﴿and they increased by nine﴾ serves as confirmation and as a removal of the possibility, similar to the exception in His words: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾, which will be explained, Allah willing. This is not without merit.

It was also said: They woke briefly and then were returned to their original state, so He mentioned the increase; and this is what is required by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And We turn them﴾ etc. This, in my view, is closer than what preceded about the solar and lunar years.

A group said: the clause is part of the speech of the People of the Book, so it is part of the saying ﴿They will say﴾ mentioned earlier, and what is between them is a parenthetical interjection. This is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: A man may explain the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between heaven and earth. Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾, the verse. Then he said: How long did the people remain? They said: Three hundred and nine years. He said: If they had remained so, Allah would not have said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾. Rather, He related the saying of the people, so He said: ﴿They will say, three,﴾ up to His words ﴿a guess at the unseen﴾. So He informed that they do not know. And he said: "They will say: they remained in their cave three hundred years and increased by nine." Perhaps this is not authentically reported from the Rabbi, may Allah be pleased with him; for it is authentically reported from him that the number of the People of the Cave was seven, and the eighth is their dog, though He followed that saying with His words: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾; and there is no difference between that and His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾. So why does the one indicate refutation while the other does not?

Indeed, Ibn Masʿud recited: "Qalu labithu kahfahum" (They said: they remained in their cave), and this requires that it be part of the speech of those disputing about their affair. However, the following of it with His words ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾ is like the following of the third saying about the number with what you have heard, in not indicating refutation.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿and they increased﴾ on this view refers to the People of the Cave, just as it does on the preceding view. Al-Khafaji said: the pronoun on this view refers to the People of the Book, unlike the first view; and the reason for departing from "three hundred and nine years" appears in it, since some of them said: they remained three hundred, and some said it was nine more. End of quote. And what is wrong with that is not hidden.

On both views, the apparent reading is that ﴿how long they remained﴾ refers to the period previously mentioned. Some claimed that it refers to the period after their discovery until the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and that is, as you see, far-fetched. It was also said: When He said ﴿and they increased by nine﴾, the nine was undefined, not known whether it was years, months, days or hours, and the Children of Israel disagreed about it, so he, peace be upon him, was commanded to refer knowledge of the nine alone to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. End of quote. This is nothing; for when a specified number precedes and something unspecified is joined to it, its specification is taken to refer to what precedes. So: "I have a hundred dirhams and ten," is clearly "and ten dirhams," and is not ambiguous, as is not hidden.

Furthermore, ﴿nine﴾ is in the accusative as the object of (izdadu), which is transitive to one object. Abu al-Baqa said: zada is transitive to two objects, and when formed as iftaʿala it is transitive to one. The apparent statement of al-Raghib and others is that zada may be transitive to one object: one says "I increased him by such-and-such, so he increased, and he increased by such-and-such." The reason for this is clear, so do not be heedless.

The majority reading, with the tanwin on "mi'ati" (hundred), has "sinin" in the accusative. They differed about its analysis. Abu al-Baqa and Ibn al-Hajib said it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to "thalatha mi'a" (three hundred). Al-Zamakhshari said it is in the accusative as an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) to "thalath mi'a." Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr, objected that this is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans.

Some claimed that it is better than the apposition, because the apposition entails that the number is not intended; and this is supported by what Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years? So Allah revealed 'years'."

Ibn ʿAtiyya permitted both analyses. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This was objected to on the ground that it entails an irregularity from two aspects, and you will know its aspect shortly, Allah willing. It was also objected, citing what al-Zamakhshari transmitted in al-Mufassal from al-Zajjaj, that it would entail that they remained nine hundred years. Ibn al-Hajib said: its justification is that it is understood from their language that the specification of a hundred is a single one out of a hundred, as when you say "a hundred men": one man is one of the hundred. So if "years" were a specification, it would be one of three hundred, and the least number of years is three, so it would be as if it were said: "three hundred of three years," which makes nine hundred years. It is answered that what was mentioned applies only when the specification is singular. As for when it is plural, the intent in it is like the intent in the specification being plural in such as "three garments," although the original for all of them is the plural; and they only turned to the singular for a reason explained in its proper place. So when the specification is used in the plural, it is used according to the original. The objection would hold only if what is used in the plural were used as the singular is used; but when the plural is used in its original sense for what the number is applied to, it does not hold. End of quote. Al-Khafaji clearly stated that this is like the plural being opposed by the plural (taqabul al-jam' bi-l-jam'). Al-Zajjaj permitted "sinin" to be in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt) of "mi'a," and this in meaning refers back to the whole number, as in the verse of ʿAntara:

*Therein are forty-two milch camels, black like the feather of the glossy black crow,*

where "black" (sudan) is described as an adjective of "milch camels" (haluba), which in meaning is an adjective of the whole number. Abu ʿAli said: It is not impossible that the poet considered "haluba" a plural and made "sudan" a description of it; and when it is meant as a plural, it is not impossible that it serves as an explanation of this kind of number, since it is in the form of singulars, as one says "twenty men" and "thirty tribes."

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read "thalathi mi'ati sinin" with the mi'a construct-attached to sinin. What was transmitted from al-Zajjaj is objected to here as well, and the same answer given there applies. There is no reason to restrict the objection to the accusative of "sinin" as a specification, since the source of the implication, assuming it is granted, is that it is a specification; and this holds even if it is in the genitive, with the specification of the hundred being by annexation, one of the two well-known usages. The second is that it is singular; and because the singular is well known in usage, it is called the original, so it is the original in terms of usage. This does not conflict with Ibn al-Hajib's statement that the original for specification in general is the plural, as you heard just now; for he meant the original rejected analogically, considering that "mi'a" is a plural like three and four and the like, as stated in al-Kashf. Sometimes it departs from the well-known usage and comes singular in the accusative, as in his saying:

*When a youth lives two hundred years, pleasure and youth have surely gone.*

Sometimes it comes plural in the genitive by annexation, as in the verse according to the reading of al-Kisa'i, Hamza and those with them. But they say that the plural mentioned there has been treated as if it lacked the plural marker, because the marker in it is not purely for plurality, since it is like a substitute for the dropped lam of its singular, to the extent that some do not inflect it with the letters but treat it like hin (a period of time). I have not found in what I have of Arabic grammar books any evidence from Arab speech for the annexation of "mi'a" to a plural. Most grammarians cite the verse according to the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i as evidence for this, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is sufficient as evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 25–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ubayy read: "thalath mi'at sanatin" (three hundred years) with the idafa (construct) and the singular, as is the common usage; and likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Dahhak read: "thalatha mi'atin sunūna" with tanwin and the nominative on sunūn, taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., "they are sunūn (years)." Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of al-Lu'lu'i from him, read: "tis'an" with a fatha on the ta', and this is a dialectal form of it. So understand this, and God the Exalted knows best.

﴿His is the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, all that is hidden in them and concealed of the affairs of their inhabitants. Al-Ghayb is a verbal noun in the sense of the hidden thing, and "the hidden" (al-khafi) has been made its very essence for emphasis. The lam is for exclusive knowledge (al-ikhtisas al-'ilmi); i.e., to Him, exalted is He, belongs that knowledge. It necessarily follows from this that His knowledge of all created things is established, glorified is He; for whoever knows the hidden knows what is other than it by a fortiori reasoning.

﴿See Him and hear Him﴾: these are two forms of exclamation (ta'ajjub), and the pronoun "hi" refers to Him, exalted is He. The speech falls under the category of saying, so the exclamation is not from Him, glorified is He, such that it might be said: the intended meaning is not its literal sense, since that is impossible for Him, exalted is He. Rather, the intended meaning is that this is a great matter which is worthy of being marvelled at, as has been said. It is not impossible that the exclamation proceed literally from some of His attributes, glorified is He, and His acts, mighty and majestic is He, from other than Him, exalted is He.

And in a hadith: "How forbearing You are toward the one who disobeys You, how near You are to the one who calls upon You, and how compassionate You are toward the one who asks You."
