They have a lengthy discussion on this question, so whoever wishes should return to it. Ibn Hisham also has a treatise on this. In any case, it contains an indication that the state of His sight and hearing, mighty and majestic is He—and they are two attributes not reducible to the attribute of knowledge—is beyond what the sight of seers and the hearing of hearers are characterized by. For the subtle and the dense, the small and the great, the manifest and the hidden, the secret and the public, are all alike in not being veiled from His sight and hearing, blessed and exalted is He. Indeed, some people have said that the non-existent and the existent are equal in this, and this is based on the thingness (shay'iyya) of the non-existent,

صفحة 255

and the disagreement on this is well known. Perhaps the reason for placing what indicates the greatness of His sight, mighty and majestic is He, first is that what we are concerned with belongs to the category of things seen. The original form is "abṣir wa-asmi'," and the hamza is for becoming (al-ṣayrūra), not for transitivity; i.e., "he became one possessing sight" and "he became one possessing hearing." This does not entail that they are not realized for Him, exalted is He far above that by a great elevation. In both there is a hidden pronoun referring to Him, glorified is He; then they were converted into the imperative form, and the subject pronoun was made explicit because the imperative form is not suited to bearing a third-person pronoun. It was made genitive by the superfluous ba', so it has two positions: genitive by virtue of the ba', and nominative by virtue of being the subject. Because it has become a complement in form, it is given the ruling of a complement, so its deletion from the second clause is permissible even though it is the subject, and the subject may not be deleted according to them. This ba' is hardly ever deleted in this position except when the thing marvelled at is an anna clause and its complement, such as: "aḥsin an taqūla" (How well it is that you say...). This verb, since it is past in meaning, is said to be built on an assumed fatha, which its appearance in the form of the imperative prevents from showing. This is the view of Sibawayh regarding this construction. Al-Radi said: this has been criticized on the grounds that the imperative with the meaning of the past is not something known; rather the past has come with the meaning of the imperative, as in the hadith: "Whoever does a good deed, let him fear God, and he will be rewarded for it."

And [it is criticized] on the grounds that "ṣāra dha kadhā" (he became one possessing such-and-such) is rare; and if what was mentioned were the case, it would be permissible to say "alḥim bi-Zayd" and "ashḥim bi-Zayd"; and on the grounds that the superfluous ba' with the subject is rare, while its use with the object is regular.

This has been answered: that the imperative's meaning of the past is not known is not conceded; do you not see that "kafā bihi" with the meaning of "iktafi bihi" (be content with him) is according to al-Zajjaj? He intended by this citation to show that it was intended for a performative meaning, namely marvelling, and that it was not intended from the past, because the performative is more fitting to the imperative form than to the past, since the past is mostly informative. And [it is answered] that the frequency of "af'ala" in the sense of "ṣāra dha kadhā" is not hidden from one who surveys the usage. The permissibility of "alḥim bi-Zayd" in the sense of marvelling is established and has no objection; and in another sense it is not established. Yes, what was mentioned about the rarity of the superfluous ba' with the subject is beyond dispute. The truth is that Sibawayh's view on this question is not free from artificiality.

The view of al-Akhfash, which al-Radi attributed to al-Farra', is that "af'il" in such constructions is an imperative both in form and meaning. So when you say "aḥsin bi-Zayd," you have commanded each one to make Zayd good, and the meaning of making him so is describing him with it; as if you said: describe him with beauty however you wish, for in him is every quality that can be in a person, as the poet said:

You have found the place of speech wide,
So if you find a tongue that speaks, then speak.

This meaning fits marvelling, unlike Sibawayh's reading. Also, the hamza of making (al-ja'l) is more common than the hamza of "ṣāra dha kadhā," though neither of them, as al-Radi said, is a consistently regular analogy. The subject is taken as the pronoun of the addressee, who is everyone, because the intended meaning is that, due to the manifestness of the matter, everyone is addressed without specification by the description mentioned. The verb "af'il" is not inflected on this view, so it is not attributed to a dual, plural or feminine, for the reason they mention: that the reason "fa'ala" for marvelling is not inflected is its resemblance to particles in being performative, and that each word of its words has become a proper name for one of the meanings. If there is a clause, the analogy is that it should not be inflected, as a precaution to secure comprehension, like proper names. Thus "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" are not inflected in proverbs. What made this easy here is that the meaning of the imperative has faded from it, just as the meaning of making has faded, and it has become purely the performance of marvelling, with no sense of address remaining in it. The ba' is superfluous with the object. Al-Zajjaj permitted that the hamza be for becoming, so that the ba' is for transitivity, i.e., "make him possessing beauty." Then he offered an excuse for "aḥsin" remaining in one form in all circumstances, because the address is to the verbal noun of the verb, i.e., "O beauty, be beautiful with Zayd." There is artificiality and awkwardness in this;

صفحة 256

moreover, we say "aḥsin bi-Zayd, O 'Amr," and two things are not addressed in one situation, unless one says that the meaning of addressing beauty has faded. The fruit of the disagreement between Sibawayh and others appears when the ba' must be deleted: on Sibawayh's view, its genitive complement must be made nominative; on the others' view, it must be made accusative.

Furthermore, Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "See by the religion of God the Exalted and hear by it"; i.e., he saw by the guidance of God the Exalted and heard by it; so the pronoun returns either to the guidance or to the glorious Name. This was transmitted from Ibn al-Anbari, but it is nothing.

Ibn 'Isa read: "abṣara bihi wa-asma'a," in the past form in both. Abu Hayyan explained this as meaning the informative and not the exclamatory, and the pronoun in the genitive refers to God the Exalted; i.e., He made His servants see by knowledge of Him, glorified is He, and made them hear. It is also permitted that "abṣar" be an elative form, and likewise "asma'," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state from the pronoun in "lahu" and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the unseen. The intended meaning is not the literal elative, but the greatness of the status of His sight and hearing, mighty and majestic is He. Perhaps this is closer than what Abu Hayyan mentioned. The resulting meaning on this reading is that He, glorious is His majesty, knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, seeing it and hearing it in the most perfect and greatest manner.

﴿What they have﴾: that is, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, indicated by mentioning them, ﴿besides Him﴾, exalted is He, ﴿of any guardian﴾, one who manages their affairs. ﴿And He does not make anyone a partner in His judgment﴾, in His decree, exalted is He, ﴿anyone whoever he may be﴾, and does not give him any part in it. It was said: the pronoun may refer to the People of the Cave; the idafa of "ḥukm" is to the known, in the sense: they have no one besides God, glorified is He, who manages their affair and protects them, and He does not make any of the creation a partner in His judgment which became manifest concerning them.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it refer to the contemporaries of the Messenger of God ﷺ among the unbelievers who opposed him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he took the verse as a parenthetical threat. It was said: it may refer to the meaning of the believers among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and the intended meaning is that they will not take any guardian besides Him, exalted is He. It was said: it refers to those who differed concerning the duration of the sojourn of the People of the Cave; i.e., no one other than God, exalted is He, manages their affair, for they cannot have power without His empowerment, glorified is He, so how could they know without His informing, mighty and majestic is He? All of these, as you see. Then, it is not hidden from you that what is in the noble composition is more eloquent in negating a partner than saying "no guardian and no partner."

Mujahid read: "wa-lā yushrik" with the yā' of the third person and the jazm; Ya'qub said: I do not know the reason for this; some explained it as the sukun being for the intention of pause. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, Zayd, Humayd ibn al-Wazir from Ya'qub, al-Ja'fi, and al-Lu'lu'i from Abu Bakr read: "wa-lā tushrik" with the tā' of the third person and the jazm, on the ground that it is a prohibition to everyone against associating partners, not a prohibition directed at him, peace and blessings be upon him. Had it been directed at him, peace and blessings be upon him, it would be an allusion to someone else, like the saying: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour." So its ultimate import returns to that. It was also permitted that the address be to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and that it be conjoined to "lā taqūlanna" (do not say), and the meaning would be: do not ask anyone about what you do not know of the story of the People of the Cave and their sojourn, and be content with what comes to you about it of revelation; or: do not ask anyone about what God the Exalted has informed you of the report of the duration of their sojourn, and be content with His explanation, glorified is He. The great deviation from the apparent sense in this is not hidden, though it is more suitable to His saying, exalted is He:

[p. 257]

The connection, according to the well-known reading and as explained earlier in its interpretation, is that when Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the story of the People of the Cave, which was among the unseen matters for the Prophet ﷺ, and the Qur'an's inclusion of it indicated that it is a miraculous revelation from the aspect of its inclusion of such matters, although the aspects of its miraculousness are not limited to this, He commanded him, may His majesty be exalted, to be constant in studying it, by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you from the Book of your Lord﴾, etc. This is a command from recitation (tilawa), meaning reading (qira'a). That is: keep reciting it to your companions, or in general, and do not be concerned with the words of one who says to you: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." It is also permissible that ﴿recite﴾ is a command from al-tulu, meaning following: that is, follow what has been revealed to you and persist in acting upon it. It has also been said that the connection is that when He, glory be to Him, forbade him from disputing about it in depth and from seeking rulings (istiftaa'), He commanded him to recite what has been revealed to him about their matter. It is as if it were said: Recite what has been revealed to you about their matter, be content with it, and do not go beyond that. Or: follow that and act upon it, do not go deep into their argument, and do not seek a ruling from any of them. So the speech is connected to the prohibitions mentioned earlier. What is meant by ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾ is the verses containing the explanation of the story of the People of the Cave. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they remained﴾, meaning: say that to them, and recite to them His report about the length of their stay. So what is meant by ﴿what has been revealed﴾ is what contains this report. But this is far inferior to what came before, rather one should not even turn to it. The reliable view is that what is meant by ﴿what has been revealed﴾ is something more general than what contains the story and other parts of His Book, exalted is He.

﴿There is none who can change His words﴾: no one other than Him can change or alter them. As for Him, glory be to Him, His power encompasses everything; He erases what He wills and confirms. From what has been mentioned, it becomes clear that the objection is refuted which says: "Substitution (tabdil) occurs, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We substitute a verse﴾." The apparent meaning is the generality of the words, which includes reports and other things. For this reason al-Tabarsi said: The meaning is: there is no changer of what He has reported, nor of what He has commanded, and the speech involves the omission of a modifier, meaning: there is no changer of the ruling of His words, end of quote. But you know that a report does not accept substitution, that is abrogation (naskh), so the will does not relate to it in such a way that power would relate to it, lest it lead to lying, which is impossible for Him, exalted is His majesty. Some have restricted the "words" to reports, because the context is about reporting the story of the People of the Cave, and according to this view there is no need to specify the indefinite negated noun, given what you have heard about the state of reports. As for the Imam's statement that abrogation in reality is not substitution, because the abrogated ruling remains in force until the time the abrogating ruling arrives, so the abrogating ruling is like something different, and how can it be substitution: this is an illusion that is not to be followed.

Some people restricted the "words" to His promises, exalted is He, to His monotheist servants. It is as if it were said: Recite what has been revealed to you and do not care about the obstinate disbelievers, for it has included the promise to the monotheists what it has included, and there is no changer of that promise. Its outcome is: recite and do not care, for Allah, exalted is He, is your helper and the helper of your companions. But this, as you see, although it is more fitting with what follows. The pronoun, as appears from Majma' al-Bayan, refers to the Book. It is also permissible that it refers to the Lord, exalted is He, as is apparent in the pronoun in His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿And you will not find any refuge besides Him﴾: that is, a refuge to which you turn when some affliction befalls. The Imam in al-Bayan wa al-Irshad said: its origin is from iltihad, meaning inclination. Al-Raghib permitted that it be a noun of place and also a verbal noun. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained it here as "an entrance into the earth." He recited, when Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him, the verse of Khasib al-Damri:

"Alas for my soul, and alas that is no use to me, and there is no refuge from the decree of Allah."

There is no need to explain it as "an entrance into the earth" in order to take refuge in it. Then, if the meaning of the address is the master of the addressed, ﷺ, the speech is based on supposition, and the estimate is: though he, upon him be prayer and peace, was [so exalted], rather he purified his community so that their souls would not whisper to them to seek any refuge other than Allah, exalted is He. We ask Him, glory be to Him, to make us among those who take refuge in Him and rely upon Him in all their affairs. Then He, may His majesty be exalted, sufficed him in what concerned him and removed from him the darkness of every distress.

* * *

[p. 258]

This is "from the path of allusion in the verses." ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book﴾. It has already been mentioned that the station of servanthood has no station like it and none close to it, and our Prophet ﷺ is at its highest levels. It has been mentioned that the true servant is one who is free from both worlds, and none is that but their master ﷺ.

﴿And has not made in it any deviance﴾, ﴿but made it straight﴾. It has been stated in the interpretation earlier that the pronoun in the genitive refers to the Book. Some interpreters made it refer to ﴿His servant﴾, meaning: He did not make in him, upon him be prayer and peace, any deviation from His presence or inclination toward anything else, and made him upright in His servanthood, glory be to Him. The command in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ is a command of creation (takwin). ﴿To warn of severe punishment from Him﴾, which is the punishment of veiling and distance from the Presence, and that is the greatest torment. ﴿No! Indeed they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord.﴾ ﴿And to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾, which are the deeds done seeking the Face of Allah, exalted is He, and nothing else. It has been said: righteous deed is disengagement from existence through the existence of the Truth. ﴿That for them is a good reward﴾, which is the vision of the Master and witnessing the Truth without veil. ﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself through grief over them if they do not believe in this statement﴾: in it is an allusion to the abundance of his compassion, upon him be prayer and peace, his concern, and his eagerness for the agreement of opponents and their inclusion in the thread of those who agree. ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth﴾, of rivers, trees, mountains, minerals, and animals, ﴿adornment for it﴾, that is, for its people, ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾ So He makes that a mirror for witnessing the lights of His majesty and beauty, glory be to Him, may He be exalted and glorified. Ibn 'Ata' said: the goodness of the deed is turning away from all of it. Al-Junayd said: the goodness of the deed is taking that as a lesson and not being occupied with it. Some of them said: the people of knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and of love for Him are the adornment of the earth, and the goodness of the deed is to look at them with reverence.

﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren wasteland﴾: a metaphor for the manifestation of its annihilation through the manifestation of the true existence and the Great Resurrection. ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a wonder?﴾ Al-Junayd, may Allah sanctify his secret, said: That is, do not marvel at them, for your condition is more marvelous than their condition, in that He took you by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, and brought you to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and you were in nearness as two bow-lengths or closer, then He returned you before the end of the night to your resting place.

﴿When the youths retreated to the cave﴾. It was said: they are the youths of knowledge who were created with the disposition of chivalry, and their chivalry is turning away from other than Allah, exalted is He, so they retreated to the cave of seclusion with Him, glory be to Him. ﴿And said﴾ when they were firm in the stations of intimacy and the witnessing of holiness, and what they tasted stirred them to seek more and to ascend the levels of happiness: ﴿Our Lord, give us from Yourself mercy﴾: complete knowledge and noble monotheism. ﴿And prepare for us from our affair right guidance﴾: by arriving at You and annihilation in You. ﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾: an allusion to their being absorbed in Him, glory be to Him, annihilated in Him, exalted is He, from all else. ﴿Then We awakened them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing what they remained in terms of time.﴾ It is an allusion to their return to sobriety after intoxication and remaining after annihilation. It is also said: it is an allusion to the unveiling after seclusion, and these two statements are close in meaning. ﴿We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord﴾, with scientific faith, ﴿and We increased them in guidance﴾ by bringing them into presence and unveiling for them. ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾: We steadied them against wavering by what We placed in them of certainty, so no suspicious conjectures or satanic whispers arose in them. It is also said: We raised them from the low ground of fluctuation to the height of establishment.

﴿When they stood up﴾, by Us, for Us, ﴿and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, the Owner of their affair and its Manager, so there is no standing for them except by His existence, which overflows from the seas of His generosity. ﴿We will never invoke besides Him any deity﴾, since there is nothing that is not in need of Him, glory be to Him, so none is fit to be invoked. ﴿For we would have then spoken an excessive transgression﴾: a statement far from the truth, extremely unjust. Some shaykhs used this verse as evidence that the seekers, when they wish to remember Allah and gather in a circle for it, should stand and remember while standing. Ibn al-Ghars said: this is weak evidence that does not support the claimant.

[p. 259]

Yet you know that there is no harm in standing and remembering, but according to what the self-styled shaykhs do today, for that never occurred in any nation and did not come in the Sharia of our Prophet ﷺ. Rather, by my life, those circles are the snares of Satan, and that standing is sitting in the midst of abandonment.

﴿And when you have removed yourselves from them and what they worship except Allah﴾: that is, when you left the company of the people of desire and turned away from the sound path, ﴿then retreat to the cave﴾: be alone with your Beloved, ﴿and your Lord will spread for you of His mercy﴾: the folded knowledge of Him, ﴿and will prepare for you of your affair a provision﴾: what you benefit from of the lights of His manifestations and the subtleties of His witnessings. Some of the knowers said: separation from other than Allah, exalted is He, necessitates union with Allah, mighty and majestic. Indeed union is not attained except after separation. Do you not see how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to withdraw to the cave of Hira' until revelation came to him while he was in it?

﴿And you would see the sun when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left, while they are in a wide space within it.﴾ So that the light does not abound in the cave and thereby presence diminish. They have mentioned that darkness aids thought and the gathering of the senses. From here you see the people of seclusion choose for their seclusion a place of little light, and yet they close their eyes during contemplation.

In the Secrets of the Qur'an: the verse contains an allusion that Allah, exalted is He, preserved them from being burned by the veils of splendor. So He made the sun of majesty incline away from the cave of their nearness, to the right of eternity and the left of perpetuity, while they were in the wide space of union with the vision of beauty and majesty, guarded and protected from the overpowering authority of the pure Eternal Essence, in whose first dawning of radiance the cosmos vanish.

In a hadith: "His veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His face would burn everything his sight reaches."

It has also been said in its interpretation: when the sun of the spirit or of knowledge and sainthood rises from the horizon of guidance and shines in the sky of spiritual visitations, which is the state of intoxication and the overpowering of ecstasy, it does not turn, during their seclusion, toward any matter related to the afterlife, which is the side of the right. And when it sets, that is, when that overpowering ends and the state of sobriety appears, the aspirations of their spirits do not turn to any matter related to the world, which is the side of the left. Rather they turn aside from both directions toward the Master, and they are in a space free of whatever would occupy them from Allah, exalted is He.

It has been mentioned that it contains an allusion that the light of their guardianship overcomes the light of the sun and turns it back from the cave, just as the light of the believer overcomes the fire of Hell. This is not something to be relied upon, although it has been narrated from Ibn 'Ata'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Whom Allah guides is the one truly guided﴾. This refers to the one from whom the veils have been lifted, so he succeeds in what he succeeds in. ﴿And whom He leaves astray, you will never find for him a protecting guardian who leads to the right way.﴾ This is because He, glory be to Him, abandons no one except on account of the badness of his receptivity (isti'dad), and when receptivity is absent, guidance becomes impossible. ﴿You would think them awake, while they are asleep.﴾ This is an indication that they are with the creation in their bodies and with the Truth in their spirits. Ibn 'Ata' said: They abide in the Presence (al-hadrah) like sleepers, with no knowledge of time or place, living yet dead, stricken yet conscious, asleep yet alert. ﴿And We turned them to the right and to the left.﴾ That is, We move them from one world to another. Ibn 'Ata' said: We turn them between the states of contraction (qabd) and expansion (bast), and between union (jam') and separation (farq). Another said: We turn them between annihilation (fana') and subsistence (baqa'), unveiling (kashf) and veiling (ihtijab), manifestation (tajalli) and concealment (istitar). It has also been said that the verse indicates that in surrender they are like the dead in the hands of the washer. ﴿And their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold.﴾ Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Sitting with the righteous and living near them is a gain, even if the species differs. Do you not see how Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the dog of the People of the Cave alongside them because of its proximity to them?

It has also been said that the verse indicates that the dog represents their souls (nufus), which are asleep and idle from actions. It has also been said that it is possible to mean that their souls have reached a state in which they obey them in all conditions and guard them from what would harm them. ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾, that is, if you had looked from your place upon what I have clothed them with of the garment of the subjugation of My lordship and the assaults of My majesty, ﴿you would have turned from them in flight﴾, that is, from seeing what is upon them of My awe and My majesty, ﴿and been filled with terror of them.﴾

(Page 260)

Just as Moses, My interlocutor, fled from the sight of his staff when I turned it into a serpent and clothed it in a garment of My majesty and awe. This flight is real on Our part, because it arises from Our manifest greatness in that mirror. So has more than one scholar established it, and it is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And thus We awakened them﴾, that is, We returned them to sobriety after intoxication, ﴿so they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ This is because they had been wholly absorbed, not knowing today from yesterday, nor distinguishing the moon from the sun. It has also been said that they considered the days of union few, and such is the condition of the lovers of beauty. The year of union is a year in their reckoning, and the year of separation is a year. It is said: The station of the lover with the Beloved, however long, is short, and the time of gathering, however great, is brief, for one is never satisfied from the Beloved, even if time is spent and passes. The lover hardly counts the nights when he is content with union, as it has been said:

*I count the nights, one night after another,
though I have lived a lifetime without counting nights.*

Then, when they returned from intoxication to sobriety and from spirituality to humanity, they sought what sustains human life and made use of the realities of the path (haqa'iq al-tariqah). This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him look for which is the purest food and bring you provision from it, and let him be discreet.﴾ The indication in this is, first, that what is fitting for the seekers of Allah, exalted is He, is to abandon asking, and this refutes those who pretend to be shaykhs whose religion and habit is asking, would that it were from what is lawful. Second, that what is fitting for them is that none of them singles out anything for himself to the exclusion of his companion. Do you not see how their speaker said, "with this silver of yours," attributing the silver to them collectively? It is related that among them was a shepherd, and perhaps he had no silver. Third, that what is fitting for them is the practice of scrupulousness (wara'). Do you not see how the speaker sought the purest, while according to some narrations it was the most lawful? For this reason Dhu al-Nun said: The gnostic is one whose light of knowledge does not extinguish the light of his scrupulousness. And it is astonishing that a man among the pretenders to shaykhhood used to take dinars from some oppressors, which were certainly unlawful. When he was asked about this, he said: Yes, they are embers, but they quench the heat of the hunger of the wayfarers. Despite this and similar things, he has today a shrine that is circumambulated by visitors, lamps are lit upon it, and vows are made to him. Fourth, that they should counsel one another to good character and gentle kindness. Do you not see how their speaker said, ﴿and let him be discreet﴾, on the basis that he commanded good dealing with the one from whom he buys?

Some of the interpreters said: It is a command to choose the subtle (latif) food, because they had not eaten for a long period, so coarse food would harm their bodies. It has also been said: They meant the subtle, because their spirits are from the world of holiness and only the subtle suits them. It is related from Yusuf ibn al-Husayn that he used to say: When you buy food for the people of gnosis (ma'rifah), let it be subtle, and when you buy for the ascetics (zuhhad) and worshippers ('ubbad), buy whatever you find, for they are still in the process of subduing their souls. Some of them said: The food and clothing of the people of struggle (mujahadat) and the practitioners of spiritual discipline (riyadat) is coarse from among what is eaten and worn, while one who has reached gnosis is suited only by what is subtle. It is related from Shaykh 'Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may Allah sanctify his secret, that toward the end of his life he wore fine clothing and ate delicate food. In my view, the obligation of this would undermine perfection. What is related from the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, and the like of him, if it is authentic, may be a matter of coincidence. Even if it was a regular practice, it may have been for a legal purpose; otherwise it contradicts what is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from his senior companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Their condition regarding food and clothing is explained in the authentic books, and there is nothing in them that supports the statement of Yusuf ibn al-Husayn and his like. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, that is, of

(Page 261)

the outsiders who are veiled from beholding the lights and standing upon the secrets, ﴿for if they come upon you, they will stone you﴾ with stones of denial, ﴿or return you to their religion﴾, which they have gathered upon and for which Allah has sent down no authority, ﴿and you will never succeed, then, ever.﴾ This is because disbelief at that point would be like Satanic disbelief. ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," ﴿except [when adding], "If Allah wills"﴾. This is guidance toward pure detachment (tajrid) and singling out (tafrid). It is related from some of the great Sufis that he commanded one of his disciples to do something, and he said, "I will do it, if Allah wills." The shaykh said to him in Persian, meaning, "O madman, then who are you?" The verse utterly rejects this statement, and in it, according to the doctrine of the people of unity (ahl al-wahdah), there is also what there is. It has also been said: The verse is a prohibition against the Prophet (ﷺ) informing about the Truth without the permission of the Truth, glory be to Him. In it is guidance for the shaykhs that it is not fitting for them to speak of realities without permission, and that they have signs of permission which they recognize.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget.﴾ It has been said: that is, when you forget the whole of existence, even yourself, for remembrance is not purified except then. It has also been said: when you forget the remembrance. For this reason al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: The reality of remembrance is annihilation in the Remembered from the remembrance. He, may his secret be sanctified, also said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this in right guidance"﴾: There is a station above remembrance which is nearer than the station of remembrance, and it is the renewal of attributes through His remembrance of you before you remember Him, majestic and exalted is He.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine.﴾ Some interpreters claimed that the total of that is twenty-five years, and they took the year mentioned in the verse to mean a lunar month. This is a claim for which there is no justification except weakness of religion and opposition to the community of Muslims. Otherwise, what harm is there in leaving it on its apparent meaning, when it is a possible matter reported by the Truthful? What indicates the possibility of this lingering is that Abu 'Ali Ibn Sina mentioned in the chapter on time in al-Shifa' that Aristotle mentioned that a condition like that of the People of the Cave befell a group of the god-seeking ones. Abu 'Ali said: History indicates that they were before the People of the Cave. End of quote.

It is also said, according to what has been stated, that the verse indicates that the disciple whom Allah, glory be to Him, nurtures without the mediation of shaykhs reaches the goal over a long period and many years, while one whom He, majestic is His majesty, nurtures through their mediation has his affair completed in forties, and it may be completed in a few counted days. I say: There is no restraint upon Allah, glory be to Him, and He, exalted is He, has brought many of His servants to Himself without intermediary in short moments.

﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens﴾, the realm of the heights, ﴿and the earth﴾, the realm of the depths. It is not hidden that the notion of the unseen (ghaybah) pertains only to created beings, for otherwise there is no unseen in relation to Him, majestic is His majesty. For this reason some have said: He, glory be to Him, does not know the unseen in the sense that there is no unseen in relation to Him for knowledge to attach to. But you know that it is not permissible to speak such words, even if they are interpreted as they are interpreted, because of what is apparently in them of conflict with the verses.

And to Allah, exalted is He, we complain of peoples who have made the Truth into a riddle and have thereby caused the creation to fall into trial.

﴿How clearly He sees and hears!﴾ That is: how seeing and how hearing He is, exalted is He, because His attributes are the very essence of His being. ﴿They have no protector apart from Him﴾, since no one other than Him, exalted is He, has any action. ﴿And He does not share His command with anyone﴾, due to the perfection of His power, glory be to Him, and the incapacity of others, exalted is His majesty. This is it, and Allah, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

[p. 262]

﴿And restrain yourself﴾: that is, hold yourself back and steady yourself. It is said, "I made Zayd patient (ṣabartu Zaydan)," meaning I restrained him. In a hadith there is a prohibition against "ṣabr al-ḥayawan" (holding an animal in restraint), meaning confining it for shooting at. Using this word for steadfastness in a matter and bearing it is a figurative extension (tawassu'), and from it comes ṣabr (patience) in its well-known sense. This sense was not taken as the meaning here because of the transitivity and the necessary connection of this usage. ﴿with those who﴾: that is, in companionship with those who ﴿call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: that is, they worship Him constantly. Expressions of this form have become common for continuity, and they are like the saying "Zayd was beaten on the back and the belly," meaning that his whole body was beaten. Some scholars kept "morning and evening" to their literal sense and did not intend the generality of all times. That is, they worship Him at the two ends of the day. These two times were singled out because they are the times of heedlessness and preoccupation with worldly affairs. As for that worship, it was said to be the remembrance of God Most High (dhikr Allah). This was narrated through the chain of Mughira from Ibrahim. It was also said to be the recitation of the Qur'an, and this was narrated from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Adi ibn al-Khiyar. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn Jubayr that it means discussion of what is lawful and unlawful.

From Ibn Umar and Mujahid it is said that it means attending the five prayers, and from Qatadah that it means attending the Dawn and Afternoon prayers. What came before supports the second of these views, and what comes after supports the apparent meaning of the first. So reflect deeply.

The relative clause refers to the poor companions: Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, Ibn Mas'ud, Bilal, and their like. The disbelievers of Quraysh, such as Umayya ibn Khalaf and other leaders of Mecca, said: "If you were to distance these people from yourself, we would sit with you, for the smell of their woolen cloaks (jibab) annoys us." Then the verse was revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Salman, who said: "Those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Uyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqra ibn Habis. They said: 'O Messenger of God, if you were to sit at the head of the gathering and absent yourself from these people and the smell of their cloaks, meaning Salman, Abu Dharr, and the poor Muslims, who wore woolen cloaks, we would sit with you, or converse with you and take from you.' So God Most High revealed: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾, up to His saying: ﴿We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾, threatening them with the Fire."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Salman that when it was revealed, "the Messenger of God (ﷺ), upon him be peace, rose seeking them, until he found them at the back of the mosque remembering God Most High. He said: 'Praise be to God who did not take me until He commanded me to restrain myself together with men of my community. Life and death are with you.'"

According to this view the verse is Medinan, and according to the first view it is Meccan. Abu Hayyan said: "The Meccan view is more sound, because the surah is Meccan." I say: most of the narrations support the second view, and according to it these verses are exceptions to the general rule of the surah, and there are many such cases. Ibn Mardawayh has reported what supports the first view through the chain of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Perhaps the verses that follow also support it. The expression of those people by a relative clause is to give the reason for the command: the quality contained in the relative clause is what motivates continued companionship.

Ibn Amir read "bil-ghadwa" (in the morning). This is explained by what Sibawayh and al-Khalil mentioned, that some Arabs make ghadwa indefinite and say "Zayd came ghadwatan" with tanwin. Al-Radi said that it is permitted to use it as an indefinite noun by consensus. The well-known view is that its most common use is as a generic proper noun (ʿalam jins) that is not declined (mamnu' min al-sarf), so the definite article al- does not enter it, because two definite markers cannot combine in one word. When one wants to add the article to it, it is intended to be made indefinite, and so it is added, just as the indefiniteness of a specific proper noun is intended in the verse:

"Among them was a companion and his cousin, Abu Jandal, and al-Zayd is the Zayd of battles."

The reading mentioned is explained on this basis. Some verifying scholars preferred the first explanation and said: it is better in both transmission and understanding, because indefiniteness in a specific proper noun is evident, whereas in a generic one there is obscurity, since it is common in its singular form before being made indefinite, so its indefiniteness can only be conceived by abandoning its presence in the mind, which distinguishes it from the indefinite noun, and this is obscure. For this reason al-Fanari denied it in his glosses on al-Talwih regarding the indefinite use of Rajab as the name of the month. The matter is open to discussion.

This verse, as in al-Bahr, is more eloquent than the one in al-An'am, which is His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face﴾: that is, desiring the good pleasure of Him, glory be to Him and exalted, not show-off or reputation, according to what Imam al-Suhayli said: when "face" is attributed to God Most High, it is meant metaphorically as good pleasure and an accepted obedience, because whoever is pleased with a person turns toward him, and whoever is angry turns away from him. It was said that "face" means the Essence, and the speech is elliptical (ʿala hadhf mudaf), with an elided noun. It was also said that it means turning toward, and the meaning is: they desire to turn toward Him and seek nearness to Him. The first is preferred. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥal) from the subject of "call" (yadʿūna): that is, they call upon Him desiring this.

﴿And let not your eyes overlook them﴾: that is, do not turn your eyes away from them toward the people of this world. The meaning is a prohibition against despising them and turning the gaze away from them to others because of their shabby condition. So ʿadā here means "to turn away," which takes an object directly and also with ʿan. The Qamus says: "ʿadāhu ʿan al-amr, ʿadwan and ʿudwanan" means he turned him away from the matter. Abu Hayyan chose this, and it is the one who estimated the object as you have heard. ʿAdā can also take a single object with ʿan, just as it takes one directly, and then it means to pass beyond or to leave. The Qamus says: "ʿadā al-amr and ʿanhu" means he passed beyond it and left it. It is possible that the meaning of the verse in this sense is: "Let not your eyes leave them," as if it said "Let not your eyes forsake them." It was also said that the literal meaning of ʿadā is to pass beyond, as al-Raghib explicitly stated, and passing beyond is not transitive with ʿan unless it means to pardon, as they also explicitly stated; and this is not intended here. So there must be an implied sense of ʿadā (taḍmīn) meaning nabā and ʿalā, as in your saying: "His eye turned away from him and rose above him" when it passed over him without settling on him. This is what al-Zamakhshari went to. Then he said: "He did not say 'let not your eyes pass beyond them' or 'let not your eyes rise above them.' He used the implied sense to give the speech the combined meaning of both senses, and that is stronger than giving a single meaning. Do you not see how the meaning returns to your saying: 'Let not your eyes thrust them aside, passing beyond them to others?'"

Abu Hayyan objected that implication (taḍmīn) is not regular according to the Basran grammarians, and it is resorted to only in cases of necessity. When it is possible to apply the word to its conventional meaning, that is better. It was also objected to what was said that it does not follow that when two verbs share a meaning they also share the same transitivity, so it does not follow from ʿadā meaning "to pass beyond" that it is transitive as "to pass beyond" is, so as to say that passing beyond is not transitive with ʿan unless it means pardon, which is not intended. Therefore ʿadā must be given the implied sense of a verb transitive with ʿan. The saying of the Qamus suffices as support for whoever opposes al-Zamakhshari. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

al-Hasan read: "wa-lā tuʿdi ʿaynayka" with a damma on the taʾ, sukun on the ʿayn, a kasra on the unstressed dal, from aʿdāhu, and the two eyes in the accusative. It is also narrated from him, and from ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash, that they read: "wa-lā tuʿaddi ʿaynayka" with a damma on the taʾ, a fatha on the ʿayn, and a shadda on the kasra dal, from ʿaddāhu yuʿaddīhi, and the two eyes also in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari and the author of al-Lawami' made the hamza and the doubling both for transitivity.

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is not good. Rather, the hamza and doubling in this word are to agree with the forms af'ala and fa''ala for the bare verb. This is because al-Zamakhshari acknowledged that before these two were added it was already transitive directly to one object, and it was made transitive with ʿan for implication. So if both the hamza and doubling are for transitivity, it would follow that it must be transitive to two objects, yet in the two readings mentioned it is not transitive to both.

﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾: that is, you seek the company of those who are not like them, of the rich and the people of this world. The clause, according to the widely transmitted reading, is a circumstantial phrase (ḥal) from the kaf in ﴿your eyes﴾, and a circumstantial phrase may come from it because it is part of the genitive construction. The governing element, according to what has been said, is the meaning of the genitive relation, but this is not correct. In al-Kashf it says: the governing element is the preceding verb, as established in His saying: ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanif﴾. You may also say: here specifically, the eye is inserted for emphasis. It is not far-fetched to make it a circumstantial phrase from the subject. The singular pronoun is either because the perception is unified, or to draw attention to the place of the insertion, or because one is sufficient in place of the other, or because they are in truth one organ. The objection to attributing desire to the eye is answered by the fact that its desire is a figure for the desire of its owner. Do you not see what is common, such as the saying:

"What the eye or the ear finds delightful, but it is in truth the person who is delighted."

Desire can also be made a figure for looking for amusement, not for taking lessons.

This is not without deviation from the apparent meaning for no reason. And the view of some that a circumstantial phrase may not come from the genitive complement in such a place, because the governing element of the circumstantial phrase and its owner differ, is not a sound reason, because it is weak. Then the apparent view is that there is no difference in permitting the clause to be a circumstantial phrase from the genitive complement, or from the complemented noun on the condition that ﴿you overlook﴾ is interpreted as "pass beyond," and on the condition that it is interpreted as "turn away." Some restricted the clause being a circumstantial phrase from the genitive complement under the first interpretation, and from the complemented noun under the second, and perhaps this is a matter of preference. This is because at the start of the speech under the second interpretation there is attribution of what is among the voluntary acts, namely turning, to the eye alone, so it fits to attribute desire to it at the end, so that the start and the end of the speech are of one pattern, while observing what is most common in circumstantial phrases, which is that they come from the complemented noun and not the genitive complement. This also avoids addressing the Beloved (ﷺ) directly by attributing desire for the life of this world to him explicitly, even though it is the target of the prohibition. There is no such thing at the start of the speech under the first interpretation, since it is apparent that passing beyond is not a voluntary act only; it is attributed to both the one who chooses and the one who does not. Moreover, making the clause a circumstantial phrase from the subject under this interpretation, along with the statement of some verifying scholars that what passes beyond in truth is the gaze, requires considering the thing and leaving it in one speech. It is not permissible to make this an instance of istikhdam (a rhetorical device) by intending from the two eyes first the figurative gaze, and intending, when returning to the pronoun in "desiring," the literal meaning, because the dual form rules this out. If it is considered first and last and not left, it requires many considerations that are not hidden from the attentive. So reflect and ponder.

In the two irregular readings, it is a circumstantial phrase from the implied subject of the verb: that is, do not pass beyond or do not turn your eyes away from them, desiring that.

﴿And do not obey﴾ in dismissing the poor from your gathering ﴿him whose heart We have made heedless﴾: that is, We made his heart heedless ﴿of Our remembrance﴾, because his capacity for remembrance has been entirely nullified, like those who urge you to drive away the poor. For they are heedless of Our remembrance, unlike those poor people who call upon Him morning and evening. In this there is an indication that what drives them to demand the dismissal is the heedlessness of their hearts toward the presence of God Most High, glory be to Him, and their attention to rational matters and their immersion in sensible ones, to the point that it was hidden from them that nobility lies in adorning the soul, not in the adornment of the body.

The meaning of "remembrance" is clear, and al-Mufaddal explained it as the Qur'an.

The verse is clear according to the position of the People of the Sunnah, but the Mu'tazilah interpreted it. It was said: the meaning is "We left his heart heedless through abandonment (al-khidhlan)," and this is the well-known interpretation among them for such cases; his condition is known to you. It was also said: the meaning is "We found him heedless," as in their saying: "We asked you but did not silence you, and we fought you but did not defeat you." This was criticised on the ground that one should not venture to interpret an act that Allah the Exalted attributed to Himself as "finding" (al-musadafah), which conveys coming upon something suddenly after prior ignorance and lack of knowledge. It was also said: the meaning is "We attributed him to heedlessness," as in the verse of al-Kumayt:

"A group has declared me an unbeliever for loving you,
and another group said: he is a wrongdoer and a sinner."

But it is as you see. Al-Rummani said: the meaning is "We did not mark his heart with remembrance, and did not make it one of the hearts in which We wrote faith, like the hearts of the believers." This is from the saying: "Fulan left his camels heedless (aghfala), when he left them unmarked, without a brand or sign by branding or the like." From this comes "ighfal al-khatt" (leaving a letter unpointed), because it has no dots. So the "ighfal" mentioned is a metaphor for making the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, which indicates belief in Him, like a mark, because it is a sign of felicity, just as the firmness of faith in the heart was made equivalent to writing. This is an interpretation of fine margin and subtle meaning, though it is contrary to the apparent sense; it is not objectionable for one whose aim in it is not to flee from the position of the People of the Sunnah.

Some have argued that the intended meaning is not the apparent sense of the verse, by His saying, glorified is He: "and followed his desire" in pursuit of appetites, since He attributed the following of desire to the servant, which shows that it is his act and not the act of Allah the Exalted. And if that were the act of Allah, glorified is He, and the attribution were metaphorical, it would have said "fa-ittaba'a" with the causal fa', since it is a consequence of it.

It is answered that the act of the servant, because it is by his acquisition (kasb) and power, and the creation of Allah the Exalted, may be attributed to him in the first respect and to Allah the Exalted in the second. The explicit statement of the consequence is not necessary; it may be omitted for a purpose, such as intending to inform of it independently, since that is more severe in censure, or leaving it to the hearer's understanding. There is no need to estimate: "so it was said: and he followed his desire."

Umar ibn Fa'id, Musa al-Aswari and Amr ibn Ubayd read "aghfalana" with a fatha on the fa' and the lam, and "qalbuhu" in the nominative, as the subject of aghfalana. In this reading it is from aghfalahu, when one finds him heedless. The meaning is: we supposed and reckoned him heedless of our remembrance of him and of his deed, by way of requital, Allah the Exalted's remembrance of him being a metonym for His recompense, glorified is He.

The prohibition against obeying those heedless ones in driving away those believers was found problematic, since it is reported that they wanted those to be driven away so that they would believe; so their faith should have been achieved thereby. The most that follows is that a great benefit results, namely the faith of those unbelievers, at the cost of a small harm, namely the loss of the honour of those pious ones; whereas by not driving them away there follows a great harm, namely the remaining of those unbelievers in their unbelief, for a small benefit.

Among the established principles of the Shari'ah: the greater harm is averted by the lesser harm. It is answered that He, glorified is He, knew that those unbelievers would not believe with true faith, but if they believed they would believe only outwardly; and such a thing does not justify the forfeiting of the honour of those poor, righteous ones. Therefore the prohibition against obedience came.

It may be said: it is possible that Allah the Exalted knew that driving away those poor, early converts who were devoted to the worship of the Most Merciful, and breaking their hearts and forfeiting their honour in order to attract the rich and to win their hearts, would cause the hearts to recoil and the thinking of His Messenger ﷺ to be evil; so perhaps one who was recently converted to Islam would apostatise, and those who entered his religion after that would be few, upon him be prayers and peace. That is a great harm, greater than the harm of a remnant of unbelievers remaining in unbelief. Therefore He, exalted and high, forbade obedience to the one whose heart We have made heedless and who followed his desire, "and his affair was" in following desire and abandoning faith "furuṭan," that is, loss and ruin, as said by Mujahid; or, going ahead of the truth and right, casting it behind his back, from the saying "faras furuṭ," meaning a horse that goes ahead of the horses; this is in the sense of what Ibn Zayd said, opposing the truth. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be that furuṭ means neglect and waste, i.e., his affair, which ought to be held to and taken seriously from the religion, was neglect; and it may mean excess and extravagance, i.e., his affair and his desire, which was his path, was excess and extravagance. Muqatil explained it as extravagance. The expression of the chieftains of Quraysh who sought the driving away of the poor believers by the relative pronoun is to signal the causality of what is within the relative clause for the prohibition against obedience.

[Page 266]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And say﴾ to those whose hearts We have made heedless of the remembrance and who follow their desires, ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. It is the predicate of a deleted subject, i.e., "this which has been revealed to me is the truth." And ﴿from your Lord﴾ is either an emphatic circumstantial phrase (hal) or a second predicate, and the first is preferred. It is apparent that His words, exalted is He, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ are part of the statement commanded, and the fa' is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, by way of threat. That is: after establishing that this is the truth, about which there is no doubt, and whose following is obligatory, whoever wills to believe in it and follow it, let him do so, like the rest of the believers, and let him not make excuses with what is hardly fit for excuse. And whoever wills to disbelieve in it and cast it behind his back, let him do so. In this there is, without concealment, a threat and a display of independence from their following, which they had promised in exchange for expelling the believers, and an indifference to them and to their faith, whether it exists or not.

It is also permissible that ﴿the truth﴾ be the subject, whose predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Al-Zamakhshari chose the first here. In al-Kashshaf he said: The reason for preferring the deletion is that the meaning is more complete in its coherence, because when He, glorified is He, commanded him to be constant in reciting this Book of great stature, among those who recite it as it should be recited, desiring His Face, blessed and exalted is He, not turning to the adornments of this world, then whoever is granted this great blessing has, in giving thanks for it, a preoccupation that averts every other preoccupation. He appended to it, to remove excuses and pretexts, His words, glorified is He: ﴿And say﴾ etc. That is: this which has been revealed is the truth, so whoever wills, let him enter the ranks of those who succeed with this happiness, and whoever wills, let him be among the perishing, immersed in error. As for making it the subject, if the definiteness is for specific reference, it returns to the first with the loss of intensification. If the definiteness is for the genus, meaning: all the truth is from your Lord and not from other than Him, and it includes the Book in a primary inclusion which has not been specified in detail, since what the statement is directed toward is not merely that it is from Him, exalted is He, but that it is truth that must be followed. End of quote.

This is a statement that bears the signs of verification, and its apparent meaning indicates that the supplication is carried by the second of the opinions concerning it. And the referent is the Book in general, not the Book specifically containing the command to restrain oneself with the believers and to refrain from obeying the heedless, as Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted. On the assumption that ﴿the truth﴾ is the subject, it was said: what is meant is that it is the Qur'an, just as what was meant by the referent under the assumption that it is the predicate. This is what was narrated from Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: it is monotheism. Al-Kirmani said: Islam and the Qur'an.

Makki said: what is meant by it is tawfiq (divine success) and khidhlan (divine abandonment). That is: say, "Success and abandonment are from Allah, the Exalted. He guides whom He wills, so He grants him success and he believes, and He leads astray whom He wills, so He abandons him and he disbelieves. It is not up to me in any of that." And this is not right, as is not hidden.

It is also permissible that His words, glorified is He, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe﴾ etc., be a threat from Him, exalted is He, not included under the statement commanded. Then the fa' is for the sequencing of what follows of threat upon the command itself. That is: say that to them, and after that, whoever wills to believe in it or to accept you in it, let him do so, and whoever wills to disbelieve in it or to deny you in it, let him do so. On both views, the intended meaning is not the literal command and choice, which is evident.

Al-Khafaji mentioned that the command to disbelieve is not intended; it is a metaphor for abandonment and leaving alone, by likening the state of one who is such to the state of one commanded to oppose, with the point of resemblance being indifference and lack of concern. This is like the words of Kuthayyir: "Treat us badly or treat us well, [I am] no blamer."

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) used this verse to argue that the servant is independent in his actions and creates them, because He made the realization of faith and disbelief depend on the pure will of the servant, since what is understood from a conditional is that it is a complete cause of the consequent. So this indicates that he is independent in bringing both into existence, and there is no difference between one act and another; therefore he is the creator of all his acts.

It is answered: even if we suppose that the servant's will is effective and creative of actions, the aim does not follow, because reason and transmitted text both indicate that it depends on the will of Allah and His desire. As for reason: they said that if it did not depend on that, it would entail circularity or infinite regress. As for transmission: He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾. And with this dependence, the matter of independence does not hold, and it is established that the servant is compelled in the form of one who chooses. This is the doctrine of the Ash'arites (an orthodox theological school). In Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din, the Proof of Islam (al-Ghazali) says: If you say: I find in myself an immediate awareness that if I will the act I am able to do it, and if I will the abandonment I am able to do it, so the act and the abandonment are by me and not by another. I say: Suppose you find this meaning in yourself. But do you find in yourself

[Page 267]

that if you will the willing of the act, that willing comes into being, or if you do not will that willing, it does not come into being? Because reason testifies that he wills the act, not because of another will preceding that will. When he wills the act, the act must come into being without capacity or choice. So the occurrence of the will in the heart is a necessary matter, and the act's following upon the occurrence of the will is also a necessary matter. This indicates that all of it is from Allah, exalted is He. End of quote.

Some people suffice, in establishing the lack of independence, with the proof that the servant's will depends on the will of Allah and His enabling of him, glorified is He, by textual evidence. They do not mention the argument of circularity or infinite regress, because of what it involves of dispute. The full discussion of this is in the books of kalam (theology). We will mention, if Allah wills, a suitable part of it in its appropriate place.

Al-Suddi said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His words, glorified is He: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾. Perhaps he meant that the obvious meaning of it should not be intended, because of the said verse. Otherwise it is a false statement. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from a group that the subject of "willed" in the two conditionals is a pronoun referring to Him, exalted is He. He argued for it with what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: whoever Allah wills for him faith, he believes, and whoever Allah wills for him disbelief, he disbelieves.

The truth is that the subject is the pronoun of "whoever". The narration from the scholar (ibn 'Abbas) was recorded by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat. When it is authentic, it may be that this statement is to clarify that whoever wills faith is the one for whom Allah, exalted is He, has willed faith, and whoever wills disbelief is the one for whom Allah, glorified is He, has willed that. It is not meant to explain the meaning of the verse or to establish the referent of the pronoun. This is supported by His words at the end of the report recorded by the group (of compilers): ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾. And Allah knows best.

Abu al-Sammal Qu'nub read ﴿wa qul al-haqqa﴾ with a fatha on the lam wherever it occurs. Abu Hatim said: that is poor in Arabic. And from him also, a damma on the lam wherever it occurs, as if following the vowel of the qaf. He also read ﴿al-haqqa﴾ with the accusative, and Sahib al-Lawami explained it as: "say the true statement," and ﴿from your Lord﴾ was said to be a circumstantial phrase, meaning "being from your Lord," and it was said to be a qualifier, meaning "the one being from your Lord." There is discussion on this.

Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿fa-li-yu'min﴾ and ﴿li-yakfur﴾ with a kasra on the imperative lam in both. ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning for those who disbelieve in the truth after it has come from Allah, glorified is He. Describing them as "the wrongdoers" is to alert that the will to disbelieve and the choice of it is an overstepping of the limit and a placing of a thing in other than its place. The sentence is a justification for the command, with what was mentioned of the threatening choice. Whoever made ﴿fa-man sha'a﴾ etc. a threat from His side, exalted is He, takes it as an emphasis of the threat and a justification of what it conveys of restraint from disbelief.

It is also permissible that it be a justification for what is understood from the apparent sense of the choice, namely indifference to their disbelief and little concern for their affair. ( And a'tadna ) is from al-'Ataad, and it originally means the storing of a thing before needing it. It was said: its origin is a'dadna, and one of the two dals was changed to a taa'. The meaning is the same: that is, We have readied for them a fire, great and wondrous. ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾, i.e., its tent. The likeness is to what surrounds them of its blaze spreading from it in all directions. Then it was used for it metaphorically (istiʿara musarrahah), with the annexation being the indicator and the encirclement being a complement. It was said: the surradiq is the enclosure around the tent that prevents reaching it. It is also applied to the rising smoke surrounding a thing. Some of them applied the verse to this, and this too is a metaphor, like its application to blaze. The lexicon's statement implies it is literal. What is narrated from Qatadah explains it as the combination of both: blaze and smoke.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is a wall of fire. Al-Kalbi related that it is a neck coming out of the Fire that encircles the disbelievers. Al-Qadi al-Mawardi related that it is the ocean surrounding the world, which on the Day of Resurrection will become fire and will encircle them. He argued for it with what Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and others narrated from Ya'la ibn Umayyah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the sea is from Jahannam," then he recited: ﴿a fire, its enclosure surrounds them﴾.

Al-Raghib said about surradiq: it is a Persian loanword (mu'arrab), and it is not among their words as a single noun whose third letter is an alif and after it two letters. The end of the quote. He was right in the claim of arabization, for most lexicographers hold that. As for his statement that it is not among their words, etc., it is refuted by the occurrence of 'ulabit, qurammis, junadif, and hulahil, all of them in the pattern of surradiq, and many like them. Such oversight from this distinguished scholar, with that abundance, is unlikely, so let it be examined what he meant. Then it is an arabization of sarayirdah, meaning the curtains of the court. It was also said: sarataq, meaning the arch of the court, which is closer in wording, except that taq is itself an arabization, its origin being ta or taq. Abu Hayyan and others said: it is an arabization of sarador, which is the vestibule. It occurs in the line of al-Farazdaq:

"You wished them [dead] until, when you met them, you left for them, before the strike, the surradiq."

It is pluralized, as Sibawayh said, with the alif and taa', even though it is masculine, so one says surradiqat. In al-Nihayah it is explained as everything that surrounds a place, whether a wall, an enclosure, or a tent. The matter of applying it to blaze, smoke, or other things mentioned, on this view, is clear.

﴿And if they ask for relief﴾ from thirst, by the indication of His words, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten metal﴾. It was also said: from what has befallen them of kinds of punishment. Al-muhl, according to what Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, is thick water like the sediment of olive oil. There is a hadith in this matter that is marfu' (traced to the Prophet). Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi, and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His words, ﴿like muhl﴾: "Like the dregs of oil. When it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it."

Others said: it is what is melted of the riches of the earth. It was said: what is melted of copper. Al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about it, so he called for gold and silver and melted them. When they melted, he said: "This is most like the muhl, which is the drink of the people of the Fire. Its color is the color of the sky, except that the drink of the people of the Fire is more intense in heat than this."

Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Mujahid that it is pus and black blood. It was also said: it is a kind of tar. His words, glorified is He: ﴿they will be given relief﴾ etc. come out in the manner of mockery toward them, like the words of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

"Tamim became angry that 'Amir was killed on the day of al-Nisar, so they were paid restitution at al-Sayhalam."

﴿It scalds the faces﴾, i.e., it cooks them when it is brought forward to be drunk, because of the intensity of its heat, to the extent that it strips off their skins, as you have heard in the hadith. So al-wujuh is the plural of wajh, which is the well-known organ, and the apparent meaning is that this alone is intended. It was also said: by "faces" He means all their bodies. The sentence is a second qualifier of "water." The first is "like muhl," or it is a circumstantial phrase from it, as in al-Bahr, since it has been described; or it is a circumstantial phrase from al-muhl, as Abu al-Baqa' said.

Al-Khafaji stated it, and the apparent meaning of some scholars' words permits that *ka* (like) be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) referring to the concealed pronoun in *ka*, since it is a noun meaning "similar," so the pronoun within it is concealed just as the pronoun in it is concealed. There is in this an excessive strain that is not hidden, since it is not a derived attribute (*sifah mushtaqqah*) so that a pronoun could be concealed in it, and no derived word is known to be built on a single letter.

It is mentioned that Abu Ali al-Farisi, in his commentary on the *Shawahid* (*Sharh al-Shawahid*), prohibited making *dhu'abati* (my forelock) in the verse of the poet, "She saw me, my forelock like the sand-scrape of a sandgrouse," to be in the nominative case governed by *ka* because it has the status of *mithl* (like). He said: "That is not easy, because *ka* is not among the words of description."

It is permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier from the concealed pronoun in the prepositional phrase. It was said: it is permissible that the intended meaning of that be a part (of the whole), except that it is a loose usage.

﴿Evil is the drink﴾, that water with which they are given relief, ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾, the Fire, ﴿a dwelling place (*murtafaqan*)﴾, that is: a place of reclining, as Abu Ubayda said, and it is narrated from al-Suddi. The origin of *al-irtifaq*, as it has been said, is reclining on the elbow of the hand.

[Page 269]

In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it is said: "So-and-so spent the night *murtafiqan*," that is, reclining on the elbow of his hand. It was also said: placing the elbow under the cheek. So *murtafaqan* is a noun of place, and its accusative case is as a specification (*tamyiz*). Al-Zamakhshari said: this is for the sake of correspondence (*mushakalah*, the attraction of one phrase to the wording of another) with His saying, ﴿and good is the resting place (*murtafaqan*)﴾, otherwise there is no reclining for the people of the Fire and no leaning, except if it is from the saying of the poet:

"I could not sleep, so I spent the night *murtafiqan*,
as if in my eyes there was poured bitter aloes."

That is, then it is not of correspondence, and the speech is in its literal sense, in that the people of the Fire have reclining in it, that is, leaning on the elbows of their hands, as the one who grieves and is distressed does. In *al-Kashshaf* it is mentioned that reclining in its literal sense may be for enjoyment and may be for grief.

It was objected that although that is possible by reason, the apparent meaning is that the punishment has occupied them from it, so it cannot come from them, so that the speech would be literal and not correspondence. It was permitted that this be mockery (*tahakkum*) or a metonymy (*kinayah*) for their not being given rest.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that *al-murtafaq* is the abode. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Qatada. In its meaning is the saying of Ibn Ata: the place of settling; and the saying of al-Utbi: the gathering place. It was said: the place of mutual companionship (*tarafuq*), that is: evil is a place for companionship and fellowship. It seems that this is the intended meaning of Mujahid in his tafsir when he said "the assembly." So al-Tabari's denial that it has such a meaning is obstinacy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: evil is a seeking place for ease (*rifq*), because whoever seeks ease from Hell will not find it. Some permitted that *murtafaq* be a mimi verbal noun (*masdar mimiyy*) meaning the reclining and leaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ is in the position of a causal clause (ta'lil) supporting the exhortation to faith (al-hath ʿala al-iman) that is understood from the expression of choice (al-takhyir). It is as if it were said: "And for those who believe..." Perhaps the change of construction (taghyir al-sabk) is to indicate (li'l-idhan) the complete contrast (kamal tanafi) between the states of the two groups. That is: indeed, those who believe in the truth that is revealed to you ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, as has been explained in its contexts (tada'if).

﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good in deed﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Hadrami... [text cut here; the passage as given continues below]

Note: The source text provided to me does not contain a reading attributed to ʿIsa al-Thaqafi in this place as stated below; the translation follows the text as given:

ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read: "lā nuḍayyiʿu" with the doubled (ta'diyf) form. On both readings, the sentence is the predicate (khabar) of the second inna, and the predicate of the first inna is the second clause together with what is within its scope (hayyiz). The linking element (al-rabit) is an omitted pronoun whose estimated form is: "one who does good in deed of them" (man ahsana ʿamalan minhum). It is not objected that this implies that among them are those who did good and among them are those who did not do good; for that holds only if min is partitive (tab'iDiyya), and it is not necessarily so, since it may be explicative (bayaniyya). And even if it is granted, there is no harm in it, for ihsan is the increase of sincerity (al-ikhlas) mentioned in the hadith of ihsan: "that you worship Allah as if you see Him." However, on this view the ruling for those among them who did not attain this degree (lam yuhsin bi-hadha al-ma'na minhum) remains. Alternatively, the linking element is the apparent noun which is the subject (mubtada') in meaning, according to what al-Akhfash held in making it a link; for "one who does good in deed" in reality are "those who believed and did righteous deeds."

It was objected that this is precluded by the indefiniteness of ﴿ʿamalan﴾, since it indicates diminution (li'l-taqlil). It was answered that this is not necessarily so, for an indefinite noun may be generalizing in affirmative contexts, and the context of praise is a witness of truth. Or the linking element is a general term (ʿumum), based on the view that generality may serve as a link, as in: "Zayd is an excellent man" (ni'ma al-rajul), according to one opinion; and in this there is evident discussion. Perhaps the preferable view is that the predicate is the statement of His, exalted is He:

[Page 270]

﴿Those, for them are Gardens of Eden﴾. The clause "Indeed We..." (*innā*) and so on is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*). Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others said that this kind of *i'tirāḍ* is like the poet's words:

*Indeed the Caliph, indeed Allah clothed him*
*in the garment of rule, by which the ends are hoped for.*

You know that *i'tirāḍ* is not definitely required in this verse either. Based on the previous possibility, this clause may be a new sentence (*mustaʾnafa*) explaining the reward. It may also be a second predicate after a predicate, according to the view of those who do not require that multiple predicates have the meaning of a single predicate.

[Page 271 marker shown below after the next sentence]

This is the correct view. That is: those described with these noble attributes, for them are gardens of residence. ʿAdan here means residence and settling. It is said: *ʿadana bi-l-makān* when one stays in a place and settles there. From this comes *al-maʿdin* (the mine), because precious stones settle in it.

It is reported from Ibn Masʿūd: *ʿAdan* is a garden among the gardens, and it is the lowest part of them. The reason for attaching *al-jinān* (gardens) to it is that, because of its vastness, every side of it is as if it were a garden.

﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾, and they are secure in the lofty chambers. ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾.
