The first *min* (from) is for beginning, and the second *min* is for explanation. The prepositional phrase is in the position of an adjective for *asāwir* (bracelets). This is what al-Zamakhsharī and others chose.

Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed that the first *min* be extra (*zāʾida*) in the object, according to the view of al-Akhfash, and this is shown by Allah's words: ﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets﴾. He also allowed that it be explanatory, meaning: something or ornament of bracelets.

Others allowed that it be partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*) occupying the position of the object, just as he and others allowed this for the second. It was also allowed that it be connected to *yuḥallawna* (they will be adorned), but as you see, this is not correct.

*Asāwir* is the plural of *asāwira*, which is the plural of *siwār* (with kasra and damma), which is the ornament worn on the arm. It is an Arabic word. Al-Rāghib said it is Arabized from *dastawāra*. It is also said: *asāwir* is the plural of *aswār*, which is the plural of *siwār*, and its origin is *asāwīr*, which was lightened by removing its *yāʾ*. So on both views it is a plural of a plural. They did not make it the plural of *siwār* from the start, because they saw that *fiʿāl* is not pluralized as *afāʿil* by analogy.

It is reported from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ that the singular is *aswār*. Ibn al-Anbārī recited:

*By Allah, were it not for young children,*
*whose faces are like moons,*
*whom the house of al-ʿAtīk gathers,*
*I would fear that poverty would strike them,*
*or a slapper who has no bracelets,*
*when a tyrant king saw me*
*at his gate, when the day had become clear.*

In the *Qāmūs* (of al-Fīrūzābādī): *al-siwār*, like *kitāb* and *ghurāb*, is the bracelet, like *al-asāwir*. Its plurals are *aswira*, *asāwir*, *asāwira*, *sūr* and *suʾūr*. This agrees with what was transmitted from Abū al-ʿAlāʾ.

This is also transmitted from Quṭrub and Abū ʿUbayda. It is indefinite (*nukkirat*) to magnify its beauty from being encircling.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Saʿd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a man of the people of Paradise looked out and his bracelets appeared, their light would obliterate the light of the sun just as it obliterates the light of the stars."

Al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ* and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* transmitted from Abū Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If the lowest of the people of Paradise in ornament had his ornament weighed against the ornaments of all the people of the world, his ornament would be greater than the ornaments of all the people of the world."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿIkrima that he said: "The people of Paradise will be adorned with bracelets of gold, pearls and silver, which are lighter upon them than anything; they are only light."

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) transmitted from Abū Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The ornament of the believer will reach where the light reaches."

Abū al-Shaykh and others transmitted from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār that he said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted has an angel, and in another narration: in Paradise there is an angel, whom, if I wished, I would name, who fashions the ornaments of the people of Paradise from the day they were created until the Hour arises. If an ornament of it were brought out, it would turn back the rays of the sun."

The objection that men wearing bracelets is a defect in this world, so how will they be adorned with them in the Hereafter? is dismissed. Its being a defect is only among a people who are not accustomed to it, not absolutely. I do not think you doubt that a thing may be a defect among one people and not a defect among others. There is nothing in our matter that is a rational judgment that it is a defect at every time, in every place and among every people. If you insist that it is so, you have adorned yourself with the ornament of ignorance and left the bond of reason.

[Page 271]

This is it. Abān transmitted from ʿĀṣim: *min asāwira* (with the alif removed and a hāʾ added), and this is one of the plural forms of *siwār*, as you have heard.

﴿And they will wear green garments﴾, because green is the most beautiful of colors, and the soul is more delighted by it than by others. It is reported in a tradition that it increases the light of sight. It is also said: three things remove grief: water, greenery and a beautiful face.

The apparent meaning is that their clothing is not restricted to what has been mentioned, since for them therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir that a man is clothed in seventy garments in a single hour, and that the least of them is like the shaqīq of al-Nuʿmān (a red flower). It is also said that restriction is possible: for them therein is what the souls desire, and this does not forbid it, since it is possible that they do not desire and their eyes do not delight in any colors other than these. The indefiniteness is to show that its beauty can hardly be described.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Kaʿb that he said: "If a garment of the garments of the people of Paradise were spread out today in this world, whoever looked at it would faint, and their eyes could not bear it."

Abān transmitted from ʿĀṣim and Ibn Abī Ḥammād from Abū Bakr: *wa-yalbisūna* (with kasra on the bāʾ). ﴿Of silk﴾. Al-Jawālīqī said: it is thin brocade in Persian, so it is Arabized. In the *Qāmūs*: it is a kind of bizyūn or a kind of thin brocade, Arabized without disagreement. Al-Layth said: the lexicographers and exegetes have not disagreed that it is Arabized. You know that there is a dispute of al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding this, and the claim that it is not from the lexicographers and exegetes is not something that sits well with me. Shaydala said: it is thin brocade in Hindi, and its singular, according to what was transmitted from Thaʿlab, is *sundusa*.

Some claimed that its origin is *sindī* (from Sind), and this kind of brocade used to be brought from Sind, so the *yāʾ* was changed to *sīn*, as was done in *sādī*, which became *sādis*. This is a statement that is only accepted by a Sindi or a Hindi. It is related that a group of people from India, from a place called *Burūj* (with the Persian *jīm*), who spoke a language called Sanskrit, came to Iskandar al-Thānī with a gift, among which was this brocade, which he had not seen. He said: "What is this?" They said: *sundūn* (with a nūn at the end). Then the Romans changed it to *sundūs*, and then the Arabs to *sundus*. So it is definitely Arabized from that word which that group used for it. But there is no doubt that it is either its name in its original language, or the name of the town from which it was brought, and it was applied to it just as the names of many goods are today. And Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the matter.

﴿And brocade﴾ (*istabraq*). Ibn Jarīr and others transmitted from Qatāda and ʿIkrima that it is thick brocade. Ibn Baḥr said: it is brocade woven with gold. In the *Qāmūs*: it is thick brocade, or brocade made with gold, or thick silk garments similar to brocade, or a red leather like pieces of bowstrings, end quote. What most exegetes and lexicographers hold is the first. It is, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, the Arabized form of *istabrah*, which is a non-Arabic word meaning thick. The well-known view is that for thick in Persian it is said *istabar*, without a *hāʾ*. Ibn Qutayba said: it is Roman, Arabized, and its origin is *istabrah*, and they changed the *hāʾ* to *qāf*. It occurs in the poetry of al-Muraqqish, who said:

*You see them wearing the cloaks at one time,*
*and at another time their clothing is brocade of silk.*

Ibn Durayd said: it is Syriac, Arabized, and he mentioned its origin as they mentioned. It is also said: its origin is *istafrah*, with a letter after the *tāʾ* between the *fāʾ* and the single *bāʾ*. Some claimed that *istabraq* is thick, fine brocade in both Arabic and Persian, so there is an agreement between the two languages. It is transmitted from al-Azharī that he approved of this. Its plural is *abārīq*, and its diminutive, as in the *Qāmūs* and others, is *ubayriq*. Ibn Muḥaysin read *wa-istabraqa* (with wasl of the hamza and fatḥa on the qāf) wherever it occurs. He made it, as the apparent statement of Ibn Khālawayh requires, a past verb on the pattern *istafʿala* from *al-barīq* (shine). Except that *istafʿala* here agrees with the bare form *barraqa*. The apparent statement of al-Ahwāzī in *al-Iqnāʿ* is that he alone read it so and made it a diptote noun, and did not make it a past verb.

The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: Ibn Muḥaysin read *wa-istabraqin* (with wasl of the hamza) throughout the Qurʾān with tanwīn, so it is possible that he dropped the hamza for lightness without analogy. It is also possible that he made it an Arabic word from *barraqa al-thawbu yabruqu bariqan*, when it shines with its newness and freshness. Then its pattern is *istafʿala* from that. When it was named with it, he treated it as a verb in the wasl of the hamza, and as a fully declinable noun in declension and tanwīn. Most exegeses hold that it is Arabic and not Arabized, end quote. It is not hidden that this contradicts the two previous transmissions. It may be said: Ibn Muḥaysin had two readings in it, with declension and without declension. So some transmitted one reading and others the other. But Ibn Jinnī mentioned that the reading with fatḥa on the qāf is a slip, or like a slip. Abū Ḥayyān said: he only said that because making it a noun without declension is not allowed, since it is not a proper name, so it would be a slip. But it is possible to make it a past verb, so it is not a slip. End quote.

In the combination of *al-sundus* and *al-istabraq* there is an indication that for those people in Paradise there is what they desire. Both are indefinite to magnify their status. How could it not be, when they are beyond what is seen of the sundus and istabraq of this world, indeed beyond what can be imagined of them.

Al-Bayhaqī transmitted from Abū al-Khayr Marthad ibn ʿAbd Allāh that he said: In Paradise there is a tree that grows sundus, from which the garments of the people of Paradise are made.

Al-Ṭayālisī, al-Bukhārī in *al-Tārīkh*, al-Nasāʾī and others transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, inform us about the garments of the people of Paradise: are they created (*khalqan tukhlaqu*) or woven (*nasjan tunsaju*)?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, the fruit of Paradise splits open and they come out of it."

Its apparent meaning is that whether they are of sundus or of istabraq, it is the same. The adornment was mentioned before the clothing because ornament is greater in the soul, more beloved to the heart, more costly in value, and sweeter to the eye. He made its verb passive, to indicate that they do not undertake that themselves, but that their servants do it, as the poet said:

*Maidens in shelter, guarded, in bounty,*
*adorned with rubies and scattered pearls.*

Likewise, all the kings in this world have their crowns and similar badges set with jewels put on them by their servants. He attributed the wearing to them, because a person undertakes that himself, especially when it covers the private parts. It is also said: he made the first passive and the second active, to indicate that the adornment is a grace from Allah the Exalted, and the wearing is their deserving. It was objected that this contains an Muʿtazilite tendency, and it is answered with the care that is required.

﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾, the plural of *arīka*, as many have said, which is a bed inside a canopy. If there is no canopy in it, it is not called *arīka*.

Al-Bayhaqī transmitted this from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Rāghib said: *al-arīka* is a canopy on a couch. Its naming in that way is either because it is in the earth made of *arāk*, which is a known tree, or because it is a place for residence, from their saying *araka bi-l-makān ʾurūkan*. The origin of *al-urūk* is residence upon grazing the arāk, and then it was extended to other residences. And this explanation was transmitted from ʿIkrima.

al-Zajjaj said: "The arā'ik (thrones/couches) are cushions set within canopied enclosures (ḥijāl). Apparently, according to all the opinions, the word is Arabic." Ibn al-Jawzi, in Funun al-Afnan, related that it means beds (surur) in Abyssinian (Habashi). Whatever the case, the statement, as one of the muhaqqiqin (verifying scholars) said, is a metaphor (kinayah) for their luxury and comfort, since reclining on arā'ik is the way of those who live in luxury and ease. And the reports speak clearly that they recline and enjoy themselves.

It was related by Ibn Abi Hatim, from al-Haytham ibn Malik al-Ta'i, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a man may recline on a couch for forty years, without turning from it or growing weary of it; there comes to him what his soul desires and what his eye delights in."

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Ibn Abbas that upon the arā'ik there are layered cushions (furush mandudah) in the sky, the distance of a farsakh (league).

Ibn Muhaysin recited: "ʿalarā'ik," by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the lam of the definite article and assimilating the lam of ʿalā into it, so the alif of ʿalā is dropped, as though the lam of the article were sukun. A similar usage is the poet's saying:

"So the surface of my self has not become a wilderness,"

meaning ʿalā al-arḍ (on the earth).

﴿How excellent a reward!﴾ That is, that which they were promised of Paradise and its delights. ﴿And how good a resting place﴾ — that is, the arā'ik or the gardens — ﴿a couch (murtafaqan)﴾, i.e. a place of reclining. The discussion of this has already been mentioned just above.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 32:

﴿And strike for them﴾ — for the believers who call upon their Lord morning and evening, and for the disbelievers who sought to drive them away — ﴿the parable of two men﴾. These are two objects of "iḍrib" (strike, i.e. set forth). The second of them is the first, because it is the one in need of detail and explanation; this was said by some of them. The verification of this point has already passed, so recall it. As for "the two men," it may refer either to two men assumed to exist, as has been said, since the coining of a parable does not require their existence, or to two men who actually existed, and this is the reliable view. It has been said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel, one of them a disbeliever named Fartus, and it has been said that his name was Qitfir; the other a believer named Yahudha, according to the words of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Muqatil said: his name was Yamlikha. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they were two sons of a king from the Children of Israel, one of whom spent his wealth in the way of Allah the Exalted, while the other disbelieved and busied himself with the adornments of this world and the growth of his wealth. It is also narrated that they were two blacksmiths who earned wealth. It is further narrated that they inherited from their father eight thousand dinars and divided them. The disbeliever bought land for a thousand, and the believer said: "O Allah, I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the maidens of paradise (ḥūr)," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother bought servants and goods for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I buy from You the everlasting youths for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then he was struck by need, so he sat on his brother's path. His brother passed by him with his retinue, and he approached him, so he drove him away and reproached him for giving his wealth in charity.

It has also been said that they were two brothers from the Banu Makhzum: the disbeliever was al-Aswad ibn al-Asad, and the believer was Abu Salama ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Asad. The purpose of striking these two as a parable is for the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, not from the standpoint of their conditions, which are understood from what was mentioned just before, that the believers have such-and-such in the Hereafter and the disbelievers have such-and-such therein. Rather, it is from the standpoint of the disbelievers' disobedience alongside their enjoyment of the blessings of Allah the Exalted, and the believers' obedience alongside their enduring the hardships of poverty. That is: strike for them a parable, in respect of disobedience with blessing and obedience with poverty, of the condition of two men.

﴿We granted to one of them﴾, namely the disbeliever, ﴿two gardens﴾ — two orchards. The Exalted did not specify their location, since no great benefit depends on specifying it.

Ibrahim ibn al-Qasim al-Katib mentioned in his book "ʿAjaib al-Bilad" that the lake of Tinnis was these two gardens, and then what happened happened, and Allah the Exalted separated them in a single night. If Allah wills, another view will come that can be known from it. The whole sentence is an explanation of the parable, so it has no place in the grammatical analysis (iʿrab). It is permissible for it to be in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) of "two men," in which case its position is accusative.

﴿of grapevines﴾ — of varied vineyards. So the speech, as has been said, is either by supposing an omitted noun (muḍāf), or "grapevines" is used metaphorically for vineyards, which are grapevine plants. What is understood from the apparent words of al-Raghib is that ʿinab (grape) is a homonym shared between the fruit and the vine, and on this basis "vineyards" is intended without need for supposition or metaphor. What prompts the intention of this is that a garden is not made of fruit but of trees. ﴿And We surrounded them with palms﴾ — that is, We made the palms encircle them, surrounding both their sides (ḥifāf), that is, their two flanks, their vineyards being girded by them. It is said: "ḥaffahu al-qawm" when the people went around him, and "ḥaffartuhu bihim" when you made them surround him; so the bāʾ makes it take a second object, as in your saying: "ghashītuhu bihi."

﴿And We placed between them﴾ — in their midst — ﴿crops﴾, so that they would be combined in providing foodstuffs and fruits, with their cultivation continuous, in a pleasing arrangement and an elegant layout.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 33:

﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce﴾, i.e., their fruit, and it reached a state fit for eating. The word ﴿kilta﴾ (both) is, according to the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), singular in form but dual in meaning; this is the well-known position. According to the Baghdadis (al-Baghdadiyyun, the grammarians of Baghdad), it is dual both in form and in meaning. According to Sibawayh, its ta' is substituted for a waw, so its root is kalawa, and the alif in it is the feminine marker. What is problematic according to this view is its inflection with letters under its condition, and it is answered with the same answer given to the difficulty concerning the "five nouns" (al-asma' al-khamsa). According to al-Jirmi, the alif is a lam substituted for its original letter, and the ta' is an added letter for the feminine. What is objected to this view is that the pattern fa'lal is not known, and that the ta' does not occur medially nor after a sound consonant. According to the well-known view, it is permissible in its pronoun to observe its wording and to observe its meaning; the first has been observed here, and the second afterwards. In the Codex of Abdullah (Mushaf Abd Allah, the codex of Ibn Mas'ud): "Kila al-jannatayni atam" in the masculine form, because the feminine form of "the two gardens" is metaphorical. Then he recited "atat", making it feminine, because the pronoun is feminine, and there is no difference between its literal and metaphorical forms. The construction is thus like your saying: "The sun rose and it shone." It is also said that Abdullah recited: "Kullu al-jannatayni atá ukulahu", in the masculine, and returned the pronoun to "kull".

﴿And did not wrong [its owner] in anything of its produce﴾, i.e., it did not reduce anything from its yield, [this being] a reduction unlike what is customary in other gardens; for fruit generally abounds in one year and diminishes in another, and likewise some trees bear fruit in some years and not in others. It is also permitted that ﴿tazlim﴾ be transitive, with ﴿shay'an﴾ as its object, and the outcome is one.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth in the midst of them﴾, i.e., between the two gardens, ﴿a river﴾, so that their irrigation would endure and their splendour would increase. Yahya ibn Abi Amr al-Shaybani said: this river is the one called the River of Abu Farts, which, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim said, is a well-known river in al-Ramla. It is also said that the meaning is: We caused a separate river to gush forth between each of the two gardens, so there would be two rivers according to this; and it is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The doubling of ﴿fajjara﴾ is said to be for intensifying the abundance of the gushing. Al-Farra' said: because the river extends, it is as if it were rivers.

Al-A'mash, Sallam, Ya'qub and Isa ibn Umar read ﴿fajara﴾ with a single letter, in accordance with the original. Abu al-Sammal, al-Iyad ibn Ghazwan and Talha ibn Sulayman read ﴿nahran﴾ with the ha' pronounced with sukun, and this is a dialectal usage applying to it and to its counterparts. Perhaps the mention of the gushing of the river is delayed after the mention of the giving of produce, although the external order is the reverse, in order to signal that each of the giving of produce and the gushing of the river is independent in completing the excellences of the two gardens, as in the story of the cow and similar. Had the order been reversed, we would understand that the whole is one quality, some parts of which follow from others; for the giving of produce ordinarily follows from irrigation. In this there is also an indication that the giving of produce does not depend on irrigation, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its oil would almost glow﴾. This is what Shaykh al-Islam said.

[Page 275]

﴿And he had﴾, that is, for the one mentioned, who is the owner of the two gardens, ﴿fruit﴾, meaning kinds of wealth, as in the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi) and others. It is said: "tamara" when one acquires wealth. Taking it to mean the fruit of trees, as Abu Hayyan and others did, is not appropriate to the wording of the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and the readers of Madinah read ﴿thumur﴾ with a damma on the tha' and the mim, and likewise in ﴿bi-thumurihi﴾ which comes later. It is the plural of thimar, with a kasra on the tha', which is the plural of thamar (with two fathas). So it is a plural of a plural, and its meaning, as previously mentioned, is: many possessions of gold, silver, animals and other things. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others explained it this way. Mujahid said that it refers specifically to gold and silver. Al-A'mash, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim for lightness, both here and in what follows, and the meaning is as you have heard. Abu Raja', in one narration, read it as ﴿thamr﴾ with a fatha and a sukun.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b), and it is taken as an explanation: ﴿And We gave him abundant fruit﴾.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾, the believer. By "companion" is meant the linguistic sense, so this designation does not contradict the view that the two were brothers, contrary to those who have erred in this.

﴿And he﴾, that is, the speaker, ﴿was disputing with him﴾, that is, disputing with his companion. The clause is in the place of a circumstantial state (hal) of the speaker. Al-muhawara means returning speech back and forth, from "haara" meaning "returned". That is, he returns the argument to him, in denying resurrection and in associating partners with Allah, Exalted is He.

It is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial state of his companion, so the pronoun in "huwa" refers to him, and the pronoun in "sahibihi" refers to the speaker. That is: the believing companion, through admonition and calling to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, returns to that disbelieving speaker, who said to him: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth﴾ ﴿and mightier in men﴾, meaning in retainers and helpers. It was also said: in male children. This is narrated from Qatadah and Muqatil. It is supported by its contrast with: ﴿less than you in wealth and children﴾. The specification of males is because they are the ones who go forth with him for his interests and to help him. It was also said: in kin, and it is their nature that they go forth with whoever is among them. It has been used as evidence that he was not his brother, because kinship (al-'ashirah) is shared between them, and the obligation of brotherhood is not explained by this. The words ﴿mალan﴾ and ﴿nafaran﴾ are in the accusative as specification (tamyiz), which, it is said, is transferred from the subject. The apparent meaning is that the elative form (af'al al-tafdil) is meant in its literal sense, and in that case this is contrary to what is found in some narrations, that the believing brother remained poor and in need after giving his wealth in charity, so he asked his disbelieving brother, who did not give to him, and rebuked him for giving in charity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 35:

﴿And he entered his garden﴾, i.e., every garden that was his, enjoying it, on the basis that the idafa (genitive construction) here is for comprehensiveness and generality, so it conveys what the dual would convey, with an addition, namely the indication that he had no garden other than that, and no share in the garden promised to those who are mindful of God. Al-Zamakhshari went to this view, and it is a subtle meaning whose conception was difficult for Abu Hayyan, so he criticized it with what he criticized it with. He chose the singular because entering cannot occur in both gardens together at one time; it occurs in one at a time, and this is devoid of the point that was indicated.

Likewise is what was said: the singular is due to the joining of one of them with the other. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that he said, concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾ etc., "the janna is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and therefore they were two gardens." He (God, glorified is He) called it a garden because of the wall surrounding it, and this is as you see. What the context and the discourse indicate is that the meaning is: he entered his garden together with his companion, ﴿while he was a wrongdoer to himself﴾. This is a circumstantial clause; i.e., he was harming himself by his disbelief, in that he exposed it to destruction and exposed its blessing to extinction, or he was placing a thing in other than its proper place, since what was fitting for him was gratitude and humility, not what is related of him.

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause, built on a question arising from the mention of his entering his garden while wronging himself, as if it were said: "What did he say at that time?" So it was said: he said: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish﴾, i.e., will be destroyed and come to an end. It is said: bada yabidu baydan and buyudan and baydudatan, meaning he perished. ﴿This﴾, i.e., the garden, ﴿ever﴾, i.e., for the length of life. So by perpetuity is meant long duration, not its immediate meaning. It was said: it is possible that he meant this, because out of his ignorance and his denial of the Hour, he thought that its species would not perish, even if each individual tree in it perished, similar to what the philosophers who hold the eternity of the world say concerning the celestial motions; but this is not so. It was also said: he only intended that this garden, as seen in its very person, would not perish, as the philosophers say, according to the well-known view, regarding the spheres themselves; and it seems that love of this world and admiration for it clouded his intellect, so he said that. Otherwise it is something no sensible person would say, and it is something no virtuous person would approve. It was also said: "this" is an indication of the heavenly bodies and the lower bodies, of the heavens and the earth and the kinds of created things; or it is an indication of this world. The end result is one, and the apparent meaning is what preceded. Whatever the case, perhaps this statement came from him in response to his companion's admonition and reminder of the perishing of his two gardens, and his prohibition against being deceived by them, and his command to acquire the righteous enduring deeds. And perhaps he (the companion) also warned him of the Hour, so he said to him:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 36:

﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever take place﴾, i.e., will occur in what is to come. So "standing" (qiyam), which is among the attributes of bodies, is a metaphor for existence and realization, but in common usage it runs in the manner of a literal meaning. ﴿And even if I am returned to my Lord﴾ by being resurrected when it (the Hour) takes place, as you claim, ﴿I will surely find﴾ at that time ﴿better than it﴾, i.e., better than this garden.

Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Bahriyya, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Munadhir, Nafi' and Ibn Amir read «minhuma» (with the dual pronoun), and likewise it is in the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria; i.e., "better than the two gardens" ﴿as a return﴾, i.e., as a place of return and outcome, in exchange for the perishing of the first and the enduring of the other according to your claim. This is a tamyiz (specification) transformed from the subject (mubtada'), as stated by Abu Hayyan. The basis of this greed and false oath is the belief that God, glorified is He, only gave him what He gave him in this world because of his intrinsic merit and his honor before Him, the Exalted. This is like His saying, related in the Qur'an: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best [reward]﴾, and he did not realize that this was a gradual lead toward ruin (istidraj). It seems that because what would be hard for him to part with, namely the Garden which he thought would never perish, came first, he said here "ruddidtu" (I am returned), and because it did not come in what follows, God willing, from the verse of Ha-Mim mentioned, it says "ruji'tu" (I am returned). So let this be considered.

﴿He said to him, his companion, while he was disputing with him﴾. The clause ﴿said to him, his companion﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as previously mentioned. The clause ﴿while he was disputing with him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), like the preceding one. Its purpose is to alert the reader from the outset that what follows is speech given special attention and directed toward debate.

Ubayy recited ﴿yukhasimuhu﴾ (he was arguing with him) instead, and this is taken as an explanation (tafsir) of the standard reading.

﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust?﴾ That is, within the creation of your origin from it, namely Adam, peace be upon him, since the creation of every individual of mankind has a share in his creation, peace be upon him. His noble nature was not confined to himself but was a model (unmudhaj) that contained, in a general way (indimaj ijmali), the nature of all the individuals of the species, and this required the operation of its effects upon all of them. Therefore, attributing the creation from dust to that disbeliever is literally true, in terms of his being the material of his origin. That this is based on the soundness of analogical equality (qiyas al-musawa) is a weak fancy (khayal wahin). It has also been said: "He created you from it" because it is the origin of your material, since a man's semen is produced from foods that return to the dust. Thus the attribution is a metaphor (majaz), by attributing to the effect what belongs to its cause. So reflect.

﴿Then from a drop (nutfa)﴾: this is your proximate material. Thus the created being is one, while the origins are many. It has been related that there is no drop from which God the Exalted has decreed a human to be created except that an angel entrusted with it casts into it a little dust, then God the Exalted creates from it whatever He wills, male or female.

Abu Hayyan (in al-Bahr) criticized this by saying that it requires establishing its soundness. I say: my strong supposition is that I have come upon its authentication, but there is a discussion, which is not hidden, regarding the application of the verse to it.

﴿Then He fashioned you into a man (rajulan)﴾: He made you balanced and complete as a human male. The original meaning of taswiya is making a thing equal (sawa'), that is, level, as in the verse ﴿...the earth would be leveled over them﴾. Then it is also used at times in the sense of creating and bringing into being, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and a soul and He who proportioned it﴾. When it is coupled with creation and bringing into being, as here, the intended meaning is creation in the most complete and most balanced state, according to what wisdom requires, without excess or deficiency.

"Rajulan" is in the accusative, according to Abu Hayyan, as a circumstantial (hal), and this requires interpretation (ta'wil).

Al-Hufi said: it is accusative as a second object of sawwa, and the intended meaning is: "He made you a man." It contains, as has been said, a reminder of the blessing of manhood, that is, He made you male and did not make you female.

The apparent meaning is that the attribution of disbelief in God the Exalted to him is due to his doubt concerning resurrection and his saying: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come﴾. And the one who doubts resurrection, as in al-Kashshaf, is a disbeliever in several respects: in doubting His power, in doubting His truthfulness in His reports, and in doubting His wisdom. Do you not see His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ This is what the context requires, since His saying ﴿Do you disbelieve...﴾ etc. came as a rebuttal of his saying ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come﴾. For this reason He arranged the denial by his creation from dust then from a drop, which points to the proof of resurrection. Most exegetes hold this view, though it has been disputed.

Some of them said: the apparent meaning is that he was a polytheist, as indicated by his companion's words, alluding to him: ﴿I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾, and his saying ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾. There is nothing in his saying ﴿if I am returned to my Lord﴾ that contradicts this, since that is according to his companion's assumption, as has passed. Moreover, acknowledging Lordship does not contradict associating partners, since idol-worshippers acknowledge it and yet are polytheists. So the meaning of ﴿Do you disbelieve?﴾ is ﴿Have you associated partners?﴾. End. Some of what relates to this will come, God willing, the Exalted.

Thabit al-Bunani recited ﴿Woe to you! Do you disbelieve?﴾ (wayl-aka a-kafarta), and this is taken as an explanation, like its similar readings mentioned earlier.

[p. 277]

[Page 278]

But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord. Its original form is *lakin ana* ("but I"). Ubayy and al-Hasan read it this way. Ibn 'Atiyya reports this reading from Ibn Mas'ud. The reader moved the vowel of the hamza of *ana* onto the nun of *lakinna*, then dropped the hamza, then dropped the vowel, then assimilated (*idgham*, merging of identical consonants) the nun into the nun. It was also said that the hamza was dropped together with its vowel, and then one of the two identical letters was assimilated into the other. This second view is closer in terms of the distance between the letters, but the deletion described is contrary to the standard analogical rule (*qiyas*, the regular pattern of Arabic). Deletion and assimilation of this kind do occur in the verse of the poet:

*"You shoot me with your glance, as if you were the guilty one, / And you hate me; but as for you, I do not hate you."*

The original here is *lakinna ana la aqlika*, meaning "but I do not hate you." This is better than the view that the original is *lakinnahu iyyaka* ("but he [is] you"), with the deletion of the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*, the pronoun referring to the situation or the fact being stated). Even weaker is the view that the original is *lakinnani iyyaki*, with the deletion of the noun of *lakinna*, as in the verse of the poet:

*"Had you been a Dabbi, you would know my kinship, / But you are a Zanji with huge lips."*

That is, *lakinnaka* together with the protective nun (*nun al-wiqaya*, the nun inserted before the pronoun suffix to protect the verb or particle's ending). The Kufans, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, and Nafi' in the transmission of Warsh and Qalun read the alif of *ana* as written at the end when stopping, and omitted it when continuing, just as it is originally in *ana*, both in pause and in connection. Abu 'Amr, in one transmission, replaced it with a *ha'* when stopping, saying *"lakinnahu"*; Ibn Khalawayh reports this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Harun reported from Abu 'Amr: *"lakinnahu huwa Allahu rabbi"* with a pronoun attached to *lakinna*.

Ibn 'Amir, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Zuhri read with the alif retained both in pause and in connection. This is also a transmission from Nafi', Ya'qub, Abu 'Amr, Warsh, Abu Ja'far, and Abu Bahriyya. This is attested in the dialect of the Banu Tamim, who retain the alif of *ana* in its original position by choice, whereas others retain it only out of necessity (*idtirar*, poetic or metrical need). Some said that retaining it in connection is not eloquent, but it is good here because *ana*, after the deletion of its hamza, resembles the attached pronoun *na* ("us"), and because the alif was made a substitute for the deleted hamza in it. It was also said that it was retained to treat connection like pause, and that retaining it prevents confusion with the doubled *lakinna*. As an example of retaining it in connection, there is the verse of the poet:

*"I am the sheikh of the clan, so know me, / Renowned, I have climbed to the summits."*

In a transmission of al-Hashimi from Abu Ja'far, it is deleted both in connection and in pause. This is also reported from Abu 'Abla, Abu Haywa, and Abu Bahriyya. He read *"lakinnana"* with the hamza deleted and the two nuns lightened. In all these readings, *lakin* is a particle of contrast (*istidrak*) that has no governing effect. *Ana* is the first subject, *huwa* is the second subject as a pronoun of the matter, and *Allahu rabbi* is a subject and predicate. The clause is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and it does not need a connecting pronoun. The clause of the pronoun of the matter and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject, and the connecting element is the pronoun of the speaker attached as a possessive (*al-mudaf ilayhi*). The construction is like your saying: "Hind, he is Zayd, one who strikes her." It is also permitted that *huwa* be a second subject, with the divine name as an apposition (*badal*) to it, and *rabbi* as its predicate; the clause is then the predicate of the first subject, and the connecting element is again the *ya'* (of *rabbi*).

In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's work), it is stated that *huwa* is the pronoun of the matter and that there is an implied verb of saying: that is, *lakin ana aqulu huwa Allahu rabbi* ("but I say: He is Allah, my Lord"). It is also permitted that it refers to the one who *"created you"* (*khalaqaka*), i.e. *lakin ana aqulu alladhi khalaqaka Allahu rabbi* ("but I say: the One who created you is Allah, my Lord"). Then its predicate is the divine name, and *rabbi* is an epithet, an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*), or an apposition (*badal*). End of quotation. Then it was permitted not to posit an implied verb of saying, and the view was restricted to taking *huwa* as the pronoun of the matter, as you have heard. It is not hidden that the possibility of an implied verb of saying is remote in this reading. The possibility that the divine name is an apposition is perhaps closer in meaning than that it is a predicate, and the pronoun refers to the one who *"created you."* Abu 'Ali permitted that *na* be a pronoun of the plural, as in *kharajna* ("we went out") and *darabna* ("we struck"), and the assimilation occurred due to the meeting of two identical letters. However, it is intended to refer to the speaker's own self in the honorific sense, so *rabbi* is singular according to the meaning. If it followed the wording, it would be *rabbuna* ("our Lord"). The distance of this is not hidden. Ibn 'Atiyya said about the verse: It is permitted that *lakinna* be the governing particle among the sisters of *inna*, with its subject omitted. The omission is eloquent when the context indicates it. The estimate is: *"lakinna qawli huwa Allahu rabbi"* ("but my saying is: He is Allah, my Lord"). This would be complete only if it were read with the alif deleted in pause and connection, and I do not know anyone who read that way. End of quotation.

You have already known who read it that way. Others have also been mentioned as reading it so: Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn 'Ali al-Hudhali, in his book *al-Kamil fi al-Qira'at* (The Complete Work on the Readings). But I do not think you will approve of deriving the grammar on that basis. 'Isa al-Thaqafi read *"lakin huwa Allahu"* with the nun of *lakin* unvocalized (sukun). Ibn Khalawayh reports it from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Ahwazi from al-Hasan. Its grammatical analysis is very clear.

It is also read as *"lakinna ana huwa Allahu la ilaha illa huwa rabbi"*, and its grammatical analysis is known from what has passed. Abu Hayyan explained the reading of Abu 'Amr according to the transmission of Harun, so that *huwa* is an emphatic of the object pronoun in *lakinnahu*, and it refers to the one who *"created you."* Then he said: It is permitted that it be a separator (*fasl*, a pronoun separating subject and predicate), because it occurs between two definites. It is not permitted that it be a pronoun of the matter, because then there would be no returning pronoun from the clause that is the predicate of the name of *lakinna*. End of quotation. I wish I knew what prevented him from permitting that the pronoun in *lakinnahu* be the pronoun of the matter, with *huwa* a subject referring to the one who *"created you,"* the divine name its predicate, and *rabbi* an epithet, an explanatory apposition, or an apposition; the clause is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter in the accusative governed by *lakinna*. Or *huwa* could be a subject, the divine name an apposition to it, *rabbi* its predicate, and the clause the predicate of the pronoun.

This is what is meant by his saying: *"And I do not associate anyone with my Lord"* (*wa la ushriku bi-rabbi ahadan*). It is a conjunction (*'atf*) on one of the two clauses. The contrast is with *"Do you disbelieve"* (*akafarta*). The summarized meaning, given the interrogative which is for affirmation in the form of denial, is: "You disbelieve in God, the Exalted, but I am a believer who professes His oneness."

Because of the clear difference between the two clauses, *lakin* is placed in its position. They have said that it occurs between two statements that differ, as in: "Zayd is present, but 'Amr is absent." Al-Zamakhshari and others went to the view that this is the meaning. In *al-Kashf* it is mentioned that there is an indication in it that disbelief in God, the Exalted, is opposed by belief and monotheism, so it is permitted that it contrast with each of them, and with both together. That is, as here: belief is conveyed by *"But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord,"* and monotheism is conveyed by *"and I do not associate anyone with my Lord."* You also know that *shirk* (associating partners with God) is often applied to disbelief in general, and they took from this His saying, exalted is He: *"Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him."* It is possible that the purpose of the whole statement is to establish belief in the most emphatic way. Perhaps the *shirk* of his companion, which he alluded to in the second clause, is what many have explicitly stated in this sense.

It was also said: *shirk* here has its commonly understood meaning, and its attribution to his companion is an allusion, on the ground that when he denied the resurrection, he made the Creator, majestic is His majesty, powerless. Whoever makes Him powerless, glorified and exalted is He, has equated Him with His creation in powerlessness, and that is *shirk*. It was also said: on the ground that when he was deceived by his worldly wealth, he claimed inherent entitlement and attributed to himself what he attributed, so he was as if he had associated partners. The believer alluded to this, and so he said as if: "But as for me, I am a believer, and I see wealth and poverty only as from Allah, the Exalted; He impoverishes whom He wills and enriches whom He wills, and I do not regard inherent entitlement as you do." The truth is that each of the two statements is forced (*takalluf*). It was also said that there is an allusion to the *shirk* of his companion in the speech, and it need not be indicated by his earlier words; it is sufficient that his being a polytheist is established in fact, and what follows contains what is clear about it. So reflect. Then know that what this verse contains is a sublime remembrance.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported "from Asma' bint 'Umays, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me words to say at times of distress: *Allahu rabbi, la ushriku bihi shay'an* ('Allah is my Lord; I do not associate anything with Him')."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 39:

﴿Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "As God willed; there is no power except through God"?﴾ This is an exhortation to speak and a rebuke for neglecting it. Placing the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) before the thing being urged upon indicates that the saying was obligatory at the very moment of entering, without delay, for restriction (li-l-qaṣr). It is permissible to front it for this purpose and to make it a separator between (lawlā) and its verb, because of the Arabs' latitude with adverbial phrases. That is: "Why did you not say, at the moment you entered it, ﴿what God willed﴾," meaning: the matter is what God willed, or "whatever God willed comes to be," where mā is a relative pronoun in the nominative position, either as the predicate of an omitted subject or as the subject of an omitted predicate.

It may also be conditional, in the accusative position governed by "shā'a" (willed), with the answer omitted; that is: "Whatever God the Exalted willed, it came to be." Whichever it is, the purpose is to urge him to acknowledge that his garden and what is in it are by the will of God the Exalted: if He wills, He preserves it, and if He wills, He destroys it. The sentence's indication of the generality that includes what has been mentioned is an initial inclusion according to the first reading, because the definiteness of "the matter" is for totality (istighrāq). On this reading the sentence conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). As for other readings, it is said: because mā is conditional, or a relative pronoun that has the meaning of a condition, and a condition and what is similar to it indicate that the existence of the consequent depends on what is in its scope, so its non-existence follows from its non-existence. The meaning is: whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. There is no objection to this for those who hold the concept of the conditional (mafhūm al-sharṭ). Some have estimated, in the second of the two possibilities for the relative pronoun, "what God willed is what exists," so that the sentence conveys what has been mentioned, but this is nothing, as is not hidden.

Al-Qaffāl of the Mu'tazila claimed that the estimate is: "This is what God the Exalted willed," and the reference is to the fruits and the like in the garden. This is like a person who, looking at a book for example, says: "This is Zayd's handwriting." His aim is to negate the indication of the verse to generality, so that the Mu'tazili doctrine remains sound for him. Likewise did al-Ka'bi and al-Jubbā'i act, when they said: the verse is specific to what God the Exalted has Himself done, and does not include what is the act of servants. And it is not impossible that there occurs in His dominion, glory be to Him, what He does not will, just as there occurs in it what He forbids. This is not hidden from one who has sound taste and a straight mind: what comes to the understanding is generality. And how many a deviation from this there is among the Mu'tazila.

﴿There is no power except through God﴾ is also part of the quoted speech; that is: "Why did you not say that, acknowledging your helplessness and confessing that what was made easy for you of its cultivation and the management of its affairs is only through His aid and empowerment, may His majesty be exalted." This verse has also included a great remembrance.

Ahmad has narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Prophet ﷺ said to me: Shall I not direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: That you say: There is no power except through God."

'Amr ibn Maymun said: I said to Abu Hurayrah: "There is no might and no power except through God," and he said: No, it is in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿Why, when you entered...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Amr ibn Murrah who said: "Among the best supplications is a man's saying: What God willed."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God the Exalted does not bestow upon a servant a blessing in family, wealth, or child, and he says: What God willed; there is no power except through God, except that God the Exalted repels from him every calamity until his appointed death comes to him." And he recited: ﴿Why, when you entered...﴾ etc.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated by another route from Anas who said: Whoever sees something of his wealth and it pleases him, and says: What God willed; there is no power except through God, no calamity will ever befall that wealth. He recited the verse. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shu'ab from Anas, raised to the Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mutarrif who said: Malik, whenever he entered his house, would say: What God willed. I said to Malik: Why do you say this? He said: Do you not hear God the Exalted saying: ﴿Why, when you entered your garden, did you say: What God willed﴾? It is transmitted from Ibn al-'Arabi that Malik takes as evidence from the verse the recommendation of the remembrance it contains for everyone who enters his dwelling.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Urwah that whenever he saw something of his wealth that pleased him, or entered one of his orchards, he would say: What God willed; there is no power except through God, and he would interpret the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Why, when you entered...﴾ the verse. Some narrations imply the recommendation of saying this upon seeing what pleases, absolutely, whether it belongs to him or to another, and that if he says it, the evil eye of admiration will not touch him.

﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ etc. "I" is an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun in the accusative as object of "tara" (you see), and the nominative pronoun has been placed in the position of the accusative pronoun. If the seeing is cognitive, then "aqall" (less) is the second object; if it is visual, it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the object. "Anā" may also be a separating pronoun (faṣl), and in that case the seeing must be cognitive, because the separating pronoun occurs only between a subject and predicate, in the present or underlying structure.

'Isā ibn 'Umar read "aqullu" with the nominative, so "anā" is the subject and "aqullu" its predicate. The sentence is then in the position of the second object on the first possibility for seeing, or a circumstantial clause on the second. "Mālan wa-waladan" is a specification (tamyīz) on both readings and what they contain of the possibility.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 40:

His saying, ﴿So my Lord may give me better than your garden﴾, stands in place of the response to the condition; that is: if you see me thus [poorer than you], then there is no harm, "it may be that my Lord..." etc. Kathir said: it is the response to the condition, and the meaning is: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope from the action of God Most High that He will turn what is in me and in you of poverty and wealth, so He will grant me, for my faith, a garden better than your garden, and will strip you of His blessing for your disbelief and will ruin your garden. Some scholars restricted this giving to His saying, "in the Hereafter," and another said, "in this world or in the Hereafter." The apparent meaning of what has been mentioned is that it is in this world, like the sending in His saying: ﴿and He sends upon it a calamity (husban) from the heaven﴾, that is, a punishment, as Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Tastari narrated from him that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to him: "Inform me about His saying, the Exalted: ﴿husban﴾." He said: "Fire." And he recited to him the verse of Hassan:

A remnant of a people upon whom were poured torrents of husban, meteors (shuhb).

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that also from al-Dahhak. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a verbal noun like al-butlan and al-ghufran, in the sense of reckoning (hisab), and what is meant by it is the reckoned/decreed thing, that is: something decreed which God the Exalted has determined and reckoned, namely the judgment of its ruin. The apparent meaning is that its application to the mentioned judgment is metaphorical. Al-Zajjaj also took husban in the sense of hisab, except that he supposed an omitted genitive (mudaf); 
Page 281
that is: "punishment of reckoning," which is the reckoning of what his hands have earned. It is not hidden that it is permissible to intend by husban in this sense the punishment, metaphorically, so there is no need to supposing an omitted genitive.

The apparent wording of al-Qamus, and likewise what was narrated first from Ibn 'Abbas, is that the application of husban to punishment is literal. It is possible, according to what has been said, that its application to fire is by considering that it is part of the punishment or of what is decreed. Al-Zamakhshari related that ﴿husban﴾ is the plural of husbanah, which is the projectile (al-mirmah), that is, that which is thrown like an arrow or a thunderbolt, and by it is meant here the thunderbolts. It was also said: it is more general than that; that is, He sends upon it projectiles of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things that He wills. ﴿Then it will become﴾ as a result of that ﴿a smooth (saʿid) ground﴾, that is: land ﴿slippery (zalaqan)﴾ with no vegetation in it. This was said by al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Suddi. It was said: the original meaning of zalaq is slipping in walking on mud and the like, but since that occurs in places where nothing grows, and similar things that prevent it, it was used metaphorically for it, or it was alluded to by it, and the verbal noun was used to express the place of slipping, as an intensification. It was also said: zalaq derives from "zalaqa ra'sahu," meaning "he shaved his head," and the statement is a comparison; that is: it becomes smooth land with no tree or plant in it, like a head that has been shaved, though this is far-fetched. It was also said: what is meant by zalaq is the slippery place in its literal, apparent sense, and the meaning is: it becomes land with no vegetation in it, and on which no foot can stand. The sum of it: it becomes stripped of its benefits, even the benefit of walking on it, so it becomes mud which produces nothing and on which no foot can stand. The apparent practice of Abu Hayyan is to prefer this. Mujahid said: that is, it becomes a vast heap of sand.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 41:**

﴿Or its water sinks away into the ground﴾. That is, it becomes sunken into the earth. The use of the verbal noun (*masdar*) here is for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), similar to what has passed.

﴿Then you will not be able to find a way to it﴾. That is, to the sunken water, through effort or action to bring it back or extract it. What is meant is the negation of the ability to reach it, and so this is expressed by negating the seeking (*talab*), as a sign that it is not possible. A sensible person does not seek the like of it. It has also been said that the pronoun in "to it" refers to water in general, not to this specific water. That is, "you will not be able to find a way to any water for it in place of that sunken water." This is what the words of al-Mawardi seem to imply, but it contradicts the apparent meaning.

The apparent meaning is that "or its water sinks away" is conjoined to "your garden becomes..." (*tusbih*). In that case, the word *husban* (reckoning, decree) must be understood as something by which the two matters would normally follow, such as the divine decree of destruction, since not every heavenly calamity results in the garden becoming a slippery barren ground (*sa'idan zalaqan*) and also in its water sinking away. It is also permissible that the conjunction be with "that He sends" (*yursila*). In that case, *husban* may be taken in the sense of one of the previous meanings. On this view, the believer has hoped for the ruin of his disbelieving companion's garden, either by a heavenly calamity or by an earthly one, which is the sinking of its water, so that everything in it of trees and crops is destroyed. However, he did not state explicitly the harm and ruin that follow from the sinking, perhaps because it is evident and because the reference to it is sufficient in his words "then you will not be able to" and so on. It has been objected that there is no defect in this conjunction, either in wording or in meaning. Yet the apparent form would have been to say: "or He makes its water sink away," or something similar in which the action is attributed to God, Exalted is He. The reason for the departure to the form in the noble text is not apparent, so reflect on this.

Then, most scholars hold that His saying "If you see me" and so on is in opposition to the disbeliever's saying "I am more than you in wealth" and so on. It seems they meant opposition in general, not complete correspondence. As for when the meaning of "company" (*nafar*) and "child" (*walad*) is not the same, this is evident. As for when it is the same, by taking *nafar* to mean child, then there are two matters, greater number and greater might (*aʿazziyyah*), and only the opposite of one of them is mentioned here, namely lesser number, which is attributed in meaning to wealth and children. Yes, it has been said that lesser children may entail lowliness, and greater number may entail might, as is observed among the Bedouin Arabs.

[Page 282]

This is it. The apparent form would have been for the answer to address the matter of children, as it addressed the matter of wealth, by saying: "and perhaps He will give me something better than your child, and afflict them with a calamity so that they become destroyed," or something similar. It has been answered that he did not address that only as an indication that love of wealth had taken hold of that disbeliever's heart, and that it suffices for his vexation and distress that his garden perish and that his believing companion be given something better than it. 

It has also been said that he did not address that because it involves hoping for the ruin of one who had not spoken to him in debate and dispute, nor had any resistance or boasting been transmitted from him, merely for the sake of vexing a disbeliever who debated, outnumbered, and boasted; and leaving that is better for the perfect and more complete for the excellent. Cursing against the unbelievers and their offspring, which proceeds from some of the prophets, peace be upon them, is not of this kind of hoping, as is not hidden from the reflective. Since he intended to leave this hoping, he left hoping for children for himself, either following it or because it was not important to him. It has also been said that he hoped for it in His saying "something better than your garden," because the intended meaning is "a thing better than your garden." An indefinite noun may be general with the help of context, so the child is included. But this is not a valid view.

It has also been said that he intended what is apparent, that is, "a garden better than your garden," except that the superiority is not complete without children, since no pleasure in wealth is complete for one who has no child. So hoping for a garden better than that garden entails hoping for children better than those children. He did not hope for the ruin of his child, so that their survival after the ruin of his garden would be a burden upon him. It is not hidden that the superiority of a garden does not come to mind except in respect of what pertains to its being a garden: abundance of trees, increase of fruit, plenty of river waters, and the like. His saying "so that it would be" and so on is a clear objection. It has also been said that he did not hope for children, being content with the children he already had, for the abundance of children is not something the perfect desire. In this there is room for doubt. It has also been said that he did not pair the hoping for the granting of children with the hoping for the granting of the garden, because that granting which is hoped for is in the Hereafter, and the Hereafter is not a place for the granting of children, since procreation ceases there. This is not hidden: even after granting that children are not given in the Hereafter to one who desires them, this is nothing. It has also been said that the hoping for children in His saying "better than your garden" is possible on the basis that he meant by "your garden" all that he had been provided with in the world, and the pronouns after it refer to it in the sense of the orchard, by way of *istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which one word is used with two meanings). This, as you see, is [weak], so reflect. And God, Exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book and is most informed.

A group read: *ghu'uran*, with a damma on the *ghayn*, a hamza after it, and a waw after both.

﴿وأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ﴾ أي أُهلِكَت أموالُه المعهودة من جنّتيه وما فيهما. وهو مأخوذ من إحاطة العدوّ، وهي استدارته به من جميع جوانبه. استُعملت في الاستيلاء والغلبة، ثم استُعملت في كل هلاك. وذكر الخفاجي أنّ في الكلام استعارةً تمثيلية (isti'ara tamthiliyya, an allegorical metaphor, in which a whole scene is figured by another)؛ شبّه إهلاك جنّتيه بما فيهما بإهلاك قومٍ أحاط بهم عدوٌّ وأوقع بهم بحيث لم ينجُ أحدٌ منهم. ويُحتمل أن تكون الاستعارة تبعية (tab'iyya, a metaphor in a verb or derived form). وبعضهم يجوّز كونها تمثيلية تبعية، انتهى. وجعلُ ذلك من باب الكناية (kinaya, metonymy or allusion) أظهر. والعطف على مقدّر، كأنه قيل: فوقع بعضُ ما تَرجّى وأُحيط إلخ. وحُذف لدلالة السباق والسياق عليه. واستُظهر أنّ الإهلاك كان ليلًا، لقوله تعالى: ﴿فَأصْبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ﴾. ويُحتمل أن تكون "أصبح" بمعنى "صار"، فلا تدلّ على تقييد الخبر بالصباح. ويجري هذان الأمران في «تُصبِحَ» و«يُصبِحَ» السابقين. ومعنى تقليب الكفّين على ما استظهره أبو حيّان أن يُبدي بطنَ كلٍّ منهما، ثم يعوّج يده حتى يبدو ظهرُ كلٍّ، يفعل ذلك مرارًا. وقال غيرُ واحد: هو أن يضع باطنَ إحداهما على ظهر الأخرى، ثم يعكس الأمر ويكرّر ذلك. وأيًّا كان فهو كناية عن النّدم والتحسّر. وليس ذلك من قولهم: قلّبتُ الأمرَ ظهرًا لبطن، كما في قول عمرو بن ربيعة:

وضربنا الحديثَ ظهرًا لبطنٍ وأتينا من أمرنا ما اشتهينا

فإنّ ذلك مجازٌ عن الانتقال من بعض الأحاديث إلى بعض. ولكونه كنايةً عن النّدم عُدّي بـ"على" في قوله تعالى: ﴿عَلى ما أنْفَقَ فِيها﴾. فالجارّ والمجرور ظرفٌ لغوٌ (zarf laghw, an adverbial phrase that is not a complement) متعلّقٌ بـ«يُقَلِّبُ»، كأنه قيل: فأصبح يندم على ما أنفق. ومنه يُعلم أنه يجوز في الكناية أن تُعدّى بصلة المعنى الحقيقي كما في قولهم: بنى عليها، وبصلة المعنى الكنائي كما هنا، فيجوز: بنى بها، ويكون القولُ بأنه غلطٌ غلطًا.

ويجوز أن يكون الجارّ والمجرور ظرفًا مستقرًّا (zarf mustaqarr, an adverbial phrase that is a complement with a specific sense) متعلّقُه خاصّ، وهو حالٌ من ضمير «يُقَلِّبُ»، أي: متحسّرًا على ما أنفق. وهو نظرًا إلى المعنى الكنائي حالٌ مؤكِّدة، على ما قيل، لأنّ التحسّر والنّدم بمعنًى. وقال بعضهم: إنّ التحسّر الحزن، وهو أخصّ من النّدم، فليُراجَع. وأيًّا كان فلا تضمينَ في الآية كما تُوُهِّم. وقُرئ: «تَقَلَّبُ كَفّاهُ»، أي: تتقلّب، ولا يخفى عليك أمر الجارّ والمجرور على هذا. و"ما" إمّا مصدريّة، أي: على إنفاقه في عمارتها، وإمّا موصولة، أي: على الذي أنفقه في عمارتها من المال، ويُقدَّر على هذا مضافٌ إلى الموصول من الأفعال الاختيارية إذا كان متعلّق الجارّ «يُقَلِّبُ» مرادًا منه يَندم، لأنّ النّدم إنما يكون على الأفعال الاختيارية. ويُعلم من هذا وجهُ تخصيص النّدم على ما أنفق بالذكر دون هلاك الجنّة. وقيل: لعلّ التخصيص لذلك، ولأنّ ما أنفق في عمارتها كان ما يُمكن صيانتُه عن طوارق الحَدَثان، وقد صرفه إلى مصالحها رجاءَ أن يتمتّع بها أكثرَ مما يتمتّع به، وكان يرى أنه لا تنالها أيدي الرّدى، ولذلك قال: ﴿ما أظُنُّ أنْ تَبِيدَ هَذِهِ أبَدًا﴾. فلمّا ظهر له أنها مما يعتريه الهلاك، ندم على ما صنع بناءً على الزعم الفاسد من إنفاق ما يُمكن ادّخاره في مثل هذا الشيء السريع الزوال، انتهى. والظاهر أنّ إهلاكها واستئصالَ نباتها وأشجارها كان دفعيًّا بآفة سماوية، ولم يكن تدريجيًّا بإذهاب ما به النماء وهو الماء. فقد قال الخفاجي: إنّ الآية تدلّ على وقوع استئصال نباتها وأشجارها عاجلًا بآفة سماوية صريحًا، لقوله تعالى: ﴿فَأصْبَحَ﴾ بالفاء التعقيبية، والتحسّرُ إنما يكون لما وقع بغتةً، فتأمّل.

﴿وهِيَ﴾ أي الجنّةُ من الأعناب المحفوفة بنخل ﴿خاوِيَةٌ﴾ أي ساقطة. وأصل الخواء، كما قيل: الخلاء. يقال: خوى بطنُه من الطعام يخوي خَوًى وخَواءً إذا خلا. وفي القاموس: خَوَتِ الدارُ تهدّمت، وخَوَتْ وخَوِيَتْ خَيًّا وخُوِيًّا وخَواءً وخَوايةً خَلَتْ من أهلها. وأُريد السقوط هنا لتعلّق قوله تعالى: ﴿عَلى عُرُوشِها﴾ بذلك. والعُروش جمع عَرْش، وهو هنا ما يُصنع من الأعمدة لتُوضع عليه الكروم. وسقوطُ الجنّة على العُروش لسقوطها قبلها، ولعلّ ذلك لأنه قد أصاب الجنّةَ من العذاب ما جعلها صعيدًا زَلَقًا لا يثبت فيها قائم. ولعلّ تخصيصَ حال الكروم بالذكر دون النخل والزرع إما لأنها العمدةُ وهما من متمّماتها، وإما لأنّ ذكرَ هلاكها على ما قيل مُغنٍ عن ذكر هلاك الباقي، لأنها حيث هلكت وهي مُسندةٌ بعُروشها فهلاكُ ما عداها بالطريق الأَولى، وإما لأنّ الإنفاق في عمارتها أكثرُ. ثم هذه الجملة تُبعد ما رُوي من أنّ الله تعالى أرسل عليها نارًا فأحرقتها وغار ماؤها، إلا أن يُراد منها مطلقُ الخراب، وحينئذٍ يجوز أن يُراد من «هِيَ» الجنّةُ بجميع ما اشتملت عليه. ﴿ويَقُولُ﴾ عطفٌ على ﴿يُقَلِّبُ﴾. وجوّز أبو البقاء وغيرُه أن يكون حالًا من الضمير المستتر فيه، بتقدير: وهو يقول؛ لأنّ المضارع المثبت لا يقترن بالواو الحالية إلا شذوذًا.

﴿يا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّي أحَدًا﴾ كأنه تذكّر موعظةَ أخيه وعلم أنه إنما أُتي من قِبل شركه، فتمنّى لو لم

[Page 284]

يكن مشركًا فلم يُصبه ما أصابه. قيل: ويُحتمل أن يكون توبةً من الشرك ونَدمًا عليه، فيكون تجديدًا للإيمان، لأنّ نَدمه على شركه فيما مضى يُشعر بأنه آمن في الحال، فكأنه قال: آمنتُ بالله تعالى الآنَ، وليتَ ذلك كان أولًا. لكن لا يخفى أنّ مجرّد النّدم على الكفر لا يكون إيمانًا، وإن كان النّدم على المعصية قد يكون توبةً إذا عزم على أن لا يعود، وكان النّدم عليها من حيث كونُها معصيةً، كما صرّح به في المواقف (al-Mawaqif, a work of kalam by al-Iji). وعلى فرض صحة قياسه بها لم يتحقق هنا من الكافر ندمٌ عليه من حيث هو كفر، بل بسبب هلاك جنّتيه. والآية فيما بعدُ ظاهرةٌ أيضًا في أنه لم يتُب عمّا كفر به، وهو إنكار البعث. والقولُ بأنه إنما لم تُقبل توبتُه عن ذلك لأنها كانت عند مشاهدة البأس، والإيمان إذ ذاك غيرُ مقبول، غيرُ مقبول؛ إذ غاية ما في الباب أنه إيمانٌ بعد مشاهدة إهلاك ماله، وليس في ذلك سلبُ الاختيار الذي هو مَناط التكليف، لا سيّما إذا كان ذلك الإهلاك للإنذار. نعم، إذا قيل: إنّ هذا حكايةٌ لما يقوله الكافر يوم القيامة، كما ذهب إليه بعضُ المفسّرين، كان وجهُ عدم القبول ظاهرًا، إذ لا ينفع تجديدُ الإيمان هناك بالاتفاق.

﴿And there was not for him﴾ al-Akhawan (the two brothers), Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ayyub, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, and Ibn Jarir read «يَكُنْ» (yakun) with the yā' of the third person masculine, because the subject that follows it, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fi'atun﴾ (a group), is not truly feminine. The verb precedes its subject, and the two are separated by the accusative (the object). In His saying, glorified is He, ﴿yansurunahu﴾ (they help him), the meaning was taken into account, so the plural pronoun was used.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: «ولَمْ تَكُنْ لَهُ فِئَةٌ تَنْصُرُهُ» (and there was not for him a group that helps him), taking into account the wording only. The intended sense of "help" (naṣrah) is its necessary consequence, which is the capacity to do it. That is: there was not for him a group able to help him, either by warding off destruction before it occurs, or by restoring the one destroyed in person, according to the view that it is permissible to restore the non-existent in the same individual, or by restoring something like it, according to the view that this is not permissible.

﴿besides God﴾ For He, exalted and glorified is He, alone is able to help him. Figurative usage (majāz) was employed, because if this were kept to its literal sense, it would imply that God Most High helps him. For when one says: "No one helps Zayd besides Bakr," it is understood from it, by customary usage, that Bakr helps him. That is not the intended meaning; rather the intended meaning is what you have heard. Its essence is: none are able to help him except God Most High, the All-Powerful. ﴿And he was not﴾ in himself ﴿one who could defend himself﴾ (munta_ṣiran), that is, unable to protect himself by his own strength from the vengeance of God Most High upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 44:

﴿Hunalika﴾ means: in that station and that state in which the destruction occurred. ﴿Al-walayatu lillahi al-haqq﴾ means: the support (al-nusrah) belongs to Allah alone, the Exalted; no one is able to provide it except Him. So the clause is a confirmation and an emphasis of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he had no party to help him﴾, etc. Or it means: in that situation He gives support to His friends, the believers, against the disbelievers, just as He, glorified is He, gave support by what He did to the disbeliever's brother, the believer. So walayah bears the meaning of support on both readings, except that on the first reading it is unrestricted, or restricted to the one under compulsion and the one upon whom destruction fell; and on this reading it is restricted to other than the one under compulsion, namely the believers. What supports that the intended meaning is their support is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is better in reward and better in outcome﴾, meaning in consequence for His friends. It has been argued that since the verse concludes with the situation of the friends, it is appropriate that its beginning be likewise.

Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Shaybah, Ibn Ghazwan from Talhah, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Isa al-Isfahani and Ibn Jarir read: "al-wilayah" with a kasrah on the waw. According to some lexicographers, it and al-walayah with a fatha have the same meaning, like al-wakalah and al-wikalah, and al-wasayah and al-wisayah. Al-Zamakhshari said: with a fatha it means support and patronage, and with a kasrah it means authority and dominion; that is, there, the authority belongs to Him, mighty and majestic, which cannot be overcome, cannot be resisted, and other than Him is not worshipped, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾.

Thus the clause serves as an indication that His saying ﴿O would that I had not associated﴾, etc., was out of compulsion and distress at what had befallen him, and not out of regret and repentance. It is reported from Abu 'Amr and al-Asma'i that they said: the kasrah on the waw is a lahn (error) here, because fi'alah comes only for what is a craft and a conferred meaning, like al-kitabah, al-imarah and al-khilafah; and here there is no assuming of a matter; rather it is al-walayah with a fatha, meaning religion with a kasrah. But this is not relied upon.

Abu Hayyan preferred that ﴿Hunalika﴾ refers to the Hereafter; that is, in that abode the walayah belongs to Allah, the Truth. This accords with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is better in reward and better in outcome﴾, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer﴾. The apparent meaning on all of this is that the pause is at ﴿munتصiran﴾ (victorious/defended), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hunalika﴾ etc. begins a new utterance. In that case, al-walayah is the subject and "lillah" the predicate, the adverbial phrase is dependent on the stative verb, and the sentence conveys restriction by definiteness of the subject, and the predicate being joined with the particle of exclusivity, as established in "al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin." Abu al-Baqa' said: "hunalika" may be the predicate of "al-walayah," or "al-walayah" may be raised by it, and "lillah" is related to the adverbial phrase, or to its governing element, or to "al-walayah"; and it may be related to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause describing it.

Some said: the adverbial phrase is related to "munتصiran" (defended), and the reference is to the Hereafter, and the intended sense is the report of the negation that he would be victorious in the Hereafter after the negation that he would have a party to support him in this world. Al-Zajjaj also made it related to "munتصiran," but he said: "and he was not victorious in that state." "Al-haqq" is an adjective of the noble Name.

Al-Akhawan, Humayd, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, al-Yazidi and Ibn Isa al-Isfahani read: "al-haqqu" with a raf', as an adjective of ﴿al-walayah﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is" or "he is" the truth, and that it be a subject whose predicate is that. Ubayy read: "Hunalika al-walayatu al-haqqu lillahi" with "al-haqq" placed first and raised, and this favors "al-haqq" being an adjective of "al-walayah" in the previous reading.

Abu Haywah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu al-Sammal and Ya'qub from 'Ismah from Abu 'Amr read: "al-haqqa" with a nasb, as an absolute object emphasizing the content of the sentence, its governing element being an implied verb, as in your saying: "this is the servant of Allah, truly (haqqan)." It is also possible that it is a cut-off (maqta') adjective.

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Hamzah, 'Asim and Khalaf read: "'uqban" with a sukun on the qaf and tanwin; and from 'Asim "'uqba" with the feminine alif maqsurah on the pattern of ruj'a. The majority read it with a damma on the qaf and tanwin. The meaning in all of them is what has preceded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 45:

﴿And set forth for them the parable of the life of this world.﴾ That is, mention to them that which resembles it in its brightness, its freshness, and the swiftness of its passing, so that they will not be deceived by it and turn away entirely from the Hereafter. Or, mention to them its wondrous description, which is so strange that it is like a parable, and make it clear to them.

﴿Like water﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence) explaining the parable: that is, it is ﴿like water which We sent down from the sky﴾. They also permitted that it be a second object (maf'ul thani) of "uḍrib" (set forth), on the basis that it carries the sense of "ṣayyir" (make). It was objected that the particle kaf (like) rejects this, unless it is superfluous (muqhamah). It was answered that this is not a valid view, because the meaning would be "make the parable this utterance," so "the parable" would mean the speech in which the comparison occurs. Al-Hufi said: the kaf is connected to an omitted element that describes an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "a striking like water." This is nothing.

﴿So there mingled with it the vegetation of the earth﴾: that is, it became intertwined, and some of it mixed with other parts because of its abundance and density, owing to the great amount of water given to it. Or the meaning is: the water entered into the plants until they were saturated and flourished. In this sense the expected wording would have been "fakhtalaṭa bi-nabāti al-arḍ" (it mixed with the vegetation of the earth), because the familiar usage in language and common practice is to use the particle bi (with) with the abundant element that is not the incidental one. Although, by the lexical convention, each of the two that interpenetrate may be said to be "mixing" and "mixed with," the wording of the noble text was chosen for emphasis on the abundance of the water, so that it is as if it were the principal, abundant element. Thus there is an acceptable inversion (qalb) in the speech.

﴿Then it became﴾ that vegetation which was intertwined, after its splendour and freshness, ﴿stubble﴾: that is, dry and crumbling. It is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). It was also said that it is the plural of hashimah (a single dry stalk). Here "asbaha" means "became," so it does not restrict the report to the morning, as in the verse of the poet:

"I have become one who no longer bears a weapon, nor owns the halter of a camel if it bolts."

It was also said that it remains on its literal sense and restricts the report to that time, because heavenly calamities most often strike at night. This was objected to: there is nothing in the verse indicating that its becoming stubble is due to a heavenly calamity. Rather, the intended meaning is to explain what it turns into after freshness, namely dryness and crumbling, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ ﴿and then made it dark stubble﴾ ﴿which the winds scatter﴾. That is, ﴿tadhruhu al-riyāḥ﴾ means "the winds scatter it," as Abu 'Ubayda said. Al-Akhfash said: "they lift it up." Ibn Kaysan said: "they bring it and take it away." Ibn Mas'ud read "tudhrīhi" (with the verb in the fourth form, from adhrā, a dialectal variant of dharā). Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Muhaysin, Khalaf, Ibn 'Isa, and Ibn Jarir read "tadhruhu al-rīḥu" with the singular. The thing compared is not the water itself, but the configuration abstracted from the whole sentence: the state of the plant that grows by water, becoming green and swaying, then becoming dry, scattered by the winds until it is as if it had never been.
