The particle fa (then) is used in the verse to indicate the swiftness of its passing and its becoming that state, so it is not an elucidatory fa (fa fasihiyya). Others said it is an elucidatory fa, and the implied sense is: "it grew, and remained for a period, then it became stubble."

﴿And Allah is over all things﴾ among the things, of which creating and annihilating are part, ﴿Omnipotent﴾, perfect in power.

[Page 286]

﴿The wealth and the children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ is an explanation of the status of what they were boasting of among the embellishments of worldly life, just as the disbelieving brother boasted of such things after the explanation of the status of the life itself through the parable mentioned earlier. The mention of wealth before children, although children are more beloved to most people, is due to the eminence of wealth in what it is associated with of adornment, support, and other things.

Its generality, with respect to individuals and times, is that it is an adornment and a support for every person, whether fathers or sons, at every time and moment. As for children, their adornment and support come only with respect to those who have reached fatherhood. Also, wealth is the means for the preservation of the self, while children are for the preservation of the species. Also, the need for it is more pressing than the need for them. Also, it precedes them in existence. Also, it is an adornment without them, but not vice versa, for whoever has children without wealth is in the narrowest state and misery. So it is stated in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary). The word "zinah" (adornment) is a verbal noun, but it is used for that with which one adorns oneself, for emphasis. For this reason it is predicated of two things. Its annexation to "the life of this world" is possessive (ikhtisasiyyah, specifying). It is also permitted that it be in the sense of "in," so the meaning is: what they boast of, the wealth and the children, is something adorned with in the life of this world. Its status in quick passing and nearness to vanishing is known, so what is to be thought of that which is among its attributes, whose nature is to pass away before it passes away?

It is mentioned that this is an indication refuting their boasting in wealth and children, as if it were said: "The wealth and the children are the adornment of the life of this world, and everything that is the adornment of the life of this world is quickly passing away. Therefore the wealth and the children are quickly passing away." The minor premise is self-evident, and the major premise is known from what has preceded regarding the explanation of the status of the life of this world itself. Then it is said: "The wealth and the children are quickly passing away, and everything quickly passing away [is such that] it is ugly for the intelligent person to boast of it. Therefore, the wealth and the children are such that it is ugly for the intelligent person to boast of them." Both premises are clear, with no concealment.

[Page 287]

﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Increase in the enduring good deeds." It was said: "What are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Takbir (saying Allahu akbar), tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah), tasbih (saying Subhan Allah), tahmid (saying al-hamdu li-llah), and la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (there is no might nor power except with Allah)."

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu li-llah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, and la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. They are the enduring good deeds, and they cause sins to fall away as a tree sheds its leaves, and they are from the treasures of Paradise."

Its interpretation has come in accordance with what has been mentioned, and in other reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas its interpretation as what has also been mentioned, but without the last statement.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated in another report from him its interpretation as the five daily prayers.

Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in another report from him, also, its interpretation as all good deeds.

In its meaning is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Qatadah, that they are everything done seeking the Face of Allah, Exalted. And from al-Hasan and Ibn 'Ata', that they are the good intentions. Al-Tabari and others preferred what is in the last report from Ibn 'Abbas, and what has come in the mentioned reports and others is included within it.

Al-Khafaji claimed that everything mentioned in its interpretation, other than the general, was mentioned by way of illustration (tamthil). This is refuted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "And they are the enduring," which is restrictive (hasr, exclusivity) after the specification of what has no generality, so reflect. In any case, "al-baqiyat" is an attribute of an implied noun, such as "al-kalimat" (the words) or "al-a'mal" (the deeds). The attribution of "al-baqiyat" to that is metaphorical (majaz), meaning "whose fruit and reward remain," by the indication of what follows. So it is an attribute applied to other than what it originally belongs to, or there is an implied subject raised by the attribute, annexed to a pronoun referring to the described noun, in which the genitive pronoun became hidden and was raised after its deletion. Likewise, the deeds of the poor believers who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening, seeking His Face, enter (into this meaning) first and foremost, for they have the greatest share of every kind of good. The statement contains an honoring of their status and a belittling of the rank of their hater. It is as if it were said: What those disbelievers boast of, the wealth and the children, is quickly passing away and should not be boasted of, while what those believers have brought is ﴿better﴾ than that ﴿with your Lord﴾, that is, in the Hereafter. This is an explanation of that in which the effects of its superiority appear, in the manner of the annexation of "adornment" to "the life of this world," for its excellence over wealth and children, although all share in the origin, since neither of them shares in the superiority in the Hereafter. It is also said: The meaning of "with your Lord" is in His judgment, Glorified and Exalted be He: ﴿as reward﴾, recompense and wage. It was also said: as benefit.

﴿And better in hope﴾, since its possessor attains in the Hereafter what he hopes for through it in this world, whereas wealth and children do not bring that to their owner. The repetition of "better" is for emphasis. It was also said: it is for the sake of the first and to indicate the difference of the two aspects of superiority.

[p. 288]

﴿And [remember] the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied «اذْكُرْ» (udhkur, "remember"). The sense is: "Remember the Day We uproot the mountains from their places and set them moving through the air like clouds, as His words indicate: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾." It has also been said that the meaning is: "We set their parts in motion after making them scattered dust," in which case the speech contains an omitted noun (hadhf mudaf, "omission of a governed noun"). It is also permissible that "setting in motion" is a figurative usage (majaz, "non-literal usage") meaning removal and annihilation, by mentioning the cause and intending the effect. The sense would then be: "Remember the Day We take them away and scatter them with a scattering," and this is like His words: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to powder﴾ ﴿and become scattered dust﴾. An objection has been raised to both views:
[p. 289]
The transformation of the mountains into scattered dust, and their removal, come after their being set in motion. Some scholars of verification (muhaqqiqun), deriving from the verses, have mentioned that first the mountains will separate from the earth and be set moving through the air, then they will fall and become a heap of sand that flows, then scattered dust. The apparent meaning here is the first state of the mountains, and there is no reason to turn away from the apparent meaning. Then the purpose of mentioning this is to warn the polytheists of the calamities in it, which are greater than the "third of the three stones" (thalithat al-athafi, the three stones of a cooking pot, a proverbial image for the smallest of hardships). Abu Hayyan and others permitted that «يَوْمَ» (yawma, "the Day") be an adverbial complement of an implied verb at His words ( قَدْ جِئْتُمُونا ) "Indeed you have come to Us" etc., meaning: "We said on such a day: Indeed you have come to Us." There is something in this which you will know there, if God the Exalted wills. Many others permitted that it is coordinated with what precedes it, His words ( عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ ) "with your Lord," so that it is governed by ( خَيْرٌ ) "is better," meaning: "The enduring good deeds are better with your Lord, and on the Day of Resurrection." In that case it is necessary that «عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ» (ʿinda rabbika, "with your Lord") be understood as His judgment, as has been said.

Ibn Amir, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, al-Hasan, Shibl, Qatada, ʿIsa, al-Zuhri, Humayd, Talha, al-Yazidi, and al-Zubayri from his transmitters, from Yaʿqub, read «تُسَيَّرُ الجِبالُ» (tusayyaru al-jibalu, "the mountains are set in motion") with «الجِبالُ» in the nominative and «تُسَيَّرُ» in the passive form with the third-person feminine prefix, following the patterns of majesty (sunan al-kibriya') and signifying that it dispenses with mention of the agent since it is determined. It is reported from al-Hasan that he read it likewise, except that he used the letter yaʾ instead of the letter tāʾ. Ubayy read «سُيِّرَتِ الجِبالُ» (suyyirati al-jibalu) in the past passive with «الجِبالُ» in the nominative. Ibn Muhaysin and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr read «تَسِيرُ الجِبالُ» (tasiru al-jibalu) in the present active with a prefixed tāʾ and «الجِبالُ» in the nominative.

﴿And you see the earth﴾: this is an address to the master of those addressed (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of seeing. The meaning: "You see all sides of the earth ﴿laid bare﴾, exposed and visible." As for the visibility of what was beneath the mountains, it is evident. As for the rest, the mountains had been blocking it from the observer's view before that. Or you see it laid bare because all that was on it has disappeared—the mountains, seas, buildings and trees. The mention is limited to the removal of the mountains because it is known from this that the removal of those things follows by a stronger inference. It has been said that attributing "being laid bare" to the earth is figurative, and what is meant is: "You see the people of the earth coming out from its inside," but this goes against the apparent meaning.

ʿIsa read «وتُرى الأرْضُ» (wa-turā al-ardu) with the verb in the passive and «الأرْضُ» in the nominative. ﴿And We gather them﴾, meaning: We assemble them at the place of standing (al-mawqif) from every direction after We have raised them from their graves. The agent is not mentioned because its intention is clear; according to what has been said, it is mentioned [implicitly]. The choice of the past tense after «نُسَيِّرُ» (nusayyiru, "We set in motion") and «تَرى» (tara, "you see") serves to indicate the certainty of the gathering, which follows from the resurrection that the deniers deny, and upon which the matter of recompense depends. The same discussion applies to what is coordinated with it, whether negated or affirmed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is for indicating that their gathering takes place before the setting in motion and the exposure, so that they may witness those terrors and great events; as if it were said: 'And We gathered them before that.'" Objection has been raised that some verses together with reports indicate that the setting in motion and exposure occur at the first blast of the trumpet, along with the breakdown of the order of the world, while the gathering and what is coordinated with it occur at the second blast. Therefore it is not appropriate to take the verse to mean "And We had gathered them before that," lest it contradict other verses; so let this be considered. Furthermore, it should not be hidden that the use of the past tense on the first reading is figurative, but on this reading it is literal, because the past and the future are considered in relation to the verb that accompanies them, not in relation to the time of speaking. According to this, the clause, as stated in al-Kashf and elsewhere, may be coordinated or be a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of «نُسَيِّرُ». Abu Hayyan said: "It is better to make it a circumstantial clause on this view," and some insisted on it, giving as reason that if it were coordinated, the past would not be relative to the setting in motion and exposure, but to the time of speaking, requiring the first interpretation. Then he said: "The verification of this is that verb forms are established for the times of speaking when they are unrestricted; but when they are made qualifiers of something that indicates a time, their past or other tense is relative to that time." This is not a valid argument. The correct view is that it is not obligatory. The verification of this is that clauses which apparently are coordinated may be either concurrent or differing in time. If this is so in reality, there is no difficulty; and if it is not, then a reason for the deviation must be present. If one of the two clauses qualifies the other, and the past tense is relative to it, then it is literal, for the reason mentioned, and the clause is not coordinated in that case. If they are coordinated, and the past is relative to one of the two coordinated elements, there is no obstacle to it; but whether it is literal or figurative is open to question. What fairness dictates is preferring Abu Hayyan's view that the circumstantial reading is more appropriate. The claim that it has no basis has no basis. In that case, «قَدْ» (qad, "indeed") is assumed by most scholars, meaning: "And [indeed] We have gathered them."

﴿So We leave out none of them﴾, meaning: We do not leave any behind. It is said: "ghadarahu" and "aghdarahu" when one leaves him behind; from it comes «الغَدْرُ» (al-ghadr, "betrayal"), which is abandoning fidelity, and «الغَدِيرُ» (al-ghadir, "pool"), which is water left by the torrent upon the land. It is read «يُغادِرُ» (yughadiru) with the third-person masculine, the pronoun referring to God the Exalted, by way of iltifat (a shift from one grammatical person to another). Qatada read «تُغادِرُ» (tughadiru) with the feminine, the pronoun referring to the earth, as in His words: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾. Abu Hayyan permitted that the pronoun refers to [divine] power. Aban ibn Yazid from ʿAsim read it likewise, or with the letter dāl vocalized with a fatha, in the passive, with «أحَدٌ» (ahadun, "anyone") in the nominative as a substitute for the agent. Al-Dahhak read «نُغْدِرْ» (nughdir) with a damma on the nun, sukun on the ghayn, and a kasra on the dāl.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 48:**

﴿And they will be presented before your Lord﴾: they will be brought to the place of His judgment and decree, may He be exalted and glorified, concerning them. ﴿In rows﴾: arranged in lines, or set in ranks.

Ibn Mandah narrated in *al-Tawhid* from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, will call out on the Day of Resurrection: O My servants, I am Allah, there is no god but Me, the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Just of judges, and the Swiftest of reckoners. Bring forward your proofs and prepare your answers, for you are to be questioned and reckoned. O My angels, set My servants in rows upon the tips of their toes for the reckoning."

In the sound hadith: "Allah, may He be exalted, will gather the first and the last into one plain, in rows; the caller will make them hear, and the sight will reach them all." The hadith is cited in full.

It has also been said: every nation and group will be set up in its own row.

In some reports: "The people of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection will be a hundred and twenty rows, of which you are eighty."

It has been said: there is no presenting in the literal sense of being displayed, and no lining up. The statement is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*): their state at the gathering is likened to the state of soldiers presented before a ruler so that he may command concerning them as he wills. It has also been said that there is an implicit metaphor (*isti'ara taba'iyya*) in which their gathering is likened to the presenting of these people. As for the word *saffan* (in rows), whether it falls within the allegorical metaphor or is a supporting element (*tarshih*) of it, its meaning is: not scattered and not mixed together. Thus there is no indication in it of the rows being one row or many.

There is no need to say that it is a singular noun used to mean the plural because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), i.e. "rows." Nor is there need to say that the original form is *saffan saffan* (row after row). Moreover, even with its distance, this would face the objection that what indicates multiplicity by repetition, such as *baban baban* (door after door) and *saffan saffan*, may not be omitted. The truth is that denying the lining up is something without basis, once its possibility and the soundness of the reports about it are established. Perhaps what we have explained about the verse is free of any blemish. In the shift to the third person (*iltifat*), the construction of the verb in the passive voice, and the mention of the title of Lordship with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is evidently the cultivation of awe, the following of the ways of Majesty, and the manifestation of kindness toward him, upon him be prayers and peace.

It has been said concerning His words, ﴿upon your Lord﴾, that it indicates Allah's anger toward them and His casting them out from the register of acceptance, because they did not live by knowledge of His Lordship, may He be exalted and glorified.

﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾ is an address to the disbelievers who denied the Resurrection, with an implied verb of speech (*idmar al-qawl*). It may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to what precedes, so it is to be read as: "saying" or "We say," if it is a circumstance of the subject of *hasharna* (We gathered); or "saying," if it is a circumstance of *Rabbika* (your Lord); or "being told," if it is of the pronoun in *ur'idu* (they were presented); or "it is said to them," if it is of the pronoun in *ur'idu*.

[Page 290]

It may also be read as an implied verb such as *qulna* (We said) or *naqulu* (We say), and then its clause has no grammatical position (*la mahalla lahu*). On this reading, it is permitted to link the earlier *yawm* (day) to it, but not if it is read as a circumstance.

Al-Khafaji said: "Because then it would become like *ghulam Zayd darban* (Zayd's servant, striking), where *darban* is a circumstance of Zayd while governing *ghulam* (servant). Such a convolution (*ta'qid*) is impermissible. It is not because that [the coming] is before the gathering and this is after it, nor because the object of a circumstance may not precede it, as is wrongly supposed." Then he said: "As for the objection raised against linking it to the verb in the second reading, that it implies that this speech is the primary purpose, it is an imagining which needs no refutation, since there is no prohibition in it." End of quotation. The truth is that linking it to the implied speech as a circumstance or otherwise is not something a sound disposition or a straight mind accepts, and such a construction hardly is permissible on the reading of it as a circumstance, even if we allow the object of a circumstance to precede it. So reflect on this.

What is meant by their coming to Him, may He be exalted, is their coming to a place where no judgment belongs to anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, from among the false objects of worship, which their worshippers claim have power to benefit and to harm, and other things. This is like what was said concerning His words, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾.

﴿As We created you﴾ is a qualifier (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a coming like your coming when We created you ﴿the first time﴾.

Or it is a circumstance of the pronoun in ﴿you have come to Us﴾, meaning: being as We created you the first time, barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, or with nothing of what you boasted of, such as wealth and helpers. This is based on His words: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you behind your backs.﴾

It is permitted that what is meant is their being living, like their first creation. The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of this is as mentioned before, but it differs in the aspect of comparison. The latter, as has been said, fits better with what precedes. This is with His words: ﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you an appointed time.﴾

This is a turning away (*idrab*) and a transition from one speech to another, both of them for rebuke and reproach. *Al-Mawid* (the appointed time) is a noun of time. *An* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, separated from its predicate by the negative particle, because the verb in the clause is a verbal sentence whose verb is inflected and not a supplication (*du'a'*). In such a case the separation by one of the known separators is required, except in rare instances. The verb *ja'ala* (appoint) is either in the sense of making (*tasyir*), in which case the prepositional phrase is its second object and *mawidan* is its first object; or in the sense of creating and bringing into being (*khalq wa-ijad*), in which case the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstance of its object, which is *mawidan*. That is: you claimed in the world that We would never make for you a time in which what We promised of the Resurrection and what follows it would be fulfilled.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (al-Alusi) on Surah 18, verse 49:

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and they will be presented﴾.

It falls under the terrifying matters for whose time-mention the warning to the polytheists was intended, as has passed. The use of the past tense form (*sigha al-madi*) indicates the certainty (*al-taqarrur*) of the event. By "the Book" is meant the books of deeds, and the *alif-lam* in it is for comprehensiveness (*al-istighraq*, totality). As for the "placing" (*wad'*), it is either the placing of each book in the hand of its owner, the right hand or the left, or the placing of each in the Balance (*al-mizan*). It is also permissible that what is meant is the angels placing those books in the midst so that they may call the responsible persons to account by what is in them. On this view, it is also permissible that "the Book" means a single book, by the angels, peace be upon them, gathering all the records of deeds into one book and placing it in the midst for the reckoning. But I have not found a narration (*athar*) supporting this. Yes, al-Laqqani said, in his commentary on his words in *Jawharat al-Tawhid*:

*And it is obligatory to take the records of the servants,*
*as is known from the Qur'an, explicitly.*

Al-Ghazali affirmed what has been said: that the records of the servants will have what is in all of them copied into one record. End of quote. The apparent reading is that al-Ghazali and his like affirmed this only on the basis of a narration, since such a thing is not said on the basis of opinion (*ra'y*), as is apparent. It has also been said that the placing of the Book is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for making manifest the reckoning of creation and their questioning, for when the reckoning of workers is intended, the ledgers are brought and placed before them, then they are called to account. Thus the necessary thing (*al-mazum*) is mentioned and its concomitant (*lazimuh*) is intended. It is not hidden that there is no need for this in our view, though it may be prompted by the denial of the weighing of deeds.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: *"wa-wada'a al-kitab"* (and He placed the Book), with *wada'a* in the active voice and its attribution to His pronoun, may He be exalted, by way of *iltifat* (the shift from third to first person, here in grammatical person), and the Book in the accusative as the object. That is: and Allah placed the Book.

﴿Then you will see the criminals﴾ all of them, so that the disbelievers who denied the Resurrection enter among them at the first level. The address (*khitab*) is similar to what has passed, ﴿fearful﴾, afraid, ﴿of what is in it﴾, i.e., in the Book, of the crimes and sins, because they are certain of the punishment that follows from them. ﴿And they will say﴾, upon their coming upon what is in its folds, small and great: ﴿Woe to us!﴾ It is a call (*nida'*) to their destruction, which they have brought upon themselves among the destructions. For *al-wayla* is like *al-wayl*, destruction. And calling it, by likening it to a person whose presence is sought, is as if it were said: "O destruction, come, for this is your time." In it is a concealed figurative metaphor (*isti'arah makniyyah takhyiliyyah*). In it is also a rebuke to them and an indication that they have no companion except destruction, and they have sought it so that they might be destroyed and not see the painful punishment.

It has also been said that what is meant is calling those present with them, as if it were said: "O you who are present with us, look at our destruction." In this there is an assumption by which that subtlety is lost.

﴿What is this Book's matter?﴾ That is: what is its condition? The interrogative is figuratively used for amazement at the state of the Book. The *lam* of the preposition was written separately in the *Imam* (the 'Uthmanic codex), and al-Tabarsi claimed there was no basis for that. Al-Biqa'i said: in writing it thus there is an indication that the criminals, because of the severity of distress, pause upon part of the word. In *Lata'if al-Isharat* it is said: Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub stopped on *ma*, while the rest stopped on the *lam*. The more correct is to stop on *ma*, because it is an independent word. Most of them did not mention anything about it. End of quote. You know that the 'Uthmani script is followed and is not to be analogized upon, and its reason is hardly known. As for the goodness of stopping on *ma* or on the *lam*, I have a hesitation about it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It leaves nothing﴾, that is, does not leave, ﴿small﴾, that is, a small matter, ﴿nor great﴾ ﴿except that it has counted it﴾, that is, except that it has numbered it. This is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for comprehensiveness. It is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*) confirming what is in the interrogative sentence of amazement, or it is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah istinafiyyah*) built upon a question arising from the amazement, as if it were said: "What is the condition of this Book, that it should be marvelled at?" Then it was said: ﴿It leaves nothing small﴾, and so on.

It is reported from Ibn Jubayr that the small is interpreted as touching (sexual touch, *al-masis*) and the great as fornication (*al-zina*). Ibn Abi al-Dunya, in *Dhamm al-Ghibah*, and Ibn Abi Hatim, reported from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the verse: "The small is smiling in mockery at the believers, and the great is laughing at that." On this the report of Ibn Mardawayh is to be understood, in which, from him, may Allah be pleased with him, the small is interpreted as smiling and the great as laughing. The difficulty raised by some scholars is thereby resolved, and it is known from it that laughing at people is among the sins.

From 'Abd Allah ibn Zam'ah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ giving a sermon and admonishing them for laughing at a wind that came out with a sound, and he said: "Why does one of you laugh at what he himself does?"

Indeed, some of our scholars mentioned that among laughter is that by which the one laughing becomes a disbeliever, like laughing at a word of disbelief. Some restricted this to the case where one is able to control himself; otherwise he does not become a disbeliever. The complete discussion of that is in its proper place.

It would have been apparent to say: "It leaves nothing great nor small," on the basis of what they stated, that in affirmation the ascent goes from the lower to the higher, and in negation it is the reverse; since the performance of the lesser does not necessarily entail the performance of the greater, unlike negation. But the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*) said: this applies when it is in its apparent sense. But if it is a metonymy for generality, as here, and as in your saying: "He did not give me little nor much," it is permissible to put the lower before the higher in negation, as Ibn al-Athir explained in *al-Mathal al-Sa'ir*. In *al-Bahr* the small is placed first for the sake of concern with it. It is reported from al-Fudayl that whenever he recited the verse he would say: "By Allah, they cry out from the small sins before the great ones." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: "The people complain, as you hear, of the counting, and no one complains of injustice. So beware of the trifling sins, for they are gathered upon their owner until they destroy him."

﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of evil deeds, or the recompense of that, ﴿present﴾, recorded in the book of each of them, or ready (*'atid*) before them, cash, not deferred. The latter meaning was chosen, though it involves departing from the apparent sense, because speech according to it is purely foundational (*ta'sis mahd*). ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ by what he did not do; that is, of them, or of them and others. The intended meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, does not exceed the limit He set in reward and punishment, even though it is not obligatory upon Him, exalted, by reason. Its verification is that He, exalted, promised to reward the obedient and increase their reward, and to punish the disobedient in proportion to their offence without excess, and that He may forgive what is other than disbelief, and that He does not punish without offence. So He, glorified and exalted, does not exceed the limit He set, nor oppose what His divine custom (*sunnah ilahiyyah*) has gone upon. He does not punish anyone for what he did not do, nor diminish the reward of what he did of what He commanded and approved, nor increase the punishment, appropriate to his deed, of what He forbade and did not approve.

This is among what the Muslims have agreed upon, though they differ on whether the impossibility of the occurrence of what is negated is by revelation (*sam'i*) or by reason (*'aqli*). The first view was taken by the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*), and the second by the Mu'tazilah. And is the naming of that exceeding (*mujawazah*) "injustice" literal or not? Al-Khafaji said: the apparent view is that it is literal. On this view there is no need to say that the meaning of the verse is that He, glorified, does not do to anyone what would be injustice if it came from servants, such as punishing without sin. For if it came from servants it would be injustice, but if it came from Him, glorified, it would not be so, since He, majestic is His affair, is the Owner of the dominion, disposing of His dominion as He wills. So no injustice whatsoever is conceivable in His affair, exalted is His affair, in any way according to the People of the Sunnah. You know that this is the well-known view among the majority, not what verification requires. So reflect. And Allah, exalted, is the Guardian of success.

From the generality of the verse it is inferred that the children of polytheists are not punished, and this is the victorious (*al-mansur*) opinion. We have previously mentioned, and to Allah, exalted, is the praise, what supports it from the reports.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 18, verse 50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We said﴾, i.e., remember the time when We said ﴿to the angels﴾, all of them, as is the apparent meaning. Some Sufis (*sufiyya*, mystics) excluded the *al-muhayyimun* (the angels absorbed in awe of God), and others excluded the angels of the heaven altogether, claiming that the one addressed was the angels of the earth.

﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, a prostration of greeting and honour; or, prostrate toward his direction, in the sense of taking him as a *qibla* (direction of prayer) for your prostration to God, the Exalted. The full discussion of this has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾, all of them, entirely, in obedience to the command, ﴿except Iblis﴾. He was not among those who prostrated; rather, he refused and became arrogant. The words of the Exalted, ﴿he was of the jinn﴾, are an independent clause brought as an explanation for what the exception concerning the accursed one from among those who prostrated implies. It was said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the excepted noun, with *qad* implied, and the connecting element is the pronoun. This is the preference of Abu al-Baqa'. The first view (that it is an independent clause) is closer to the mind, as if it were said: "What is his case, that he did not prostrate?" And it was answered: "His origin was of the jinn." This is apparent in showing that he was not of the angels. Yes, he was with them and counted among their number.

Ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] has transmitted from Sa'd ibn Mas'ud, who said: The angels used to fight the jinn, and Iblis was taken captive while he was young, so he was with the angels and worshipped by prostrating with them. Something similar has been transmitted from Shahr ibn Hawshab, and this is the view of many scholars. So much so that al-Hasan said, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim: "God fight against peoples who claim that Iblis was of the angels, while God, the Exalted, says: ﴿he was of the jinn﴾." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Anbari in *Kitab al-Adda'* (*The Book of Homonyms*), and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama* transmitted from him that he said: "Iblis was not of the angels for the blink of an eye, and he is indeed the origin of the jinn just as Adam, peace be upon him,

[Page 293]

is the origin of mankind." In this is an indication that there was no jinn before him, just as there was no mankind before Adam, peace be upon him. There is in the heart's acceptance of its soundness what there is. Closer to soundness than this is what a group of scholars said: that there were jinn before him, but they perished and had no offspring other than him. So the jinn and devils today are all his descendants. Thus he is to the jinn as Noah, peace be upon him, is to mankind, according to what is well known. It was also said: He was of the angels, and the jinn are a tribe of them. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas.

In another narration from him, may God be pleased with both of them, that Iblis was among the nobles of the angels and the most honoured of them in lineage. He was a guardian over the gardens, and he had authority over the lowest heaven, and he had the meeting place of the two seas, the sea of Rome and the sea of Persia, and authority over the earth. He saw that by this he had greatness and nobility over the people of heaven, so pride entered his soul, which no one knew of except God, the Exalted. When he was commanded to prostrate, his pride that was in his soul appeared, so God, the Exalted, cursed him until the Day of Resurrection. According to what Qatada transmitted from him, he would say:

"If he had not been of the angels, he would not have been commanded to prostrate."

This has been answered with what we indicated just now and with other things that are not hidden. Ibn Jubayr also took this view, and a group transmitted from him that he said: "The jinn in the verse is a tribe of the angels who never ceased fashioning the adornments of the people of Paradise until the Hour arrives." In another narration from him, the meaning of ﴿he was of the jinn﴾ is that he was of the guardians of the gardens, and this is a strange interpretation. Similar to it is what Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama* transmitted from Qatada, that the meaning of his being of the jinn is that he was concealed (*ajinna*) from obedience to God, the Exalted; that is, he was covered and prevented. The majority narration from him is that he holds what has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them. It was said: He is of the angels, and the meaning of ﴿he was of the jinn﴾ is that he became of them by transformation (*maskh*). It was said: The meaning of that is that he was counted among them because of his agreement with them in disobedience, since they had been disobedient before, so a group of angels, peace be upon them, was sent to fight them.

You know that the answer is difficult for the one who claims that Iblis was of the angels, along with his claim of their infallibility (*'isma*), and he must commit something contrary to the apparent meaning in this verse. Yes, the question of their infallibility, peace be upon them, is a matter of disagreement, and there is no definitive proof for infallibility, as the scholar al-Taftazani said. Al-Qadi 'Iyad mentioned that a group held the infallibility of the messengers among them and the near ones (*muqarrabun*), peace be upon them, but did not say that other than them was infallible. If the one who claims that Iblis was of the angels takes this view, he cannot escape the objection except by claiming that he was not among the near ones, and the transmitted reports do not support that. The verse also remains against his claim. Likewise, if he adopts what has been reported from some Sufis, that the angels of the earth were not infallible and that Iblis, may the curse be upon him, was among them.

﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾, i.e., he departed from His obedience, glorified is He, as al-Farra' said. Its origin is from *fasaqa al-rutab* (the date fruit departed from its skin), and they called the mouse *fasiqa* (a transgressor) because it comes out of its hole from both sides. For this reason it is followed by *'an*, as in the words of Ru'ba:

"They go down into Najd and the deep valley, *fawasiqan* (departing) from their aim, deviating."

The apparent view is that *fisq* in this sense is something the Arabs spoke of before. Abu 'Ubayda said: "We have not heard that in any of the poetry of the pre-Islamic age nor in its narratives; the Arabs only used it after the Qur'an was revealed." Al-Mubarrad agreed with him on that, saying: "The matter is as Abu 'Ubayda mentioned, and it is an eloquent word on the tongues of the Arabs." What al-Farra' mentioned seems to be an explanation of the sum of the meaning, since *amr* here does not mean obedience at all. Rather, it means either the thing commanded, which is the prostration, and his departing from it means not being characterised by it; or it means the words of the Exalted, ﴿prostrate﴾, and his departing from it means his opposing it. That the sum of the meaning is this under both interpretations is clear. It was also said that *'an* is causal, as in the saying "his clothing was from nakedness, and his food was from hunger"; that is: he became a transgressor, a disbeliever, because of the command of God, the Exalted, to the angels, of which he was counted among them, since without that command no refusal would have been realised. Qutrub took this view, except that he said: "That is, he defied his refusal of the command of his Lord." It is possible that this is a semantic supposition and that it is a grammatical supposition. On the causal interpretation it is permissible to take *amr* to mean the will: that is, he defied because of God's will for his defiance, and had it not been so, he would have obeyed. The more evident is what was mentioned first, and the *fa'* is causal, joining what follows it to the words of the Exalted, ﴿he was of the jinn﴾, and it indicates that his defiance was caused by his being of the jinn, since the nature of the jinn is rebellion, due to the turbidity of their substance and the wickedness of their essence. What is wicked does not come forth except poorly, though some of them obeyed and believed. It is also permissible that the conjunction is with what is understood from the exception, as if it were said: "They prostrated except Iblis, who refused to prostrate, so he defied," and in that case it indicates that his defiance was caused by his refusal and his abandonment of prostration. It was also said that here it is not conjunctive, since it is not valid to make his refusal and abstention from prostration caused by his defiance of the command of his Lord, the Exalted.

The words of al-Radi: "The *fa'* that is not for conjunction, which is called the *fa'* of causality, is also not free of the meaning of sequence, and it is restricted to sentences and enters upon what is a consequence with the conditional particle preceding it and without it." End of quote. This is not correct, because it is sufficient for the validity of the sequence of the second that its causing is established, as in ﴿So Moses struck him and he died﴾, as clarified in *al-Tashil*. Here it is the same. The mention of the title of lordship, which is incompatible with defiance, is to show the ugliness of what he did. The meaning of the command, by mentioning the time of the story, is the story itself, because in it there is a strong rebuke of the arrogant who boast of their lineages and wealth and who disdain to be aligned with the poor believers, by showing that this is the work of Iblis, and that they in this are followers of his enticement, as what comes later indicates, God willing. From this the connection is known. It was also permissible that its connection is that when He, the Exalted, explained the state of the one deluded by the world and turning away from it, and the cause of delusion by it was love of desires and the enticement of Satan, He first made them abstain from the adornments of the world by showing that it is subject to decline and swift to pass, and that the enduring good deeds are better in reward and better in hope than the world itself and what is highest in it. Then He warned them against Satan by reminding them of the ancient enmity between them.

Abu Hayyan chose, as its connection, that when He, the Exalted, mentioned the Day of Resurrection and the gathering, and mentioned the fear of the criminals of what is written in their records, and Iblis the accursed was the one who led them to sins and to taking partners, it was fitting to mention Iblis and warn against him, as a way of keeping them far from sins and from obeying what he whispers and calls to. In any case, mentioning this story here, given that it was mentioned before, is not repetition, because its mention here is for a benefit other than the benefit for which it was mentioned earlier, and so with its mention in every place where it is mentioned in the Glorious Book. The same is said of everything that is apparently repetitive. It is not hidden that most apparent repetitions differ in their styles and vary in their wording and expressions, and in that there are divine secrets that are in it, so let not Satan cause you to slip.

﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾ The interrogative *hamza* is for denial and wonder, and the *fa'* is for consequence. The meaning is either a denial that taking him and his offspring as allies should follow from the knowledge of what proceeded from him, with wonder at that; or the consequence of denying the aforementioned taking and wondering at it, to inform them by God, the Exalted, of the ugliness of the accursed one's conduct. So reflect. The apparent meaning is that *dhurriyya* here means offspring, so the verse indicates that he has children, and a group said this.

It has been transmitted from Ibn Zayd that God, the Exalted, said to Iblis: "I do not create for Adam a descendant except that I create for you the like of it." So no child is born to Adam except that a devil is born with him, joined to him.

From Qatada it is transmitted that he said: "He marries and begets as the children of Adam beget." It is mentioned in *al-Bahr* that among those who held this view were also al-Dahhak, al-A'mash, and al-Sha'bi.

It is transmitted from al-Sha'bi that he said: "There is no offspring except from a wife," so he would be one who holds that he has a wife. In *al-Durr al-Manthur*, by the narration of

[Page 294]

Ibn al-Mundhir from him, it is reported that he was asked about Iblis: "Does he have a wife?" He said: "That is a wedding I have never heard of." Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Maka'id* and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "Iblis has five children: Thabr, who is the owner of calamities; al-A'war (the one-eyed); Dasim, I do not know what the two of them do; Musawwat, who is the owner of uproar; and Zalabnur, who is the one who sows discord among people and shows a man the faults of his family."

In another narration from him: al-A'war is the owner of adultery; Musawwat is the owner of false news, which he throws onto people's mouths, and they find no basis for it; Rasim is the owner of houses: when a man enters his house without mentioning God's name, he enters with him, and when he eats without mentioning God's name, he eats with him; and Zalabnur is the owner of the markets. These five were from five eggs that the accursed one laid. It was also said that the accursed one inserts his tail into his posterior and lays an egg, and the egg splits open into a group of devils. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sufyan that all his offspring are from five eggs that he laid. He said: "It has reached me that more than Rabi'a and Mudar gather against one believer." God, the Exalted, knows best the soundness of these reports. Some said: "He has no offspring, and the meaning of *dhurriyya* is the followers from among the devils, and it is metaphorical, figuratively describing them as children." It was also said: "Perhaps the truth is that he has children and followers." It is permissible that by *dhurriyya* is meant their totality together by way of predominance (*taghlib*), or a combination of the literal and the metaphorical according to one who holds that, or the generality of the metaphor.

Some reports have come down that among those said to be his offspring by birth are those who believed in Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and our Prophet (ﷺ), and Hama, may Allah be pleased with him. Glory be to Him who brings the living out of the dead. It is not incumbent upon us to know the manner of his begetting, for many things are of unknown manner to us, and we affirm them; so let this be of that kind, if the report concerning it is sound.

As for the argument for his being an angel from the apparent sense of the verse, since it indicates that he has offspring (dhurriyyah) while the angels do not have that, the proponent of this view may say: granting that dhurriyyah is taken to mean offspring, he was transformed (musikh) after he disobeyed and went out of the angelic state, and so he came to have offspring; the verse does not indicate that he had offspring before the disobedience, and the argument from it is not complete without that. The words ﴿min dūnī﴾ (apart from Me) are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); that is: "Will you take them as protectors, passing beyond Me to them, and exchange Me for them, obeying them instead of obeying Me?" ﴿wa-hum﴾ (while they) means: while the state is that Iblis and his offspring ﴿lakum ʿaduwwun﴾ (are an enemy to you), that is, enemies, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿fa-innahum ʿaduwwun lī illā Rabb al-ʿālamīn﴾ (for they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds), and His words: ﴿humu al-ʿaduww﴾ (they are the enemy). This form is used in imitation of verbal nouns (maṣādir), like qabūl and walūʿ. Restricting the taking (ittikhādh) to a circumstantial clause serves to emphasize and intensify the denunciation, for its content prevents the taking from occurring and is absolutely incompatible with it:

And among the miseries of this world for the free man is that he sees an enemy for whom there is no escape from being his friend.

﴿Bi'sa lil-ẓālimīn﴾ (Evil is it for the wrongdoers), that is, those who place a thing in other than its proper place, ﴿badalan﴾ (as a substitute), that is, in place of Allah, glory be to Him. It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). The subject of (bi'sa) is a concealed pronoun explained by what follows it, and the object of blame (al-makhṣūṣ bil-dhamm) is omitted; that is: "Evil is the substitute from Allah, the Exalted, for the wrongdoers, namely Iblis and his offspring." In the shift to the third person with the use of "the wrongdoers" in place of the pronoun of the addressees, there is an indication of the complete extent of wrath, and an indication that what they did is clearly a hideous wrong, which is not hidden.

[Page 296]

﴿I did not make them witness﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) brought to explain that Iblis and his offspring do not deserve to be taken as allies, as mentioned, after the preceding explanation of what diverts them from that: the corruption of their origin, their wickedness, and their enmity. That is: I did not bring Iblis and his offspring to witness.

﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, since I created them before creating those (beings). ﴿Nor the creation of themselves﴾, that is: nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. So both pronouns, the plural pronoun in the accusative and the one in the genitive, refer to Iblis and his offspring, and they are the ones meant by "the misleaders" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor would I take the misleaders as helpers﴾. The pronoun was placed in the position of their pronoun only to censure them, to record their misleading against them, and to emphasize what preceded concerning the denial of their being taken as allies. The word *ʿaḍud* (helper) originally means the part between the elbow and the shoulder, and it is used metaphorically for a helper, like the hand. This is the meaning intended here. Because it is an indefinite noun in a negative context, it is general. It was interpreted in the plural and in the singular to match the verse-endings (*ruʾus al-ayy*). It has also been said that it was not put in the plural because the whole group is, in terms of being unfit to be relied upon, like one person. That is: nor would I take them as helpers in the affair of creation, or in any of My affairs, so that it could be supposed that they share in the management, let alone in the substitution that would follow from their doing so, on the basis of sharing in some of the attributes of lordship. Returning the pronoun in *anfusihim* (themselves) to Iblis and his offspring has been said by everyone who holds that the pronoun in *ashhadtuhum* refers to them. The eminent scholar Shaykh al-Islam explained this by saying: out of caution against separating the two pronouns, and in keeping with the apparent wording of *anfus*. Then he said: you may also return the second pronoun to the wrongdoers, and the separation is accepted on the basis that the meaning returns to them. The denial of their being taken as allies revolves around the negation of making witnesses of the devils who are their allies, on the basis that the minimum that validates taking someone as an ally is that the ally be present at the creation of the one he takes as ally. Where that presence does not occur, there is certainly nothing that validates the alliance. As for making some of the devils witness the creation of some of them, it does not fall within the scope of the aforementioned denial at all. Moreover, if the witnessing of some of them of the creation of others validates the witness's alliance, on the basis that it indicates his perfection, in the sense that he has some part in the creation of what is witnessed in general, then it is nonetheless detrimental to the alliance with what is witnessed, on the basis of its deficiency relative to the one who witnessed its creation. Therefore the negation of the aforementioned witnessing is not purely a negation of the perfection that validates alliance with all of them, and that is the basis of the aforementioned denial.

The verse contains mockery of the disbelievers and an announcement of the complete weakness of their minds and the feebleness of their opinions, in that they do not understand this clear matter, which is hardly confused even for the simpleminded and children, so that they would need to have it stated explicitly. The choice of negating witnessing rather than negating their presence, and of negating their being taken as helpers rather than negating their being such, serves to indicate that they are subjugated under His power, exalted is He, and follow His will and His desire, glory be to Him, and are far from deserving witnessing and assistance of their own accord, without being brought or taken. The most that could be supposed of them is that they reach that level by the command of Allah, majestic is His majesty, and that would not even happen. End of quotation.

This is a passage that bears the marks of investigation. However, it has been objected: it is possible that by "the heavens and the earth" is meant what includes their inhabitants, and this is often what is meant by them. Then the disbelievers are included, and the verse would indicate the negation of the devils' witnessing of their creation, which is the subject of the aforementioned denial, without any need to adopt the separation of the pronouns, which is contrary to what is immediately understood. The apparent meaning of his words, and likewise of many others, is to take the negated witnessing in its literal sense.

It has also been permitted that it means consultation, metaphorically. This is what the apparent meaning of what is in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit) seems to require. On this reading there is no obstacle to taking "the heavens and the earth" as including their inhabitants. It is as if it were said: I did not consult them about the creation of anyone, neither the disbelievers nor others. So what is the matter with these disbelievers, who take them as allies, when the minimum that validates alliance is that the ally be one whose opinion is sought regarding the affair of the one allied with or the affair of another? The negation of their being taken as helpers in any way at all, after the negation of consulting them about creation, would then make the statement apparently express the general negation of their having any role in any respect, whether in opinion, in bringing into being, or otherwise, in anything. Perhaps the verse in that case is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It leaves out nothing small or great without recording it﴾, in one respect. It has been said: the negation of witnessing in the second part may mean the negation of consultation, and from this also the negation that they were created according to their own will, and from this also the negation that they were created perfect, since it is said: "he was created as he willed," meaning "he was created complete." The poet said:

*You were created free of every defect, as if you had been created as you wished.*

On this reading, among creatures there is someone who witnessed the creation of his own self, in the sense that he was created complete. This is not hidden in what it entails. Perhaps it is enough to infer from this that the negation of perfection is expressed with less of this burden. Understand.

He claimed that the perfect ones witnessed the true creation of themselves, in the sense that they saw, while they were fixed entities, their own creation, that is, the bestowal upon them of external existence, which a non-existent thing does not possess. I do not see that a perfect person would undertake or give ear to this.

After relating the view that the two pronouns return to the devils, al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The closer view to me is that they return to the disbelievers who said to the Messenger ﷺ: "If you do not drive these poor men away from your gathering, we will not believe in you." So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: These who came with this corrupt suggestion and this baseless obstinacy were not My partners in governing the world. The proof is that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, and I did not seek support from them in the governance of this world and the next. Rather, they are like the rest of creation. So why did they make this corrupt suggestion? A parallel is this: if someone makes great demands of you, you say to him: "You are not the ruler of the city, that we should accept from you these enormous demands, so why do you make them?" What confirms this is that a pronoun must return to the nearest antecedent mentioned, and in the verse that is "those disbelievers," because they are what is meant by "the wrongdoers" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the substitute for the wrongdoers﴾. End of quotation.

It has also been said: on the assumption that the two pronouns return to those disbelievers, the meaning is that these wrongdoers are ignorant of what the Pen has written from eternity concerning the states of happiness and their opposite. For they were not witnesses to the creation of the world, so how could they judge that their own state is good in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, and that they are honored and exalted among creation, while the poor are the opposite of these states? It has also been said that the meaning on this reading is: I did not make them witness that, nor did I inform them of the secrets of creation, nor did I single them out with distinctions that others do not possess, so that they would be examples for people and people would believe through their belief, as they claim. So do not pay attention to their words, hoping for their support of the religion, for it is not fitting for me to rely on the misleaders to support My religion. This is strengthened by the reading of Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan and Shaybah: «وما كُنْتَ» (*wa-ma kunta*, "nor were you") with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, addressing him ﷺ. The meaning is: it was not proper for you to rely on them. Perhaps the description of those wrongdoers as misleaders is because their intention in driving away the poor was to repel people from him ﷺ, and that is clear misleading. It has also been said: every astray person is a misleader, because misleading is either by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of condition, and the second is something no one who is astray is free of. It has also been said: the two pronouns refer to the angels, and the meaning is: I did not make them witness that, nor did I seek their help in anything. Rather, I created them so that they would worship Me, so how could they be worshipped? This is refuted by: ﴿Nor would I take the misleaders as helpers﴾, unless it is said that this is a negation of taking the devils as helpers, from which the negation of the validity of worship of both groups is inferred from the two clauses.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The two pronouns refer to the disbelievers and to people in general. Thus the verse contains a refutation of groups of astrologers, adherents of the doctrine of natural temperaments, physicians, and others who wade into their wading. This view was held by 'Abd al-Haqq al-Saqalli, and some of the scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) mentioned it. End of quotation. What has been said about the last clause applies to it generally, as was said before.

It has been cited as evidence that it is not proper to seek help from a disbeliever in matters of religion, such as fighting the disbelievers or fighting the rebels (*ahl al-baghy*). This is the view of some of the imams, and some of them have a detailed position on this. As for seeking their help in worldly affairs, what appears is that there is no harm in it, whether the matter is menial, such as emptying latrines, or other, such as making pulpits and prayer niches, sewing, and the like. Perhaps the Jewish man or the dog that died in the words of al-Faruq, may Allah be pleased with him, was counted as using them in religious matters, or it is based on the choice of a distinction in worldly matters as well.

The Shi'ah have related that 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, said, when he was resolved to dismiss Mu'awiyah, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, advised him to leave him in his post until the matter of the caliphate became firmly established: "What prevents me from that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor would I take the misleaders as helpers﴾. So I will never take Mu'awiyah as a helper." This is a lie that no one believes except a misled misleader.

Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Sikhtiyani, 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Muqsim read: «ما أشْهَدْناهُمْ» (*ma ashhadnahum*, "We did not make them witness") with the royal "we."

'Ali, may Allah honor his face, read: «مُتَّخِذًا المُضِلِّينَ» (*muttakhidhan al-mudillin*) with the active participle governing its object.

al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah read: «عُضْدًا» (*ʿudhdan*) with the *ḍad* sukun and its vowel moved to the *ʿayn*. 'Isa read «عَضْدًا» (*ʿadhdan*) with the *ḍad* sukun for lightness, as they say for "rajul" and "sabuʿ" "rajl" and "sabʿ" with sukun, and this is a dialect of Tamim. From him also it is reported that he read with two *fatha*s.

Shaybah and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Harun, Kharijah, al-Khifaf and Abu Zayd read: «عُضُدًا» (*ʿududan*) with two *damma*s. This is also reported from al-Hasan, and likewise it is reported from him that he read with two *fatha*s. On this reading it is either a dialectal form of *ʿadud* as in al-Bahr, though he did not mention it in al-Qamus, or the plural of *ʿadid* (helper), like *khadam* as the plural of *khadim*, from *ʿaddahu*, meaning "he strengthened him and helped him." In that case there is no metaphor.

al-Dahhak read: «عِضَدًا» (*ʿidhadan*) with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* and a *fatha* on the *ḍad*. We have not found this among its dialects. Indeed, in al-Qamus, "ʿadhid" like "katif" is counted among them, which is the reverse of this reading.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 52:

﴿And on the Day He says﴾: that is, Allah, the Exalted, says to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and a challenge, through an intermediary or without one. Al-A'mash, Talhah, Yahya, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamzah and Ibn Muqsim read "naqulu" (We say) with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), and the speech is by way of: "Remember also"; that is, "And remember the Day He says: ﴿Call upon My partners whom you claimed﴾ [to be partners] for your intercession."

That is, you claimed them to be intercessors. The attribution (idafah) is in regard to what they also claimed, for they claimed that they were partners just as they claimed that they were intercessors. More than one scholar has permitted here that the speech be understood as "you claimed them to be partners," and the intended meaning of them is Iblis and his offspring. Making them a substitute (badal) in what preceded is based on what results from the act of their worshippers who obeyed them in what they whispered to them, or [it refers to] everything that was worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn Kathir read "shurakayi" (My partners), with the final long vowel shortened and attached to the ya' (of the first person). ﴿Then they will call upon them﴾: that is, they will call out to them for aid, and in this there is a clarification of the completeness of their concern for their being helped, through the way of intercession; since it is known that there is no way to defend against [the punishment]. ﴿But they will not respond to them﴾: so they will not help them, since there is no possibility of that. It has been said: in mentioning it despite its being obvious, there is mockery of them and an announcement that they are in such foolishness that they will not understand it except by explicit statement.

﴿And We will place between them﴾: that is, between those who call and those who are called upon, ﴿a barrier (mawbiqan)﴾. Mawbiq is a noun of place from wabaqa, wubuqan, like wathaba, wuthuban, or from wabiqa, wabaqan, like fariha, farahan, when one is destroyed; that is, a place of destruction in which they share, and it is the Fire. It has come from Ibn 'Umar, Anas and Mujahid that it is a valley in Hell that flows with blood and pus. From 'Ikrimah it is that it is a river in the Fire that flows as fire, and on its two banks are serpents like dark-coloured mules; when they rise up toward them to seize them, they seek help by plunging into the Fire away from them. The interpretation of mawbiq as "destruction" is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and from Mujahid and others. From al-Hasan, its interpretation is "enmity"; so it is a verbal noun (masdar) applied to the cause of destruction, which is enmity, just as "ruin (talaf)" is applied to the hatred that leads to it, in the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred ruinous."

From al-Rabi' ibn Anas, its interpretation is "prison." The meaning of mawbiq being between them, according to all its interpretations, is that it encompasses them and that they share in it, as one says: "I placed the wealth between Zayd and 'Amr." It is as if "ja'alna" was made to include the meaning of "qasamna" (We divided); and in that case it is not possible to include 'Isa, 'Uzayr and the angels, peace be upon them, and the like among the partners according to the second opinion.

Some have said: the meaning of mawbiq, that is, destruction or prison, being between them is that it is an intervening barrier placed in the middle, and that was made between them to cut off the greed of the disbelievers that they would be reached by those whom they called upon for intercession. It has come from some who interpreted it as "valley" that Allah, the Exalted, separates by it between the people of guidance and the people of misguidance; and according to this there is no obstacle to the second meaning of "partners" including those noble ones.

al-Tha'alibi said in Fiqh al-Lughah: mawbiq in the sense of a distant barrier, on the basis that wabaqa also means "perished"; that is, We placed between them a far-off interval in which the long stretches are lost because of its great distance. Upon this too the said inclusion is permissible, for those noble ones, peace be upon them, are in the highest gardens, while these base ones are in the depths of the fires. Anyone with the slightest reflection will not fail to see the situation if mawbiq is meant as enmity.

﴿Between them﴾ according to all that has been mentioned is an adverbial complement of place (zarf), and it is the second object of "ja'ala" when it means "made/rendered" (sayyara), with mawbiqan as its first object; and if it is taken to mean "created" (khalaqa), the adverbial complement is attached to it, or to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of its object, which was placed before it for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawasil), and so it became a circumstantial (hal).

al-Farra' and al-Sirafi said: al-bayn here means "connection (wasl)", for it can carry that meaning just as it can mean "separation (firaq)". It is the first object of "ja'alna", and mawbiqan, meaning "destruction (halaka)", is its second object. The meaning is: We made their connection in the world a destruction on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾. He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to make explicit their criminality and to censure them for it. The seeing is visual.

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, as recorded from him by Ahmad, Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the disbeliever will see Hell from a distance of forty years' journey."

﴿Then they will be certain﴾, meaning they will know, as recorded by ʿAbd al-Razzaq and a group of others from Qatadah. This is the apparent meaning of their state after Allah's statement and their calling for help from their partners, the partners not responding to them, and Allah placing a barrier (mawbiq) between them.

It has also been said that the verb "ẓanna" retains its literal sense of supposing, and that they had not attained certainty, ﴿that they are about to be thrown into it﴾, meaning that they will be mingling with it and falling into it, since they had not despaired of the mercy of Allah before entering it. It has also been said that when they saw it from afar, as you have heard in the hadith, they supposed that it would seize them immediately, since the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is employed for the present moment. So what is certain is the basic fact of entering, and what is supposed is entering at once. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), the reading is "mulaqūhā" (meeting it), and likewise al-Aʿmash and Ibn Ghazwan from Talhah read it so. Taking it as an explanation (tafsir) was preferred because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (sawad al-mushaf). From ʿAlqamah it is reported that he read "mulaffūhā" with a doubled fa' from laffa al-shay' (to wrap up the thing). ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾, meaning a place to which they could turn away.

Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

"O Zuhayr, is there any escape for Shaybah from a place of turning away, or is there no eternity for one who spends and strains?"

So it (maṣrif) is a noun of place. It has also been permitted that it be a noun of time, and likewise Abu al-Baqa' permitted it, and others followed him, that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "turning away." In ad-Durr al-Masun it is said that this is an error, for he made the pattern maf'il with a kasra on the ʿayn a verbal noun from the sound present form yaf'il with a kasra, whereas the grammarians have explicitly stated that its verbal noun has a fatha on the ʿayn only, and that its noun of time and place has a kasra on it. Indeed, the view that it is a verbal noun is acceptable in the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, "maṣrafan" with a fatha on the rāʾ.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 18, verse 54:

﴿And We have certainly varied﴾, that is, repeated and presented in many different forms of expression, ﴿in this Qur'an﴾, which is of great standing, ﴿for the people﴾, for their benefit and advantage, ﴿from every example﴾. That is: every example. Here "min" (من, "from") is what the grammarians call *sayf khatib* (سيف خطيب, literally "a sword of an orator", meaning an extra or emphatic particle) according to the opinion of al-Akhfash (d. c. 215 AH, a grammarian of Basra), and the prepositional phrase is the object of ﴿varied﴾. Or it may mean "an example from every example", with "min" being original (not extra), and the object being a modified noun of the omitted prepositional phrase. It has also been said that the object is implied, and "from every example" means "some part of every kind of example". In any case, "example" (*mathal*) here means either its well-known meaning or the strange attribute which, in its beauty and its capacity to attract the soul, is like an example. The meaning is that God, exalted is He, diversified the striking of examples, mentioned strange attributes, and mentioned from every kind that which is needed, which calls to faith and which benefits them, as an example. It does not mean that He, glorified is He, mentioned every single example. It seems that the verse contains an omission, or it means: "We indeed did this so that they would accept, but they did not."

﴿And man has been, by his nature, the most contentious of things﴾. That is, the most contentious of the things from which dispute may arise. Dispute (*jadal*, جدل), as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani, d. 502 AH) and others said, is contention through exchange of speech. What is most fitting to the context is that it means here quarrelsome disputing for falsehood and obstinate argument, which is its most common usage. Several scholars have mentioned that the word is derived from *jadal*, which means twisting, and that *mujadalah* (debate) is a wrestling, because each of the two disputants twists against the other. The word is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*, تمييز, an accusative noun clarifying the meaning of the preceding word). The meaning is that the dispute of man is greater than the dispute of every disputant. It is explained by the breadth of his range, for he lies between the height of angelhood and the depth of animality, and so in both directions of ascent and descent he has no known station.

It is apparent that the intended "man" is not a specific individual. It has been said that the reference is to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it has been said Ibn al-Za'bara'. Ibn al-Sa'ib said it was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and his dispute was about the resurrection when he brought a bone that had crumbled and said: "Will God, exalted is He, be able to restore this?" and crushed it in his hand. The first opinion is preferred, and it is supported by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ali, may Allah honor his face: "The Prophet (ﷺ) visited him and Fatimah at night and said: 'Will you not pray?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed our souls are in the hand of Allah, exalted is He; if He wills to raise us, He raises us.' He turned away when I said that and did not answer me. Then I heard him striking his thigh and saying: 'And man has been, by his nature, the most contentious of things.'"

This clearly indicates that "man" is taken in its general sense. There is no doubt about the soundness of the hadith, but it contains a difficulty that is known upon reflection, and it is not resolved by what al-Nawawi (d. 676 AH) mentioned when he said: "The preferred meaning is that he (ﷺ) was amazed at the speed of his reply and that he did not agree with him in excusing himself with this. For this reason he struck his thigh. It has also been said that he (ﷺ) said that to accept their excuse, and that there is no blame." End of quote. So consider this carefully.

[p. 300]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 55:

﴿And what prevented the people﴾ Ibn 'Atiyyah and others said: What is meant by them are the disbelievers of Quraysh whose falsehoods were related, and "mā" is negative.

Some (scholars) claimed, and it is of great strangeness, that it is interrogative; that is: "What thing prevented them ﴿from believing﴾," that is, from their belief in Allah the Exalted and abandoning what they were in of associating partners (with Him), ﴿when guidance came to them﴾, that is, the Qur'an, the Mighty, which guides to belief through its various kinds of meanings that necessitate it, or the Messenger (ﷺ); and the application of "guidance" to each (of them) is for emphasis. ﴿And that they should seek forgiveness from their Lord﴾ through repentance from what they had committed of kinds of sins, among which is their disputing the truth with falsehood. The benefit of mentioning this after belief is generalisation, according to what has been said. And whoever claims that belief, if it is not accompanied by seeking forgiveness, does not wipe out what came before it has taken this as evidence; but this contradicts what the apparent meanings require.

Some (scholars) said: There is no doubt that belief together with seeking forgiveness is more complete than belief alone, so it was mentioned along with it so that the verse conveys what prevented them from being characterised by the most complete of what is required of them. It is not hidden that this is nothing. It was also said: seeking forgiveness was mentioned after belief to emphasise that what is meant by it is the belief that is not mixed with hypocrisy, as if it were said: what prevented them from believing with true belief ﴿except that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them﴾, and those are the peoples of the past nations who were destroyed. The attribution of "the way" to them is said to be because it applied to them, while in reality it is the way of Allah the Exalted concerning them, and what is meant by it is destruction by the punishment of annihilation. If "the way" is interpreted as destruction, there is no need for what has been mentioned. "That" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun, and it is the subject of "prevented," and the sentence is with an elided genitive; that is:
Page 301
what prevented them from that except the seeking of destruction in this world; so said al-Zajjaj. Ṣāḥib al-Faynān permitted the estimate "waiting" (intizār); that is: what prevented them except waiting for destruction. al-Wahidi estimated "decree" (taqdīr), that is: what prevented them except Allah the Exalted's decree that destruction come upon them. He said:

The verse concerns those among the polytheists who were killed at Badr and Uhud, and the apparent sense of the surah being Meccan, except what is excepted, refutes this. What motivates the estimate of the elided genitive is that if the preventer of their belief and seeking forgiveness were the very coming of destruction, they would be excused; and that the punishment of the Hereafter prepared for the disbelievers, meant by His saying: ﴿or the punishment comes to them face to face﴾, is certainly awaited, which inclines toward the view that the time of the coming of punishment is later than the time considered for their belief and seeking forgiveness, so what you have criticised from both does not hold.

The estimate of "seeking" has been objected to: their seeking the way of the earlier peoples results from their not believing, and that is due to their being prevented from belief; so if their prevention were due to seeking, circularity would follow. It was answered that what is meant by "seeking" is its cause, namely their obstinacy and stubbornness which made them seekers of punishment, like their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾, etc. It was objected that some of them deny the truth of Islam, just as some of them are obstinate; and it does not appear how the seeking arises from denying its truth, nor likewise does it appear that it arises from obstinacy. It was also objected that the non-belief, which precedes the seeking and continues, means the seeking cannot be a preventer.
