It was answered that what precedes the seeking is the earlier non-belief, and seeking is not a preventer of it; rather it is a preventer of what is realised afterwards, and this, as you see, is weak. It was also said: what is meant by seeking is verbal, outward seeking, not true inward seeking of the heart; for whoever has even a little intellect does not truly and inwardly seek destruction and punishment. And from outward seeking, its source and what is a sign of it is the denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) of what he threatened of punishment and destruction for whoever does not believe in Allah the Mighty and Majestic; so it is as if it were said: what prevented them from believing in Allah the Exalted, which the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, commanded, was only their denial of him concerning what he threatened for abandoning it; and this is not free from being shaky.

It was also said: The truth is that the verse, on the estimate of seeking, is like your saying to one who disobeys you: "You want me to strike you," and this is placing entitlement in the position of seeking; so it is as if it were said: what prevented them from that was only the entitlement to worldly destruction or the otherworldly punishment. It was objected that disbelief and being characterised by unbelief is the cause of the mentioned entitlement, so it would be prior to it; and whenever entitlement is a preventer of it, the order of priority and posteriority is reversed, so one thing would be both prior and posterior in the same respect, which is invalid. It was answered by denying that non-belief is in reality a cause of entitlement; it is merely a formal cause, while the real cause is the badness of their dispositions and the corruption of their quiddities in reality; and just as it is a cause of entitlement, so it is a cause of being characterised by disbelief. If you wish, say: it is a preventer of belief. Hence it was said: what is meant by seeking is seeking in the language of disposition, and the outcome of the verse is: what prevented them from that was only their dispositions and the seeking of their quiddities for its opposite; for seeking their dispositions for destruction or the punishment that follows from the opposite is a disposition toward the opposite and a seeking of it. And perhaps it is said, on this basis, that what is understood from the verses is that if a messenger had not come to the disbelievers to awaken them from the slumber of heedlessness, they would argue, were they punished, by his non-coming, and they would say: what prevented us from belief is that no messenger came to us; and its outcome is: what prevented us from that is heedlessness; and they would find no more eloquent proof than this, nor more beneficial for deliverance. As for poor disposition and the badness of essence, they are far from their using it as an argument and making it a preventer. So there is no distance in estimating the seeking and taking its apparent meaning, and the verse would be of the kind of His saying:
Page 302

"And there is no fault in them..."

the verse. What is meant is the negation that there should be for them any preventer from belief and seeking forgiveness, after the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ), that could serve as a proof for them at all; as if it were said: there is no preventer for them from believing or seeking forgiveness from their Lord, and no proof after the coming of the Messenger who conveyed what he conveyed of guidance, except the seeking of what they were threatened with, of the coming of worldly destruction or otherworldly punishment; since that, on the supposition of its realisation from them, is not fit to be a preventer or a proof, no preventer or proof remains for them at all. End.

It is not hidden that, after overlooking what is objected to it, this is far-fetched, and denying that is obstinacy; and the better course is the estimate of the estimate, which is undoubtedly a preventer, except that those who hold the view of disposition, as you know, make its source the disposition; and in its meaning is the estimate of will, that is: His will, the Exalted; and 'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam confined himself to this, and he resolved the apparent conflict between the restriction derived from this verse and the restriction derived from His saying: ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, except that they said: Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ by saying that the first restriction concerns the true preventer, for the will of Allah the Exalted is the preventer in reality, and the second concerns the customary preventer, which is the strangeness of a human being being sent as a messenger; for the meaning is: what prevented the people from believing except that strangeness. What benefits you in combining the two restrictions has already been mentioned in Surat al-Isra', so remember it, for what is in the covenant is no antiquity.

The Imam claimed a plurality of preventers, and that what is meant by the verse is the absence of one kind of them. He said: The companions said: knowledge of their non-belief is contrary to the existence of their belief; so if that knowledge is present, the preventer is present. Also, the presence of the motive to disbelief is present, otherwise it would not have occurred, for the occurrence of a voluntary act without a motive is impossible; and the existence of a motive to disbelief is a preventer from the occurrence of belief. So it must be said: what is meant is the absence of the sensible preventers. End; so consider this carefully.

The "qubul" (with two dammas) is the plural of "qabil," which means kind; that is: or the punishment comes to them in kinds and varieties; or it is in the sense of "qibalan" (with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba'), as many have read; that is: face to face, for Abu 'Ubaydah related both with this meaning; and its origin is in the sense of confronting, so when it indicates face-to-face witnessing, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. If it is a state of the pronoun object, its meaning is: witnessing them (with the ya' kasra or fatha), or being witnessed by the people in order to be disgraced; and if it is from the punishment, its meaning is: witnessed by them or by the people. A group read: "qiblan" with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', which, as in al-Bahr, is a lightening of "qubul" according to the dialect of Tamim.

Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zamakhshari mentioned that it was read: "qabalan" with two fathas; that is: confronting. And Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Ghazwan from Talhah read: "qabilan" with an open qaf, a kasra on the ba' followed by a quiescent ya'; that is: face to face and in confrontation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 56:

﴿And We send not the messengers﴾ to the nations in any state whatsoever, ﴿except﴾ as being ﴿bearers of good tidings﴾ to the believers of reward, ﴿and warners﴾ to the disbelievers and the sinners of punishment. We did not send them so that signs would be demanded of them after the manifestation of the miracles, and so that they would be treated in a manner unworthy of their station. ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood﴾ by demanding that, and by asking about the story of the People of the Cave and the like, out of obstinacy, and by their saying to them ﴿You are but mortals like us﴾ and ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, and so on. The restriction of the disputation to falsehood is to clarify the blameworthy kind of it, for it is, as has passed, not far from being general in lexical usage, not specific to falsehood, so that what was mentioned would be taken as a figurative usage (tajrid). What is meant here is its lexical meaning and what is applied to it technically of what truly fits it. ﴿That they may refute﴾, i.e., that they may remove and nullify, ﴿thereby﴾, i.e., by the disputation, ﴿the truth﴾ which the messengers, peace be upon them, brought. The root of idhha' (refutation) is causing to slip, and dahd is the mud in which one slips. The poet said:

I came, and al-Yashkuri's fear of him saved him, and he swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery mud.

And another said:

O Abu Mundhir, you desired loyalty and feared it, and you swerved as the slipping camel swerves.

Its use for the removal of truth has been said to be from the use of what was laid down for the sensible in the intelligible. It has also been said: you may say that there is in it a comparison of their speech to disagreeable mire, as in the words of al-Khafaji:

He came to us with mire for his thoughts, to make slip the feet of the guidance of the proofs.

﴿And they take My signs﴾ with which I strengthened the messengers, whether they were words or deeds, ﴿and what they were warned of﴾, i.e., what they were warned of from the striking calamities announcing punishment and torment, or their warning, ﴿in mockery﴾, i.e., as derision and ridicule.

Hamzah read: "huz'an" with sukun and hamza. Others among the seven, other than Hafs, read it with two dammas and hamza. It is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis, and it may be interpreted as that which is mocked.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 57:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord﴾ Most scholars hold that what is meant by them is the Mighty Qur'an, because of the phrase ﴿that they should understand it﴾; the genitive (idafah) is thus one of specific reference (li-l-'ahd).

It is also permissible that what is meant by them is the category of verses (jins al-ayat), with the Mighty Qur'an entering it in the primary sense (dukhulan awwaliyyan). The interrogative is one of denial, having the force of negation. Several scholars have verified that what is meant is the negation that anyone may be equal in injustice to one who has been admonished with the verses of God, the Exalted ﴿but turns away from them﴾, not reflecting upon them and not taking admonition from them. The indication of this meaning from what is mentioned is by way of metonymy (kinayah). The attribution of greatest injustice is based upon what falls within the relative clause (hayyiz al-silah), namely turning away, to indicate that the injustice of one who disputes the verses and takes them in mockery is beyond all bounds. ﴿And forgets what his hands have sent forth﴾, i.e., his deeds of disbelief and sins, of which disputing with falsehood and mocking the truth are among the most prominent. Forgetting that is a metonymy for not contemplating its consequences. According to most scholars, what is meant by ﴿man﴾ is the polytheists of Makkah.

It is also permissible that what is meant by it is whoever possesses the attribute within the relative clause, whoever he may be, and the polytheists of Makkah enter it in the primary sense. The pronoun in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We have placed over their hearts﴾, refers to them on both interpretations, and the reason for the plural is evident. The clause is a explanatory resumptive (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: what is the cause of their turning away and forgetting? It is answered: its cause is that We have placed over their hearts ﴿coverings (akinnah)﴾, i.e., veils, the plural of kinan; the tanwin, as some have indicated, denotes multiplicity. ﴿That they should understand it﴾: the pronoun in the accusative refers, according to most scholars, to the verses, and its masculine and singular form is due to the meaning intended from them, which is the Qur'an.

It is also permissible that it refers to the Qur'an, not as what is meant by the verses, and the sentence contains an ellipsis, the estimate being: lest they understand it (karahata an yafqahuhu); and it has been said: so that they do not understand it, i.e., understanding that benefits. ﴿And in their ears is a deafness (waqran)﴾, i.e., We have placed in them a heaviness, so that they do not hear it with such hearing. ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever (idhan abadan)﴾, i.e., for the entire duration of the obligation. ''Idhan'' is a conditional particle and an answer, as its meaning has been verified in its proper place; so it indicates the negation of their guidance in response to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, in the sense that they have made what should have been the cause of attaining guidance a cause of its absence. It is also said to be an answer to the Messenger (peace be upon him) on the presumption of his saying: "What is wrong with me that I do not call them, out of eagerness for their guidance?" And although there was mentioned to him ﷺ of their affair what was mentioned, hoping that those coverings might be lifted and torn away by the hand of the call, it was said: 
Page 304
"And if you call them..." etc. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. In al-Kashf, in explaining this: as for the indication, the explicit interposition of "idhan" points to this, since the meaning is "idhan law da'awta" ("then, even if you called"), and this is inversion (ta'kis) without strain. As for its being an answer in the aforementioned manner, its meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ was placed in the position of one asking, as an exaggeration regarding the non-guidance that results from their being sealed upon their hearts; so this does not conflict with what they preferred, that it is on the presumption of a question: "Why did they not become guided?" For the question in this form is more fitting. End of quote. This is a precious statement, by which the veil is lifted, one is safe from following error blindly, and the attentive reader is spared what has been said: that the estimate "what is wrong with me that I do not call them" implies prohibiting them from the call, so it was taken from a verse like His words, "So turn away from one who turns his back on Our remembrance"; and it has been said it was taken from His words, "over their hearts coverings"; and it has been said it was taken from His words, glorified is He, "if you call them." This is so. The meaning of guidance is not hidden from you, and it may be intended to mean the Qur'an, in which case it is the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun; and perhaps the intention of that here favors the intention of the Qur'an in the earlier guidance. And God knows best.

The verse concerns people whom God, the Exalted, knew would die upon disbelief among the polytheists of Makkah at the time of its revelation; so it does not conflict with the reports that they are sealed (bi-l-tab') and that they do not believe, either by verification or by imitation, with the belief of some polytheists after the revelation. The possibility that what is meant is all the polytheists, in the sense of "and if you call them all to guidance, they will never all be guided," and that only some of them are guided, is as you see. The Jabriyyah have used this verse to support their doctrine, and the Qadariyyah the verse preceding it. The Imam said: You rarely find in the Qur'an a verse supporting one of these two groups without a verse alongside it supporting the other group; and this is nothing but a severe trial from God, the Exalted, which He placed upon His servants so that the firmly rooted scholars may be distinguished from the mere imitators.

Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on surah 18, verse 58:

﴿Your Lord is the All-Forgiving﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). His words ﴿Full of mercy﴾, meaning the One who possesses mercy and is characterized by it, are a second predicate following the first. The Imam said: The intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha) was used for forgiveness rather than mercy, because forgiveness is the abandonment of harm, whereas mercy is the conveying of benefit. God's power relates to the first, since it is the abandonment of harms without end, and does not relate to the second, since doing what has no end is impossible.

Al-Nisaburi criticized this: It is a subtle distinction, if transmission supported it, but God's words ﴿Full of mercy﴾ are not free of intensiveness, and in the Qur'an (Ghafur Rahim, "Forgiving, Merciful") intensiveness is used a great deal on both sides. As for the relation of power to the abandonment of what is unlimited, there is room for doubt, because His determinations (muqaddarat) are limited, and there is no difference between what is abandoned and anything else. End of quote. It has been objected to him: They explained al-Ghaffar as the one who wills the removal of punishment from one who deserves it, and al-Rahim as the one who wills benefaction to creation. The intent of intensiveness in one respect does not preclude its absence in another, since it is not required there. They have also stated that God's determinations are unlimited, and what enters existence of them is limited, by the proof of correspondence (burhan al-tatbiq, a proof from one-to-one correspondence). This is a good reply, and it dispels what was raised against the Imam. The philosophers claimed that what enters existence of the determinations is also unlimited, and the proof of correspondence does not apply to it in their view, because they require simultaneity and sequence. By my life, my hair stood on end at the apparent sense of al-Nisaburi's statement that God's determinations are limited, for its apparent sense is a limitation of God, exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say. Yet it can be dealt with by charitable interpretation, so reflect.

Next, the explanation of the distinction between the two predicates here, according to what al-Khafaji said: What is mentioned after the non-punishment of them for the great crime they committed is a great forgiveness, and the postponement of hastening is a mercy from Him, preceding His wrath. But He, glorified be He, did not will to complete His mercy upon them and bring it to its end, for if He, exalted is His majesty, had willed that, He would have guided them and spared them punishment altogether. This point does not depend on the discussion of limitedness and unlimitedness that the Imam mentioned, although it is sound in itself, as has been said. The objection to it, that it requires the unlimitedness of the related objects in every case where intensive forms are attributed to God, is not necessary. For intensiveness regarding what is limited may be taken as increase in quantity and strength in quality. Even if what was mentioned were granted, it would follow that intensive forms are invalid
[page 305]
regarding attributes of established existence, such as Rahim and Rahman, and this has no basis. It is answered that what was mentioned is the reason for the distinction between the two matters here: intensiveness is taken with respect to abandonment, not its opposite, because abandonment is a negation, in which unlimitedness is permissible, unlike the other. Do you not see that the abandonment of their punishment indicates the abandonment of all kinds of punishments in this world, even though they are unlimited? So it was said. But there is room for doubt in this.

Some have said, in explaining what al-Nisaburi said, that ﴿Full of mercy﴾ is not free of intensiveness: this is either because mercy is joined with the definite article (al), so that the complete mercy is restricted, or the known mercy which encompassed everything. Or it is because of dhu: its indication of attribution in such a construction is stronger than the indication of derived forms of it, and God does not indicate His attribution of a quality by this indication except that the quality is intended in its most eloquent form. Otherwise, what is the benefit in turning away from the shorter derived form that indicates the basic attribution, such as al-Rahim (the merciful) for example, to that? This is not disturbed by the objection that if intensiveness were intended, why was the shorter form also turned away from, which conveys it, such as al-Rahim or al-Rahman, to what was mentioned? For it may be said: it is intended that the intensified mercy should not be restricted to being in this world or in the Hereafter. These two names convey restriction according to the well-known view, and for this reason one turns from them to ﴿Full of mercy﴾. If you say they are like it in not restricting, it is said that its indication of intensiveness is stronger than their indication of it, in that it is claimed that this indication is through two matters, which the indication of the two majestic names does not equal in strength. On this basis, dhu al-rahma is more eloquent than each of al-Rahman and al-Rahim, although both together are more eloquent than it. For this reason they were used in the basmala (the invocation) and not it. Whoever is fair will not doubt that your saying "Fulan dhu al-'ilm" (so-and-so possessor of knowledge) is more eloquent than your saying "Fulan al-'Alim" (so-and-so the Knowing), in that the former indicates that he is the possessor and owner of the essence of knowledge, and the latter two do not. In that case the difference between the two predicates in the verse is the greater eloquence of the second, and the reason for this is clear, for mercy has a wider scope than forgiveness, as is well known. The point here is the increase of consolation for him, may God bless him and grant him peace, after God informed him of the sealing of the hearts of some of those sent to them, and despaired him of their guidance, although God, exalted is His majesty, knows his great eagerness for their guidance, upon him be blessing and peace. This is the secret of choosing the title of Lordship (Rububiyya) joined to his pronoun, peace be upon him. End.

This is a statement standing at the threshold of acceptance and rejection in noble consideration, and whoever examines it closely will know what is in it of both matters. He placed the first attribute first because clearing away precedes adorning, or because it is more important according to the situation and context. The context, according to what the verifying scholars said, is the context of explaining the delay of punishment for them after they deserved it, as His words indicate: ﴿If He were to take them to account﴾, that is, if He were to will to take them to account ﴿for what they earned﴾, that is, what they did. Ash'ari's acquisition (kasb, the doctrine that human acts are acquired by God's creation) is not understood by the Arabs. The word "ma" may be verbal (masdariyya), meaning "for their earning", or relative (mawsula), meaning "for what they earned" of sins, among which is what is related of their disputing with falsehood, their turning away from the signs of their Lord, and their indifference to the destructive things they committed. ﴿He would have hastened for them the punishment﴾, because their deeds required that. It is said: The choice of the expression "take to account", which indicates the severity of seizing with speed, over "punish" and "chastise" and the like, is to signal that the negation derived from the protasis of the conditional relates to the attribute of speed, as its consequent indicates. The choice of the future form, although the meaning is past, is to convey that the absence of the hastening of punishment for them is due to the continuing absence of the will to take them to account, for the present tense used in the place of the past indicates the continuation of the action in the past.

﴿Rather, for them there is a appointed time﴾, which is the day of Badr or the Day of Resurrection, with "appointed time" being a noun of time. It is also permitted that it be a noun of place, meaning Hell. The sentence is conjoined to an implied element, as if it were said: "But they are not being taken to account
[page 306]
suddenly; rather, for them there is an appointed time." ﴿They will not find besides Him any refuge﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, a place of escape. It is said: "Wa'lat nafs fulan" meaning it fled. On this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"I sometimes steal the heedlessness of the master of the house, though he is wary of me there, where there is no refuge."

Ibn Qutayba said: It is the place of shelter. It is said: "Wa'la fulan ila kadha ya'ilu wa'lan wu'ulan", meaning he sought refuge. The meaning is one, and the difference is only in transitivity with "ila" and its absence. Interpreting it as refuge is transmitted from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid interpreted it as a safe place, and al-Dahhak as a means of deliverance. The matter in this is easy. According to what Abu al-Baqa' said, it may be a noun of time or a noun of place. The pronoun in the genitive refers to the appointed time, as is apparent. It was said that it refers to the punishment, and in that there is the intensiveness that is in it, since it indicates that they have no deliverance at all, for one whose refuge is punishment, how can he see a way to deliverance and salvation?

You know that the matter of intensiveness is also present in the apparent sense. It was also said that it refers to God, exalted is He, but this contradicts the apparent sense together with the absence of intensiveness. Al-Zuhri read "mawallan" with a doubled waw, without hamza or ya'. Abu Ja'far, from al-Halwani, from him, read "mawillan" with a light waw kasra, also without hamza or ya'.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 59 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And those towns﴾ means the towns of ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lot, and their like. The speech is elliptical, with an omitted noun: the meaning is "the people of those towns," as shown by His words ﴿We destroyed them﴾. The demonstrative is used because they are, for the listener's knowledge of them, treated as though present to the senses. Some have supposed the omitted noun before ﴿those﴾; both readings are permissible. ﴿Those﴾ (tilka) is used for the feminine, whether rational or not. It has also been allowed that "the towns" is a metaphor for their people. In any case, the demonstrative is the subject (mubtada'), and "the towns" is its attribute (sifah). Describing a demonstrative by a non-derived noun is well known in this construction. The predicate is the clause ﴿We destroyed them﴾. Abu Hayyan preferred that "the towns" be the predicate and the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal), as in His words ﴿So those are their houses, fallen into ruin﴾. It has also been allowed that ﴿those﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that the following clause explains, so that the sense is: "And We destroyed those towns, We destroyed them." ﴿When they did wrong﴾ means at the time of their wrongdoing, as the polytheists of Mecca did with the evil deeds related about them. The omission of the object either generalises the wrong or treats the verb as intransitive; that is, "when they committed wrong." According to the majority of grammarians, ﴿lamma﴾ ("when") is an adverb of time, as has been indicated. It does not mean a specific moment in which they committed the wrong, but a period extending from the beginning of the wrongdoing to its end.

Abu al-Hasan Ibn ʿUsfur said: it is a particle (harf). One of the proofs he cited for its being a particle is this verse, since it indicates that the cause of the destruction was wrongdoing, and an adverb of time does not indicate causation. It was objected that your saying "I destroyed him at the time of his wrongdoing" implies that wrongdoing was the cause, even if the adverb itself does not signify causation. It was also said: there is no objection to its being an adverb that has been used to express causation.

﴿And We appointed for their destruction﴾, that is, for their ruin, ﴿an appointment﴾, a fixed time from which they would not delay by a single hour, nor advance. Thus the first noun (mahlik) is a verbal noun (masdar), and the second (mawʿid) is a noun of time. The fixing of the time is because an appointment is never anything but fixed; otherwise a noun of time would be indefinite. The reverse is weak. Some claimed that the object of destruction in this reading, which is the reading of Hafs according to the well-known transmission from him, namely with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, is one of the rare verbal nouns, like al-marjiʿ and al-mahid. This was justified by saying that the present tense of the verb is yahlik, with a kasra on the lam, and grammarians have stated that a mim-prefixed verbal noun with a kasra on its root vowel where the present-tense root vowel is also a kasra is rare. This was rebutted: the Qamus explicitly states that halaka comes in the patterns daraba, mana, and ʿalima, so how can rarity be established? The truth is that it is a verbal noun that is not rare, and it is in the genitive construction with the agent. That is why it was explained as above. It was also said that halaka can be both intransitive and transitive; in the dialect of Banu Tamim one says halakani fulan ("so-and-so destroyed me"). On this transitive usage, the noun is in the construction with its object.

[Page 307]

Abu ʿAli cited in support of this a line of verse: "and the destroyer of him who went crooked through the wilderness", meaning its destroyer. Abu Hayyan objected that it is not necessarily so in the line; rather some grammarians hold that halik there is intransitive and belongs to the category of the adjectival form of the active participle (sifah mushabbahah), the original being halikin man taʿarraja, with man as the agent of halikin. Then a pronoun referring to mahmah was implied within halikin, and man was put in the accusative by analogy to the object, and then the construction was made genitive with nasb ("accusative"). The correct view is that it is permissible to use the relative pronoun in the adjectival form construction, and this is attested in Arabic poetry. ʿAmr ibn Abi Rabiʿa said:

*Soft of body, slender of waist, and full-bodied, whom the quilts have not wrapped.*

Hafs, Harun, Hammad, and Yahya from Abu Bakr read with a fatha on both the mim and the lam. The reading of the majority has a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, and it is also a verbal noun. Taking it as a passive participle (ism maf'ul) would mean: "and We appointed for those among them whom We destroyed in this world an appointment in which We would take vengeance upon them with the utmost vengeance," which is the Day of Resurrection or Hell. The problems with this are not hidden. The apparent meaning is that the verse is an argument regarding what was done to the Quraysh: a fixed appointment is set so that they may take warning and not be deceived by the delay of punishment from them. This supports taking the "appointment" mentioned earlier as referring to the Day of Badr. So reflect upon it. And God the Exalted knows best and is most aware.

* * *

**From the subtle allusions (ishara) in the verses:** ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. This is a command to keep company with the poor who have devoted themselves to serving their Master. Its benefit for him, upon him be blessings and peace, returns to them. That is because they are lovers of the Presence, and he (ﷺ) is its mirror, the throne of its manifestation, the mine of its secrets, and the dawning-place of its lights. Whenever they see him (ﷺ), they live; whenever he is absent from them, they grieve and are bewildered. As for keeping company with the poor in relation to other than him (ﷺ), its benefit returns to the one who keeps their company, for they are a people whose companion does not suffer. ʿAmr al-Makki said: keeping company with the righteous and the truthful poor is the life of the people of Paradise; their companion turns with them from contentment to certainty and from certainty to contentment. From the famous qasida of Abu Madyan, which Shaykh Muhyi al-Din expanded into a quintain (may his secret be sanctified), come the lines:

*What pleasure is there in life except the company of the poor? They are the sultans, the lords, and the princes.*

*So keep their company and be courteous in their gatherings, and set aside your own portion, however they put you behind them.*

*Seize the time, and be always present with them, and know that contentment belongs to whoever is present.*

*Keep silence unless you are asked; then say, "I have no knowledge," and remain veiled in ignorance.*

*Until he said:*

*If a fault appears in you, acknowledge it, and make your excuse for what is in you of wrong.*

*And say, "Your servants have more right to your forgiveness, so be lenient and take gently, O poor ones."*

*They are more inclined to bounty, and that is their nature, so do not fear any reckoning or harm from them.*

By these lords he meant the Sufis, and the designation "poor" has become common for them, because poverty in the familiar sense predominates among them. Their poverty accompanies righteousness, and for this reason poverty is praised. But if it is joined with corruption, we seek refuge in God the Exalted from that. Whenever you hear encouragement to sit with the poor, know that what is meant is the righteous poor. The reports on this are numerous. From Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as a statement attributed to him: "Be humble, and sit with the needy, and you will be among the great servants of God the Exalted, and you will be freed from pride." In al-Jami': "Sitting with the poor is a form of humility, and it is among the best of struggle (jihad)." In another report: "Love the poor and sit with them." Among the benefits of sitting with them is that the servant sees the blessing of God the Exalted upon him, is content with little of this world, and in their company is safe from flattery, fawning, bearing obligation, and other such things. Yes, sitting with them is contrary to what the soul is disposed to; therefore its excellence is great. It has been said that in His words ﴿keep yourself patient with those who…﴾ and so on, rather than "remain with those who…" and so on, there is an allusion to this. But this applies in relation to others than him (ﷺ), for his noble self was created with the best nature and formed with the best disposition.

Some of the people of inner meanings said: the phrase "keep yourself patient" was used rather than "keep your heart patient," because his noble heart (ﷺ) was always with the Truth. So he was commanded to keep company with the poor openly, and God the Glorified singled out his heart for Himself secretly.

﴿Desiring the adornment of the life of this world﴾, that is, seeking the company of nobles, the wealthy, and the people of this world. This is blameworthy when accompanied by inclination toward them and humility before their wealth.

It has come in a hadith: "Whoever humbles himself before a rich man for the sake of his wealth has lost two-thirds of his religion, so let him fear God the Exalted regarding the remaining third."

The harms of keeping company with them are many, and they are not hidden from anyone who knows the benefits of keeping company with the poor. The least of their harm is what you bear from them, for the wealthy rarely escape reminding his poor companion of his favours, even by mere companionship, and that is an unbearable burden. Among the witticisms of al-Zamakhshari: "The taste of blessings is sweeter than reminders of favours, and they are more bitter than blessings when reminders are made." And one of the poets said:

*We have a companion who ever follows up his kindness with reminders, and the giving of reminders with kindness is worth nothing.*

*We left him, not out of hatred or weariness, but because for the sake of his reminders the quail is used (as bait).*

﴿And do not obey him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair is ever excess﴾. This is a prohibition against obeying the veiled and heedless. In the story they wanted to drive away the poor and to prevent the Prophet (ﷺ) from sitting with them. But the lesson lies in the generality of the wording, not in the particular cause. So among the people of allusion, the heedless and veiled person who has the desire of the soul in everything is not to be obeyed. They counted among obeying him the humility shown to him, for he seeks that outwardly, even if he does not express it in words.

﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. They said: this contains an allusion to not concealing the truth, even if it leads to the denial of the veiled and the aversion of the ignorant. Among the matters counted as part of the secrets of the Qur'an is the disclosure of divine secrets. It was said: the true lover does not mind the exposure of secrets before strangers, and does not fear the blame of any blamer, nor is he bound by the belief or denial of creatures. For the pleasure of love in that is more complete. Do you not see the words of the speaker:

*Ah, give me wine and say to me, "It is wine," and do not pour it for me in secret when it is possible to pour it openly.*

*And declare the name of the one I love, and leave me aside from allusions, for there is no good in pleasures without the veil of disclosure.*

It is not hidden that this is contrary to what is accepted among the Sufis, may God the Exalted sanctify their secrets. For they have kept their secrets from strangers and enjoined this. And as proof on this matter, what is attributed to Zayn al-ʿAbidin, may Allah be pleased with him, suffices:

*Indeed I conceal from my knowledge its jewels, lest the ignorant one see the Truth and be tempted by us.*

*Abu Hasan has already gone before in this, to al-Husayn, and he enjoined it before him upon al-Hasan.*

*For many a jewel of knowledge, if I were to disclose it, it would be said to me, "You are one of those who worship idols."*

*And men who are Muslims would make my blood lawful, seeing the vilest of their own deeds as good.*

Yes, the one overpowered and likewise the one under command is excused, and in necessity the forbidden is permitted. How excellent are the words of al-Shihab al-Qatil:

*Alas for the mercy upon lovers, who strain to conceal love and passion, though it is a revealer!*

*If they disclose the secret, their blood is made lawful; and likewise the blood of those who disclose is made lawful.*

*And if they conceal, the tearful eye tells of them in the presence of the informers.*

What was mentioned first can serve as a defence of Shaykh al-Akbar (may his secret be sanctified) and his like. For they did not mind disclosing the realities which they claimed, even though it was a cause of the misguidance of many people and a summons to denounce them. Some have used the verse in refuting them, on the basis that the true meaning is what comes from God the Glorified, and what they brought is not from Him, since no verse testifies to it, no hadith confirms it, and no report supports it. It has been answered that this is nothing but from the verses and hadiths, except that it is derived from them only by holy power and divine lights. So the deniers' failure to understand it does not prove that it is not true, since they lack that power and are veiled from those lights. How many a truth has their understanding not reached! It has been objected that if this were so, such realities would have appeared in the earliest period, for the possessors of holy powers and divine lights were many in it, and the eagerness to make the truth manifest was greater. It has been answered that it is possible that there was an impediment, or the absence of a factor requiring the manifestation of what has been made manifest of realities. There is in this a kind of unease, and perhaps what may benefit you here will come to you, God willing. In sum, the matter of Shaykh al-Akbar and his like (may God sanctify their secrets) in what they said and wrote is, to me, problematic, especially the matter of the Shaykh, for he brought the greatest calamity, despite the greatness of his undeniable rank. That is why you see many people denouncing him and turning away from him. How elegant is what was said by Firaq Janin al-ʿIsabah al-Faruqiyyah and the one who ascends the ladders of the descents of Mawsil, in his poem in which he set the elixir of praise for the red sulphur, so that it became a sun on the horizons of the praises of Shaykh al-Akbar. It is his saying:

*A man denies from it a matter, then it forbids him, and his forbidding denies the denial.*

*It turns away from him, then turns toward him with tongues that resemble the sober as drunkards.*

[End of part 1]

﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾. It was said: this indicates that they will be adorned with the realities of the Essential Oneness (al-tawhid al-dhati, the unity of the Divine Essence) and the meanings of the Essential, Unitary self-manifestations (al-tajalliyat al-ʿayniyya al-ahadiyya). ﴿And they will wear green garments﴾ indicates that they are characterized by bright, good, fresh attributes that produce joy, ﴿of fine silk﴾ (the states and gifts, and it is expressed by "fine silk" because they are more delicate), ﴿and brocade﴾ (the characters and acquisitions, and it is expressed by "brocade" because they are thicker). ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾: it was said, that is, the couches of the Divine Names (asma larr ilahiyya). ﴿And strike for them an example: two men...﴾ etc. In this there is, from the consolation of the poor who rely upon God, the Exalted, and the alerting of the deluded rich, what there is. Al-Nisaburi said: the two men are the sinful soul (al-nafs al-kafira) and the believing heart (al-qalb al-mu'min). ﴿We made for one of them﴾, and it is the soul, ﴿two gardens﴾, which are desire (al-hawa) and the world (al-dunya), ﴿of grapevines﴾ (the appetites), ﴿and We surrounded them with palm trees﴾ (love of leadership), ﴿and We placed between them a field﴾ (of bestial enjoyments), ﴿and We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ (of human powers and the senses). ﴿And he had fruit﴾ (of the kinds of appetites), ﴿and he said to his companion, while conversing with him﴾, that is, he contends with the soul: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth﴾, that is, in inclination, ﴿and mightier in men﴾ (of blameworthy qualities). ﴿And he wronged himself﴾ in enjoying the garden of this world according to the whim (hawa). ﴿He said: I shall surely find better than it﴾, he said that out of delusion in God, the Exalted, and His generosity. ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent therein﴾ of his life and the goodness of his readiness. End.

This pattern has been adopted in most of the verses, and there is no novelty in it, for it is the practice of many interpreters.

﴿There, guardianship belongs to God, the True. He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾. Ibn ʿAta said: (guardianship belongs) to those seeking Him, glorified be He, not to Paradise. ﴿And best in outcome﴾ is for those who desire (Him). ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: it was said they are the lasting love, the complete gnosis (maʿrifa), intimacy with God, the Exalted, sincerity in His Oneness, glorified be He, and singling Him out, exalted is He above other than Him. So they remain for the one who is characterized by them, and they are sound, with no crookedness in them, and they are the best of abodes. It may also be explained as encompassing them and other than them of sincere deeds and truthful intentions.

﴿And on the Day We set the mountains in motion and you see the earth laid bare﴾. Ibn ʿAta said: by this, glorified be He, indicates the manifestation of His majesty, the completeness of His power, and the greatness of His might, so that the servant may prepare for that station and set right his inward and outward state for the address of that scene and its answer. ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ is a report about all the children of Adam, even if the addressee in His words, glorified be He, ﴿Nay, you claimed...﴾ etc. is some of them. It is mentioned that each category will be presented in a row. It was also said: the prophets, peace be upon them, are one row, the saints are a row, and the rest of the believers are a row, while the hypocrites and disbelievers are a row, and they are the last of the rows. So it is said to them: ﴿You have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾, in the description of the original nature, weak and cut off toward Him, glorified be He. ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, that is, the books, so the book of acts of obedience will be placed for the ascetics and worshippers, and the book of obedience and disobedience for the general people, and the book of love, longing and passion for the elite. And one of them said:

"I deposited in the heart a book of longing,
whose folds will be unfolded on the Day of Reckoning."

﴿And they will find what they did present﴾. Abu Hafs said: the most severe verse in the Qur'an upon my heart is this verse: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾. It was said: that is, I did not make them witness the secrets of that and the subtleties deposited therein, and God, glorified be He, only made His beloved and friends witness that. ﴿And man is most contentious of things﴾, because he is the locus of the diverse Names and the lesser world in which the greater world is enfolded. This, and God, the Exalted, knows best the secrets of His Book.

﴿Wa-idh qala Musa﴾ (And when Musa said). He is the son of 'Imran, the Prophet of the Children of Israel, peace be upon him, according to the sound opinion. al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group of others narrated through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: Nawf al-Bikali claims that Musa, the companion of al-Khidr, is not Musa, the one of the Children of Israel. He said: "The enemy of Allah has lied." Then he related a long hadith in which he reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ something that is explicit that he was Musa of the Children of Israel. The People of the Book also went to denying this, and those among the muhaddithun (hadith scholars) and historians who followed them also followed them, and they claimed that the Musa here is Musa ibn Misha, with a dotted sh, son of Yusuf ibn Ya'qub. It was also said: Musa ibn Ifra'im ibn Yusuf, and he is the first Musa. It was said: The People of the Book only denied it because they deny that the Prophet learned from someone other than himself. It was answered: We accept that he learned from a prophet, and there is no disgrace in one prophet learning from another prophet. It was objected: Even if they accepted that and acknowledged the prophethood of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, they would not accept that he was Musa ibn 'Imran, because their souls do not permit them to say that their most excellent Prophet learned from someone who is not equal to him in excellence. Al-Khidr, peace be upon him, even according to the view of his prophethood, or indeed of his messengerhood, does not reach the rank of Musa, peace be upon him. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: Their denial is not merely for that alone, but for that and for their saying that Musa, peace be upon him, after the exodus from Egypt, he and his people came to be in the wilderness (al-tih), and he died there, and his people did not come out of it except after his death. The story requires his, peace be upon him, leaving the wilderness, because it did not take place while he was in Egypt by consensus (ijma'). It also requires his absence for days, and if it had happened, many of the Children of Israel who were with him would have known it. And if it had been known, it would have been transmitted, because it contains an extraordinary matter, and the motives to transmit it would be abundant. Since it was not transmitted, it did not happen.

It was answered: Their unwillingness to accept that their Prophet, peace be upon him, learned from someone who is not equal to him in excellence is a matter that reason does not support, and it is nothing but a kind of jahili zealotry (hamiyya jahiliyya). For it is not far-fetched by reason that the more excellent and more knowledgeable learns something that he does not have from one who is lower than him in excellence and knowledge. Among the well-known proverbs: "Something may be found in the discarded (al-asqat) that is not found in the boxes (al-asfat)." And they said: "Something may be found in the one who is less excellent that is not found in the excellent." And some of them said:

"There is no obstacle that Allah, glorified and exalted, has concealed from Musa, peace be upon him, the knowledge of the matters that the story includes, despite his greater knowledge and excellence, for a wisdom. That does not detract from his being more excellent and more knowledgeable than al-Khidr, peace be upon him. And that is nothing, as is not hidden."

And [it was answered] that it will come, if Allah wills, shortly that the story took place after Musa, peace be upon him, had prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel and settled after the destruction of the Copts. So there is no consensus that it did not take place in Egypt. Yes, the Jews do not say that they settled in Egypt after the destruction of the Copts, and many of us also hold this view. Then it is said: That Musa, peace be upon him, did not leave the wilderness is not accepted. Likewise, the claim that this requires his absence for days is not accepted, since it may be in a way that breaks habit, like the wilderness they fell into, and the lifting of the mountain over them, and other extraordinary things that happened to them. And it may be said: It is possible that he, peace be upon him, went out and was absent for days, but they did not know that he, peace be upon him, had gone for this matter, and they thought he had gone to commune and worship, and he did not inform them of the reality of his absence after he returned, knowing the weakness of their understanding, and he feared that his rank would be diminished in their eyes. They are the ones who said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ and ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾. And he instructed his young man (fata) to conceal that from them as well. It is also possible that he, peace be upon him, was absent and they knew the reality of his absence, but they did not transmit it generation after generation, out of a presumption that there was in it something that would lower his noble rank, peace be upon him. So its transmission continued to decline until they perished at the time of Bukhtnassar, just as most of the bearers of the Torah perished. It is also possible that a very small number of them remained until the time of our Prophet ﷺ, and they agreed among themselves to conceal it and deny it, in order to cast doubt into the hearts of the weak Muslims. Then that small number perished and it was not transmitted from them. It is not hidden that the door of possibility is wide. In sum, their denial is not to be heeded, after the possibility of its occurrence is accepted by reason and Allah, exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ have reported it, for the verse is manifest in that. Close to this denial is the denial of the Christians of the speech of 'Isa, peace be upon him, in the cradle. We have already mentioned that it is not to be turned to after Allah, exalted, has reported it. So hold fast to the Book of Allah, exalted, and leave aside the whisperings.

[p. 312]

"Idh" is in the accusative as an object (maf'uliyya) of "udhkur" (remember), which is omitted, and the meaning is: say, "Musa said." ﴿To his young man (fatahu)﴾ Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Ifra'im ibn Yusuf, peace be upon him, for he used to serve him and learn from him, and that is why he is attributed to him. The Arabs call a servant "fata" because servants are most often in the age of youthfulness (al-futuwwa). He was, it is said, the son of the sister of Musa, peace be upon him. It was also said: He was the brother of Yusha', peace be upon him, and the Jews denied that he had a brother. It was also said: He was his servant, and the attribution is to ownership, and he was called "fata" for what is in the authentic hadith: "Let none of you say: 'My fata and my fataat,' and let him not say: 'My slave and my slave-girl.'" This is among the etiquettes of the Sharia. Using that is not disliked, contrary to some, but rather contrary to the preferable (khilaf al-awla). This view contradicts the well-known position, and al-Nawawi ruled that it is an invalid view. The permissibility of owning people among the Children of Israel is a matter of discussion. The second view is similarly invalid, because it contradicts all the authentic reports.

﴿La abrah﴾ (I will not cease) from "barah" the defective verb, like "zala yazal" (to cease), i.e., "la azal asir" (I will not cease traveling). He omitted the predicate (khabar), relying on the indication of the situation (qarina al-hal), since that was at the time of setting out on the journey, and relying on what follows it, his saying: ﴿until I reach﴾, for a terminal point (al-ghaya) necessarily has something it ends, and what fits it here is travel, and what comes after also indicates this. The omission of the predicate in such a case is rare, as al-Radi mentioned, and of it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"They did not cease until their women swayed in the valley of Dhi Qar, with the perfumed boxes of scent."

[p. 313 would be next]

Abu Hayyan said: Our companions have stated that omitting the predicate of kana and its sisters is not permissible, even if evidence indicates its omission, except what came in poetry, in his saying:

"Alas for you, like the grief of one fearful who seeks your protection when there is no protector."

That is: when there is no one in the world. al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the original was: "My journey will not cease until I reach," so the predicate is "until" together with its genitive, and the pronoun of "sir" (journey) was omitted, which became in the nominative and concealed form, and the verb changed from third person to first person. It was said: Likewise the verb occurring in the predicate, which is ﴿abligh﴾, as if its original was "yablugha," so that the connection is achieved, and the attribution is metaphorical. Otherwise the predicate would be without a connecting element, unless it is estimated: "until I reach with it," or it is said that the hidden pronoun in "ka'in" suffices for the connection, or that the existence of the connection after change is formally sufficient, even if what is estimated is in the force of what is mentioned. In my view there is no subtlety in this option, although al-Zamakhshari found it subtle.

It was also permitted that "abrah" is from "barih" (complete), like "zala yazul," so it needs no predicate. Yes, it was said: a supplied object (maf'ul) must be estimated for the meaning to be complete, i.e., "I will not depart from what I am undertaking until I reach ﴿the meeting place of the two seas (majma' al-bahrayn)﴾." Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) criticized this, saying it requires a sound transmission.

Al-majma' is the place of meeting, and it is a noun of place. It was said to be a verbal noun, but that is not the case. The two seas are the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome, as narrated from Mujahid, Qatada and others. Their meeting point is on the side of the east. Perhaps what is meant is a place where their meeting is near, for otherwise the two do not meet except in the Ocean (al-bahr al-muhit), and they are two branches of it.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that the meeting place of the two seas, according to what the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya implies, is on the side of the land of Syria. A group among them, including Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, said: It is near Tangier, where the Ocean and the sea that flows out of it meet, from the south-west to the east. And it is narrated from Abu [...] that it is in Ifriqiya. It was said: The two seas are al-Kurr and al-Rass in Armenia, and this is narrated from al-Suddi. It was said: The Sea of al-Qulzum and the Blue Sea. It was said: They are a salt sea and a fresh sea, and their meeting is in the Green Island (al-Jazira al-Khadra) on the western side. It was said: They are a metaphor for Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, because they are two seas of knowledge, and the intended meaning of their meeting is a place where their gathering happens by chance. This is a Sufi interpretation, and the context rejects it, and likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿until I reach﴾, for the apparent sense would be to say: "until the two seas meet," for example.

Al-Dahhak and 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read "majma'" with a kasra on the second mim (majmi'). And al-Nadr, from Ibn Muslim, read "mijma'" with a kasra on both letters. This is anomalous in both readings, because the analogy for nouns of place and time from "fa'ala yaf'alu" with a fatha on the 'ayn is fatha in both, as in the reading of the majority.

﴿Aw amdiya huquban﴾ (or I go on for a long time) is coordinated to ﴿abligh﴾ and "aw" is for one of two things. The meaning is: until one of two things occurs, either my reaching the meeting place, or my passing a period (huqub), that is, my journey for a long time.

It was permitted that "aw" means "illa" (except/until), with the verb after it in the subjunctive by an implied "an," and the exception is incomplete from the most general circumstances. That is: "I will not cease traveling in every state until I reach, except that I pass a time with which I am certain of missing the meeting place." Abu Hayyan reported the permissibility of "aw" meaning "ila" (to), but it is not sound, because it requires his certainty of reaching the meeting place after his journey of a huqub, and that is not intended.

"Huqub" is with two dammas and it is said with one damma then a sukun, and al-Dahhak read it that way. It is a singular noun, and its plural, as in the Qamus, is "ahqub" and "ahqab." In the Sihah (al-Sihah), it is stated that huqub with a damma is pluralized as "hiqab," like "quff" and "qifaf." It is, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the lexicographers, a long age (dahr). It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayra that it is eighty years, and from al-Hasan that it is seventy. al-Farra' said it is a year in the dialect of Quraysh. Abu Hayyan said: The hiqab are years, and its singular is hiqba. The poet said:

"If you turn away from her for a hiqba, you will not meet her, for you are, from what you have made, in the [thing] tried."

What he mentioned, that the hiqab are years, was mentioned by more than one lexicographer, but his saying "its singular is hiqba" is open to scrutiny, because the apparent sense of their speech is that it is a singular noun, and al-Khafaji explicitly stated that. Also, hiqba is the plural of hiqab (with a kasra then a fatha), and the Qamus says: "al-hiqba with a kasra from the age is a period with no fixed time, and a year; its plural is hiqab, like 'inab, and huqub, like hubub." al-Raghib and al-Jawhari restricted themselves to the first.

The origin of Musa's, peace be upon him, determination to go, according to what is mentioned, is what al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Musa, peace be upon him, stood up as a preacher among the Children of Israel, and he was asked: Who is the most knowledgeable of people? He said: I am. So Allah, exalted, rebuked him, because he did not refer knowledge back to Him, glorified be He. So Allah, exalted, revealed to him that I have a servant at the meeting place of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you." The hadith [continues].

And in another narration from him, from Ubayy as well, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Musa of the Children of Israel asked his Lord, saying: O Lord, if there is among Your servants anyone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him. He said to him: Yes, among My servants is one more knowledgeable than you. Then He described to him his place and permitted him to meet him."

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary on surah 18, verse 60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Harun, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Musa (peace be upon him) asked his Lord, glorified is He, saying: "O my Lord, which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Then which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow his desire." He said: "Then which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him away from ruin." He said: Musa had said to himself that there was no one more knowledgeable than him. So when it was said to him, "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own," he said: "O my Lord, is there anyone on earth more knowledgeable than me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Where is he?" It was said to him: "By the rock where the spring is." So Musa set out seeking him, until what Allah the Exalted mentioned took place.

Then, these reports do not indicate that the story occurred in Egypt or elsewhere. Yes, some narrations do explicitly state that it was in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Awfi, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Musa (peace be upon him) and his people prevailed over Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt. When the land was settled for them, Allah the Exalted revealed that he should remind them of the Days of Allah the Exalted. So he addressed his people and mentioned the good and blessings that Allah the Exalted had given them, and reminded them when Allah the Exalted delivered them from the family of Pharaoh, and reminded them of the destruction of their enemy and of how Allah, glorified is He, had made them successors on the earth. He said: "Allah the Exalted spoke to your Prophet directly, He chose me for Himself, He placed upon me love from Him, and He gave you everything you asked of Him. So your Prophet is the best of the people of the earth, and you read the Torah." He did not leave out any blessing Allah the Exalted had bestowed upon them without making them aware of it. Then a man from the Children of Israel said to him: "O Prophet of Allah, is there anyone on earth more knowledgeable than you?" He said: "No." So Allah the Exalted sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to Musa (peace be upon him), who said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted says: 'And what will make you know where I place My knowledge? Rather, there is on the shore of the sea a man more knowledgeable than you.'" Then occurred what Allah, glorified is He, related.

Ibn Atiyya denied this, saying: "It is not seen at all that Musa (peace be upon him) settled his people in Egypt except in this statement, and I do not think it is sound. Rather, what is widely attested is that Musa (peace be upon him) died in the land of the wandering (al-Tih) before the conquest of the lands of the tyrants." End quote. What he mentioned about Musa (peace be upon him) not settling his people in Egypt is, in my view, the more acceptable position, even though al-Khafaji criticized his statement after quoting it, saying: "In it there is room for consideration."

Furthermore, the reports mentioned clearly indicate that the servant to whom Musa (peace be upon him) was guided was more knowledgeable than him. The discussion of that will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

[p. 314]

**﴿So when they reached﴾**: the *fa'* (the particle *fa*) here is *fasīḥa* (expressive, implying an unstated antecedent). The sense is: so they set off walking to the meeting place of the two seas. **﴿When they reached the meeting place of the two of them﴾**, that is, of the two seas. The original form of *bayn* (between) is the accusative, used as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyya*).

It has been taken out of this (accusative) by putting it in the genitive through the *iḍāfa* (construct phrase), as a form of extended usage (*ittisā'*). The intended meaning is "their meeting place." It has also been said: "a meeting place in the middle of them," so that it serves as an elaboration of "the meeting place of the two seas." It is mentioned that this fits the explanation of the meeting place as Tangier or Ifriqiya, since by "the meeting place" is meant the point where the branches of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea join from the Ocean, and that is there.

It has also been said that *bayn* is a noun meaning "junction." This has been criticized on the ground that it is weak, since there is no elegance in saying "the meeting place of their junction." It has also been said that there is in it extra emphasis, like the saying "his grandfather's grandfather" (*jadd jaddihi*). It is also permissible that it means "separation": the place where the separating of the two seas meets, that is, the two seas which are separated. The apparent reading is that the dual pronoun, under both possibilities, refers to the two seas.

Al-Khafaji said: It is possible, under the possibility that it means "separation," that it refers back to Musa and al-Khadir, peace be upon them both; that is, they reached the place of the promised meeting of their companionship in it. Likewise if it means "junction." He ended. In this there is what is not hidden. Under all the other possibilities, *majma'* is a noun of place, and the possibility of its being a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) here is like what preceded.

**﴿They forgot their fish﴾**, which was made the sign of finding the sought one, its loss being the indication.

It is established that when God, exalted is He, said to Musa, peace be upon him: "Indeed I have at the meeting place of the two seas one who is more knowledgeable," Musa said: "O Lord, how can I come to him?" He said: "Take with you a fish, and put it in a basket. Wherever you lose the fish, he is there." So he took a fish and put it in a basket, then set off, and his young man set off with him, until they came to the rock, and it was at the meeting place of the two seas. They put down their heads and slept, and the fish stirred in the basket, went out of it, and fell into the sea.

The apparent reading is that forgetting is attributed to both of them together, and this is the view of the majority of scholars (*jumhūr*). The statement is according to an omitted element (*muḍāf*), that is: they forgot the condition of their fish. But the condition that each of them forgot differs. The condition that Musa, peace be upon him, forgot was its remaining in the basket or being lost. The condition that Yusha', peace be upon him, forgot was what he saw of its life and its falling into the sea. This is the view that Yusha' witnessed its coming back to life, and there is in this a sound report.

In a ḥadīth narrated by al-Shaykhān and others: "God, exalted is He, said to Musa: Take a dead Nun (fish), and it is wherever the spirit is breathed into it. So he took it and put it in a basket. He said to his young man: I will not burden you except that you inform me of the place where the fish leaves you. He said: You have not been asked for much. While they were in the shade of a rock, suddenly the fish stirred until it entered the sea, and Musa was asleep. His young man said: I will not wake him. When he woke up, he forgot to inform him."

In a ḥadīth narrated by Muslim and others: "God, exalted is He, said to him: The sign of that is that you take with you a salted fish, and it is wherever you lose it. He did so, until when they reached the rock, Musa set off seeking, and his young man placed the fish on the rock. It stirred and entered the sea. His young man said: When the Prophet of God comes, I will inform him. So Satan made him forget."

Some have claimed that the one who forgot was only the young man, who forgot to inform Musa, peace be upon him, about the matter of the fish. The reason for attributing forgetting to both of them is that a thing may be attributed to a group even if the one who did it was only one of them. What is mentioned here is similar to the phrase "the people forgot their provision" when the one responsible for their affairs forgot it. It has also been said that the statement involves the omission of an element: that is, one of them forgot, and what is meant is the young man. But this is, as you see, weak. The cause of this fish's coming back to life, according to what is in some reports from Ibn 'Abbas, is that by the rock there was water of life; whoever drinks from it becomes immortal, and no dead thing comes near it without coming back to life. Some of it reached the fish, and it came back to life.

It is also narrated that Yusha', peace be upon him, performed ablution with that water, and some of it splashed onto the fish, and it lived.

It has also been said: it was not touched except by the spirit and coolness of the water, so it lived by God's permission, exalted is He. The mention of this water, and that nothing of it touched anything without that thing coming back to life, and that the fish was touched by it, is found in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī in connection with Surat al-Kahf as well, but there is nothing in it that whoever drinks from it becomes immortal, as in some of the previous reports. It is a difficulty for this view that it is narrated that Yusha' also drank from it, yet he did not become immortal. Only, it may be said that this does not hold. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Then this fish was, as you have heard earlier, salted, and in one report it was roasted. In some reports it was among what they took as provision, and they would eat from it at supper and lunch. God brought it to life, and they had eaten half of it. **﴿And it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾**: a path like a tunnel (*sarab*), and the sarab is the underground passage.

It is established from the ḥadīth of al-Shaykhān, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasā'ī and others: "God, exalted is He, held back from the fish the flow of the water, so that over it was something like an arch." What is meant by it is a curved building like a bridge.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related through al-'Awfī from al-Ḥabr (Ibn 'Abbas): the fish did not touch anything of the sea without that thing drying up until it became a rock. This, and likewise what preceded of the extraordinary matters contrary to custom which God, glorified is He, shows to whomever He wills of His prophets and saints, is what al-Damīrī mentioned, the trace of the first extraordinary event persisting. He said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Andalusī said: I saw a fish near the city of Sabta, of the offspring of the fish which Musa and his young man took as provision, and they ate from it. It is a fish whose length is more than an arm's length and whose width is a span. One of its sides has thorns and bones, and there is a thin skin over its entrails. It has one eye, and its head is half a head. Whoever sees it from this side finds it disgusting and supposes it is a dead carrion. Its other half is sound, and people seek blessing from it and send it as gifts to distant places. He ended.

Abū Shujā' said in the book of al-Ṭabarī: "I came with it and saw it; it was half a fish, and it had only one eye." Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: "I too saw it, and on its half there was a thin skin under which there was no thorn." In this there is a contradiction with what is in the statement of Abū Ḥāmid. I asked many of the sea travellers and followers of the wonders of traces, and they did not mention that they had seen that, nor was it presented to them in any of the kingdoms. So perhaps the matter, if it is sound, each of affirmation and negation, has become today like the phoenix, which once existed and then ceased to exist. And God, exalted is He, knows the reality of the situation best.

The *fa'* according to what their statements imply is *fasīḥa*: that is, so it came to life and fell into the sea, then took (its way). Some of them supplied the element that the *fa'* hints at, with a *wāw* (and) contrary to what is usual, in order to avert the objection to the condition that Yusha' forgot being what he saw of its life and its falling into the sea. The objection was that the *fa'* indicates that his forgetting, peace be upon him, was before its life and its falling into the sea and its taking the tunnel, so that it is not valid to count that in the forgotten condition. It was answered that what is considered in the condition is life and falling into the sea themselves, without considering anything else. What in fact lies after them, insofar as taking (the path) is consequent upon them, is that they are in themselves prior to forgetting, and insofar as taking is subsequent, they are subsequent; and from this aspect they are conjoined to "they forgot" by the *fa'* of consequence. It is not hidden that what will come in the answer, God willing, will reject this answer, unless it is required in it to deviate from what is well known among the scholars. So consider.

The accusative of **﴿tunnel﴾** is because it is a second object of *ittakhadha* (took), and **﴿in the sea﴾** is a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) from it. Had it come later, it would be a qualifier, or from "the way." It is also permissible that it be connected to *ittakhadha*. The *fī* in all of that is for place.

Perhaps it might be imagined from the statement of Ibn Zayd, where he said: "He only took his way on land until he reached the sea, and then swam", that the *fa'* is causal, like the saying that a woman entered the Fire because of a cat. It is as if it were said: so he took his way on land as a tunnel for the sake of his reaching the sea. Some agreed with him that the making of the tunnel was on land, and they claimed that on his path on land he encountered a stone and bored through it. It is not hidden that saying this contradicts what is found in the sound reports which you have heard, and the verse hardly supports it. It has been permitted that *sabīlahu* (his way) is the object of *ittakhadha*, with **﴿in the sea﴾** and **﴿tunnel﴾** as a circumstantial phrase from "the way," but this is not the right view. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial phrase from the subject of *ittakhadha*, and it has the sense of free movement and roaming, from the saying "a stallion sārib", that is, left unrestrained, grazing wherever it wishes. From this is the verse **﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾** (13:10). It is in the sense of a description, that is: he took that in the sea, moving freely. It is not hidden that this is similar to what preceded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 62:

﴿Then when they had passed beyond it﴾ That is, beyond the place where their destination, the meeting-point of the two seas, lay. It is related soundly that they continued on the rest of their day and their night, until, when it was the next day and the day had risen high, Musa, peace be upon him, felt hunger. At that point ﴿he said to his young man, "Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ The ghada' (morning meal) is the food eaten at the start of the day, and what is meant by it is the fish, as the apparent sense of the reply indicates. It has also been said that they travelled through the night until the next day, and then he said that.

﴿Indeed we have suffered from this journey of ours, nasaban﴾ That is, weariness and exhaustion. This refers to their journey, which they were engaged in, but by considering some part of it.

It is soundly related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Musa did not experience any fatigue until he passed the place he had been commanded to go to."

It has been mentioned that this is understood from the implication (fahwa), and the specification by mention indicates that he was not fatigued during his other journeys. The wisdom in the occurrence of hunger and fatigue to him once he had passed the place was that he should seek the morning meal, whereupon he would recall the fish and return to the place where he would meet what he sought.

And from Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn Atiyya, father of Abu Abd al-Haqq the exegete, who said: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his preaching: Musa walked to the private conversation (with his Lord) and remained forty days without needing food, and when he walked to a human being, hunger overtook him on some day.

The clause is in the position of giving the reason for the command to bring the morning meal, either by considering that fatigue arises only because of the weakness that results from hunger, or by considering the brief rest that occurs during the taking of the meal.

Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr read: "nuṣuban" with two dammas. The author of al-Lawamih said: this is one of the four dialectal forms of this word.

﴿He said﴾ that is, his young man said. The resumption is explanatory (bayani), as if it were said: What did the young man do when Musa, peace be upon him, said what he said? It was said: He said: ﴿"Do you see? When we took refuge at the rock, indeed I forgot the fish"﴾, that is, we sought shelter by it and stayed there.

In some sound narrations it is reported that when Musa, peace be upon him, said to his young man: ﴿"Indeed we have suffered from this journey of ours, nasaban"﴾, he said: "God has removed the fatigue from you."

Accordingly, it is possible that after he said that

[p. 317]

"He said: ﴿Did you see?﴾ etc." Shaykh al-Islam said: He mentioned the taking refuge at the rock, although what was mentioned earlier was reaching the meeting place of the two seas, in order to specify further the place of the incident. The meeting place is a wide area, so it is not possible to pin down the intended meaning by attributing the incident to it. The reference to the rock also serves to prepare an excuse, since taking refuge there and sleeping beside it commonly lead to forgetfulness. End of quote.

This last point holds only according to some of the reports that they slept beside the rock. It is mentioned that this rock was near the River of Olive Oil, a specific river with many olive trees around it. As for ﴿Did you see?﴾, it has been said to mean "Tell me." Abu Hayyan objected to this: if it has this meaning, it must have two things: the noun asked about must follow it, and the sentence after it must have the form of a question. Neither of these is present here. Abu Hayyan and the army's supervisor (Nazir al-Jaysh) in their commentary on al-Tashil reported from Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash that he held that when "a'ara'ayta" is not followed by an object or a question, but by a sentence introduced by the particle fa', as here, it is taken out of its usual use and is understood to mean "either" or "take note," so that the fa' is its answer, not the answer of "idh," since it is not used as a conditional except when accompanied by "ma," without disagreement. The meaning is therefore: "Either, or take note, when we took refuge at the rock: ﴿I forgot the fish﴾."

Shaykh al-Islam said: The verb "to see" is used figuratively for complete knowledge and full witnessing. Its purpose in the question is to make Musa (peace be upon him) marvel at the forgetfulness that overcame him there, given that what he had witnessed was among the great wonders that are hardly ever forgotten. The loss of the fish has been made a sign of finding what was sought.
