This is a common manner of speech among people: when one of them is afflicted by a calamity, he says to his companion, "Do you see what has befallen me?" He intends by this to magnify the matter and to make his companion marvel at it, since such a thing is not known to happen and one does not usually ask about it, as has been said. The object is omitted, relying on what is indicated by his words ﴿Indeed I﴾ etc. This includes emphasis on the wonder and an encouragement to regard the forgotten matter as weighty. End of quote. There is in this some deficiency.

Al-Zamakhshari took it as a real question. He said: When Yusha' (peace be upon him) asked Musa (peace be upon him) for the meal, he mentioned what he had seen of the fish and what had overcome him of forgetting it up to that point. He was astonished and began to ask about the cause of this, as if he said: "Did you see what overcame me when we took refuge at the rock? For I forgot the fish." So he omitted that. End of quote. This indicates that the object of ﴿Did you see?﴾ is omitted: it is either the interrogative clause, if "ma" in "ma dahani" is interrogative, or the very word "ma" if it is a relative pronoun. It also indicates that "idh" is an adverb of time connected to "dahani," and it is the cause of what follows the fa' in ﴿Indeed I﴾, and this fa' is causal. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And when they are not guided by it, they will say, "This is an ancient lie."﴾ The implied meaning is: "And when they are not guided by it, their obstinacy appears, so they will say," etc. This is the view that "a'ara'ayta" means "tell me," and you have heard what has been said against it. In its interpretation according to the second possibility there is also the matter of omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause, on the basis that ﴿Indeed I forgot﴾ is part of that clause. In general, the intended meaning of the question is not its literal sense but also the magnification of the matter.

Furthermore, it should not be overlooked that if "ra'a" is visual, or means "to know," it requires one object. According to some of the verifiers, the implied meaning is: "Did you see, or did you know my state when we took refuge?" This involves reducing the omission, and its merit is not hidden. If it is of the sort of knowledge, it requires two objects. On this basis Abu Hayyan said: It is possible that it belongs to the category in which both objects are omitted for brevity, and the implied meaning is: "Did you see our affair when we took refuge, what its outcome is?"

Attributing the forgetting to the name of the fish rather than to a pronoun for the meal, although it is the meal that he was commanded to bring, has been explained as follows: it is to point out from the very beginning that this is not like forgetting one's provisions at a stopping place, and that what he witnessed is not one of the states connected with the meal insofar as it is a meal and food, but insofar as it is a fish like the other fish, with an added feature. It has also been said that it serves to make clear what was lost, and to bring joy to Musa (peace be upon him) while the answer is also obtained. It was previously reported that he said to him: "I will not burden you except that you tell me the place where the fish left you." Then, the apparent meaning is that the forgetting is in its literal sense, and it is not connected to the fish's essence but to the mention of it.

It is also permitted that it be used figuratively for loss, in which case it is connected to the fish itself. Most scholars take the first meaning, that is: "I forgot to mention to you the matter of the fish and the wondrous affair I witnessed." ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan.﴾ Perhaps he was occupied with whisperings about his family and about leaving his homeland, and this was a cause of forgetting, by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. Otherwise, that state is not something that can be forgotten.

Some have said: Yusha' had witnessed from Musa (peace be upon him) many overpowering miracles, so this miracle had no great impact on him that whisperings could affect, and so he forgot.

The Imam said: When Musa (peace be upon him) exaggerated his own knowledge, God Most High removed this necessary knowledge from the heart of his companion, as a reminder to Musa (peace be upon him) that knowledge is not attained except by God's teaching and by its preservation in the heart and mind. You know that if God Most High had made the one witnessing and forgetting Musa (peace be upon him) himself, the reminder would have been more complete. It may also be said that he was made to forget as a discipline for him, based on what was previously mentioned: that when Musa (peace be upon him) said to him, "I will not burden you," etc., he said to him, "You were not burdened much, since you made the matter seem easy and did not show reliance on God Most High by saying, 'I will tell you, God willing.'" There is also in this a rebuke to Musa (peace be upon him) for relying on him for knowledge of the fish's departure, so that he did not obtain it until he became weary. Moreover, this whisper does not harm the station of Yusha' (peace be upon him), even if we say that he was a prophet at the time this story took place.

[p. 318]

Some verifiers said: Perhaps he forgot that because he was absorbed in contemplation and his innermost being was drawn toward the sacred presence, due to what overcame him of witnessing the striking signs. He attributed it to Satan, although its real agent is God Most High and its figurative agent is the absorption mentioned, out of humility toward himself, by making that absorption and attraction the cause of his distraction from watching for the appointed time that God Most High had set, like whisperings. So there is a figurative usage here, by borrowing the term "Satan" for any kind of distraction.

In a hadith: "Indeed, my heart is veiled over, so I seek forgiveness from God Most High seventy times a day."

Or, because the inability of a faculty to bear both sides, and its being occupied with one of them to the exclusion of the other, is counted as a deficiency in its possessor and as neglect of striving and purification. Thus the deficiency has been figuratively described by this, since it is its cause.

Hafs read the ha' in "ansaniyhu" with a damma, which is rare in such a construction. The forgetting of such an event is rare. The majority read it with a kasra, and al-Kisai inclined the fatha of the sin.

God Most High's words ﴿that I mention it﴾ are a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the ha' (pronoun). That is: "None made me forget mentioning it to you except Satan." It has been said: In attaching the verb first to the pronoun of the fish, and then mentioning it explicitly, by way of substitution that indicates the replaced item is set aside, there is an indication that the object of forgetting is not the fish itself but the mention of its matter.

In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud and his reading it is: "an udhakkirakahu" (that I remind you of it). In preferring "an" with the verb over the verbal noun there is a kind of emphasis that is not hidden.

﴿And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner.﴾ The apparent meaning, which most commentators hold, is that the whole of this is the speech of Yusha', and it is a continuation of his words ﴿Indeed I forgot the fish﴾. It conveys another aspect of the matter, and what lies between them is a parenthetical statement placed earlier for the sake of giving attention to the excuse, as if it were said: "It came to life, moved, fell into the sea, and took its way in it, a wondrous way." So "its way" is the first object of "took," "in the sea" is a circumstantial phrase from it, and "wondrous" is the second object. In mentioning "the way," then its being attributed to the pronoun of the fish, then making the adverbial phrase a circumstance of the attributed noun, there is a general hint that the second object is of the kind of strange affairs. It also contains an arousing of interest in the second object and a repetition that conveys the emphasis suited to the context. So this construction, in conveying the meaning or in its eloquence, is superior to saying "and it took in the sea a wondrous way."

It is permitted that "in the sea" be a circumstantial phrase of "wondrous," or that it be connected to "took," or that the second object be "wondrous" as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "a wondrous taking," namely that its course was like a tunnel and a hidden passage. It is also permitted, on the assumption that the adverbial phrase is the second object, that "wondrous" be put in the accusative by a verb hidden from it, that is, "I marvel at a marvel." This too is from the speech of Yusha' (peace be upon him): he marvelled at the matter of the fish after informing about it. It has also been said that Yusha's speech ends at "the sea," and that "I marvel at a marvel" is the speech of Musa (peace be upon him), as if it were said: "And Musa said: 'I marvel greatly at that state you have told me of.'" You know that if this were so, the following sentence would have been introduced with the conjunction "wa" on this assumed phrase. It has also been said that the whole may be the speech of the Mighty and Majestic, and in that case it has two possibilities. One is that it is a report from Him, Most High, about the fish, that it took its way in the sea as a wonder for people. The other is that it is a report from Him, Glorified, about Musa (peace be upon him), that he took the fish's way in the sea as a wonder to be marvelled at. On this view "wondrous" is the second object, and there is no awkwardness in delaying the subsequent "he said" from it, since it is a resumption to explain what came from him (peace be upon him) afterwards. That this is the speech of Yusha' (peace be upon him) is supported by the reading of Abu Haywa: "wa-ittikhada" in the accusative, as a conjunction with the accusative in "adhkurahu."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 64:

﴿He said﴾ i.e., Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿That is﴾ what you mentioned of the matter of the fish, ﴿that which we were seeking﴾, i.e., that which we were seeking insofar as it is a sign of success
Page 319
in that which is the sought-after thing in its own right. It has been read as "nabgh" without a yā' in pause, and its affirmation (in connected speech) is better; this is the reading of Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'. As for pausing, the majority omit the yā' following the orthography of the Mushaf, while Ibn Kathir affirmed it in both situations. ﴿So they both turned back﴾, i.e., they returned ﴿upon their traces﴾, the former ones, and what is meant is their path by which they had come. ﴿Retracing﴾, i.e., they were tracing it, meaning they were following its tracks closely; that is, it is derived from "qassa athararahu" (he traced his track) when he followed it, as is the apparent meaning. Its accusative case is because it is an object of a verb understood from its own root. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) interpreted as a descriptive phrase; i.e., ﴿following closely﴾ until they both reached the rock where the fish was lost beside it.

[p. 320 marker not included]

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 18, verse 65, part 1 of 5]**

﴿and they found a servant from among Our servants﴾. The majority hold that he is al-Khidr (the Green One), spelled with a fatha on the kha' and sometimes with a kasra, and with a kasra or sukun on the dad. It has also been said that he is Alyasa', or Ilyas, or that he is an angel among the angels. The last is a strange and false view, as stated in the commentary on Muslim. The truth, which the sound reports support, is the first view. "Al-Khidr" is a title, and he was given it as al-Bukhari and others narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): because he sat on a white carpet (farwa), and it would shake behind him and turn green.

Ibn 'Asakir and a group narrate from Mujahid that he was given this title because whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrates from 'Ikrimah that this was because whenever he sat in a place, the area around him turned green, and his garments were green.

It is narrated from al-Suddi that whenever he stood in a place, grass grew beneath his feet until it covered his feet.

It has been said that the title is due to his radiance and beauty. The correct view, as al-Nawawi said, is the first. His kunya (byname) is Abu al-'Abbas. His name is Balya, with a fatha on the ba', a sukun on the lam, a ya' with two dots beneath, and an alif at the end, said by some to be long. It has been said that it is Abliya, with an added hamza at the beginning. It has also been said that his name is 'Amir, or Ahmad. Ibn Dihya rejected the last, on the grounds that none of the earlier nations heard the name Ahmad before our Prophet (ﷺ). Some claimed that the name of al-Khidr is Alyasa', and that he was named so because his knowledge encompassed six heavens and six earths. Ibn al-Jawzi rejected this. You know that it is not merely weak but false. Similar is the view that his name is Ilyas.

They differed about his father. Al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn 'Asakir, narrate through Muqatil ibn Sulayman, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he was a son of Adam by his own loins (li-sulbih). Ibn 'Asakir narrates from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that his mother was Roman and his father Persian, but he did not mention his name, and he mentioned that Ilyas was his brother from this mother and this father. It is also narrated from Asbat, from al-Suddi, that he was the son of a king among the kings, who was devoted to the worship of Allah the Exalted. His father wished to marry him off, but he refused, then agreed, and was married to a virgin, but he did not approach her for a year. Then he was married to a previously married woman, but he did not approach her either. Then he fled, and his father sought him but could not find him. Then his first wife remarried. She had become a believer, and she was the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife. He also did not mention his father's name. It has been said that he was the son of Pharaoh, on the basis of the claim that Pharaoh was his father. Glory be to Him who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living.

Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrate from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he was the son of 'Amil, and that he set out with a group of his companions until he reached the Sea of India, which is the Sea of China. He said: "O my companions, guide me." They guided him into the sea for days and nights. Then he rose and said: "An angel met me and said to me: 'O sinful human, where to, and from where?' I said: 'I wanted to see the depth of this sea.' He said to me: 'How, when a man from the time of David, peace be upon him, has descended into it and has not reached a third of its depth until now.'" That is three hundred years. I think you have no doubt that this report is a lie. Even if it is said, "Speak of the sea and there is no blame," it is still not sound. It has been said that he was the son of al-'Is. It has also been said that he was the son of Kalyan, with a fatha on the kaf, a sukun on the lam, a ya' with two dots beneath, followed by an alif and a nun. Ibn Qutayba, in al-Ma'arif, says: Wahb ibn Munabbih said that he was the son of Malkan, with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the lam, son of Faligh, son of 'Abir, son of Shalikh, son of Arfakhshadh, son of Sam, son of Noah, peace be upon him.

[p. 320]

None of these views is sound in my judgment. However, al-Nawawi's conduct in the commentary on Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him, suggests a preference for the view that he is Balya ibn Malka, and this is the view of the majority. And Allah knows best.

It is established from the hadith of al-Bukhari and others that the two of them returned to the rock, and there was a man covered with a garment, having placed one end of it beneath his feet and the other beneath his head.

In Sahih Muslim: "They came to an island, and found al-Khidr standing, praying on a green prayer rug on the heart of the sea."

Al-Tha'labi said: "They reached him while he was sleeping on a green prayer rug on the surface of the water, covered with a green garment." It has also been said that the path of the fish returned to a stone, and when they came to it they walked upon it until they reached an island where al-Khidr was.

It is sound that when they reached him, Musa greeted him with salam. Al-Khidr said: "And how is there salam in your land?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes."

It is narrated that when he greeted him while he was covered, he informed him that he was Musa. He raised his head, sat up, and said: "And upon you be peace, O Prophet of the Children of Israel." Musa said: "How do you know me, and who informed you that I am a prophet of the Children of Israel?" He said: "The One who made you known to me and guided you to me." Then he said: "O Musa, is it not enough for you that the Torah is in your hand and that revelation comes to you?" Musa said: "My Lord sent me to you so that I may follow you and learn from your knowledge."

The tanwin in ﴿a servant﴾ is for magnification, and the idafa in ﴿Our servants﴾ is for honour and special relation; that is, a servant of exalted rank, from among those specially chosen by Us and honoured by being attributed to Us.

﴿We had given him mercy from Us﴾. It has been said that the mercy means lawful provision and a pleasant life. It has been said that it means seclusion from people and not needing them. It has been said that it means long life together with soundness of body. The majority hold that it means revelation and prophethood, and this term has been used for that in several places in the Qur'an. Ibn Abi Hatim narrates this from Ibn 'Abbas. This is the view of those who hold that he was a prophet, and on this there are three views. The majority hold that he was a prophet but not a messenger. It has been said that he was a messenger. It has been said that he was a saint (wali), and al-Qushayri and a group held this. The preferred view is that of the majority. The evidences from the verses and reports are many, and with their totality certainty is almost attained. Just as there was disagreement about his prophethood, there was disagreement about whether he is alive today, and a group held that he is not alive today.

Al-Bukhari was asked about him and about Ilyas, peace be upon them both: "Are they both alive?" He said: "How could this be, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said, shortly before his death, that: 'No one alive upon the earth today will remain at the end of a hundred years'?"

What is in Sahih Muslim from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said before his death: "There is no soul living upon which a hundred years will pass while it is still alive on that day."

This is further from ta'wil (figurative interpretation). Other imams were asked about this, and one of them recited: ﴿And We did not grant immortality to any human before you﴾. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya was asked about him and said: "If al-Khidr were alive, it would be obligatory upon him to come to the Prophet (ﷺ), to fight before him, and to learn from him."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of Badr: "O Allah, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on the earth."

They were three hundred and thirteen men, known by their names, the names of their fathers, and their tribes. Where then was al-Khidr at that time?

Ibrahim al-Harbi was asked about his survival and said: "Whoever refers to an absent one has not been fair to him. Nothing but Satan has put this among people."

In al-Bahr, from Sharaf al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, the view that he has died is also transmitted. Ibn al-Jawzi transmitted it from 'Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Likewise from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Harbi. He also said: "Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Munadi used to find repugnant the statement of whoever says that he is alive."

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la related his death from some of the companions of Muhammad. And how can the existence of al-Khidr be conceived when he does not pray with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on Friday or in congregation, nor witnesses jihad with him, despite the words of the Prayer and Peace be upon him: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

And the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My covenant on that?" They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾

[p. 321]

And the established fact that when 'Isa, peace be upon him, descends to the earth, he will pray behind the imam of this nation and will not precede him at the beginning of the matter. How far from understanding is the one who affirms the existence of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and forgets what is folded within his affirmation of turning away from this Shari'ah. Then he said:

We have, by reasoning, several grounds for his non-survival. The first: the one who said he is alive said that he is a son of Adam, peace be upon him, by his own loins, and this is corrupt for two reasons. The first: it would follow that his age today would be six thousand years or more, and such a thing is far-fetched in ordinary experience regarding humans. The second: if he were a son of his by his own loins, or the fourth of his descendants, as they claimed, that he was the vizier of Dhu al-Qarnayn, then he would have been of awe-inspiring form, exceedingly tall and broad.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Adam was created, his height was sixty cubits, and creation has continued to decrease after him."

No one who claims to have seen al-Khidr has mentioned that he saw him in a great form, and he is among the earliest of people. The second ground: if al-Khidr had been before Noah, peace be upon him, he would have boarded the ship with him, and no one has transmitted this.

The third: the scholars agreed that when Noah, peace be upon him, came out of the ship, all those with him died, and none remained except his offspring. The proof of this is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And We made his descendants the ones who remain﴾. The fourth: if it were sound that a human from the time of Adam survived until near the ruin of this world, that would be among the greatest signs and wonders, and his story would be mentioned in the Qur'an in several places, because it is among the signs of Lordship. Glorified and Exalted is He, mentioned the one whom He gave life for a thousand years less fifty years and made him a sign, so how would He not mention the one whom He gave life for many times that?

The fifth: the claim that al-Khidr is alive is a saying about Allah the Exalted without knowledge, and this is forbidden by the explicit text of the Qur'an. As for the second premise, it is evident. As for the first: if his life were established, it would be indicated by the Qur'an, or the Sunnah, or the ijma' (consensus) of the Ummah. Here is the Book of Allah the Exalted: where is the life of al-Khidr in it? And here is the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ): where in it is anything that indicates this in any way? And here are the scholars of the Ummah: when did they agree on his life?

The sixth: the most that is relied upon for his life is narrated stories in which a man reports that he saw al-Khidr. Alas, for the sake of Allah the Exalted, what a wonder! Does al-Khidr have a sign by which whoever sees him recognises him? Many of those who claim to have seen him are deceived by his saying: "I am al-Khidr." And it is known that it is not permissible to accept the claim of one who says that without a proof from Allah the Exalted. From where does the one who sees him know that the one who informs him is truthful and does not lie?

The seventh: al-Khidr separated from Musa ibn 'Imran, the interlocutor of the Merciful, and did not accompany him, and said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾. How then would he be content for himself to be separated from someone like Musa, peace be upon him? Then he associates with ignorant worshippers who have stepped outside the Shari'ah, who attend neither Friday prayer, nor congregation, nor a gathering of knowledge, and each of them says: "al-Khidr said to me, al-Khidr came to me, al-Khidr advised me." So how strange: he leaves the one who spoke with Allah to frequent the company of an ignorant person, who keeps company with none but an accursed devil. Glory be to You, this is a great slander.

The eighth: the Ummah is in agreement that whoever says, "I am al-Khidr," if he said, "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say such and such," his words would not be heeded, and he would not be taken as evidence in religion. The only way out for the one who holds that he is alive from this conclusion is to say that he did not come to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, nor pledge allegiance to him, or to say that he was not sent to him. And in this is what is in it of disbelief.

The ninth: if he were alive, his fighting the disbelievers, his garrisoning (ribat) in the way of Allah Most High, his standing in the row for an hour, his attendance at Friday and congregational prayers, and his guiding the ignorant of the Ummah would be far better than his wandering among the wild beasts in the deserts and wastelands, and other such things. What is for and against this will come, if Allah Most High wills.

It is widely cited as evidence the report: "If al-Khadir were alive, he would have visited me." According to the scholars of hadith (al-huffaz), this is a fabricated report (mawdu') with no basis. Even if it were authentic, it would have ended the dispute and debate. The majority of scholars hold that he is alive and present among us

[Page 322]

and this is agreed upon among the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified. This is what al-Nawawi said. It is reported from the exegete al-Tha'labi that al-Khadir is a prophet who has been granted long life according to all opinions, hidden from the sight of most people. Ibn al-Salah said: "He is alive today according to the majority of scholars, and the common people agree with them on this." Only some hadith scholars denied his life, and they relied on many reports, among them what al-Daraqutni recorded in al-Afrad and Ibn 'Asakir recorded from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Al-Khadir is a son of Adam, from his loins, and his term was extended so that he would refute the Dajjal (Antichrist). Such a statement cannot be made on the basis of opinion."

Among them is what Ibn 'Asakir recorded from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "Our companions related to us that when death approached Adam, peace be upon him, he gathered his sons and said: 'O my sons, Allah Most High is sending a punishment upon the people of the earth. Let my body be with you in the cave, and when you descend, take me out and bury me in the land of al-Sham.' His body was with them. When Allah Most High sent Nuh, he took that body with him, and Allah Most High sent the flood upon the earth, and it was submerged for a time. Nuh came and descended at Babil and instructed his three sons to take his body to the cave where he had ordered them to bury him. They said: 'The earth is desolate, with no one to keep us company, and we do not know the way. But wait until people become safe and multiply.' Nuh said to them: 'Adam asked Allah to prolong the life of whoever buries him until the Day of Resurrection.' The body of Adam remained until al-Khadir was the one who undertook its burial. Allah Most High fulfilled for him what He had promised, and so he lives until what Allah Most High wills for him to live."

This is the reason for his long life, though it seems a remote cause. Otherwise, the well-known explanation is that he drank from the Spring of Life when he entered the darkness with Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he was at his vanguard. Among the reports is what al-Khatib and Ibn 'Asakir recorded from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and honour his face, who said: "While I was circumambulating the House, I saw a man clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, saying: 'O You whom no hearing distracts from another hearing, O You whom questions do not confuse, O You whom the insistence of the insistent does not weary, let me taste the coolness of Your pardon and the sweetness of Your mercy.' I said: 'O servant of Allah, repeat the words.' He said: 'Did you hear them?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of al-Khadir,' and he was al-Khadir, 'no servant says them after the obligatory prayer except that his sins are forgiven, even if they are like the sand of 'Alij, the number of rain drops, and the leaves of trees.'"

Among them is what al-Tha'labi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: 'When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died and we began preparing his body, the people went out and the place was emptied. When I placed him on the washing platform, a voice called out from a corner of the house at the top of its voice: "Do not wash Muhammad, for he is pure and has been purified." Something troubled my heart and I said: "Woe to you, who are you? The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded us with this, and this is his sunnah." Then another voice called out to me from the corner of the house at the top of its voice: "Wash Muhammad, for the first caller was the accursed Iblis, who envied Muhammad (ﷺ) for entering his grave washed."' I said: 'May Allah reward you with good. You have told me that was Iblis, so who are you?' He said: 'I am al-Khadir. I attended the funeral of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

Among them is what al-Hakim recorded in al-Mustadrak from Jabir, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died and the Companions gathered, a man entered with white-streaked beard, large and handsome. He stepped over their necks, wept, and then turned to the Companions and said: 'In Allah Most High there is consolation for every calamity, a substitute for everything lost, and a successor to everything that perishes. So turn to Allah Most High in repentance, and desire Him, and look to His regard for you in affliction. The one truly afflicted is he who is not consoled.' Abu Bakr and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: 'This is al-Khadir, peace be upon him.'"

Among them is what Ibn 'Asakir recorded: that Ilyas and al-Khadir fast the month of Ramadan in Bayt al-Maqdis, perform Hajj every year, and drink from Zamzam a single sip that suffices them until the same time the following year.

Among them is what Ibn 'Asakir, also al-Uqayli and al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Khadir and Ilyas meet every year at the season (of Hajj), and each of them shaves the head of the other, and they part with these words: 'In the name of Allah, what Allah wills. No good brings but Allah. What Allah wills; there is no power nor might except through Allah.'"

[Page 323]

Among them is what Ibn 'Asakir recorded with his chain from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: "While 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was praying over a funeral, a voice called out from behind him: 'Do not precede us in the prayer, may Allah have mercy on you.' He waited until the man reached the first row, and 'Umar said the takbir and the people said it with him. The voice then said: 'If You punish him, he has disobeyed You much; and if You forgive him, then he is in need of Your mercy.' 'Umar and his companions looked at the man. When the deceased was buried and the earth was leveled over him, the man said: 'Blessed are you, O owner of the grave, if you were not a headman, a tax collector, a treasurer, a scribe, or a policeman.' 'Umar said: 'Bring me the man so that we can ask him about his prayer and his speech, and who he is.' But he vanished from them, and they looked and found the trace of his footprint to be a cubit long. 'Umar said: 'By Allah, this is the one the Prophet (ﷺ) told us about.'" The argument from this report rests on the premise that by "the one spoken of" he meant al-Khadir, peace be upon him, and so on.

Much of what has been mentioned, although it does not prove that he is alive today, indicates that he was alive in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). His being alive then does not necessarily mean he is alive today. Yet it suffices to refute the opponent, since he denies his life then just as he denies it today. However, if there were someone who affirmed it then and denied it now, what has been mentioned would not benefit against him. But there is no one among us like that. The accounts of the righteous from the Successors and the Sufis about meeting him and taking knowledge from him in every age are more numerous than can be counted and too famous to be mentioned. Yes, the hadith scholars who hold that he is alive all agree that he has no narration from the Prophet (ﷺ), as al-'Iraqi explicitly stated in his takhrij of the hadiths of Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din. This contradicts what the Sufis hold, for Shaykh 'Ala' al-Din claimed to have derived prophetic hadiths directly from him without intermediary.

Al-Suhrawardi mentioned in al-Sirr al-Maktum that al-Khadir, peace be upon him, narrated to us three hundred hadiths which he heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) directly from his mouth. Some of those who hold that he is alive now use the principle of istishab (presumption of continuity) as evidence: his life was previously established by proof, so it remains so until a proof to the contrary appears, and none has appeared. They also answered what the opponent cited from among the aforementioned reports. They answered what al-Bukhari recorded of the hadith which does not necessitate denying his life in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), but by its apparent meaning it requires denying his life after a hundred years from the time of the statement, meaning that he was not then on the surface of the earth but rather on the surface of the water. And the hadith is general regarding what people witness, as shown by the exception of the angels, peace be upon them, and the exclusion of Satan. Its conclusion is the breaking of the first century. Yes, it is an explicit text in refutation of one who claims long life, such as Kartan ibn 'Abdullah al-Hindi al-Tabrizi, who appeared in the seventh century, claimed to have been a Companion, and narrated hadiths.

In it there is also the point that what is apparent regarding those who are on the surface of the earth is that they are of its people and settled in it by custom. There is no doubt that this includes those who are at sea, and if those at sea were not counted among those on the surface of the earth, the hadith would not be an explicit text in refuting Ratn and his like, because they might have been at sea at the time of the statement. Indeed, if this interpretation were accepted, many people would be excluded from the general scope of the hadith, and the generality would be weakened, as in the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿And if Allah were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ [35:45]. Let one consider the statement of the one who said:

"It may be that at the time of the statement he was in the air." In this there is also what is not hidden to the discerning reader. And the second answer is objected to: if al-Khadir existed, he would be among those people witness, as is the usual case with humans, and that he, peace be upon him, is exempt from this cannot be established except by proof, and where is that? So reflect.

They also answered what Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya said, that the obligation to come to him is not granted, for many believed in him (ﷺ) in his time and never came to him, peace be upon him. Thus Uways al-Qarani, may Allah be pleased with him, the best of the Successors, never had the opportunity to come to him, accompany him in jihad, or learn from him without an intermediary. The same applies to al-Najashi, may Allah be pleased with him. Moreover, we say: al-Khadir, peace be upon him, did come to him and learned from him (ﷺ), but in secret, because he was not commanded to come openly, for a divine wisdom required that.

As for his presence in jihad, Ibn Bashkuwal recorded in Kitab al-Mustaghithin bi-Allah from 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, who said: "I was on a military campaign when my horse fell dead. I saw a man of handsome face and pleasant fragrance. He said: 'Would you like to ride your horse?' I said: 'Yes.' He placed his hand on the horse's forehead until it reached its rear and said: 'I adjure you, O ailment, by the might of Allah's might, by the majesty of Allah's majesty, by the power of Allah's power, by the sovereignty of Allah's sovereignty, by "There is no god but Allah," by what the pen has written from Allah, and by "There is no power nor might except through Allah," that you depart.' The horse rose to its feet by Allah's leave. The man took hold of my stirrup and said: 'Ride.' I rode and caught up with my companions. On the following day, when we prevailed over the enemy, he was in front of us. I said: 'Are you not the one who was my companion yesterday?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'I ask you by Allah, who are you?'"

He rose to his feet, and the earth beneath him trembled, turning green. He said: "I am al-Khadir."

This is explicit that he may attend some battles. As for the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement at Badr: "O Allah, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on earth"...

[p. 324 continues] Its meaning is: he is not worshipped in the manner of prominence, dominance, and the strength of the community. Otherwise, how many believers there were in Medina and elsewhere who did not attend Badr! It is not hidden that placing al-Khidr (peace be upon him) in the same category as Uways al-Qarani, al-Najashi, and others like them, who were unable to come to the Prophet (ﷺ), is far from fairness, even if we do not say that it is obligatory for him (peace be upon him) to come. How can a fair-minded person affirm that the Prophet (ﷺ) is the imam of all the prophets (peace be upon them all), and that all of them followed him on the night of the Mi'raj, yet not see that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) must come to him and meet with him (ﷺ), when there is apparently no obstacle preventing him from doing so? Whoever claims that his relationship to our Prophet (ﷺ) is like his relationship to Musa (peace be upon him) should renew his Islam. The claim that he used to come and learn secretly, because he was not commanded to do so openly, for a divine wisdom, is something for which no proof has been established. Moreover, if this were the case, he would have mentioned it (ﷺ), even once. Where is the evidence for such a mention? Furthermore, the wisdom in preventing him from coming once or twice is not apparent, unlike the coming of Jibril (peace be upon him) in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi (may Allah be pleased with him).

If it is said that this claim is merely a possibility, it is answered: one does not give attention to such a thing except in case of necessity, and it cannot be realized except after its existence has been established, for at that point it is established by evidence, and his existence is like his existence in our view. As for what is narrated from Ibn al-Mudrik, we do not accept that it is authentic from him. If you consider the wording of the narrative closely, you will find its soundness improbable. Anyone who is fair knows that his presence (peace be upon him) on the day when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him): "Shoot, may my father and mother be your ransom," was more important than his presence with Ibn al-Mubarak. The possibility that he was present and no one saw him is nearly sophistry.

As for what they have mentioned regarding the meaning of the hadith, one may say that it is far-fetched. What is apparent from it is the negation that Allah (glorified is He) be worshipped if He destroys that group absolutely, in the sense that if they neglect (the religion) while Islam is still fresh, the rest will apostatize, and hardly anyone will believe after them, so no human being on earth will worship Him (glorified is He) at that time. The hadith of apostasy may also not be taken as a continuous statement, but rather the meaning may be: "O Allah, if You destroy this group, who are the crown of the head of Islam, and the disbelievers overpower all the Muslims after them and destroy them, then no human being will worship You at that time." In any case, using the hadith as evidence for the non-existence of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) has some basis. If they answer it by saying that what is meant is the negation of seeing anyone who worships Him (exalted is He) afterwards, while al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is not seen, then what has been mentioned above applies to this answer.

They answered the argument from the words of Allah (exalted is He): ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾ by saying that what is meant by immortality is perpetual endless duration, and those who hold that he exists today do not claim that he is perpetual. Rather, some of them say he will fight the Dajjal and die; some say he will die at the time of the lifting of the Qur'an; and some say he will die at the end of time. What they mean is one of these two matters, or something close to them.

It was objected that khuld (immortality) means lasting, and according to what the apparent meaning of Allah's words requires, ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, it is literally a reference to long duration of stay, not to permanent continuance. The apparent purpose is to establish (a new meaning), not to emphasize. Al-Raghib said: "Everything that is slow to undergo change and decay, the Arabs describe as khalid (lasting), as they say of the three stones of a hearth, khawalid, because of their long remaining, not because of their permanence and survival." End of quotation.

You know the strength of the answer, because long duration of life was established for some humans, such as Nuh (peace be upon him). They also answered what was transmitted from Ibn al-Jawzi regarding the rational aspects. As for the first of the two flaws in the view that he is the son of Adam (peace be upon him), after accepting the soundness of the report, it is answered that ordinary remoteness does not harm the one who holds that he lived this very long span, because that, in his view, is among the breaking of customary patterns. As for the second, it is answered that what has been mentioned about the great stature of earlier people is an exception given in the general case. Otherwise, Ya'juj and Ma'juj are from the lineage of Yafith ibn Nuh, and among them there is one whose height is a span, as is reported in the traditions. Moreover, there is no novelty in al-Khidr (peace be upon him) having been given the power of taking forms and appearing in any shape he wishes, like Jibril (peace be upon him). The Sufis (may their secrets be sanctified) have affirmed this power for the saints, and they have famous stories about it.

You know that what has been mentioned about Ya'juj and Ma'juj, that among them is one whose height is a span, even if granted, one may say about it that this will be when the barrier is opened, which occurs at the end of time, and the argument from their condition cannot be complete unless it is established that among them there was someone like that in ancient times. What has been mentioned about his being given the power of taking forms is a remote possibility, and its establishment for the saints is disputed by many of the later scholars.

Some people have said: "If anyone among humans were given this power, it would have been given to him (ﷺ) on the day of the Hijra, so that he could have dispensed with the cave and made it a veil for him from the disbelievers." The matter of this has room for discussion.

As for the second of the objections, it is answered that the absence of a report that he was on the ship does not necessarily mean his non-existence, if we say that he (peace be upon him) was before Nuh (peace be upon him), since it is possible that he existed and was not transmitted, and it is also possible that he boarded and was not seen. This is as you see.

Some people have said: "If the possibility of being given the power of taking forms is established according to those who hold the prolongation of life, then let them say: it is possible that he (peace be upon him) took a form and became so tall that he waded through the water and did not need to board the ship, in the manner that the proponents of superstitions claim about Awj ibn Anaq." Also, they say: "He has the ability to stay in the air. What prevented them from saying that it is possible he did not board and was protected from the water by the air, just as they said, regarding the answer to the hadith of al-Bukhari, that it is possible he was in the air?"

Also, some have mentioned, from al-Allami in his tafsir, that al-Khidr circulates in the seas guiding whoever goes astray in them, and Ilyas circulates in the mountains guiding whoever goes astray in them. This is their practice by day, and at night they meet at the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, guarding it. So why did they not say that he (peace be upon him) remained in the sea when others boarded the ship? Perhaps they did not say this because what has been mentioned was narrated in something close to it by al-Harith ibn Abi Usama in his Musnad, from Anas, as a marfu' report, and its wording is: "Al-Khidr is in the sea and Ilyas is on land, and they meet every night at the dam which Dhu al-Qarnayn built," and the report continues.

They have said that its chain is weak, or that they do not affirm for him this divine service at that time. They are close to saying the same about his being given the power of taking forms and of being in the air.

As for the third objection, it is answered that we do not accept the consensus that everyone on the ship died and that after the disembarkation nothing remained except the offspring of Nuh (peace be upon him). The restriction in the verse is relative to those who denied Nuh (peace be upon him). Also, the intended meaning is that everyone who was apparent and visible died, other than his descendants (peace be upon him), as evidenced by the fact that Satan was also on the ship. Furthermore, the intended meaning of the verse is the survival of his descendants (peace be upon him) through procreation, and this does not negate the survival of others without procreation. We claim this for al-Khidr. However, the view that he was before Nuh (peace be upon them both) is a weak view, and the relied-upon view is that he was after that. What is in some of what has been mentioned is not hidden.

[p. 325] As for the fourth objection, it is answered that it does not follow, from his prolonged life being among the greatest signs, that it must be mentioned repeatedly in the Glorious Qur'an. Allah (glorified is He) mentioned Nuh (peace be upon him) as consolation for our Prophet (ﷺ), for what he suffered from his people during this period, while they remained insistent upon disbelief until they were drowned. This benefit would not be present if the lifespan of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) were mentioned. Furthermore, it may be said that from the mention of the long life of Nuh (peace be upon him) explicitly, there is understood implicitly the permissibility of a longer life than that.

It was objected that we may return and say: at the very least, this great matter should be mentioned in the Glorious Qur'an once, because it is one of the signs of divine lordship over the human species. It is not that it is rationally necessary that its being so requires its mention; rather, we claim that mentioning it is a matter of good taste, especially since the prolonged life of the enemy of Allah (exalted is He), Iblis (may he be cursed), has been mentioned. If it is mentioned, the Qur'an would include mention of a long-lived one from the jinn who is distanced and mention of a long-lived one from mankind who is brought near, and its beauty is not hidden. It may perhaps be said that it also includes bringing joy to the Prophet (ﷺ). And as for the aforementioned possibility of a longer life lying within the scope of an addition, that is not what is being disputed; what is disputed is its occurrence, and without establishing it, one does not attain the water of life.

Some answered that in the words of Allah (exalted is He): ﴿We gave him mercy from Us﴾ there is an indication of his long life (peace be upon him), according to what you have heard from someone in its tafsir. It was rebutted: his interpretation of it in this way is based on the view of prolongation of life. If that view is accepted, then it is accepted; otherwise, it is not.

As for the fifth, it is answered: we choose that it is established by the Sunnah, and part of it has already been mentioned to you.

It was objected with what al-Qari transmitted from Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, that he said: "The narrations in which al-Khidr (peace be upon him) and his life are mentioned are all lies, and not a single hadith about his life is authentic. Whoever claims authenticity bears the burden of proof." It was also said: the consensus of the great shaykhs and the majority of the eminent scholars suffices for its establishment. This consensus has been reported by Ibn al-Salah, al-Nawawi, and others of the eminent great ones. It was objected that the consensus of the shaykhs is not accepted. For Sadr al-Din Ishaq al-Qunawi, in Tabsirat al-Mubtadi and Tadhkirat al-Muntahi, reported that the existence of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is in the world of imagination ('alam al-mithal).

Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashi went to the view that al-Khidr is an expression for expansion (bast), and Ilyas for contraction (qabd). Some have gone to the view that Khidriyya is a rank held by some of the righteous, following the footsteps of al-Khidr who was in the time of Musa (peace be upon them both). With the existence of these views, the consensus cannot be complete, and their not being accepted by the verifying scholars among them does not complete it either. The consensus of the majority of scholars, as reported by Ibn al-Salah and al-Nawawi, is accepted, but it is not the consensus which is one of the legal proofs, and the opponent is not satisfied except with that, and that is what he denied, so how can it be established? Perhaps the opponent also does not count the consensus of the shaykhs (may their secrets be sanctified) as a consensus that is one of the proofs.

As for the sixth, it is answered that he has signs known to his people, such as the earth turning green at his foot, and that the length of his foot is a cubit. Perhaps some extraordinary feats of customary patterns appear from him that bear witness to his truthfulness. Moreover, the believer accepts his statement on the basis of good opinion about him. It has become widespread among those who claim to have seen him (peace be upon him) that one of his signs is that the thumb of his right hand has no bone, and that the pupil of one of his eyes moves like mercury. It was objected: by what proof was it established that these are his signs? "Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful."

[Page 327]

What is established in the sound hadith is that he was called al-Khidr (the Green One) because he sat on a white patch of land (*farwa*), and it turned green behind him as it shook. Yet there is nothing in it indicating that this was permanently his. As for the claim that his foot measured a cubit long, it comes only in the report of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir mentioned earlier, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and we do not accept its authenticity. Moreover, those who claim to have seen him say they see him in different forms, and no single form is ever fixed for him, peace be upon him. The appearance of extraordinary events (*khawariq*) is shared between him and other saints (*awliya*) of this community. So it is possible that a saint may manifest an extraordinary event and say, "I am al-Khidr," figuratively, because he is on his path, or for some other consideration, and a legitimate motive may prompt him to say so.

[Page 328]

In the hadith of the Hijrah it is related that when the Prophet ﷺ was asked, "Which people are you?" he replied, "We are from Ma'," so the questioner thought that "Ma'" was the name of a tribe.

He ﷺ meant only that they were created from "gushing water" (*ma' dafiq*). Similarly, it may be said to a Sufi who says, "I am al-Khidr": despite the appearance of extraordinary events, there is no certainty that the speaker is al-Khidr in the apparent sense in reality, because that speaker may be one who has passed away in his shaykh (*fana' fihi*) through unity of spiritual path (*ittihad al-mashrab*). Often a passed-away disciple says of his shaykh, "I am so-and-so," naming his shaykh. Also, whenever some of them say, "I am the Truth" (*ana al-Haqq*), or "There is nothing in the cloak but Allah," it is not far-fetched that they say, "I am al-Khidr." Many of them have been reported, in verse and prose, saying, "I am Adam, I am Noah, I am Abraham, I am Moses, I am Jesus, I am Muhammad," and so on, as is not hidden from you. They have mentioned a sound interpretation (*mahmal*) of this among themselves, so let the saying "I am al-Khidr" be understood in the same manner, as coming from one who is not al-Khidr. With this possibility remaining, how can certainty be attained? Good opinion (*husn al-zann*) does not produce that certainty.

As for the seventh objection, we do not accept that he meets the ignorant worshippers who have departed from the Shariah, and their words are not regarded. Lying charlatans lie against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, so it is not far-fetched that they lie against al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and say, "He said" and "He came." The claim of his meeting is only with the great Sufis and the worshippers who observe the legal limits of the Shariah. His meeting with them has become widely known, to the extent that some of them asked al-Khidr to accompany them, and he refused. This is related of ʿAli al-Khawwas (may Allah have mercy on him) during his journey to Hajj. When he was asked the reason for his refusal, he said, "I feared a deficiency in my reliance upon Allah (*tawakkul*) if I depended on his presence with me."

It has been objected that his meeting with them and their meeting with him may be of the kind they describe regarding their meeting with the Prophet ﷺ and his meeting with them, peace be upon him. For the sacred spirits (*al-arwah al-muqaddasah*) may appear in embodied forms, and the perfect among the servants may meet them. It is sound that the Prophet ﷺ saw Moses, peace be upon him, standing and praying in his grave, saw him in the heavens, and saw him circumambulating the House.

[Page 329]

The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn al-ʿArabi), may his secret be sanctified, claimed to have met most of the prophets, peace be upon them, especially Idris, peace be upon him. He mentioned that he met him many times and took much knowledge from him. Indeed, the perfect person may even meet one who has not yet been born, such as the Mahdi. The Greatest Shaykh also mentioned his meeting with him. This is evident to those who say that eternity (*al-azal*) and everlastingness (*al-abad*) are one point, and that the difference between them is only by consideration, according to those who have stripped themselves of the cloaks of their bodies. Perhaps the frequency of this manifestation and embodiment is one of the special qualities of al-Khidr, peace be upon him. And with this possibility remaining, certainty also cannot be attained that the Khidr who is seen exists in external reality in the same way as the existence of other people, as is not hidden.

Based on his meeting, peace be upon him, with the perfect ones among the people of Allah, there is some chain of transmission (*turuq*) for our authorization (*ijazah*) in the Salat al-Bashishiyyah. I narrate it through some chains from my shaykh ʿAla al-Din ʿAli Effendi al-Mawsili, from his shaykh and father Salah al-Din Yusuf Effendi al-Mawsili, from his shaykh, the seal of guides, the Sayyid ʿAli al-Bandinijji, from the Prophet of Allah, al-Khidr, peace be upon him, from the perfect saint Shaykh ʿAbd al-Salam ibn Bashish, may his secret be sanctified.

As for the eighth objection, we do not accept that the claim that he was not sent to by the Messenger ﷺ amounts to disbelief (*kufr*). Even granting that it is not disbelief, it is a false statement by consensus (*ijma'*). We choose that he came and pledged allegiance, but inwardly, in a way that no one perceives. Indeed, a group of the scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence (*arbab al-usul*) counted him among the Companions. Perhaps the non-acceptance of his narration is due to the lack of certainty about his existence and his witnessing during his vision. But this is, as you see, weak.

As for the ninth objection, it is a reckless claim in speech. From where is it known that what he mentioned, the absence of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, from jihad and other matters, is negated? Especially since the one who possesses the knowledge of the "divine presence" (*al-ʿilm al-ladunni*) does not occupy himself except with what Allah has taught him, in every place and time, according to what the matter and the circumstance require. It has been objected that the negation rests on the absence of evidence, so we say accordingly, until evidence is established, and perhaps it will not be established until people stand before the Lord of the worlds. Later, if Allah wills, the discussion of the divine knowledge and the one who possesses it will come. In sum, the state of most of the evidence of both groups has become clear to you. What remains is what some have argued from istishab (presumption of continuity).

You know that it is a valid proof according to al-Shafiʿi, al-Muzani, and Abu Bakr al-Sayrafi, in every matter, whether affirmation or negation, that has been established as real by evidence, and then doubt arises about its continuation, unless a supposition of its non-existence arises. As for us, and likewise the theologians (*mutakallimun*), it is among the weak proofs that are not suitable for establishing a ruling, but are suitable only for repelling it, in the sense that a ruling is not established, and the non-existence of a ruling rests on the absence of its evidence. The default regarding non-existence is its continuation until evidence of existence appears. Thus the one who is missing (*al-mafqud*) inherits according to them, but not according to us, because inheritance belongs to the category of establishing, so it cannot be established by it, and cannot be inherited, because the absence of inheritance belongs to the category of repelling, so it is established by it. Several other branches follow from this disagreement, but this is not the place to mention them.

Since the ruling of istishab according to us is as mentioned, the Hanafi's argument from it for establishing the life of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, today, and that it is certainly so, is not free of defect. Indeed, al-Shafiʿi's argument from it for that is likewise, based on the condition that the validity of inference from it is conditional on no supposition of non-existence arising. For custom (*al-ʿadah*) decides that a human being does not remain for such a long period and so many ages. It has been said that custom is a valid proof. Otherwise, the breaking of custom through a miracle would not have an effect in obliging belief and following. If it does not yield certainty of non-existence in what we are discussing, it yields supposition of it, and thus the condition for the validity of the inference is not fulfilled. In light of this, what is relied upon, purified from the turbidity of discord, is inference from one of the four sources of evidence. You have already known the state of their inference from the Book and the Sunnah, and what they call consensus. As for inferring by analogy (*qiyas*) here, it is something no sensible person would undertake, let alone a learned one.

"Then know," after all this reckoning, that the sound prophetic reports and the preponderant rational premises support those who hold that he has died, peace be upon him, with every kind of support, and reinforce their claim with every kind of reinforcement. There is no reason to depart from the apparent meanings of those reports except to respect the apparent meanings of the narrated accounts, and Allah knows best their authenticity, which come from some righteous and good people. Likewise, good opinion of some Sufi masters, for they said that he exists until the end of time in a manner that does not admit the earlier interpretation. In the seventy-third chapter of *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah*: "Know that Allah, exalted is He, has in every kind of created being distinctions and a choice portion. The highest of the distinguished among the servants are the messengers, peace be upon them, who possess the station of messengership, prophethood, sainthood, and faith. They are the pillars of the house of this kind. The Messenger is the most excellent of them in station and the highest in state, in the sense that the station from which he was sent is higher in rank with Allah, exalted is He, than all other stations. Next are the poles (*aqtab*), the imams, and the pegs (*awtad*), through whom Allah, exalted is He, preserves the world and protects the house of religion that stands on the four pillars: messengership, prophethood, sainthood, and faith. Messengership is the comprehensive pillar and is the intended purpose of this kind. Thus this kind is never without a messenger, as long as the religion of Allah, exalted is He, endures. That messenger is the pole who is the focus of the Real's regard, and through him the kind remains in this abode even if all disbelieve. This name is not applicable to a human being unless he has a natural physical body and a spirit, and exists in this kind in this abode in his body and spirit, nourishing himself. He is the locus of manifestation of the Real from Adam, peace be upon him, until the Day of Resurrection. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away, after establishing the religion that is not abrogated and the law that is not changed, and all the messengers, peace be upon them, entered into that religion, and the earth was never empty of a sensible messenger in his body, because he is the pole of the human world, and if the messengers are many, one of them is the intended one; Allah, exalted is He, preserved after his death, peace be upon him, from the living messengers in their bodies in this abode four: Idris, Elias, Jesus, and al-Khidr, peace be upon them. The first three are agreed upon, and the last is disputed among others, but not among us. So He made to dwell"

[Page 330]

The Ṣūfiyya (Sufis) are the Sufis.

Glorified is He, placed Idris in the fourth heaven. The fourth heaven and the rest of the seven heavens belong to the lower abode (al-dār al-dunyā), because they are transformed in the abode of the Hereafter, just as this earthly creation of ours is transformed into another creation. He left the others on the earth, and they all remain in the lower abode with their bodies. All of them are the awtād (the pegs, a spiritual rank of saints). Two of them are the two imams, and one of them is the qutb (the pole, the axis of spiritual order), who is the point of the Truth's regard toward the world. He is the corner of the Black Stone among the corners of the House of Religion. The messengers have not ceased, and do not cease, to be in this abode until the Day of Resurrection, even though they follow the law of our Prophet (ﷺ). But most people do not know this. Through one of them God preserves faith (al-īmān), through the second guardianship (al-wilāya), through the third prophethood (al-nubuwwa), through the fourth messengerhood (al-risāla), and through all of them together the upright religion (al-dīn al-ḥanīfī). The qutb among these never dies, that is, he is not struck senseless. This knowledge is not known among the people of our path except for the trustworthy individuals. Each one of this community, in every age, has a person upon his heart alongside their presence, and they are called the nuwwāb (deputies). Most of the awliyā' (saints) among our common companions know only those deputies and do not know those messengers. For this reason, each one of the community aspires to attain the rank of qutbiyya, imāmiyya and watadiyya. When they are granted these, they realise that they are deputies of those messengers, peace be upon them.

Among the honours of our Prophet (ﷺ) is that he made messengers from among his community and followers, even though they were not sent to them from among the people of this rank from which messengers are sent, though they had already been sent. For this reason, on the night of the Isrā', the Prophet (ﷺ) led the prophets, peace be upon them, in prayer, so that the imamate over all of them would be valid for him, living in his bodily and physical form. When he, upon whom be prayers and peace, passed away, the matter remained preserved through these messengers, peace be upon them. Thus the religion remained established, by the praise of God Most High, even though corruption appeared in the world, until God inherits the earth and whatever is upon it. This is a subtle point, so understand its value, for you will not find it in the words of anyone other than us. Had it not been cast into my heart to make it known, I would not have made it known, for a secret that God Most High knows, which He has informed us of. Only their deputies know what we have mentioned, not others among the saints. So praise God Most High, O our brothers, that He has made you among those whose hearing has been struck by the hidden secrets of God Most High in His creation, which He has reserved for whom He wills of His servants. So be receptive to them, believe in them, and do not forbid yourselves the affirmation of them, lest you be deprived of their good. (End of quotation.)

From this it is known that he holds the view of the messengerhood of al-Khiḍr, peace be upon him. This view is weaker according to the majority of scholars. Also known is the view of his life and survival until the Day of Resurrection, and likewise the survival of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. The well-known view is that after his descent to the earth he will marry, have children, die, and be buried in the noble chamber alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Let one consider what is the basis of his statement, sanctified be his secret, that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, remains on the earth, when he is today in the heavens like Idrīs, peace be upon him.

Furthermore, if you take such statements into account and accept them merely because of the eminence of their speaker and good opinion of him, then say that al-Khiḍr, peace be upon him, lives until the Day of Resurrection. But if you do not take that into account, and make evidence, present or absent, the criterion of acceptance and rejection, and the eminence of the speaker does not deceive you, since everyone's words are accepted or rejected except those of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then that is the proper course.

It is reported from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, that he said: "Do not look at who said it, but look at what was said. Then consult your heart after standing on the proofs of both sides, what supports them and what counts against them, and then act upon what it gives you as a verdict." I see many people today, and indeed in many eras, calling whoever opposes the Ṣūfiyya in any matter they hold to a denier, and considering him of corrupt belief. They believe in whoever agrees with them and accepts their words as good. Similar things appear in the words of the Ṣūfiyya too. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar, sanctified be his secret, transmitted in the preceding chapter from Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī, sanctified be his secret, that he said to Abū Mūsā al-Daybilī: "O Abū Mūsā, when you see someone who believes in the words of the people of this path, tell him to pray for you, for he is answered in prayer." He also mentioned that he heard Abū ʿImrān Mūsā ibn ʿImrān al-Ishbīlī say to Abū al-Qāsim ibn ʿUfayr al-Khaṭīb, when he denied what the people of the path mention: "O Abū al-Qāsim, do not do that, for if you do this you combine two deprivations: we do not know it from our own souls, and we do not believe it from others, and there is no proof that refutes it, nor any defect in it, in terms of the law or reason." (End of quotation.) From this it is understood that what the legal or rational proof refutes is not accepted, and this is what I hold and what I say. I ask God Most High to grant success to me and to you in everything that is pleasing and acceptable to Him, glorified is He.

The tanwīn in His saying, Most High: ﴿mercy﴾ is for magnification, and likewise in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and We taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾, that is, knowledge whose essence cannot be grasped and whose extent cannot be measured, and it is the knowledge of the unseen and the secrets of hidden sciences. As for the mention of ﴿from Our presence﴾ (ladun), it is said that this is because knowledge is among the most specific of His essential attributes, Most High. They have said that power does not relate to anything unless will relates to it, and will does not relate unless knowledge relates to it. So the thing is first known, then willed, and then power relates to it, and so it comes into existence.

It is also mentioned that it is understood from the implication of ﴿from Our presence﴾, or from placing it before ﴿knowledge﴾, that this is specific to God Most High, as if it were said: knowledge that is specific to Us and cannot be known except through Our instruction. In choosing ﴿We taught him﴾ over ﴿We gave him﴾, there is an indication of the magnification of the matter of this knowledge.

This teaching may be through revelation heard in the tongue of an angel, which is the first category of the apparent revelation (al-waḥy al-ẓāhirī), as happened to our Prophet (ﷺ) in his report of the unseen which God Most High revealed to him in the noble Qur'ān. It may also be through revelation that arises from an angel's indication without explanation in words, which is the second category of that, and is called nafth (inspiration breathed into the heart), as in the ḥadīth: "Indeed the Holy Spirit (Rūḥ al-Qudus) breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it completes its provision, so fear God Most High and be gracious in seeking." As for ilhām (inspiration), as some expressions of the people indicate, it is of this kind. They affirm for it an angel which they call the angel of inspiration (malak al-ilhām). It is for the prophets, peace be upon them, and others by consensus. For them there are ways of reaching the unseen which branch out from the purification of the inner self.

The verse is for them a foundation for affirming ʿilm laduni (knowledge from God's presence). The term "knowledge of reality" and "inner knowledge" has become widely applied to it, though some did not approve this application. The gnostic of God Most High, Shaykh ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Shaʿrānī, may God have mercy on him, said in his book called al-Durar al-Manthūra fī Bayān Zubad al-ʿUlūm al-Mashhūra the following words: "As for the essence of the science of tasawwuf, in which the people have written their treatises, it is the fruit of acting upon the Book and the Sunna. Whoever acts upon what he knows speaks what they spoke, and all that they said becomes part of what he possesses, for whenever a servant advances in the courtesy with God Most High, his speech becomes subtle to understanding. Some of them said to their shaykh: 'The words of my brother so-and-so are subtle to my understanding.' He said: 'Because you have two shirts and he has one shirt; so he is higher in rank than you.' This is what led jurists and their like, from among the people of veils, to call the science of the Ṣūfiyya the inner science, and it is not inner, for the inner is only the knowledge of God Most High. As for all that the creatures know, across their different levels, it is of the outer knowledge, for it appeared to the creatures, so know this." (End of quotation.)

The truth is that applying the term "inner knowledge" as a technical term to what they have attained is correct, and there is no dispute over terminology. Its basis is that it is not apparent to most people, and its attainment depends on holy power rather than intellectual premises, although every knowledge is described as being inner and as being outer in relation to the one who is ignorant of it and the one who knows it. This is like applying the term "strange knowledge" (al-ʿilm al-gharīb) to the science of talismanic correspondences, the talismans, and the jafr (the science of letters and their numerical values), because of their rarity and the scarcity of those who know them. So understand this.

Some have claimed that the rulings of inner knowledge and the knowledge of reality differ from the rulings of the outer and the knowledge of the Sharia. This claim is false, empty, corrupt and worthless. The texts of the Ṣūfiyya that refute it will come, God willing, and it will be shown that they have no basis for the story of Mūsā and al-Khiḍr, peace be upon them both.

Abū Zayd transmitted from Abū ʿAmr the reading "لَدُنا" (ladunā) with the nūn lightened, and it is one of the dialects of "لَدُنْ" (ladun).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 66:

﴿Musa said to him﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istinaf), answering a question that arises from the context, as if it were said: "What speech passed between them?" So it is said: Musa, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿Shall I follow you on condition that you teach me﴾. This is Musa, peace be upon him, asking permission to follow him on the condition of being taught. This is understood from the word "ʿalā" (on condition). The jurists of legal theory (al-Usuliyyun) have said that "ʿalā" may be used in a meaning from which it is understood that what follows it is a condition for what precedes it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they will pledge allegiance to you on condition that they do not associate anything with God﴾, meaning: on condition of not associating. Its being for a condition is, according to the jurists (al-Fuqaha'), equivalent to its literal meaning, as in al-Talwih (al-Talwih, a commentary on al-Tawdih), because in its original use it is for obligation, and the consequent is necessarily bound to the condition. Al-Fanari's words in Badai' al-Usul also hint at this, though they are apparent in indicating that it is not a literal meaning for condition. Al-Sarakhsi mentioned that it is a literal meaning for it, but the grammarians did not address it. Al-Subki hesitated over its occurrence in the speech of the Arabs. The truth is that it is a correct usage, attested by the Book, whether literal or figurative, and the understanding of conditionality does not contradict the particle's being attached to the verb before it, as they said regarding the verse we mentioned. Likewise, it does not contradict its being attached to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as has been said here. So the meaning becomes: "Shall I follow you while spending my effort in your teaching me ﴿of what you have been taught, [as] right guidance﴾", i.e., knowledge that has rushd, which is attaining good. Abu ʿAmr, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Munadhir, Yaʿqub, Abu ʿUbayd and al-Yazidi read "rashadan" with two fatha vowels, while most of the Seven read it with a damma and sukun. Both are dialectal variants, like "al-bukhl" and "al-bakhal" (stinginess). Its accusative case, originally, is because it is an attribute of the second object of "tuʿallimanī" (you teach me). It was described by it for emphasis, but it was placed in its position after its omission. The second object of "ʿullimta" is the pronoun returning to the relative "mā", i.e., "from that which you were taught". Both verbs are derived from "ʿalima", which is transitive to one object. It is also permitted that ﴿of what you have been taught﴾ be the second object of "tuʿallimanī", and "rushdan" be a substitute (badal) for it, though this is contrary to the apparent sense. It is also permitted that "rushdan" be an object of purpose (maful lahu) for "atabiʿuka", i.e., "Shall I follow you for the sake of attaining good?" In that case, the second object of "tuʿallimanī" must be ﴿of what you have been taught﴾, interpreted as "some of what you have been taught" or "knowledge of what you have been taught". It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdar) with its verb omitted, i.e., "he guided rushd", and the sentence is then resumptive, with the second object again being ﴿of what you have been taught﴾. The request of Musa, peace be upon him, for teaching has been raised as a difficulty, since he is a messenger of the Resolute Messengers (ulu al-ʿazm), so how could he learn from someone else, when a messenger must be the most knowledgeable of the people of his time? For this reason Nawf and those like him said: this Musa is not the son of ʿImran, although the apparent sense of his unqualified mention suggests that he is him. It is answered that what is required of a messenger is that he be the most knowledgeable in matters of belief and what relates to his law, not absolutely in everything. For this reason our Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life."

Therefore, it does not harm his rank that he learns hidden sciences and secret mysteries from another, which have no connection to his mission, especially if that other is also a prophet or messenger, as has been said of al-Khidr, peace be upon him. A parallel to what has been mentioned, in terms of a scholar who is a mujtahid, like Abu Hanifa and al-Shafiʿi, may God be pleased with them both, learning the science of jafr (a science of occult letters) for example from someone lower than himself, is that it does not diminish his rank, and denying this is obstinacy.

It is not objected to this that the knowledge of the unseen is not knowledge with rushd, i.e., attaining good, while Musa, peace be upon him, was in the process of learning a knowledge by which he would attain good, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good, and no harm would have touched me﴾. Some have said: what is required is that the messenger be more knowledgeable than his community, and al-Khidr, peace be upon him, is a prophet to whom no messenger was sent, nor is he commanded to follow the law of anyone, so it is not denied that he alone knows what no one else knows.
