It is not hidden that according to this view al-Khidr, peace be upon him, is not from the Children of Israel, because the apparent sense is that Musa, peace be upon him, was sent to all of them; so it is said.

Then, what I incline to is that Musa, peace be upon him, possessed knowledge of the reality (ʿilm al-haqiqa), which is called the inner knowledge (al-ʿilm al-batin) and the knowledge bestowed directly from God (al-ʿilm al-ladunni), except that al-Khidr knows more of it than he does. And al-Khidr, peace be upon him, whether a prophet or messenger, has knowledge of the law (ʿilm al-shariʿa), which is called the outer knowledge (al-ʿilm al-zahir), except that Musa, peace be upon him, knows more of it than he does. So each of them is more knowledgeable than the other in some respect. The description of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, in the preceding hadiths as more knowledgeable than Musa, peace be upon him, does not mean that he is more knowledgeable than him in every respect, but rather in some respects and in some sciences. However, since the speech came out in the manner of rebuke and discipline, it was expressed in a way that outwardly implies generality. A parallel to this is the verses of threat, according to what is said, that they are restricted by God's will, but this restriction was not mentioned for the sake of greater intimidation. The superlative form (afʿal al-tafdil), although it indicates an increase in the reality of the act, does so in a way that encompasses an increase in a particular instance of it. This is indicated by the validity of restricting it to a specific category, as you say: "Zayd is more knowledgeable than ʿAmr in medicine, and ʿAmr is more knowledgeable than him in agriculture." If its meaning were an increase in knowledge in general, your saying "Zayd is more knowledgeable than ʿAmr" would necessitate that ʿAmr not be more knowledgeable than him in any science, and thus preferring ʿAmr over him in the science of agriculture would not be valid. Denying the truth of the absolute superlative while affirming the truth of the restricted one entails affirming the truth of the restricted without the absolute. The superlative has indeed come in an unrestricted use while intending preference in one respect, as Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib mentioned in his Amali al-Qur'an among the aspects for resolving the famous difficulty in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We show them no sign except that it is greater than its sister﴾, namely that the meaning is: "except that it is greater than its sister in one respect." Then he said: Two things may each be superior to the other in some respect. Our master Jalal al-Din al-Dawani has elaborated on this matter in what he wrote on the new commentary on al-Tajrid, and verified it fully.

Among what indicates that Musa, peace be upon him, had a knowledge that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did not have, is what al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that: "al-Khidr, peace be upon him, said: 'O Musa, I am upon a knowledge from the knowledge of God, exalted is He, which He taught me, that you do not know; and you are upon a knowledge from the knowledge of God, exalted is He, which God, glorified is He, taught you, that I do not know.'"

You know that if the saying of God, exalted is He, to Musa, peace be upon him, mentioned in the preceding hadiths, "Indeed I have a servant at the meeting place of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you," did not mean "more knowledgeable in some sciences" but rather "more knowledgeable in all sciences," then its reconciliation with what we have mentioned from the speech of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, would be problematic. Then, according to what we have mentioned, it is appropriate that what al-Khidr said he knows and Musa does not know, peace be upon both of them, be understood as some of the knowledge of reality, and what he said Musa knows and he does not know, peace be upon both of them, be understood as some of the knowledge of the law. So each of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon both of them, has knowledge of both the law and the reality, except that Musa, peace be upon him, has more of the knowledge of the law, and al-Khidr, peace be upon him, has more of the knowledge of reality. But given the present situation, as you will know its reason, God willing, and the fact that each does not know some of what is with the other, does not harm his rank.

The statement of one who said, such as al-Jalal al-Suyuti, "Reality and law were not combined except for our Prophet (ﷺ), and the prophets had only one of them," should be understood to mean that they were not combined in the most perfect manner except for him (ﷺ), and the prophets, peace be upon them, did not have, in that manner, except one of them. Interpreting it as meaning that they were not combined in the form of the command to convey except for our Prophet (ﷺ) is also possible, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to convey reality just as he is commanded to convey the law, but only to those who are prepared for it, and it does not lack something. It is understood from the words of some of the great scholars that the knowledge of reality is among the sciences of sainthood (wilaya), and then it is necessary that every prophet have a share of it, and this does not necessitate equality in its sciences.

In al-Jawahir wa'l-Durar: I said to al-Khawwas, may mercy be upon him: "Do messengers differ in knowledge?" He said: "Knowledge follows the mission, for every messenger has only the knowledge that his community needs, and no more." I said to him: "This is in terms of their being messengers. Is their state, in terms of being saints, likewise?" He said: "No. One of them may have from the sciences of sainthood more than the sciences of sainthood of the Resolute Messengers, who are higher than them, end quote." I see that what they obtain of the knowledge of reality, based on the view that it is among the sciences of sainthood, is more than what is obtained by saints who are not prophets. And you will not find me preferring a saint who is not a prophet in the knowledge of reality over a saint who is a prophet. And I do not hold that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, is a saint without being a prophet. Those who hold that necessarily face, apparently, the claim that what he has of the knowledge of reality, while being a saint, is more than what Musa, peace be upon him, has of it, if they affirm for him, peace be upon him, some of that while he is a prophet. But they do not see in that a demeaning of the rank of Musa, peace be upon him. The apparent sense of some of them is that he, peace be upon him, was not given any of the knowledge of reality at all, and yet his rank is not lower than the rank of al-Khidr, peace be upon both of them, since he has other aspects of excellence. The investigation of what those who go to his sainthood, peace be upon him, say will come, God willing.

Then, what I see, and praise be to God, is further from what has been transmitted from some of the Sufis, that sainthood in absolute terms is superior to prophethood, even if the saint does not reach the rank of the prophet. This is rejected by the verifiers (al-Muhaqqiqun) without hesitation. Yes, there may be a disagreement regarding a prophet's prophethood and his sainthood: which of them is superior? Some say his prophethood is superior to his sainthood, and some say his sainthood is superior.

Some of the gnostics ('urafa') chose this, giving as reason that legislative prophethood is connected to the benefit of the time, whereas sainthood has no connection to one time over another, and in the prophet it is at the utmost perfection. But what I choose is the first. The Karramiyya have erred in this matter, claiming that the saint may reach the rank of the prophet, or even higher. Their refutation is evident. Arguing for it from this story, based on the view that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, is a saint, is of no account, as is not hidden.

This, and it is not hidden to whoever has even a little taste for the styles of speech, is how Musa, peace be upon him, observed, in arranging his speech, his lofty rank, along with the utmost humility toward al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and the highest degree of courtesy and gentleness. The Imam counted many kinds of this, reaching twelve kinds. If you want them, return to his tafsir. What the verse indicates, in the enumeration of what the entire story's verses indicate, from what is mentioned in books of hadith and others, will come, God willing, exalted and majestic is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 67:

﴿Qāla﴾ — that is, al-Khidr said to Musa, peace be upon them both: ﴿Innaka lan tastaṭīʿa maʿiya ṣabrā﴾ (“Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me”). This is a negation of his being able to be patient with him in the most emphatic way, since it is introduced with inna (إنَّ, the particle that conveys emphasis) and with lan (لَنْ), and the negation with lan is stronger than the negation with other particles. He moved away from “lan taṣbira” (“you will not be patient”) to ﴿lan tastaṭīʿa﴾ (“you will not be able”), which conveys the negation of patience by way of a demonstrative argument (ṭarīq burhānī), because ability (istiṭāʿa) is something on which the act depends, so the negation of the ability entails the negation of the act. He made ﴿ṣabrā﴾ indefinite (nakkara) in the context of negation, and this conveys generality: that is, “you will not be patient with me at all, not even any degree of patience.” He justified this with his saying:

﴿And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ This indicates that he, peace be upon him, would be taking charge of matters that were hidden. The meaning is matters whose outward forms are objectionable. A righteous man, especially the owner of a Shari'ah (law), cannot help but recoil when witnessing them. It seems that [Musa] knew, along with this, the sharpness of Musa, peace be upon him, and his excessive zeal, which led him to seize his brother by the head and drag him.

﴿خُبْرًا﴾ is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the subject. The original would be: ما لَمْ يَحُطْ بِهِ خُبْرُكَ (that which your knowledge has not encompassed). It derives from the triliteral خَبَرَ, of the pattern نَصَرَ and عَلِمَ, and its meaning is عَرَفَ (to know). It is also permissible for it to be a verbal noun (masdar), with ﴿تُحِطْ﴾ as its governing verb, because it corresponds to it in meaning, since الإحاطة (encompassing) is commonly used for knowledge. So it is as if it were said: لَمْ تَخْبُرْهُ خُبْرًا (you did not gain any real acquaintance with it). Al-Hasan and Ibn Harmuz read «خُبُرًا» with a dammah on the ba'.

The scholars, as the Imam and others said, used this verse as evidence that istita'a (capacity to act) does not exist before the act. They said: If istita'a were present before the act occurred, then the istita'a for patience would be present before patience occurred, and so its negation would be a lie, which is false. Therefore it is necessarily the case that it does not exist before the act.

Al-Jubba'i answered that what is meant by this statement is that patience will be burdensome for you, just as it is said in common usage: "So-and-so cannot bear to see so-and-so or to sit with him," when that is burdensome to him.

The Imam criticized this by saying that it is a departure from the apparent meaning. The argument was supported by what was cited in support of it. The fair view is that
صفحة 334
using this verse as evidence for what was mentioned is not clear, because the intended meaning is nothing other than the negation of patience by negating what it depends on, namely istita'a. This is true whether istita'a existed beforehand or existed concurrently with the act. Furthermore, the view that istita'a precedes the act is not specific to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school). Rather, what is understood from the words of Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani is that it is also the doctrine of the Salaf (the early generations). The verification of this is in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 69:

﴿Said﴾ Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿"You will find me, God willing, patient"﴾, with you, not objecting to you, ﴿"and I will not disobey any command of yours."﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to ﴿patient﴾. The verb is conjoined to a derived noun (mufrad mushtaqq), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ranks (ṣāffāt) and those who grasp (wa-yaqbiḍna)﴾, by interpreting one of them in terms of the other. In this case, the preferable option is to interpret the conjoined element: that is, "you will find me patient and not disobeying." In promising this "finding" there is an emphasis that is absent from a promise of patience itself and of abstaining from disobedience. Alternatively, it is conjoined to ﴿you will find me﴾. According to the first view, the clause is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb), since it is conjoined to the second object of "finding" (wijdān). According to the second view, it has no grammatical position (lā maḥalla lahā min al-iʿrāb) according to what is in the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari). It has been objected that the apparent position of the clause is also accusative, because of the preceding "said." It has been answered that the content of the saying (maqūl al-qawl) is the whole of the conjoined and the conjoining element together, so its parts do not have a position in terms of the original (bi-iʿtibār al-aṣl). It has also been said: al-Zamakhshari's intention is to explain the status of the conjunction within the saying reported of Musa, peace be upon him. It has also been said: his intention is that it is not interpreted as a single noun, as in the first case. It has also been said: this is based on the view that the content of the saying is omitted, and this clause explains it. The apparent answer is the first one, and the first of the two views on conjunction is preferable, for what you have come to know, and because the connection of the conjoined element to the exception (istithnāʾ) is evident. As for mentioning the will of God (mashīʾa): if it is for conditionality (taʿlīq), then there is no difficulty in the non-fulfilment of what he promised.

It cannot be said that he, peace be upon him, broke his promise, even if the mention of God's will was for blessing (tayammun). If we say that a promise, like a threat, is a performative utterance (inshāʾ) that does not admit of truth or falsehood, or that it is restricted by a condition known from the context, such as "if you wish" or "if no legal or other obstacle prevents," then likewise there is no difficulty. But if we say that it is an informative statement (khabar) and that it is not intended as restricted, the difficulty appears clearly, for breaking the promise then is a lie, and this is unfitting for the station of prophethood, since it contradicts infallibility (ʿiṣma). It has been answered that what proceeded from him, peace be upon him, in the last two instances was forgetfulness, as in the first instance, and such a breaking of promise does not harm the station of prophethood, because forgetfulness is an excuse. It has been criticised: we do not accept that there was forgetfulness in the last two instances. In al-Bukhari and its commentary by Ibn Hajar, it is stated: the first was forgetfulness, the second was a condition, and the third was deliberate. In another narration: the second was deliberate and the third was separation. Some of them said: you may say that nothing proceeded from him, peace be upon him, that would harm his station, because the breaking of promise in the first instance is pardoned, and where it occurred the last two were not breaking of promise. In this there is room for reflection. Al-Qushayri said: Musa, peace be upon him, promised himself two things: patience, which he attached to the will of God, and so he was patient regarding what al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did; and that he would not disobey him, which he stated absolutely without attaching the will of God, and so he disobeyed him when he said: ﴿do not ask me﴾, and he kept asking him. So what he attached to the exception, he did not break, and what he stated absolutely, the breaking occurred in it. End of quotation.

This is based on the conjunction being to ﴿you will find me﴾. You know that this is contrary to the preferable view. Also, the meaning of patience is persistence, steadfastness in the act and not objecting, as the subsequent dialogue indicates, and this did not come about from him, peace be upon him. Also, the discussion of breaking the promise remains, as is not hidden. And you know that it is far from the state of Musa, peace be upon him, to be certain of patience and of not disobeying the command, after al-Khidr, peace be upon him, indicated to him that unusual matters contrary to the principles of his law would proceed from him. Therefore it is not far from him to take the conditional sense in both clauses. He did not state it after both, but placed it in the middle between the two objects of "finding" in the first clause, for greater care for its matter. With this the difficulty is removed without need for lengthy debate. In this there is evidence that the actions of the servant are by the will of God, exalted is He, for if some voluntary actions proceed by His, glorified is He, will, then all of them must proceed by it, since there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist school) chose that the mention of the will is for blessing (tayammun), and this does not indicate what has been stated. Some of the researchers said: the argument also applies to the possibility of blessing, since there is no sense in seeking blessing through what has no reality. The Imam (al-Razi) also indicated this, so understand. The verse has been cited as evidence that the command (amr) denotes obligation (wujūb), but there is room for consideration in this. Then, the apparent meaning is that by "command" is not meant the opposite of prohibition (nahy), but rather any demand (muṭlaq al-ṭalab). The purport of the verse is the negation that he would disobey him in anything he demands.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 70:

﴿He said﴾ al-Khidr (peace be upon him), ﴿"If you follow me"﴾. He (peace be upon him) permitted him to follow, after the two previous occasions (al-latayya wa-al-lati). The fa' (the particle "then") introduces a consequence (tafri') of the conditional clause (al-shartiyya, the conditional sentence) upon what preceded, namely Musa's (peace be upon him) promise to be patient and obedient.

﴿"Then do not ask me about anything"﴾ that you witness of my actions, let alone object to or dispute it, ﴿"until I myself mention it to you"﴾, that is, until I begin to explain it to you. The limit (al-ghaya, the terminal point) is, as has been said, attached to what is understood from the speech, as if it were said: "Disapprove in your heart of what I do until I explain it to you." Or it is for the permanent prohibition of asking, since asking after explanation is not fitting, all the more so. On both views, there is an indication that everything that proceeds from him has a wisdom and a praiseworthy end, definitely. It has also been said that ḥattā (until) here expresses causation (ta'lil), but this is not correct.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿فَلا تَسْألَنِّي﴾ (fa-la tas'alanni) with the doubled nun and the hamza. From Abu Ja'far: ﴿فَلا تَسَلَنِّي﴾ (fa-la tasalanni), with fatha on the sin and the lam and the doubled nun, without hamza. All the readers, as Abu Bakr said, have a ya' at its end (i.e., in the first person ending, the ya' of the pronoun). Regarding the omission of the ya' from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), there is a strange (gharib, anomalous) disagreement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 71:

﴿So they set off﴾, meaning Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. Yusha' (Joshua), peace be upon him, is not counted among them because he was in the position of a follower (tab'). It is also said that Musa, peace be upon him, sent him back to the Children of Israel.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Prophet (marfu'), that the two of them "set off walking along the shore of the sea. A ship passed by them and they asked its people to carry them, and they recognised al-Khidr and carried them without a fare."

In the narration of Abu Hatim from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, the people of the ship thought they were thieves, because the place was dangerous, so they refused to carry them. Their leader said: "I see men upon whose faces is light. I will indeed carry them." So he carried them.

﴿until, when they boarded the ship﴾. The alif-lam in al-safina (the ship) is the alif-lam of generic definition (ta'rif al-jins), since no previous mention had been made of a specific ship. According to some narrations it was a new, sturdy ship, and no ship that passed them was better, more beautiful or stronger. It was also, as some authentic narrations indicate, one of the small ships by which the people of this coast carried passengers to the people of the other coast. In the narration of Abu Hatim, it was heading to Ayla.

It is authentically related that when the two of them boarded, a sparrow came and landed on the edge of the ship, then pecked at the sea. Al-Khidr said to him: "My knowledge and your knowledge, compared with the knowledge of God the Exalted, have diminished only as much as this sparrow has diminished from the sea."

This is treated as an illustrative example (tamthil). The use of the verb rakiba (to board) in such contexts with the preposition fi (in), while in other places it is used without it, as in His saying ﴿that you may ride them and as adornment﴾, is explained by its transitive usage, and the reason for this has already been indicated in His saying ﴿And he said, "Board it"﴾. It is also said that this is intended to convey the meaning of entering, as if it were said: "until, when they entered into the ship". ﴿he made a hole in it﴾. It is authentically related that when the two of them boarded the ship, they were only surprised to find that al-Khidr had pulled a plank from its planks with an adze. Musa, peace be upon him, said to him: "These people carried us without a fare, and you deliberately went to their ship and made a hole in it."

It is also authentically related that he, peace be upon him, made a hole in it and drove a peg into it. It is said that he pulled up two planks on the side facing the water.

In a narration from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Prophet (marfu'), the two of them, "when they had boarded and settled in it, and the ship was tossed about with its people, he brought out his auger and his hammer, then went to one side of it and struck into it with the chisel until he made a hole in it. Then he took a plank and pressed it over the hole, then sat upon it, patching it."

This narration clearly indicates that his making the hole in it occurred when the ship had reached the deep part of the sea, its greatest depth. In the narration from al-Rabi', the people of the ship carried them and they sailed until, when they were close to the land, he made a hole in it. It is possible to reconcile these by saying that the initial resolve was while the ship was in the deep water, and the completion of the act was when it was close to the land. The apparent sense of the reports is that he, peace be upon him, made a hole in it while its people were in it, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿He [Musa] said: "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?"﴾ Whether the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), on the basis that Musa, peace be upon him, had a good opinion of al-Khidr, or the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), on the basis that this is more fitting to the context of denunciation, [either way]. Some scholars did not permit the lam to be the lam of causation, imagining that this implied a breach of good manners. This is not so; rather, it is nearly certain that it is the lam of causation, because the apparent sense is that the answer is built upon it, as we shall indicate, God willing.

In a report narrated by Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh, it is said: "They set off until, when they boarded the ship, those who were in it left, and he remained behind to make a hole in it. Musa said to him: 'Are you making a hole in it to drown its people?' Al-Khidr said to him: [what] God the Exalted has related."

This apparently indicates that he resolved to make the hole, and Musa objected to him at that point, which contradicts what the verse implies. If it is interpreted (ta'wil) as meaning: "he remained behind to make a hole in it, and so he made a hole in it", and that Musa's use of the present tense is to bring the scene vividly before the mind, or if it is said that al-Khidr first set his mind on making the hole and prepared its means, and then secondly made the hole in fact, and Musa objected to the first act first and to the second act second, then the hadith reports the first of what happened from each of them concerning this matter, and the verse reports the second of what happened from each of them. There remains, as is said, another discrepancy between the apparent sense of the hadith and the apparent sense of the verse: the first implies that the people of the ship were not in it when it was made a hole in, while the second implies that they were in it at that time. It has been answered that the hadith says no more than that they left it while he remained behind to make the hole, and it does not say that they left and then he made the hole. So it is possible that he, peace be upon him, remained behind to make the hole after they had left, but he did not do it until after they had returned to it and were inside it. You know that this conflicts with what has been said regarding how to reconcile the report from Sa'id with the report from al-Rabi'. In general, reconciling the three reports with one another and with the verse is difficult.

Some scholars said in this regard: it is possible that when the ship was tossed about with them, they came upon an island in the deep water, so they went out for some of their needs, and al-Khidr remained behind, resolved to make the hole, and Musa, peace be upon him, was with him. Musa sensed this from him, so he hastened to object. Then its people returned and boarded it again, and the resolve remained the same. He, peace be upon him, began to carry out what he had resolved, and Musa, peace be upon him, did not notice until it was complete, by which time the ship was close to the land. The distance of this is not hidden.

Some scholars mentioned that the apparent sense of the verse implies that his making the hole in it occurred immediately after boarding, because the consequent follows the condition. It has been answered that this is not necessary; what is necessary is only that the consequent be caused by the condition and occur after it. Do you not see that you say: "If Zayd rebels against the sultan, he kills him", and "If you give the sultan a poem, he gives you a reward", although killing often does not immediately follow rebellion, and giving does not immediately follow giving? Ibn al-Hajib has explicitly stated that it is not necessary for the condition and the consequent to occur at the same time, so one says: "If you come to me today, I will honour you tomorrow." On this basis is His saying ﴿"When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾. Whoever insists on this, like al-Radi, makes the time indicated by "idha" (when) extended, and in the aforementioned verse he supposes the meaning to be: "Shall I, when I am dead and have become dust, be brought forth?" On this basis too, immediacy is not necessary. Yes, some scholars said: the report "When they boarded the ship, they were only surprised to find that al-Khidr had pulled a plank from its planks" indicates that the making of the hole followed the boarding. Also, making the endpoint of their departure the content of the conditional sentence requires this, because if the making of the hole were delayed after the boarding, the endpoint of the departure would not have been the content of the sentence, since it would not have ended with it. It has been answered that the immediacy indicated by the report is understood as meaning that not many days, or the like, had passed. It is also answered that there is no barrier to the endpoint being a continuous matter, and the ending of what is limited by it coinciding with its beginning, like your saying: "So-and-so ruled until the year such-and-such was his reign." Consider this carefully.

Furthermore, there is some doubt about the soundness of al-Rabi''s report, and God the Exalted knows best its soundness. The apparent sense is that the people of the ship did not see him when he began making the hole, otherwise they would not have allowed him to do it. Ali al-Qari explicitly stated this. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, through Hammad ibn Zayd, from Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab, that he said: "al-Khidr was a servant whom no one could see except those whose eyes God wished to show him. Therefore none of the people saw him except Musa, peace be upon him. Had the people seen him, they would have prevented him from making the hole in the ship, and likewise from killing the boy." This is not a report traced back to the Prophet, and God the Exalted knows best its soundness. However, it will come soon, God willing, from al-Rabi' too, that they later came to know that he was the one who did it. The apparent sense also is that Musa, peace be upon him, did not intend to include his own noble self in His saying ﴿to drown its people﴾, even though it is suitable to be included in it, on the basis that "its people" means those who were riding in it.

Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read ﴿لِتُغَرِّقَ﴾ (litughriqa, with doubled ghayn) to indicate an increase in the object. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Zayd ibn Ali, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan and Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani read ﴿لِيَغْرَقَ أهْلُها﴾ (liyaghraqa ahluha), attributing the verb to its people. That the lam in this reading is the lam of consequence is very clear.

﴿You have indeed committed a grave thing (shay'an imra)﴾, meaning a calamitous, abhorrent matter, from amira al-amr, meaning it became abundant. This is what al-Kisa'i said, so its root meaning is "abundant". Ibn Jinni said in Sirr al-Sina'a that the Arabs describe calamities by abundance. According to some, it is originally on the pattern of kibd (liver) and was lightened. It is said that they did not say amran imra, despite the paronomasia (tajnis) it contains, because that is an affectation to which no attention is paid in eloquent speech, as al-Marzuqi explicitly stated in his commentary on the lines of al-Samaw'al:

"The love of death brings our lifetimes near to us,
while their lifetimes, hating it, are made long."

This was a rejection of the choice of some who related the line as "The love of death shortens (yuqassiru)". This was supported by the line of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

"Imminent the departures, far the returns."

Where it was possible for him to say "slow the returns" (bati'u al-qufuli), but he did not say it. Perhaps it may be said here that he did not say that for the reason mentioned, together with its giving the misleading sense of the opposite of what is meant, and its falling short of the level of the magnificent wording, which contains greater severity. In the report from al-Rabi' it is said that when Musa, peace be upon him, saw what he saw from al-Khidr, he was filled with anger, wrapped his garments tightly around himself, and wanted to throw al-Khidr, peace be upon him, into the sea, saying: "You intended the destruction of its people, so you will know that you are the first to perish." Every time his anger increased, the sea roared, and every time he calmed, the sea was like oil. Yusha' ibn Nun said to him: "Do you not remember the covenant and the pledge you made upon yourself?" And al-Khidr, peace be upon him, turned to him, reminding him of what he had said before:

He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?" This implies a rebuke for his not having shown patience, and at that point Moses (peace be upon him) was overcome by shame. He said, "Do not hold me to account for what I forgot." This is an apology on the ground of having forgotten the stipulation, in the most emphatic form. It is as though his forgetting were a matter already established for al-Khidr (peace be upon him), who had no need to be informed of it independently; rather, Moses was only asking him to refrain from holding him accountable for it. Here *ma* is a verbal-masdar particle (*ma masdariyya*), and the *ba'* (with) is attached to *mu'akhadha* (holding to account). That is: "Do not hold me accountable for my forgetting your stipulation, that I should not ask about anything until you yourself mention it to me." He asked to be spared being held accountable for forgetting, because even a perfect person may be held to account for it. This is a holding to account for the lack of carefulness that led to it, as occurred with the first of mankind, who was the first of people. Otherwise, holding him accountable for forgetting itself is not valid, since it is not within one's power.

It has also been said that the *ba'* expresses causality (*sababiyya*) and is connected to the verb. Although forgetting is not the immediate cause of being held to account, the immediate cause being the abandoning of the stipulation's requirement, it is a remote cause, because without it the abandonment would not have occurred. It was also permitted that the *ba'* be connected to the sense of negation (*nahy*), as was said regarding *bi-ni'mati rabbika* in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾, that it is connected to the sense of negation. Thus forgetting would be the cause of the prohibition against holding him accountable for abandoning the requirement of the stipulation.

Some have claimed that the *ba'* must be for accompaniment (*mula-basa*). The word *ma* may be a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) or a qualifying noun (*mawsufa*). That is: "Do not hold me accountable for that which, or for something, I forgot, namely the stipulation." However, this apparently requires supplying an omitted genitive (*mudaf*, a noun governed by a construct phrase that is elided), that is: "for the abandoning of what I forgot," because holding one accountable is for abandoning the stipulation, i.e., abandoning acting upon it, not for the stipulation itself.

It has been said that the omitted noun may not be needed, since the stipulation is itself a cause of being held accountable, for without it there would be neither abandoning of action nor being held accountable. A parallel to this is what was said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾. Then, that what has been mentioned is an apology for forgetting the stipulation is the apparent meaning, and it is established in al-Bukhari that the first time was out of forgetfulness.

Some have claimed that it is possible that he (peace be upon him) did not forget the stipulation, but rather forbade being held accountable for forgetting, giving the impression that what proceeded from him was due to forgetting it, whereas he only meant the forgetting of something else. This is one of the figurative (*ma'arid*) forms of speech by which a lie is avoided while still reaching one's aim, like the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿This is my sister﴾ and ﴿I am sick﴾. Ibn Jarir related this from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Ibn Abi Hatim related it from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

It was also permitted that forgetting be a figurative expression for abandoning, that is: "Do not hold me accountable for what I abandoned of your stipulation the first time." ﴿And do not burden me﴾: do not overwhelm me, and do not impose upon me ﴿from my affair﴾, which is following him, ﴿hardship﴾, that is, difficulty. It is the second object of *turhiqni*. The meaning is: do not make my following you difficult for me, and make it easy for me by overlooking and refraining from questioning. Abu Ja'far recited it as *'usuran* with two dammas.

He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?" This implies a rebuke for his not having shown patience, and at that point Moses (peace be upon him) was overcome by shame. He said, "Do not hold me to account for what I forgot." ﴿So they set off﴾. The fa' (the "fa" of an implied condition, fa'ihah) here means: so he accepted his excuse, and they went out of the ship and set off, walking along the shore, as is in the Sahih. In another narration, they passed by a village. ﴿Until, when they met a boy﴾. It is claimed, as al-Bukhari said, that his name was Jaysur, with a jim, though it was also narrated with a ha'. It was also said that his name was Jinbitur, and other things were said. It is established that he was playing with the boys, and they were, as it has been said, ten, and that there was none among them more handsome or cleaner than him. So he took him ﴿and killed him﴾. Al-Bukhari reported in one narration that he (peace be upon him) took hold of his head from its top and pulled it off with his hand.

In another narration, he took him, threw him down, and then slaughtered him with a knife.

It was said that he struck his head against a wall until he killed him. It was said that he crushed him with a stone. It was said that he struck him with his foot and killed him. It was said that he put his finger into his navel and pulled it out, and he died. The first three narrations are reconciled by saying that he first struck his head against the wall, then threw him down and slaughtered him, then pulled off his head. It may be that all of them are reconciled, but both of these reconciliations are far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that the boy was not mature, because "ghulam" (boy) in its common usage literally means this, and the majority held this view. It was said that he was a mature young man. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz that he was twenty years old. The Arabs continue to apply the name "boy" to a young man, and from this is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj:

"He healed her of the disease that had afflicted her, a boy who, when he shakes the spear, gives her to drink."

And his saying:

"Ward off from me the edge of the sword, for I am a boy, and when I am mocked, I am no poet."

It was said that it is literal of the adult, because its root is from "al-ightilam," which is intense sexual desire, and that occurs only in one who has reached puberty. Its application to a small child is a metaphorical extension, by naming a thing with the name of what it will become. The view of the first group is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Moses (peace be upon him), ﴿Have you killed a pure soul﴾, i.e., one pure from sins, for an adult rarely becomes pure of sins.

[p. 339 marker as given in source]

It has come in a hadith from Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet, that "pure" is explained as "without a minor sin," and this is an explanation by necessary implication. Whoever says he was an adult says: he (peace be upon him) described him thus because he had not seen him commit a sin, so this is a description arising from good assumption. It is cited as evidence that he was an adult by His saying: ﴿without a soul﴾, i.e., without a right of retaliation (qisas) that you have against him. Al-Nawawi and al-Karmani answered that the intention is to point out that he killed him without right, but the right of retaliation was singled out for negation because it is the most fitting to the context of killing. Or, their law required retaliation to be imposed on a child. The hadith scholars, such as al-Bayhaqi in the book al-Ma'rifah, have transmitted that in our law too it was so before the Hijrah.

Al-Subki said: before Uhud, and then it was abrogated (naskh). The prepositional phrase, Abu al-Baqa' said, is connected to "you killed," as if it were said: you killed a soul without right. It is also permitted that it be connected to an implied element, i.e., a killing without a soul, and that it be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), i.e., he killed it while wronging it or while it was wronged.

Ibn Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, Nafi', al-Yazidi, Ibn Muslim, Zayd, Ibn Bukayr from Ya'qub, Ruways from him also, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read "zakiyah" with a lightened ya' and an alif after the zay, which is zakiyah (زاكية). They read "zakiyyah" (زكية) with shaddah and without an alif, as Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Ibn Amir, and the Kufans read. The latter is more emphatic than that, because it is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) indicating permanence, and the pattern fa'il transformed from fa'il, as Abu Hayyan said, indicates intensity. Abu Amr distinguished between zakiyah (with alif) and zakiyyah (without alif): zakiyah with the alif is the one who never committed a sin at all, and zakiyyah without the alif is the one who sinned and was then forgiven.

This was criticized as an unclear distinction, because the original meaning of "zakah" is growth and increase, so it occurs in the sense of spiritual increase, and it is applied to purity from sins even if only by natural creation and beginning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That I may give you a pure boy﴾. So from where did this implication come? Then it was justified by saying that it is possible that "zakiyah" with the alif derives from the intransitive form zaka, which requires that it is not another verb and that the quality is established in itself, while "zakiyyah" means "made pure" (muzakkah), since fa'il may come from a non-triliteral root, like rada' meaning "suckling ones." The purification of one soul by another from sins happens only through forgiveness, and he (the grammarian) understood this from the speech of the Arabs, since he is the imam of Arabic and lexicography. Thus, by this consideration, "zakiyah" with the alif is more eloquent and more fitting to the context, on the basis that he holds that the boy had not reached puberty. This is why he chose that reading, though each of the two readings is mutawatir (transmitted by continuous multiple chains) from him (peace be upon him). This, as is said, does not contradict that "zakiyyah" without the alif is more eloquent in terms of indicating elevation (raf'), which is stronger than mere removal (daf'). So understand.

Whichever it is, describing the soul with this is for the sake of increasing the abhorrence of what he did.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that when al-Khidr (peace be upon him) killed the boy, Moses (peace be upon him) was struck by an extraordinary fright, and said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without a soul?﴾

﴿Indeed you have done a thing, an unthinkable thing﴾. Nukr means very reprehensible. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: al-munkar is what the intellects deny and souls recoil from, and it is more eloquent in condemning a thing than "amr" (affair). It was also said the reverse. Al-Raghib said: al-munkar is a calamity, and "amr" is a hard matter that is not known. Because of this greater eloquence, some said: the intended meaning is a thing more reprehensible than the first. Al-Tibi preferred that it is less than "amr" and said: what the composition requires is that he mentioned the more severe and then descended to the lighter. Killing a soul is lighter than tearing the ship, because it involves destroying a group, and it is more severe than setting up the wall without a wage. In al-Kashf he said: the apparent meaning is that the emphasis of "nukr" is either by the wording, which is obvious; do you not see how the poet explained it:

"The rivals have met from me a nukr, a calamity, a great calamity, a grave affair."

Nukr is with a calamity whose attributes are such-and-such, and he made "amr" one of its attributes. As for its reality, the tearing of the ship led to destruction, and this was an immediate act, although that was not an inevitable cause. The saying of one who said that it descended in argument, reasoning that setting up the wall is lighter than killing, is nothing, because it was narrated in the order of existence, not in descent or ascent. This is considered only relative to what came after it, and that ends his words. The view of emphasis by eloquence was also narrated from Qatada. What supports this is what al-Qurtubi related from the author of al-Urs wa al-Ara'is: when Moses (peace be upon him) said to al-Khidr (peace be upon him) what he said, al-Khidr became angry, tore out the boy's left shoulder, stripped the flesh from it, and there was written on it: a disbeliever who will never believe in God, exalted is He.

He based the reason for changing the magnificent wording on the ugliness of killing, and it was said: the wording was changed to what you see because killing is uglier, and the objection to it is more appropriate and more deserving. So the objection was worthy of being made the main point of the speech. This is based on the principle that in a conditional sentence the main judgment is the consequent (jaza'), and the condition is a qualifier of it, like a circumstantial phrase according to the grammarians. Its verification is in al-Mutawwal and its glosses.

The conjunction with fa' of consequence was used to convey that the killing occurred right after the meeting, without delay, as the objection implies. For if time had passed between the meeting and the killing, it would have been possible, by considering ordinary matters, that al-Khidr had gained knowledge from the boy's condition of what Moses (peace be upon him) had not known, and so this objection would not be raised against him. And it does no harm here to claim that the tearing of the ship is also like this, because the aim is to justify the choice of fa' rather than waw or thumma, after justifying the choice of the conjunction itself by the fact that this allows the objection to be made the main point. The summary is: since the objection in the second story was of great concern and importance, it was made the consequent of the conditional "idha," and once it was designated as the consequent for this reason, it was necessary to make the killing part of the condition by coordination. The fa' was chosen among its particles so that consequence would be conveyed. Since the objection in the first story was not like it in the second, it was made an independent sentence, and the tearing was made the consequent.

Al-Tashkandi claimed that it is permissible for both objections in the two stories to be independent sentences, with the consequent in both being the act of al-Khidr (peace be upon him), except that "qad" must be assumed in the second consequent, because the affirmative past verb not connected to it, verbally or by implication, is not suitable as a consequent.

This was taken into account in the second case and not in the first, because killing is uglier, so it deserves to be emphasized, and the tearing is not like that.

Some learned men objected to this, saying that the consequent fa' cannot enter upon an affirmative past verb except with an implied "qad," to make the effect of the conditional particle on it clear, by turning its meaning to the future. So there is no need for a connecting particle in order for it to be a response. But with an implied "qad," the fa' enters because the conditional particle has no effect on it, so it requires a connecting particle. So his saying, exalted is He: ﴿he tore it﴾ (kharaqaha), and likewise his saying, glorified is He: ﴿so he killed him﴾ (faqatalahu), since both are future relative to what preceded them, come as consequents without need for linking the consequent fa'. So there is no room in the second for making the fa' a consequent marker, and likewise there is no room in the first for assuming "qad" in order to bring the fa' into it. So consider this well, for it is not free of something.

Mir Badshah replied to this: the sound taste refuses to assume "qad" if the killing were made the consequent, since the context does not require it. How, when the tearing had already come as consequent without it? And it is known that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) did what the one who observes the law cannot bear to endure. What needs verification is only the second objection by Moses (peace be upon him), after what had already passed from him in speech, and his being sent by God for learning. In this there is turning away from explaining the subtle point in verifying it, and neglect of it, as some learned men said, concerning the position of the consequent fa' and the assumption of "qad." Perhaps the truth is that one should say: even if the assumption is permitted, it is very much contrary to the apparent meaning.

He also claimed that it is possible to say, in explaining the arrangement of the two stories as we have set it out, that meeting the boy was a cause of compassion and gentleness, not of killing, so it was not fitting to make it a consequent. And making the consequent of the condition and of boarding the ship may be a cause of tearing it, so it was made a consequent.

In this there is the objection that the opponent may deny the difference and say: just as meeting the boy is a cause of gentleness and not of killing, so too boarding the ship is a cause of guarding and preserving it, not of tearing it. How, when its safety is a cause of al-Khidr's own safety outwardly? Among the common proverbs: do not throw a stone into the well from which you drink. And if it is granted to him that he may say: the meeting with the boy is a cause of gentleness, not of killing, then killing is more strange, and the objection to it is more appropriate. So the objection is worthy of being made the consequent, and the matter, in explaining the subtle point, comes back to something like what preceded. The matter in this is easy, as is not hidden.

Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) said, regarding the reason for the change (in wording): the occurrence of extraordinary acts (khawariq) from al-Khidr, peace be upon him, came, through its happening once, to be in the manner of the habitual, and the soul became familiar with it, as it becomes familiar with ordinary matters. So its expectation turned away from hearing it toward expecting to hear the condition of Musa, peace be upon him: would he keep to observing his stipulation, in accordance with his promise, when witnessing another extraordinary act, or would he hasten to object as he did the first time? Thus the intended purpose was to convey what came from him, peace be upon him, and so the consequence was made his objection, rather than what came from al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. "To God, the Exalted, belongs the excellence of the composition of the revelation!" As for what has been said, that killing is more reprehensible and objection to it is more fitting, and so it was deserving of being made the main point of the discourse, this does not remove the doubt at all; rather it supports it. For the fact that killing is more reprehensible is among the reasons it rarely issues from a believing rational person, and its report rarely reaches the ears; and that calls for making it the object of the account. And the fact that objection to it is more fitting is among the reasons for its frequent issuing from every rational person, let alone a prophet; and that does not require making it so. End.

It has been criticised: what he mentioned of the nuance, even if granted, does not harm, among its (other) nuances, what preceded, since there is no conflict among the nuances. As for his objection, his saying "that calls for making it the object" – if he means it is an object in itself, this is not correct; and if he means it is an object in the sense that it is to be objected to and prevented, then this requires making the objection the consequence, as has passed. As for it being among the causes of its frequent issuing from every rational person, this necessitates attention to the objection to it.

You know that whenever a thing is rare, reporting it and conveying it to the hearer has a greater effect on the soul, and that strange reports receive more care in their conveyance than non-strange ones, since few know the strange, unlike others; and denying this is obstinacy. So the Shaykh's meaning is that the killing being more reprehensible is among the reasons for its rarely issuing from a believing rational person and its report rarely reaching the ears; and that calls for making it the object of conveying, as is the case with things that rarely occur and are rarely realised. And the objection to it being more fitting is among the reasons for frequent occurrence; but that does not require that it be treated in that way. On this basis, there is no objection to what he mentioned for the impartial. Furthermore, what he mentioned of the nuance applies both on the view that killing is more reprehensible than breaching the boat and on the opposite view as well. This differs from what preceded, for that was based on the greater reprehensibility of killing, so whoever does not hold this needs another explanation of the nuance. By this, it is preferred over what preceded. It is also supported by the fact that the flow of the discourse from its beginning is to explain the condition of Musa, peace be upon him; so making his objection the main point fits the flow better. Except that he departed from this in the story of the breaching, and made what came from al-Khidr, peace be upon him, the main point rather than his objection, because when the soul heard the description of al-Khidr it thirsted to hear what proceeds from him, so it quenched its thirst, and made what proceeded from him the object of conveying, because it is what the soul seeks while awaiting it. Then, after the soul heard that and its thirst subsided, he returned the discourse to its first course and aimed in conveying at the state of the one whose condition the discourse had been explaining from its beginning. It is not hidden that this is a statement that the original arrangement, looking at the flow,

is that the first story should be in the pattern of the second story; but he departed from that for what has been mentioned, and departure from the original is measured by the extent of need: "But whoever is forced, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him" (Qur'an 2:173). The fifteenth part is complete; followed, God willing, by the sixteenth part, whose beginning is: (Qala alam aqul laka).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 75–76:

Page 2

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ The addition of "laka" (to you) is for the increase in opposition to rejecting the counsel, and the lack of firmness and patience, since he repeatedly showed aversion and disapproval, and he did not heed the reminder until he increased in denial the second time.

"He said" — that is, Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿If I ask you about anything﴾ that you do of the marvels, "after this" — that is, after this time or after this question — ﴿then do not keep company with me.﴾ Ibn Amir, Isa and Ya'qub read (فَلا تَصْحَبْنِي) with a fatha on the ta' from sahiba (to accompany), meaning: "then do not be my companion." Also from Isa (فَلا تُصْحِبْنِي) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha' from asḥaba, and Sahl narrated it from Abu Amr, meaning: "then do not make me accompany you, and do not make me your companion." Some of them supplied the second object as "ilmaka" (your knowledge), but that is not correct.

Al-A'raj read (فَلا تَصْحَبْنِي) with a fatha on the ta' and the ba' and a shadda on the nun, and the intent is emphasis in the prohibition, meaning: "then do not be my companion at all." This supports the view that the prohibition, where there is no emphasis, means prohibition, and that what is meant by it is firm resolve to leave and part ways, not permission, in the sense of "if I ask you again, you are then permitted to leave my company." ﴿You have indeed reached from my side an excuse﴾ — that is, you have found an excuse from my side. Al-Nawawi said: its meaning is "you have reached the point at which you are excused for parting from me, since I have opposed you time after time."

It is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, that he said: "May Allah have mercy on us and on Musa. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders. But he was seized by embarrassment before his companion, so he said that." Nafi' and Asim read (مِن لَدُنِي) with the nun lightened, and it is a proof against the one who forbids that (s). Most of them hold that he omitted the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) and kept the original nun, kasra-d, according to the analogy for nouns that are annexed, that the nun of protection does not attach to them, as in "watani" and "maqami." It was said: it is possible that the mentioned element is the nun of protection and the annexed word is "lad" without a nun, a dialectal form of "ladun." Thus there is no omission at all. This was challenged on the grounds that the nun of protection occurs only with a word built on sukun, to shield it from kasra, whereas "lad" without nun is built on damma. It was answered that there is no obstacle to saying that the nun protected it from the disappearance of the damma, and that Shu'ba gave the dal a light damma (ishmam) and it was narrated from Asim that he made it sakin. Mujahid said: "It is a gross error." Perhaps he meant a narration; otherwise they have mentioned that "lad" with fatha and sukun is a dialect of "ladun."

Isa read (عُذُرًا) with a damma on the dhal, and it is narrated from Abu Amr and from Ubayy (عُذْرِي) with annexation to the first-person pronoun ya'.

[Page 3]

﴿So they set out, until, when they came to the people of a town﴾. The majority hold that it is Antioch (Antakiyah), and al-Tha'labi reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim related, through Qatadah from him, that it is Barqah. In the *al-Qamus* (the dictionary), it is stated that Barqah is the name of several places. In *al-Mawahib*, it is said that it is a town in the land of the Romans, and Allah knows best. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Suddi that it is Bajarwan. This is also the name of several places, except that some have mentioned that what is meant by it is a town in the regions of Armenia. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Sirin that it is al-Ubullah, with a hamzah, a single b661 ba', and a doubled lam. It has also been said that it is a town on the seashore called Nasirah, from which the Christians (al-Nasara) are named. Al-Tabrisi (in *Majma' al-Bayan*) said: "This is what is narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him." It has also been said that it is a town in al-Jazirah al-Khadra' in the land of al-Andalus. Ibn Hajar said: "The disagreement here is like the disagreement concerning *Majma' al-Bahrayn*, and nothing from it can be relied upon." In a hadith: "They came to the people of a town, miserly (*lu'ama*)." [The phrase] ﴿they asked them for food﴾ (*istat'ama ahlaha*) is in the genitive position as a description of "town." The response of "when" (*idha*) is the later ﴿he said, "If Allah wills"﴾. By this, he followed the same approach as in the second story, making the interjection the main part of the speech, for the reason that Shaykh al-Islam mentioned there. Abu al-Baqa' and others held that it is the response itself, and the later clause is a fresh statement, similar to what is in the first story. The descriptive reading is the one preferred by the researchers, as you will know, if Allah wills. Here there is a well-known question, which al-Salah al-Safadi put into verse and submitted to the Imam Taqi al-Din al-Subki, saying:

*O our master, judge of judges, and one whose face, when it appears, makes the two moons feel shy,*
*And whose hand on the day of generosity, and whose pen on his page, are two seas that meet,*
*And one who, when the issues of difficult matters grow dark, clears them with a mind of ever-shining brilliance.*
*You have seen the Book of Allah as the greatest miracle for the best of those whom the two worlds (humans and jinn) are guided by.*
*And among the aspects of its miraculousness is that its brevity is in concise words while its meanings are expansive.*
*But in the Cave I have seen a verse whose thought has held my reins for a long time:*
*"They asked them for food" (istat'ama ahlaha); yet we see that "they asked them" (istat'amahum) is similar to it in clarity.*
*So what is the splendid wisdom in placing a noun in place of a pronoun? That is indeed a matter of significance.*
*So guide my bewilderment by the customs of your excellence, for I have no means to reach this speech.*

Al-Subki answered that the clause (*istat'ama*) may be in the genitive position as a description of "town," and may be in the accusative position as a description of "people," and may be the response of "when"; there is no other possibility. Whoever reflects will know that the first is definite in meaning, and that the second and third, although the verse permits them, are far from its intended meaning. As for the third, it would entail that the aim is to report the asking for food upon arrival, and that this is the full meaning of the speech; it would also entail that the greater part of their intention, or all of it, is the request for food, although the intention is what your Lord willed of what is recounted after it, and to show Moses, peace be upon him, the wonderful matter. As for the second, it would entail that the concern is with describing the condition of the people in themselves, with the town having no effect on that, while we find the rest of the speech pointing to the town itself. So the first is determined, and in it ﴿they asked them for food﴾ is required, and ﴿they asked them﴾ (*istat'amahum*) is not permitted at all, since the clause would be empty of a pronoun referring to the described noun.

On this basis, it is understood from the whole set of verses that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did what he did in a town whose people were blameworthy, for there had already come from them bad conduct, from the elders, regarding the right of the guest, despite his request. Places have an influence on dispositions. He did not hesitate there, although it was apt for corruption and waste, but rather engaged in reform purely for the sake of obedience. Peace be upon him did not concern himself with the action of its miserly people. To this are added these benefits: the second "people" may be the first, or others, or some of them and some others. It is usual that whoever comes to a town does not find all of its people at once, but his sight first falls on some, then he may survey them. Perhaps when these two righteous servants came, Allah decreed for them the surveying of all of them gradually, so that the completeness of His mercy and His not holding His servants accountable for the bad conduct of some of them might become evident. If it had been said "they asked them," the first group would have been intended specifically. So the noun was used to indicate emphasis on generality in it, and that they did not leave any one of its people without asking him, and he refused. Despite this, they were met with the best recompense. Consider how these secrets are concealed from many commentators behind veils, so that some of them did not address anything at all, some claimed that this was emphasis, and another asserted what is not to be relied upon. I heard about a person who said: "The turning away from *istat'amahum* is because the gathering of two pronouns in one word is heavy." This is a view cited only to be refuted, for the Qur'an and eloquent speech are full of such usage, including what occurs in this verse. Among the completions of what has been mentioned is that if *istat'ama* is taken as a response, it comes after the arrival, whereas if it is taken as a description, it may be that the arrival had happened before this time. It is mentioned for definition and to draw attention to the fact that it did not lead them to refuse arrival for the sake of goodness. This is what Allah opened to me, and poetry falls short of the answer. I have said:

*For the secrets of the verses of the Book there are meanings, subtle, so that they do not appear to every meaning-seeker.*
*In them, for the disciplined, intelligent one, are wonders whose lightning's radiance makes the two moons bow.*
*When a flash from them has appeared to my heart, I have been eager, comforted in eye, to fly.*
*With joy and delight, reaching the heights, as if my place had risen above the Pleiades.*
*So what are kingship and rivals, what are the white swords and the spears, when I have faces that have shone with congratulations?*
*And these are what I have granted you the secret of; so thanks to the one who gave you the excellence of my expression.*
*I see "istat'ama" as a description that applied to a town, though it has no pronoun, and grammar is like a balance.*
*Its craft requires that a concealed element referring back to it is not possible.*
*It is not a response, nor does the people's row (ahluha) allow it, so there is no basis for the pronoun or concealment.*
*These are three, and no other is possible; one of them is determined, and it captivated me.*
*I trained my thought with them until there was churned out from it the cream of ages long past.*
*My life is in the surge of seas of knowledge in my heart, which extends my tongue.*

And he continued enthusiastically in this vein, and there is in it what there is of argument. Some have objected that, on the assumption that the clause is a description of the town, one could use a more concise construction than what has been mentioned, saying: "When they came to a town, they asked its people for food." So what is the reason for mentioning "the people" first on this assumption? It is answered that "the people" was brought in to indicate that they intended the arrival at their town, and they were asked and refused. There is no doubt that this is more eloquent in stinginess and further from any good being done toward any of them, so that what came from al-Khidr, peace be upon him, becomes exceedingly strange. It cannot be said: "Let the construction be so, and let the people be understood by implication or metaphor, as in His saying, ﴿and ask the town﴾," because we say: arrival is attributed to a place, as in "I came to Arafat," and to those in it, as in "I came to the people of Baghdad." So if it were not mentioned, it would defeat the intended meaning. This is not like what is mentioned in the verse, because it is not customary to ask the town itself.

Shaykh Izz al-Din 'Ali al-Mawsili, in answering al-Safadi, preferred that the repetition of "the people," and the turning away from *istat'amahum* to *istat'ama ahlaha*, is for belittlement. This is one of the purposes of placing a noun in place of a pronoun. He elaborated on this in prose, and said in verse:

*I asked why "istat'ama ahlaha" came instead of "istat'amahum," though that is indeed a matter of significance.*
*In it there is brevity, not found there, and you have not stood upon the reason for its preference since a long time.*
*So take an answer lifting its veil, by which the meaning becomes like an eyewitness opinion.*
*When the two states are equal in the ruling, the pronoun is preferred; but when the two differ,*
*such that in the explicit statement there is the showing of a wisdom, like the elevation of rank or the lowliness of a wrongdoer,*
*like the Commander of the Faithful saying "this," and what we are discussing, they have declared with security.*
*This came in brevity and expansion in my answer, in prose, with the beauty of expression.*

In prose he mentioned another reason for the turning away, which is what al-Subki transmitted and refuted. Al-Nisaburi also mentioned it, and by my life, it is as al-Subki said. It returns to what has been mentioned, that the noun is for belittlement. The statement of some researchers that it is for emphasis, its intended purpose being an increase in censure, is a sound view for every discerning person. An example of this is His saying, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong﴾, and the verse goes on. Similar examples are numerous in eloquent speech. Some said: "The two people are different, so they were brought together." And the saying of some: "When the previously mentioned noun is repeated as a definite, the second is the same as the first" is not a consistent rule. This is because the intended meaning of the first "people" is some of them, since at the beginning of entering the town it is not ordinarily possible to come upon all of its people, especially according to what is related, that their entry was before sunset. And the intended meaning of the second "people" is all of them, because it is reported that they, peace be upon them both, were walking through the gatherings of those people, asking them for food. If the pronoun had been used, it would have been understood that they asked only some of them. Some reversed the matter and said: The intended meaning of the first "people" is all of them, and the meaning of arriving at them is reaching them and settling among them, similar to arriving at a country, which clearly means reaching a part of it and settling in it. The intended meaning of the second "people" is some of them, because asking every single individual among the elders and young, males and females, rich and poor of the town is highly unlikely, and the report does not indicate it. Perhaps it is evident that they asked the men. It has been narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and Allah knows best the soundness of the report, that he said: "A woman from the Berbers fed them after they had asked the men, and the men did not feed them. So they prayed for their women and cursed their men. For this reason the noun was used instead of the pronoun." Something similar is reported from Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, in *al-Risalah*.

It is objected against these two views that they contradict what is customary in repeating the first mention as a definite. And against the second, that the difference mentioned in it has no benefit worth considering. This objection does not apply to the first, because the benefit of the difference mentioned in it is an increase in censure upon the people of the town, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 77 (part 2 of 2):

Some scholars, preferring the view of emphasis (ta'kid), held that by "the people" (al-ahl) in both places is meant those whose outward condition gives reason to expect that the purpose will be achieved from them, and that despair of obtaining it from others arises from despair of obtaining it from them: namely, the residents who were settled and established in the village. Whoever does not take custom into account says that the two of them, peace be upon them, went to everyone and asked them, because, as is said, they were in need. ﴿But they refused to entertain them﴾ (fa-aba an yudayyifuhuma), with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Razin, Abu Muhsin, 'Asim in the transmission of al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it without doubling (takhfif), from the verb of hospitality (al-idafah). One says dayafahu when he has become his guest, and adafahu and dayyafahu when he housed him and made him a guest. The root meaning of dafa is "to incline," as in "the arrow deviated (dafa al-sahm) from the target" (yadifu), and one says "the sun declined (adafat al-shams) toward setting," and "it inclined (tadayyafat)" if it leaned. Its counterpart is zarrahu, from al-izwirar (turning aside). The expression "refused" (al-iba') carries an indication of the great baseness of the people, for, as al-Raghib said, it is the intensity of refusal. For this reason it did not say "they did not entertain them" (fa-lam yudayyifuhuma), even though that is shorter, since it falls short of what is in the sublime wording in indicating their blame. Perhaps that request for food (al-istita'am) was a request for food by way of hospitality, such that they may have said: "We are strangers, so entertain us," or something similar, as the expression of God Most High, ﴿they refused to entertain them﴾, indicates, rather than "they refused to feed them," although the apparent sense of ﴿they asked them for food﴾ requires the latter. He said "asked them for food" rather than "asked them for hospitality" only to indicate that the main aim of the two was food, not inclining toward a dwelling or seeking shelter in a place.

Some have mentioned that ﴿they refused to entertain them﴾ contains a condemnation that "they refused to feed them" does not, because a generous person may turn away a beggar who asks for food without being blamed, as when he turns away a stranger he is asked to host. Rather, one hardly turns away a guest except a miser. Among the greatest insults of the Arabs is the saying, "So-and-so drives away the guest." It is reported from Qatadah: "The worst of villages is the one where the guest is not entertained and the traveler's right is not recognized."

Zayn al-Din al-Mawsili said: God, glory be to Him, specified asking for food for Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them, and entertaining for the people, because asking for food is the role of the one who asks, and entertaining is the role of the one who is asked, since custom requires this; so the resident calls the newcomer to his home, asks him, and brings him there. End of quote. And this, as you see, is not sound. Among things that sensible people laugh at is what al-Nisaburi and others transmitted: "When the people of that village heard the revelation of this verse, they were ashamed and came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a load of gold and said: 'O Messenger of God, we will pay this gold so that you change the ba' in (aba) into ta'.' But he (ﷺ) refused." Some relate that this story occurred in the time of 'Ali, may God honor his face, but there is no basis for any of this. Even if it were sound, it would show the weakness of the intellect of the people of the village in Islam, just as their baseness is known from the Qur'an and the Sunnah beforehand.

﴿So they found﴾ (fa-wajada) is conjoined (ma'tuf), as al-Subki said, to ﴿a wall in it﴾. It is reported that they came to it when they found no shelter, and their night was a cold night, and it was on the edge of the road. ﴿It wanted to collapse﴾, meaning to fall. Its past tense is inqadda, on the pattern infa'ala like injarra, and the nun is an augment, because it derives from qadadtuhu in the sense of "I broke it." But since what is broken falls down, inqidad was said to mean falling. The well-known meaning is falling rapidly, like the swooping of a star or a bird. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is from al-qadda, which means small pebbles, and from it comes ta'am qadad, meaning food containing pebbles. On this meaning, it means "it wants to crumble and become pebbles." End of quote.

Abu 'Ali mentioned in al-Idah that its pattern is af'ala from al-naqd (breaking down), like ahmar. Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd: this is an error, and the verification of that belongs elsewhere. The nun, on this view, is original (asliyyah), and the meaning of the wall's "wanting to fall" is that it is near collapse, either by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) with the relation of causation, where the wanting of falling is the cause of nearness, or by way of metaphor (isti'arah), by likening the nearness of falling to willing because of the inclination found in both. It may also be considered that the statement contains a metaphor that is both implicit (makniyyah) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah). It is frequent in their speech to attribute to non-rational things actions that belong to rational beings. Among that is the verse:

"The spear seeks the chest of Abu Bara'
and turns aside from the blood of the Banu 'Uqayl."

And the words of Hassan, may God be pleased with him:

"Indeed, a time that gathers my scattered affairs in a single heap
is a time that intends goodness."

And the words of another:

"The buttocks and the breasts refused, in their garments,
to touch the bellies, and to touch the backs."

And the words of Abu Nuwas:

"He made the lute speak, though its silence had lasted long;
pleasure does not speak until the lute speaks."

And many other examples, to the point that it has been said that whoever has even slight acquaintance with the speech of the Arabs does not need a witness for this point. Some scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) transmitted from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Isbahani that he denies the occurrence of metaphor in the Qur'an, and so he interprets the verse by saying that the pronoun in "wants" refers to al-Khidr or to Musa, peace be upon them. It was also allowed that the subject is the wall, and that God created in it life and will. All of these are artificial and forced interpretations, by which the eloquence of the speech is diminished.

Abu Hayyan said: perhaps the transmission from this man is not sound, for how could he say that, when he is one of the eminent, proficient poets who excelled in verse and prose? Ubayy read (yunqadu) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the qaf and the dad, in the passive voice. In the codex of 'Abdullah and in the reading of al-A'mash, it is (yuridu li-yanqadda), likewise, except that it is in the subjunctive, governed by the implied an after the lam.

'Ali, may God honor his face, 'Ikrimah, Khulayd ibn Sa'd, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (yanqas) with the unpointed sad and an alif. Its pattern is yanfa'il, the intransitive of qastuhu, so infas means when you break it and it breaks. Ibn Khalawayh said: the Arabs say "the tooth split (ansaqat al-sinn)" if it split lengthwise. Dhu al-Rummah, describing a wild bull, said:

"He covers the thicket with his two horns and tears it down,
out of the great sand, a split one and one that is bent."

In al-Sihah: qays al-sinn is its falling out from its root. And he cited the words of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"A separation like the falling of a tooth; so patience,
for indeed it is for every person a stumble and a joy."

Al-Umawi said: "insaqat al-barr" means it collapsed. Al-Asma'i said: al-munqas is that which is uprooted, and al-munqad with the pointed dad is that which splits lengthwise. Abu 'Amr said: the two have one meaning. Al-Zuhri read (yanqad) with an alif and a dad with a dot. The well-known explanation is "it collapses."

Abu 'Ali mentioned that the well-known reading from al-Zuhri is (yanqas) with the unpointed letter.
