﴿So he set it up﴾ (fa-aqamahu): he wiped it with his hand, and it stood, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Qurtubi said that this is the sound view, and it is more fitting to the circumstances of the prophets, peace be upon them. It was objected that this is not appropriate to what follows, for one does not deserve a wage for such an act. It was answered that the lack of deserving a wage, given that the purpose was achieved, is not granted, and that its ease for the doer does not harm it. It was also said: he set it up with a pillar that he propped it with. Muqatil said: he leveled it with plaster. It was also said: he demolished it and sat down to rebuild it.

Ibn al-Anbari transmitted in al-Masahif from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he read: "They found in it a wall wanting to collapse, so he demolished it, then sat down to rebuild it."

The height of this wall up to the sky, according to what al-Nawawi transmitted from Wahb ibn Munabbih, was a hundred cubits. Al-Suffayri transmitted from al-Tha'labi that its thickness was two hundred cubits by the cubit of that village, and its length over the surface of the earth was five hundred cubits, and its width was fifty cubits, and people used to pass beneath it in fear of it.

﴿Musa said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ This is an exhortation to al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and an urging to take a reward and wage for what he did, so that by it they would both gain sustenance and strength for their livelihood. It is therefore a question to him: why did you not take the wage? And an objection to his leaving off taking it. So the meaning is the necessary implication of the benefit of the report, since there is no benefit in reporting his action. It was also said: he did not say this as an urging, but said it by way of allusion (ta'rid), that his action was superfluous and a voluntary act done without being requested, and without benefit or entitlement for the one for whom it was done, while he was in complete need of the opposite. When the Speaker, peace be upon him, saw deprivation, the touch of need, and occupation with what does not matter, he could not restrain his patience, so he objected.

"Ittakhadha" is of the pattern ifta'ala. The first ta' is original, and the second is the ta' of ifti'al, into which the first was assimilated. Its root is takhadha, not akhadha, even though it has the same meaning, because the first radical of a word is not changed when it is a hamza or a ya' that has been changed from one. For this reason it was said that "iytazara" is an error or irregular, and this is common in eloquent speech. Also, if its change in ifti'al were granted, it would not account for the form takhidha, and this is the view of the Basrans. Others said that ittikhadh is ifti'al from akhadha, and this does not stand as stated above, and they say that the lengthened vowel that arises is also changed to ta'. Because of its frequent use here, they treated it as though it were original, and said takhidha is triliteral, following it, just as they said taqiya from ittaqa.

'Abdullah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Bihuriyya, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Yazidi, Ya'qub, Abu Hatim, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read (la-ttakhadhta) with an open ta' and a kasra on the kha', meaning la-akhadhta ("you would have taken"). Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub, and Hafs made the dhal clear, and the remaining seven idghamed it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 78:

﴿He said﴾ al-Khidr, peace be upon him, ﴿"This is the parting between me and you"﴾ — with the idafa of the verbal noun (masdar) to the adverb of place (zarf) in a broadened usage (ittisa'an). Ibn al-Hajib makes the idafa in such a case carry the sense of "in" (fi). What is useful for you here has already been discussed, so reflect on it.

Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿firaqu bayni﴾ with tanwin and the accusative of bayn as an adverb of place (zarfiyyah). Bayn is repeated, even though it is not normally made to govern a plural, because it cannot be conjoined to a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition. Abu Hayyan said: The departure from "baynina" (between us) serves emphasis and points to the parting that is implied by His words earlier, ﴿So do not accompany me﴾, and the predication (haml) is meaningful, because the subject spoken of is the parting considered as existing in the mind, and the predicate is the parting considered as existing in external reality, as has been said. Or [the demonstrative refers] to the present time, meaning: this time is the time of our parting. Or [it refers] to the third objection, meaning: this objection is the cause of our parting, just as you requested. The reason for specifying the parting with the third objection is evident.

The first scholar (al-'Allamah al-Awwal) said: This was the cause of the parting rather than the first two, because the apparent meaning of those two was objectionable, so Musa was excused, unlike this one, for he does not object to doing good to the one who does evil but rather praises it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, regarding its reason, that Musa's words about the ship and the boy were for the sake of Allah, while in this case they were for his own self, seeking worldly gain, and so it was the cause of the parting. al-Qushayri related something similar from some of them. In al-Kashf it was rejected on the grounds that it is not befitting to their dignity, and perhaps the report from the rabbi is not authentic. It is transmitted in al-Bahr from the masters of meanings that these events which occurred to Musa with al-Khidr were a proof against Musa, peace be upon him. When he denied the piercing of the ship, he was called: "O Musa, where was this management of yours while you were cast adrift in the chest on the river?" When he denied the killing of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this, and your striking of the Copt and the judgment against him?" When he denied the rebuilding of the wall, he was called: "Where is this from your lifting the stone for the two daughters of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, without a wage?" I have seen in some books that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, said: "O Musa, you objected to me over the piercing of the ship, while you yourself threw down the tablets of the Torah so that they broke; you objected to me over the killing of the boy, while you yourself struck the Copt so that he was judged against; and you objected to me over the rebuilding of the wall without a wage, while you yourself watered the flocks of the two daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage. So whoever does the like of what you did will not object to me." The apparent meaning is that none of this is sound, and the difference is clear between what came from Musa, peace be upon him, and what came from al-Khidr, and he is too exalted to argue against the bearer of the Torah with such things, as is not hidden.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman and Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu 'Abd Allah, and I think he is al-Multi, who said: When al-Khidr wished to part from Musa, he said to him: "Advise me." He said: "Be beneficial and do not be harmful; be cheerful and do not be angry; withdraw from contentiousness; do not walk without need; do not reproach anyone for his sin; and weep over your own sin, O son of 'Imran." Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir related from Yusuf ibn Asbat, who said: It reached me that al-Khidr said to Musa when he wished to part from him: "O Musa, learn knowledge in order to act upon it, and do not teach it in order to be talked about." It reached me that Musa said to al-Khidr: "Pray for me." Al-Khidr said: "May Allah make His obedience easy for you." And Allah knows best about the soundness of this as well.

﴿I will inform you﴾ — Ibn Abi Wathhab read ﴿sa-unbiyuka﴾ with the yа sincerely pronounced without hamza, and the sin (sa) is for emphasis, since the informing is not delayed; that is, I will certainly inform you ﴿of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾. The apparent meaning is that this was not at Musa's request, peace be upon him. It has been said that when al-Khidr resolved to part from him, he seized his garments and said: "I will not part from you until you inform me of what permitted you to do what you did and what called you to it," and so he said ﴿I will inform you﴾. Ta'wil means returning a thing to its end, and what is meant here is the outcome and consequence, since that is what is informed about, not ta'wil in the sense mentioned. "Ma" refers to the actions issued by al-Khidr, peace be upon him, namely the piercing of the ship, the killing of the boy, and the rebuilding of the wall; and their outcome was the deliverance of the ship from the usurping hand, the deliverance of the boy's parents from his evil, together with the better replacement, and the extraction of the two orphans' treasure. In making the relative clause express Musa's inability to be patient, rather than saying "by the interpretation of what you did" or "of what you saw" and the like, there is a kind of allusion and rebuke directed at him, peace be upon him. It may also be said that this was to solicit greater attentiveness and readiness on his part to receive what would be conveyed to him. ﴿Patience﴾ is the object of ﴿could not hold﴾, and ﴿over it﴾ is connected to it; it was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fasilah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 79:

﴿As for the boat﴾, which he damaged, ﴿it belonged to poor people﴾, weak folk who could not defend themselves against the oppressors. The plural *masakin* (the needy, the poor; the singular *miskin* is pronounced with either a kasra or a fatha on the mim) also has the plurals *masakin* and *miskinun*. It means one who is weak and incapable, and this meaning includes one whose incapacity stems from a condition of the soul or the body. For this reason it has been said that they were called *masakin* because of their disability. They were ten, five of whom were disabled (*zamna*, chronically ill or handicapped). Applying the term *masakin* to all of them on this basis is an instance of *al-taghlib* (the figure of speech in which the term for the majority is used to cover the whole group).

This sense of *miskin* is different from the one over which the jurists have differed concerning the distinction between the *miskin* and the *faqir* (the poor). Accordingly, the verse is not a proof for those who say that the *miskin* is one who possesses something but not enough to suffice him, because in this sense the consideration of whether he has wealth or not is set aside.

It may also be interpreted as "the needy" (*al-muhtaj*), and in that case the verse clearly supports what the aforementioned speaker claims. Those who say that the *miskin* is one who has nothing at all, and that this is the *faqir* according to the first view, claim that the boat was not their property but that they were hired workers (*ujara'*) on it. It has also been said that they had it as a loan (*ariyya*) and that the *lam* (in *lahum*) indicates specific association (*lam al-ikhtisas*), not ownership. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning and is not accepted without evidence. It has also been said that they were treated as though they had nothing at all, and that they were called *masakin* out of compassion.

Ali, may God honour his face, recited *li-masakkin* (with a shadda on the sin) as the plural of *massak*. It has been said that the meaning is *mallahin* (sailors). It has also been said that the *massak* is one who holds the rudder (or the leg) of the boat, and that they took turns at this. It has further been said that the *masakun* are tanners of hides (*musuk*, singular *misk*). The meaning of sailors is probably the most apparent.

﴿who work on the sea﴾, that is, they work with it on the sea and make their living from what it brings them. The attribution of the work to all of them is either on the basis that some of them were disabled, by way of *taghlib*, or because the work of agents is equivalent to the work of those who appointed them.

﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, that is, to make it defective by puncturing it, and I did not intend to drown its people, as you supposed. The word "wished" was used to express this meaning, and the phrase "I made it defective" was not used. This shows that the *lam* in *li-a'iba* (the *lam* of purpose) is causal, and to take it in the sense of consequence requires departing from the apparent meaning here, as is not hidden from the careful reader.

﴿And behind them was a king﴾, that is, in front of them. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Abu Ubayda, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Zajjaj also read it this way. The usage of *wara'* (behind; also used for in front) is found in the verse of Labid:

*Is there not, behind me, if my death is delayed, the staff that the fingers bend upon?*

And in the verse of Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrib al-Sa'di:

*Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people, Tamim, and the wilderness are behind me?*

And in the verse of another:

*Is there not, behind me, that I totter upon a staff, so that my enemies feel safe and my family becomes weary of me?*

It is also found in the Qur'an in many places. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that *wara'* can mean "in front of," but they differ regarding other meanings. Most of them hold that it is a genuine meaning which may be intended in any context, and they said it is one of the words with contrary meanings (*al-adad*). The apparent view of some is that it has one single meaning which covers both opposites. Ibn al-Kamal, quoting al-Zamakhshari, said that it is a name for the direction which a person conceals from behind or in front. Al-Baydawi said, in summary, that it is originally the verbal noun of *wara* (yari') like *qada* (yaqdi), and when it is annexed to the subject (*fa'il*) it means the object (*maf'ul*), namely the concealed, which is what is behind; and when it is annexed to the object it means the subject, namely the concealer, which is what is in front.

This was refuted by the verse ﴿Return behind you﴾, where *wara'* is annexed to the object and the intended meaning is "behind."

Al-Farra' said: it is not permissible to say of a man, "He is behind you" when he is in front of you, and likewise with all bodies. It is only permissible in reference to the times of nights and days. Abu Ali said: the use of *wara'* in the sense of "in front" is by extension (*ittisa'*), because it is a direction opposite to another direction, so each of the two directions is "behind" the other when the meaning of facing is not intended. This is permissible with bodies that have no face, such as two stones facing each other, each of which is behind the other.

It has also been said that *wara'* here means "behind them," as is the well-known meaning of *wara'*.

It has been objected that if he was behind them, then they had escaped from him. It is answered that the intended meaning is that he was behind them, overtaking them and passing by them; or that their return would be upon him. His name, as they claim, was Hadad ibn Bidad, and he was an unbeliever. It has been said that he was Jalandi ibn Karkar, king of Ghassan. It has also been said that he was Mifwad ibn al-Jalandi ibn Sa'id al-Azdi, and that he was in the island of al-Andalus.

﴿who seizes every boat﴾, that is, every sound one. Ubayy ibn Ka'b also recited it this way. If the generality were kept on its apparent sense, there would be no benefit in the act of damaging it.

﴿by force﴾ from its owners. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) explaining the type of seizing. The apparent meaning is that he used to seize boats from their owners and then not return them. It has been said that he would commandeer them and then return them.

The *fa'* in *fa-aradtu* (so I wished) is for consequence (*tafri'*), and it indicates that the reason for the intention to damage was that the boat belonged to poor, incapable people. But since the connection between this cause and its effect was hidden, it was clarified by mention of the king's custom of seizing boats. The meaning comes to this: as for the boat, it belonged to poor, incapable people who earned their living by it, so by what I did I intended to help them against what they feared and could not repel: the force of a king behind them whose custom is to seize sound boats.

Some have said that the cause is the combination of the two matters, poverty and seizure, except that the *fa'* of consequence was placed between the two matters. The apparent arrangement would have been to place it after both, for the sake of the goal: since that act was the reprehensible thing which needed explanation of its interpretation; and to signal that the stronger of the two in causation is the first matter. For this reason he did not care about rescuing the boats of others, although the last part of the cause was present. And because placing it later would have separated the boat from its pronoun, with the possibility of the pronoun referring to the nearer noun. So let this be understood.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Moses, peace be upon him, did not know the interpretation of this act beforehand.

What is reported from al-Rabi' is problematic for this: that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, after he had damaged the boat and it was saved from the unjust king, came to its owners and said: "I only intended what is better for you." They praised his opinion, and he repaired it for them as it had been. This clearly indicates that he, peace be upon him, made them understand the reality of the matter. And it is apparent that Moses, peace be upon him, was present and heard that. It may be said that this report is not to be relied upon, and that the possibility of its authenticity together with Moses, peace be upon him, not hearing it is not something to be considered.

[p. 10]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 80:**

﴿As for the boy﴾, who he killed, ﴿his parents were﴾, meaning his father and his mother. The masculine is used to cover both (taghlib). The word for "father" is used here, as in al-Itqan (al-Suyuti's book), "ka'zīr" (كَأْزِيرُ), while "mother" is included by oversight. In the Codex of Ubayy and the reading of Ibn Abbas, it reads: (﴿As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his parents were believers﴾). The meaning on that reading, according to the reading of the Seven, is the same, except that he omitted an explicit statement of his disbelief, indicating that there is no need to mention it because it is evident. Whoever held that the boy was an adult used that reading as evidence, because a child is not described as truly disbelieving or believing. Al-Nawawi answered this in two ways. The first is that the reading is irregular (shādhdha) and cannot be used as evidence. The second is that he was called by what he would become had he lived. In Sahih Muslim, it is reported that the boy was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever, and this was interpreted in a similar way. The same applies to the report mentioned earlier about the man of the wedding and the brides. However, I have reservations about its soundness, because on its surface it may imply Moses's knowledge of the interpretation of the killing before parting. According to the interpretation I have heard, nothing mentioned here applies to the preferred view regarding children, namely that they are in Paradise absolutely. Moreover, it has been said that the discussion concerns only someone whom the Truthful One (the Prophet ﷺ) informed was a disbeliever. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Jahdari read: (﴿fa-kāna abawāhu mu'minān﴾, "and his parents were believers"). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi explained it as the dummy pronoun (ḍamīr al-sha'n), with the clause in the position of its predicate. Abu al-Fadl permitted that mu'minān be in the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, in which case it would be in the accusative. He also permitted that the pronoun in kāna refer to "the boy", with the clause in the position of its predicate.

﴿So we feared that he would overburden them﴾, meaning we feared greatly that he would cover over the two believing parents if he remained alive, ﴿with rebellion﴾, transgressing the divine limits, ﴿and disbelief﴾ in God, the Exalted. This would happen by his love leading them to follow him, as is narrated from Ibn Jubayr. Perhaps the conjunction of disbelief with rebellion is to make the matter more terrible. Perhaps the mention of rebellion, although the apparent context is limited to disbelief, is so that this horror may be realized; or the meaning may be: we feared he would defile their faith at first and remove it at last. On this view, it is necessarily more hideous and abominable than its removal without a prior defilement. Some commentators on al-Bukhari explained "fear" as "knowledge", saying: that is, we knew that if he came of age and reached maturity, he would call his parents to disbelief, and they would answer him and enter his religion because of their excessive love for him. It has also been said: the meaning is that we feared he would cover them with rebellion against them and disbelief in their blessing upon him, through his raising them and their being the cause of his existence, because of his disobedience and bad conduct, so that evil and affliction would befall them. It has also been said: the meaning is that we feared he would cover them and join his rebellion and disbelief to their faith, so that two believers and a rebellious disbeliever would be in one house. In some reports, the boy used to corrupt, and in one narration he used to commit highway robbery and swear to his parents that he had not done it, so they would swear to his oath and protect him from whoever sought him. Whoever held that he was an adult used this as evidence, while the one who holds that he was a child says this is not sound, and perhaps the truth is with him. Apparently, this is from the words of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, which he gave in reply to Moses, peace be upon him, on his behalf. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that this is a report of the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, and that the intended meaning is "He wanted", with the fear being a metonymy (majāz mursal) for its concomitant, which is dislike, as has been said. In al-Kashf it says: this is because the place of address is one: Moses, peace be upon him, asked from Him, Exalted, and al-Khidr, peace be upon him, by God's permission, answered on His behalf, and in that there is subtlety. But the apparent meaning is the first. It has been said: on this possibility, it is with the supposition: "God said: we feared", and the "fa" is from the narration. This is also far-fetched, and this possibility hardly fits the verse afterwards, unless the expression by the apparent in it is considered a shift of person (iltifāt). In the Codex of Abdullah and the reading of Ubayy: (﴿fa-khāfa rabbuka﴾, "so your Lord feared"). The interpretation is what you have heard.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: fear and dread, like the expression of hope with "la'alla" and similar words occurring in the speech of God, are directed to the addressees; otherwise God, may His majesty be exalted, is far above all of that.

Page 11

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 81:

﴿So We intended that their Lord should replace for them one better than him﴾ by granting them, in his place, a son better than him ﴿in purity﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, in religion (dinan). This is an explanation by way of what necessarily follows (tafsir bil-lazim), and the majority of scholars said: in purity from sins and bad character traits. The mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) and the attribution of the two to Him (i.e., "their Lord") carries an indication, which is not hidden, of the intention that good should reach them. ﴿And nearer in mercy﴾, that is, in compassion (rahmatan). Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

O You who sent down mercy (al-ruhm) upon Idris, and sent down the curse upon Iblis.

Both (ruhm and rahmah) are verbal nouns (masdar), like al-kathr and al-kathrah. The intended meaning is "nearer in compassion toward them and kinder to them." Abu Hayyan preferred this reading. Perhaps its basis is the frequent use of the verbal noun in the active sense, together with what this carries here of agreeing with the verbal noun preceding it. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Atiyyah that the meaning is: "they are more merciful to him than they are to the boy." Perhaps the intended meaning according to this view is that he was more beloved to them than that boy, either because of the increase in the goodness of his character, or his character, or both together. This meaning is closer to giving new information (ta'sis) than the first meaning, given the interpretation of the element it is coordinated with as explained above. However, what supports this interpretation is what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: that they exchanged him for a girl who gave birth to a prophet. Al-Tha'labi said: she reached Yunus ibn Matta, and a prophet among the prophets married her, and she gave birth to a prophet through whose hand God guided a nation among the nations. In a narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from Yusuf ibn 'Umar, she gave birth to two prophets. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas and Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with them both, she gave birth to seventy prophets. Ibn 'Atiyyah considered this unlikely and said: the multiplicity of prophets (peace be upon them) is not known except among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not of them. There is clear room for objection to this. The basis of the support is that a girl, by custom, loves her parents, shows them mercy, inclines toward them, and is kinder to them more than a boy is. It was said: He replaced them with a believing boy like them. The two masdars are in the accusative as specifications (tamyiz), and the governing element of each is the word before it, the comparative adjectives (af'al al-tafdil). It is not hidden what subtlety there is in first mentioning the ambiguity and then the clarification, which is why he did not say: "So We intended that their Lord should replace for them one purer than him and more merciful," since in "khayr" (better) with "zakah" there is a praise that is not in "azka," as becomes clear upon sincere reflection.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that af'al is not here for comparison, because there is no purity in that boy nor mercy. It was objected to that he was pure and clean from sins in fact if he was a child, and according to outward appearance if he was an adult; therefore Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿a pure soul﴾ (nafsan zakiyyah), and this is in contrast to him; so the better is the purity of one who is pure in the present and the future, according to outward appearance and inward reality. Even if it is granted, the hypothetical sharing (al-ishtirak al-taqdiri) suffices for the validity of the comparison. As for his saying "nor mercy," it is a claim without evidence, end of quote.

Al-Khafaji said: The correct answer here is to be content with hypothetical sharing, because al-Khidr, peace be upon him, knew the inward reality; he knows that there is no purity in it nor mercy. So his saying that there is no evidence for it has no basis. You know that mercy, on the second interpretation, is something whose negation is not valid, because it is the basis of fear (of God), so understand. The apparent reading is that the fa' is for consequence, so it indicates that fear is the cause of the aforementioned intention, and it is understood from the consequence of the killing, though he did not state the killing itself explicitly, although it is the intended object of interpretation, relying on its being clearly understood from this sentence in the most subtle way. In it there is also an indication of rejecting what the words of Musa, peace be upon him, hint at, that his killing was injustice and corruption on the earth.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Humayd, al-A'mash and Ibn Jarir read (yubaddilahuma) with the doubled consonant (tashdid).

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far in one transmission, Ya'qub and Abu Hatim read (ruhman) with a damma on the ha'. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, read (rahman) with a fatha on the ra' and a kasra on the ha'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 82 (part 1 of 5):

﴿As for the wall﴾, the one previously mentioned, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys﴾. It has been said that they were Asram and Sarim. ﴿Young ones﴾: their father had died, and this is the apparent meaning, because orphanhood among the children of Adam is by the death of the father. There is a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that they were both adults, and the description of them by this term is in view of what they had been, in terms of compassion for them. It is very far-fetched, as is clear. ﴿In the city﴾: this is the village mentioned earlier. Perhaps the reference to it here as a "city" is to show a kind of regard for it, given the orphans in it and the one who was from its people, namely their righteous father. Since the flow of the preceding speech was not in this manner, it referred to it there as a "village."

﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: wealth buried in gold and silver, as al-Bukhari recorded in his History, and al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'. Ikrimah and Qatadah said the same. The word (kanz, treasure) is originally a verbal noun, then it is used to mean the object (ism al-maf'ul).

Page 13

Al-Raghib said: "Kanz" is placing some wealth upon other wealth and preserving it, and its origin is from "kanaztu al-tamr fi al-wi'a" (I stored the dates in the container). An objection has been raised to explaining "treasure" in this way: the apparent meaning is that the one who hoarded it was their father, since the wording "belonging to them" implies that it belonged to them; so it would only be theirs if it was an inheritance, or if they had themselves extracted it, and the second is ruled out, so the first is determined. And he (the father) was described as righteous. This conflicts with what has come in condemnation of the hoarder. It is answered that what is condemned is wealth from which rights have not been paid; indeed, it is not called "kanz" in the sharia sense for what has had its dues paid, as is indicated by the hadith held by those who uphold the argument from implication (mafhum): "Every wealth whose zakat is not paid is a treasure." The Prophet (ﷺ) was concerned with explaining the legal rulings, not linguistic meanings, since the latter are known to the addressees, and nothing of extraction or its absence is required in its linguistic meaning intended here. The description as righteous is evidence that it was not of the blameworthy kind of treasure. As for the one who said that "treasure" is prohibited absolutely, he claimed that it was not so in the law of those before us, and argued for it with what al-Tabarani narrated from Abu al-Darda' regarding this verse, that he said: "Treasures were permitted for them and spoils were forbidden to them, while spoils were permitted for us and treasures were forbidden to us."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah something similar, and in it: "So let not a man marvel and say: What of the treasure, which was lawful for those before us and is forbidden to us? For Allah, exalted is He, makes lawful from His command what He wills and forbids what He wills, and these are the sunnahs and obligations: they are lawful for one nation and forbidden to another." Al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It was not gold or silver, but pages of knowledge." This was also related from Ibn Jubayr. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), in a marfu' report, and al-Bazzar from Abu Dharr similarly, and al-Kharaiti from Ibn 'Abbas as a mawquf report, that it was a tablet of gold on which was written: "I marvel at the one who believes in destiny, how he grieves; I marvel at the one who believes in provision, how he toils; I marvel at the one who believes in death, how he rejoices; I marvel at the one who believes in reckoning, how he is heedless; I marvel at the one who knows the world and its turning with its people, how he is content with it. There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

In the narration of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, it is written on one of its two sides: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I marvel..." etc. On the other side: "I am Allah; there is no god but Me, alone, without partner. I created good and evil, so blessed is the one whom I created for good and whose hands I have made to accomplish it, and woe to the one whom I created for evil and whose hands I have made to accomplish it."

Some have reconciled by saying that the intended meaning of "treasure" encompasses all of these, based on the view that it is wealth buried in general, and each of the mentioned items was wealth that had been buried, but in each of the narrations only one of them was mentioned. In this there is that, despite its remoteness, it is contradicted by the apparent meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's words (may Allah be pleased with them both): "It was not gold or silver."

﴿And their father was righteous﴾: the apparent meaning is that he was the nearest father who begot them. It is mentioned that his name was Kashih and the name of their mother was Dahna. It has been said that he was the tenth father, and from Ja'far al-Sadiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was the seventh father.

Whichever it was, the verse indicates that the righteousness of fathers brings care for their children. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Khaythamah that he said: "'Isa (peace be upon him) said: Blessed are the descendants of the believer; then blessed are they, how they are protected after him." Khaythamah recited this verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Wahb that he said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, protects by the righteous servant a tribe of people." And from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said to one of the Kharijites in a discussion that took place between them: "By what did Allah, exalted is He, preserve the wealth of the two boys?"

He said: "By the righteousness of their father." He said: "My father and my grandfather are better than him." The Kharijite said: "Allah, exalted is He, has informed us: 'Indeed you are a contentious people.'" It was mentioned of the righteousness of this man that people would deposit their trusts with him, and he would return them to them as they had deposited them.

It is also narrated that he was a swimmer.

﴿So your Lord intended﴾, your Owner and the manager of your affairs. In the attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun of Musa (peace be upon him) rather than their pronoun, there is an alert to him regarding the necessity of complete submission and surrender to His will, and the obligation of avoiding dispute over what occurred in accordance with them, from which is perceived the seeking of what achieves the upbringing and management of the body.

Page 14

﴿That they reach their maturity﴾. It was said: that is, puberty and perfection of judgment. In al-Sihah: strength, which is what is between eighteen and thirty. It is a singular form that is in the pattern of a plural, like "anukka," and there is no parallel to them. It is said: it is a plural with no singular from its own form, like "asal," "ababil," "'abadid," and "madhakir." Sibawayh used to say: its singular is "shuddah," and this is good in meaning, because it is said "the boy reached his shiddah (full strength)," but "fa'lah" is not pluralized as "af'al." As for "an'um," it is the plural of "na'am," from their saying: "a day of misery (ba's) and a day of ease (na'am)." As for the statement of one who said: its singular is "shadd," like "kalb" and "aklub," or "shidd," like "dhi'b" and "adhu'ub," this is merely analogy, as they say concerning the singular of "ababil": "abbul," by analogy with "ujul," and it is not something heard from the Arabs.

﴿And they extract their treasure﴾ from beneath the wall. Had I not set it up, it would have collapsed, and the treasure would have come out from beneath it before they were able to safeguard it and benefit from it. They mentioned that the two orphans were unaware of the treasure, and they had a guardian who knew of it, but he was absent, and the wall had nearly fallen; so if it had collapsed it would have been lost. For this reason he set it up. ﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾: an object of purpose for "intended," and the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. It is not an object of purpose for "they extract," because the subjects differ. Some permitted that, since the condition of unity of subject is not stipulated, or by making the verbal noun from the passive form. It was also permitted that the accusative be a circumstantial state, from the pronoun of "they extract," in the sense of "being shown mercy." Al-Zamakhshari (held) the accusative to be an absolute object of "intended," since the intending of that is a mercy from Him, exalted is He.

It was objected: if "your Lord intended" means "had mercy," then mercy is necessarily from the Lord, so what is the benefit of mentioning "from your Lord"? The same applies if it is an object of purpose. It was said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is "I did what I did as a mercy from your Lord," so it is then an object of purpose by estimating "intending" or "hoping for the mercy of your Lord," or it is accusative by removing the preposition. "Mercy" in the sense of "revelation" means: by the mercy of your Lord and His revelation. Thus His saying "and I did not do it of my own accord" is emphasis for that: that is, not by my opinion or my own effort. ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned of the consequences arranged in the thread of explanation, and the sense of distance in it is to signal the great elevation of its rank in grandeur.

﴿The interpretation of that which you could not bear﴾: that is, you could not be patient. It is the imperfect of "istata'a," with a hamzat al-wasl, and its origin is "istatha'a" on the pattern "istaf'ala." Then the ta' of the iftti'al was deleted for lightness, and the ta' which is original remained. Some claimed that the sin is a substitute for the converted waw into alif, and the origin is "ata'a," and there is no need to say that the deleted letter is the ta' which is the first radical of the verb, then the claim that they replaced the ta' of the iftti'al with ta' because it occurs after the sin. It is said "tastati'" by converting the ta' into ta', and "tasti'" by deleting the ta' of the iftti'al, so the variants are four, as Ibn al-Sikkit said. How delicate is the deletion of one of the two close letters and the retention of the other at the end of this speech, at which the departure of al-Khadir from Musa (peace be upon them both) occurred.

Some researchers said: this was specifically made light because, since it recurred in the story, it was fitting to lighten the last. It was objected that this too is repeated, and the other is lighter than it, so why was it not used? It is answered that the difference between this and that is evident. It was said: it was specifically lightened to indicate that what he met was light for Musa (peace be upon him) by explaining its cause. It was objected that this is distanced by the fact that it is in the narration, not the narrated matter, and you know this. Likewise what we have mentioned is a flower that does not bear rubbing and interpretation according to the previous meaning which he mentioned as the intended one, that is: that is the outcome and consequence of what you could not bear ﴿upon which you could not be patient﴾ of the matters which you saw. So it is a fulfilment of the promised explanation. He also permitted that the reference be to the explanation itself, so the interpretation would be in its well-known meaning. In any case, it is a summary of what preceded.

Page 15

In making the relative clause other than what passed is a repetition of the indefinite and an intensification of the rebuke. It was said: perhaps the attribution of the intending first to the pronoun of the speaker alone is because he is the direct agent of the defect, and second to the pronoun of the speaker together with another, because the killing of the boy by his action and act, and the change of another, depends upon him, and it is by the pure act and power of Allah, exalted is He; so the pronoun "we" is shared between Allah, exalted is He, and al-Khadir (peace be upon him). Third, to Allah, exalted is He, alone, since he (peace be upon him) had no part in the maturity of the two boys.

The directing of the plural pronoun was objected to: that the joining of a created being with Allah, exalted is He, in one pronoun, especially the pronoun of the speaker, contains the abandonment of courtesy that is in it. This is confirmed by what has come: "that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas used to give a sermon in his assembly, (ﷺ), whenever delegations of the Arabs came. It happened that a delegation of Tamim came, and their orator stood and mentioned their glories and their distinctions. When he finished his sermon, Thabit stood and gave a sermon in which he said: 'Whoever obeys Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger (ﷺ), has been guided, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What an evil orator of the people you are.'" Al-Khattabi stated that he (peace be upon him) disliked from him what it contained of equating them.

It was answered that the like of this has occurred in verses and hadiths. Among that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾, for the apparent meaning is that the pronoun of "send blessings upon" refers to Allah, exalted is He, and to the angels.

And His saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of faith: "that Allah and His Messenger be dearer to him than whatever else is besides them both."

[p. 16]

Perhaps what the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked from Thabit was that he paused at his saying "yu'ṣihimā" (which would be followed by the dual pronoun) and did not make the pronoun match in this way. The apparent meaning of this is that there is no dislike at all for this kind of pronoun agreement, and this is one of the opinions on the question. The second opinion is that of al-Khattabi, who held that it is disliked as a matter of *tanzih* (disliked but not prohibited). The third opinion is what the words of al-Ghazali imply, that it is disliked as a matter of *tahrim* (prohibited). According to the view that it is disliked in the sense of *tanzih*, some scholars have inferred that this is not a consistent rule, so that it may be disliked in one context and not in another. On this basis, the answer to what we are discussing is built: when the context in which Thabit was speaking was one of oratory and prolixity, in the presence of idolaters while Islam was still fresh and new, the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked him using the pronoun in that way. But in a context like the one in which the speaker and the addressee are known, and where the purpose is a point (*nukta*) of the kind that is intended here, namely that the one referred to has no independence, there is no dislike in using this pronoun. Some have restricted the dislike to other than the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case the answer to what was mentioned becomes stronger, because if it is permissible for the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is all the more permissible in the speech of Allah the Exalted, and in what He related, glorified be He, by a fortiori reasoning.

The conclusion of what was determined on this question is that the truth is that there is no dislike in this in the speech of Allah the Exalted and of His Messenger (ﷺ), as has been indicated in the commentaries on al-Bukhari. As for human beings, the preferred view is perhaps that it is disliked in the sense of *tanzih* in some contexts and not in others. This is my statement. I do not hold that this pronoun is shared between Allah the Exalted and al-Khidr (peace be upon him), not because it involves a lack of courtesy (*adab*), but because the apparent meaning is that it is like the pronoun in *khashīnā* (We feared), and the apparent meaning in that case is that it is not shared, because sharing it would require resorting to metaphor (*majāz*). Moreover, the point (*nukta*) that they mentioned in choosing the shared pronoun in *aradnā* (We wished) does not appear in choosing it for the pronoun in ﴿فَخَشِينَا﴾ (so We feared), because the first statement did not contain two actions in the way that the second statement contained them. So reflect on this. It has also been said regarding the reason for the variation in style: the first action is evil, so it is not fitting to attribute it to Him, glorified be He, even though He is the doer, exalted be He. The third is good, so He attributed it to Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone. The second is a mixture, since its good is the replacement with something better and its evil is the killing, so it was attributed to Allah the Exalted and to Himself, taking both into account. But the objection to this is that the attribution in ﴿فَخَشِينَا﴾ is also of this kind, and where is the mixture of good and evil in it? Making the point lie in the expression is refuted by the mere agreement with what follows, which is nothing, as is not hidden. It has also been said: the apparent meaning is that in the first two cases he attributed the wish to himself, but he varied the expression, so he expressed it with the pronoun of the plural speaker after having expressed it with the pronoun of the singular speaker, because the rank of joining is posterior to the rank of singularity. In addition, there is an indication in it that he is among the great ones in the sciences of wisdom, so he would not have undertaken this killing except for a lofty wisdom, unlike the spoiling of the boat. The act of replacement was attributed to Allah the Exalted [p. 17] as an indication that He, glorified be He, is independent in the act, and that what the servant obtains is merely the concomitance of the will to act without any influence on it, as is the true doctrine. The statement ends here. You know that replacement itself is something to which the will of the servant has no concomitance at all; the concomitance belongs only to the killing, on which it depends. Moreover, in this explanation there is more to be said.

In al-Intisaf it is said: perhaps the attribution of the first to himself alone is from the standpoint of courtesy toward Allah the Exalted, because what was intended there was a defect, so he behaved courteously by attributing the damaging to himself. As for the attribution of the second to "we," the apparent meaning is that it is in the manner of the courtiers of a king who say "we ordered such-and-such, and we arranged such-and-such," while meaning the order of the great king. "Arranged" (*dabbara*) also indicates this, and it is supported by His saying in the third case: ﴿فَأَرَادَ رَبُّكَ أَنْ يَبْلُغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا﴾ (so your Lord wished that they should reach their maturity). This is, as you see, [a weak view].

It has also been said: the variation of style is due to the variation in the state of the knower of Allah, glorified be He. At the beginning of his affair he sees himself as effective, so he first attributed the will to himself. Then he becomes aware that he cannot be independent in the act without Allah the Exalted, so the will was attributed to that pronoun. Then he sees that he has no part at all, and that the one who effects and wills is only Allah the Exalted, so he attributed it to Him, glorified be He, alone. This is the station of annihilation (*fana'*), and there is a station of "Allah was, and nothing was with Him, and He is now as He was." This has been criticized: if it is meant that these states passed over al-Khidr (peace be upon him) and that he was characterized by each of them during the dialogue, then this is false. How could he be, at that time, among those who attain even the second rank, let alone the first, when he is the one who was given knowledge from a direct source (*'ilm ladunnī*)? And if it is meant that he expressed himself in the manner of one who is characterized by each of those ranks, even though he (peace be upon him) was at the highest of them, then if this was intended as teaching Moses (peace be upon him), Moses (peace be upon him) is too exalted for al-Khidr (peace be upon him) to teach him the question of the creation of actions. And if it was teaching someone else (peace be upon him), then the situation is not that situation, given that there is someone else from whom this speech is heard. And if it is meant that he expressed himself in the three places in a particular manner from among those manners, but that Allah the Exalted expressed himself in each place in a different manner, so that the manners multiplied in His relating of the story to us, as teaching and as an indication of those ranks, while the speech of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) was not like that, then Allah the Exalted is too exalted and too great to relate from anyone a speech that he did not say, or did not say in its meaning, and to claim this is a kind of fabrication against Him, glorified be He.

What occurs to the mind of this poor servant is that in the answer the state of the objection was taken into account, and what it contained and indicated. Since the first objection was based on the assumption that the *lam* in ﴿لِتُغْرِقَ﴾ (to drown) is causal, and so contained the attribution of the will to drown to al-Khidr (peace be upon him), and since the denunciation in it was less than the denunciation in what follows, based on what the scholars chose, namely that *nukran* (a dreadful thing) is more emphatic than *imran* (a grave matter), it was fitting to explain it by attributing the will to damage to himself, which indicates the negation of the will to drown, which Moses' statement points to. And he did not bring anything indicating glorification, or the joining of anyone with him in the will, because the matter of denunciation was not magnified, and it did not require being met with something indicating the magnification of the will to the opposite of what he (peace be upon him) supposed and denounced.

Since the second objection was at the extreme of emphasis and denunciation, and there it was at the peak of denunciation, it was fitting to indicate that what he was objected to and whose denunciation was exaggerated was intended to be a great matter, and that if it had not happened, one would not be safe from the occurrence of a grave calamity. Therefore he attributed the fear and the will to the pronoun of one who magnifies himself, or of the speaker together with someone else. For in attributing the will to that, there is magnification of its matter, and in magnifying the one who wills there is magnification of the matter willed. Likewise, in attributing fear to that, there is magnification of its matter, and in magnifying the one who fears there is magnification of the matter feared. Perhaps it may be said, on the basis of the intention of joining us: in that attribution there is an indication that what is feared and what is willed has reached such greatness that Moses (peace be upon him) shares in the fear of it, and in the will of it, with al-Khidr, and not that he is independent in denouncing [p. 18] what is among the beginnings of that willed matter, and by it the root of corruption is cut off from both roots.

Since the third objection was very light, being in words with no harshness and no disturbance in its outward or inner meaning, and since it was not about the act itself but about not taking a wage for it, so that it could be used to repair the wall of the body and remove what had afflicted it of weakness, it was fitting that the answer to it be gentle, and that he not attribute to himself independence or participation in any act whatsoever. Therefore he attributed the will to the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, and did not suffice with that until he added it to his own pronoun (peace be upon him). And this does not conflict with the repetition of the denunciation and reproach, because that is related to the whole of what had first come from that quarter.

This is what there is to say. Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the secrets of the Book. He, glorified be He, is the one who grants success to what is right.

Those who held that he (peace be upon him) was a prophet used as evidence His saying: ﴿وَمَا فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أَمْرِي﴾ (I did it not on my own accord), and it is evident in this. The possibility that there was a prophet there who commanded him to do it through revelation, as claimed by those who hold that he was a saint (*wali*), is a remote possibility. Moreover, in His description of him by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿آتَيْنَاهُ رَحْمَةً مِنْ عِنْدِنَا وَعَلَّمْنَاهُ مِنْ لَدُنَّا عِلْمًا﴾ (We gave him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Us), there is no great benefit on this view. Indeed it may be said: what is the benefit of this knowledge from a direct source if, in displaying wonders to Moses (peace be upon him), he needed the mediation of a prophet like himself?

Some have said that it was by inspiration (*ilham*). But this entails the claim that inspiration was a proof in some of the sacred laws (*shara'i'*), and that al-Khidr was one of those obligated by that law. Otherwise, the apparent meaning is that his authority does not lie in the law of Moses (peace be upon him), and likewise he is not a proof in our law according to the correct view. Whoever deviated and held that inspiration is a proof stipulated for it that no legal text contradict it. So if Allah the Exalted had given one of His servants, through inspiration, knowledge of the kind of thing He gave al-Khidr (peace be upon him) about the state of the boy, it would not have been lawful for him to kill him.

What Imam Ahmad transmitted from Ata', who said: Najdah al-Haruri wrote to Ibn Abbas asking him about killing children. He wrote back to him: "If you are al-Khidr, who knows the unbeliever from the believer, then kill them." Ibn Abbas, as al-Subki said, intended by this a rebuke and an appeal to what cannot be realized with certainty, out of his desire to argue from the story of al-Khidr. And it was not his meaning, may Allah be pleased with him, that if that knowledge were obtained it would be permissible to kill. What al-Yafi'i said in his *Rawd* is also to be considered: that if Allah the Exalted permitted one of His servants to wear, for example, a silk garment, and he knew the permission with certainty and wore it, he would not be violating the law. And the certainty that he had from the perspective of al-Khidr's having it when he killed the boy is, since he is a saint and not a prophet according to the correct view, a stumble such that one can almost not say to its owner "may he stumble." This is because the likely source of certainty today is inspiration, and inspiration is not a proof according to the imams. Whoever deviated stipulated what he stipulated. And obtaining it through news from Jesus (peace be upon him), if he descends, is impossible, because he (peace be upon him) will descend under the law of our Prophet (ﷺ), and in his law it is prohibited for men to wear silk except for medical treatment.

What he mentioned of denying the prophethood of al-Khidr is not to be relied upon or taken into consideration. Among those who explicitly stated that inspiration is not a proof among the Sufis is the Imam al-Sha'rani, who said: "Many have slipped in this matter, and they have gone astray and led others astray. For us in this regard is a work I named *Hadd al-Husam fi 'unuq man aṭlaqa ījāb al-'amal bi'l-ilham* (The Sharp Sword against the Neck of One Who Makes Acting on Inspiration Absolutely Obligatory), a small volume." The statement ends here. He also said in his book named *al-Jawahir wa'l-Durar* (The Jewels and Pearls): "I have seen in the words of Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, the following text: Know that when we use the term 'angel of inspiration,' we mean only the subtle emanations from the angelic spirits, not the angels themselves. For an angel does not descend with revelation upon any heart other than that of a prophet at all, nor does it command a divine command all at once. The law has been firmly established and the obligatory and the required have been made clear, so the divine command ended with the ending of prophethood and messengerhood, and no one remains whom Allah the Exalted commands with a command that would be an independent law to be worshipped by forever. For if He commanded him with an obligation, the Lawgiver had already commanded it. And if He commanded him with something permissible, then either that permissible thing commanded becomes obligatory or recommended for him, and this is exactly the abrogation (*naskh*) of the law he is under, since it makes the legally permissible obligatory or recommended; and if He leaves it permissible as it was [p. 19]"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 82 (part 3 of 5):

What benefit is there in the command that the angel of inspiration (malak al-ilham) brought to this claimant? If he says: "The angel of inspiration did not come to me with that, but God, exalted is He, commanded me directly, without any intermediary," we say: he is not to be believed in such a matter, and it is a deception from the self (nafs). If he claims that God, glorified is He, spoke to him as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, then no one holds this view. Moreover, if God had spoken to him, He would only have conveyed to him in His speech knowledge and information, not rulings (ahkam) and law (shar'), and He would not command him at all. End of quotation.

The Rabbani Imam, Mujaddid of the Second Millennium (Mujaddid al-Alf al-Thani), may his noble secret be sanctified, has stated clearly in his Letters (al-Maktubat) in many places that inspiration does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful. From this it is known that there is no contradiction between the Sharia (the sacred law), the Haqiqa (inner truth), and the outward and inward meanings. His words, may his secret be sanctified, in the Letters are full of this. Thus, in Letter 43 of the first volume: "A people inclined toward atheism and heresy (zandaqa), imagining that the true purpose lies beyond the Sharia. Far from it, far from it, and again far from it. We seek refuge in God, glorified is He, from this evil belief. Each of the Tariqa (spiritual path) and the Sharia is the very essence of the other; there is no contradiction between them even to the extent of the head of a barley grain. Everything that contradicts the Sharia is rejected, and every truth (haqiqa) that the Sharia rejects is heresy (zandaqa)."

He also said in the course of Letter 41 of the same volume, in the discussion of Sharia, Tariqa and Haqiqa: "For example, the tongue's refraining from speaking falsehood is Sharia, and the removal of the thought of lying from the heart, if it is done with effort and exertion, is Tariqa, and if it is easy without effort, it is Haqiqa. In sum, the inner dimension, which is the Tariqa and the Haqiqa, completes the outer dimension, which is the Sharia. So the travelers on the path of Tariqa and Haqiqa, if there appear from them in the course of the journey matters whose outward form contradicts and opposes the Sharia, these are from the intoxication of the moment (sukr al-waqt) and the dominance of the state (ghalabat al-hal). When they pass that station and return to sobriety (sahw), that opposition is entirely removed, and those contrary knowledges become altogether 'scattered dust' (haba'an manthuran)."

He also said, may God benefit us by his knowledge, in the course of Letter 36 of the same volume: "The Sharia has three parts: knowledge, action, and sincerity (ikhlas). As long as these parts are not realized, the Sharia is not realized. When the Sharia is realized, the pleasure of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is obtained, and it is above all worldly and otherworldly felicities, and 'the good pleasure of God is greater' (wa-ridwanun min Allahi akbar). So the Sharia encompasses all felicities, and no aim remains beyond the Sharia. The Tariqa and the Haqiqa, by which the Sufis are distinguished, both serve the Sharia in perfecting its third part, which is sincerity. Thus their purpose is the perfection of the Sharia, not some other matter beyond that..." to the end of what he said.

He, may his mercy be upon him, also said in the course of Letter 29 of the said volume, after much investigation: "It is established that the path to attaining the degrees of nearness to God, exalted is His majesty, whether the nearness of prophethood or the nearness of sainthood (wilaya), is confined to the path of the Sharia to which the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, called, and to which he was commanded, as in the verse: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾ [12:108], and the verse: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [3:31] also indicates this. Every path other than this path is misguidance and a deviation from the true goal. And every path that the Sharia rejects is heresy (zandaqa). The evidence for this is the verse: ﴿And that this is My path, straight﴾ [6:153], the verse: ﴿What, then, is there after the truth but error?﴾ [10:32], the verse: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [3:85], and the hadith: 'The Prophet (ﷺ) drew a line for us,' the report (to the end), and the hadith: 'Every innovation is misguidance' (kullu bid'atin dalala), and other hadiths," to the end of what he said, may the mercy of the Exalted King be upon him.

He, may his secret be sanctified, also said regarding the knowledge of the Sufis: "Know that the knowledge and gnosis (ma'arif) of the Sufis at the end of their journeys and their wayfaring is nothing but the knowledge of the Sharia, not other knowledges distinct from the knowledge of the Sharia. Yes, in the course of the path many knowledges and gnoses appear, but one must pass beyond them. Thus at the ultimate end, their knowledge is the knowledge of the scholars, which is the knowledge of the Sharia. The difference between them and the scholars is that those knowledges, in relation to the scholars, are speculative and inferential, while in relation to them they become unveiling (kashfiyya) and necessary (darurIyya)."

[Page 19]

He also said: "Know that the Sharia and the Haqiqa are one in reality, and there is no difference between them except in terms of the general and the detailed, in terms of inference and unveiling of the unseen and the seen, and in terms of effort and absence of effort. The Sharia has the first of these, and the Haqiqa has the second. The sign of reaching the reality of certainty (haqiq al-yaqin) is that his knowledge and gnoses correspond to the knowledge of the Sharia and its gnoses. As long as there is any contradiction, even the smallest hair's breadth, that is a proof of not having arrived. As for what occurs in the expression of some shaykhs, that the Sharia is the husk and the Haqiqa is the kernel, although it indicates the uprightness of its speaker is lacking, it is possible that what he meant is that the general, in relation to the detailed, has the status of the husk in relation to the kernel, and that inference in relation to unveiling is likewise. The upright masters do not permit the use of such expressions that give a misleading impression, when his noble expressions, which can scarcely be counted, can be read otherwise."

My master, the Rabbani Pole (al-Qutb al-Rabbani), Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified, said: "All the saints (awliya') draw only from the word of God, exalted is He, and of His Messenger (ﷺ), and they act only according to their outward meanings." The leader of the sect, al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: "All the paths are closed except to him who follows the footsteps of the Messenger, peace be upon him." He also said: "Whoever does not memorize the Qur'an and does not write down the hadith, he is not to be emulated in this science, because our science is bound by the Book and the Sunna." Al-Sari al-Saqati said: "Tasawwuf is a name for three meanings: the light of its gnosis does not extinguish the light of its piety (wara'), it does not speak of a hidden inner secret in a knowledge that the outward text of the Book contradicts, and its charismatic wonders (karamat) do not lead it to violate the sacred prohibitions of God." He also said, may his secret be sanctified: "Whoever claims an inner knowledge that the outward ruling contradicts, he is mistaken."

Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri said: "Whoever you see claiming with God a state (hal) that departs from the fundamentals of the sacred knowledge, do not approach him. And whoever you see claiming a state for which no outward preservation (of the Sharia) bears witness, then suspect him in his religion." Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz said: "Every inner outpouring (fayd batin) that an outward matter contradicts is false."

Abu al-Abbas Ahmad al-Dinawari said: "The tongue of the outward does not change the ruling of the inward." In al-Tuhfa of Ibn Hajar, al-Ghazali is quoted as saying: "Whoever claims that he has a state with God, exalted is He, by which he drops from himself such things as prayer or the prohibition of drinking wine, must be killed, although there is room to consider whether he is to be eternally in the Fire. Killing such a person is better than killing a hundred unbelievers, because his harm is greater." End of quotation. There is no consideration regarding his eternal abode, because he is an apostate for permitting what is known to be forbidden, or for denying the obligation of what is known to be obligatory by necessity in both cases. For this reason, in al-Anwar he firmly affirmed his eternal abode in the Fire. End of quotation.

He said in the Ihya': "Whoever says that the inward contradicts the outward is nearer to disbelief than to faith..." and so on.

Part of the Risala of al-Qushayri is also similar. What should be known is that the words of the realized knowers (al-'arifin al-muhaqqiqin), although they indicate that there is no contradiction between the Sharia, the Tariqa and the Haqiqa in reality, also indicate that within the Haqiqa there are unveilings and hidden knowledges. That is why you see them saying: "The science of Haqiqa is the knowledge of the divine gift (ilm al-ladunni), the science of unveiling (mukashafa), the science of bestowal (mawhiba), the science of secrets (asrar), the hidden knowledge (al-'ilm al-maknun), and the science of inheritance (ilm al-wiratha)." However, this does not indicate contradiction, for unveilings and hidden knowledges are the fruit of sincerity, which is the third part of the components of the Sharia. Thus they are, in reality, consequent upon the Sharia and a result of it. Yet these unveilings and hidden knowledges do not change any legal ruling, nor do they restrict what is absolute, nor make absolute what is restricted. This contrasts with what Sajiqli-zada (Sajaqli Zadeh) imagined when he said in explaining the aforementioned expression of the Ihya': "Al-Ghazali means by the inward what is unveiled to the scholars of the inward regarding the permissibility of some things for them, although the Lawgiver forbade it to His servants absolutely. So it must be said: its permissibility was unveiled to them because a hidden cause that makes it lawful for them was unveiled to them. The Lawgiver's prohibition, exalted is He, of that to His servants is restricted by the absence of the unveiling of the cause that makes it lawful for them. Whoever has that cause unveiled to him, it becomes lawful for him, and whoever does not, it does not. But the Lawgiver, glorified is He, forbade it to His servants absolutely and omitted that restriction because its occurrence is rare, for the one to whom it is unveiled is very few. An example is the unveiling of the place of the ship's breaking and the killing of the boy for al-Khidr, peace be upon him. Thus, for him, the breaking and the killing became lawful by that unveiling, and their permissibility for him contradicts the general prohibition of the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, forbidding his community from harm and from killing a child. But these two are restricted: the first is restricted to when there is no known usurper, for example, and the second to when it is not known that the child will become a misguided misleader. Yet the Lawgiver omitted the two restrictions because their occurrence is rare, and relying on the understanding of those firmly grounded in knowledge of them..." to the end of what he said. But the preceding texts call out against this, as you have heard.

Moreover, those hidden matters and unveilings, indeed all that happens to the Sufis of theophanies (tajalliyyat), are not among the ultimate aims, and the perfected person does not stop at them or turn toward them. The Rabbani Imam, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in Letter 36 (part of which was quoted earlier) that they serve to train the children of the path, and that one should pass beyond them to reach the station of contentment (rida), which is the end of the stations of the wayfaring and of attraction (jadhba). It is rare; only one in thousands reaches it. Then he said: "Those of little insight count states and ecstasies (mawajid) among the stations, and the witnessings (mushahadat) and theophanies among the goals. Therefore they remained in the bonds of illusion and imagination and became deprived of the perfections of the Sharia." ﴿It is hard for the polytheists what you call them to; God chooses for it whom He wills and guides to it whoever turns in repentance﴾ [42:13]. End of quotation.

From this it is known that the perfected in the Sharia pass over these and do not turn toward them, nor do they consider them a goal. The bulk of their aim is attaining the station of contentment. In light of this, the verse of the Mathnawi comes out, where he says:

*"Zani tarafi ke ishq min afzud, dard abu hanifa shafi'i dersi nakardi."*

["The one who increased love in one direction (yet) the pain (of love) did not learn the lessons of Abu Hanifa or al-Shafi'i."]

[Page 20 continues]

And the perfect person may be veiled from all of that and, in this respect, join the common folk. It is known from what has been mentioned that Musa (peace be upon him) is more perfect than al-Khidr. The superiority of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) in the knowledge of the Reality (al-haqiqa, the inner, mystical truth) was relative to the present state. Musa (peace be upon him) expressed this and did not stop at it, because he was in the station of legislation (al-tashri', the giving of sacred law). Perhaps his request to be taught was by command, as a trial for him because of that slip. They have said that the more lofty the ascent of the perfect person, the lower his descent will be, and the lower his descent, the more perfect he will be in guidance and the more complete his outpouring, because of the greater closeness between the guide and the one seeking guidance. For this reason, they said in what is related: al-Hasan al-Basri stood on the bank of a river waiting for a boat. Habib al-'Ajami came up and said to him: "What are you waiting for?" He said: "A boat." He said: "What need do you have for a boat? Do you not have certainty?" Al-Hasan said: "Do you not have knowledge?" Then Habib crossed over the water without a boat, and al-Hasan realized that the superiority belonged to al-Hasan, for he combined the knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqin) and the eye of certainty ('ayn al-yaqin), and he knew things as they are. In reality, power was concealed behind wisdom, and wisdom lies in causes. Habib was a man of intoxication who did not perceive causes, so he was treated by having them removed. From here the secret of the scarcity of extraordinary events among the Companions becomes clear, together with the saying of the Rabbani Imam: "The end of Uways, the master of the Successors, is the beginning of Wahshi, the killer of Hamza, on the day he embraced Islam." So what is to be thought of anyone other than Uways, and anyone other than Wahshi?

I say: the perfect person, although he is as you have come to know, yet above him is the most perfect, who is always ascending in his descent and descending in his ascent. That is none other than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Were it not for that, the higher and lower worlds would not be sustained. Here is the source of the Reality and the sacred law for him (ﷺ) in the most complete manner, as we indicated earlier. Praise be to Allah, the Exalted, for making us of his community and his descendants.

What al-Imam al-Ghazali said in the Ihya' does not conflict with what we have mentioned, namely that the knowledge of the Hereafter is of two kinds: the knowledge of unveiling (mukashafa) and the knowledge of conduct (mu'amala). As for the knowledge of unveiling, it is the knowledge of the inner, and it is the highest of the sciences. It is the knowledge of the truthful (al-siddiqin) and of those brought near (al-muqarrabin). It is an expression for a light that appears in the heart when it is purified and cleansed of blameworthy qualities. By this, what was previously heard of their names and was imagined to have vague, unclear meanings becomes disclosed, and so it becomes clear

[Page 21]

at that time, until knowledge of the Essence of Allah, the Exalted, of His perfect attributes, of His acts, and of His wisdom in creating this world and the next is attained. End of quotation.

Because the intent is that this is from the inner knowledge, which is the knowledge of the Reality, and this part cannot be absent from a prophet. How could it be, when the rank of the truthful is below the rank of the prophets (peace be upon them), as they established in the verse: ﴿So those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾.

From what we have mentioned about there being no contradiction between the sacred law (shari'a) and the Reality (haqiqa), we know what al-Balqini said in answering the difficulty he raised regarding al-Khidr's words to Musa (peace be upon them both): "Indeed, I have knowledge..." (the earlier hadith). He claimed that its apparent meaning indicates the impossibility of teaching both kinds of knowledge together, though this is not impossible. He answered that the knowledge of unveilings and realities contradicts the knowledge of the outward, so one who judges by the outward should not know the realities, due to the contradiction; and likewise, one who knows the Reality should not know the outward knowledge that he is not charged with, since it contradicts what he has of the Reality. But by my life, he erred in what he said, and men are known by the truth. It seems he did not rely on it, so he followed it with another answer that is contrary to the apparent meaning.

You know that there is no need for any of that, and the difficulty arises from weakness of reflection. Moreover, the story of al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is not suitable as proof for one who claims there is contradiction between the two kinds of knowledge. For the greatest difficulty in it is the killing of the boy, because he was created an unbeliever, and it was feared that if he remained alive, his parents would apostatize. That too is a sacred law, but it is specific to him (peace be upon him). For, as the scholar al-Subki said: "It was revealed to him to act according to the inner and contrary to the outward, which accords with wisdom. So there is no difficulty in it, though it is known from our sacred law that it is not permissible for anyone, whoever he may be, to kill a child, especially between two believing parents. How is it permissible to kill him for a cause that has not occurred? The newborn is not described as truly disbelieving or truly believing." The agreement of the sacred laws on rulings is something no one from among mankind has held, let alone the eminent scholars. This is clear on the view that he was a prophet. As for the view that he was a saint (wali), it is said that the saint's action by inspiration was then a sacred law, or, as it has been said, he was commanded to do so through a prophet other than Musa (peace be upon him).

As for the rebuilding of the wall without wages, there is no difficulty in it, because it is a kindness. The most that can be imagined is that it was for the wrongdoer; so let it be so, and there is no harm, for it is among the noble characteristics. As for the breaking of the boat so that it would be saved from the seizure of the tyrant, they have said that this is something with no harm in it. Indeed, al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam said: "If a person has in his keeping the property of an orphan, or a foolish or insane person, and fears that a tyrant will seize it, it is obligatory for him to damage it in order to preserve it. And the word of the one who damaged the orphan's property or the like is accepted when the orphan or the like disputes with him after maturity or the like, that he did it to preserve it, in its various aspects," as al-Qadi Zakariyya said in his commentary on al-Rawd, just before the chapter on deposits.

A similar case: if he had in his keeping, for example, the property of an orphan, and knew that if he did not give up some of it to a wicked judge, the judge would seize it and hand it over to some traitors, and this would lead to its loss, then it is obligatory for him to give something to the judge, aiming to give the least amount that would satisfy him. And the word is his also.

Some have said: the most that this story indicates is the establishment of inner knowledge, and this is granted; but applying the term "inner" to it is relative, as has been explained earlier. And in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, of knowledge is something like the hidden treasure, which none knows except the scholars of Allah, the Exalted. When they speak of it, none denies it except those heedless of Allah, the Exalted," there is an indication of this. By "those heedless" are meant the scholars of the outward who were not given that. Some of those who affirm it cite the saying of Abu Hurayra: "I memorized from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) two vessels of knowledge. As for one, I have spread it; as for the other, if I spread it, this throat of mine would be cut." It is also cited as proof of the contradiction between the two kinds of knowledge.
