You know that it is possible that by the other, the one whose spreading would lead to his throat being cut, he meant the knowledge of trials, and what occurred under the Banu Umayya, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) censure of certain individuals among them. And there is no doubt that spreading that in those eras would lead to killing. And even granting that he meant by it the inner knowledge called the knowledge of the Reality, we do not grant that his throat would be cut for spreading it because it contradicts the outward knowledge in itself. Rather, it would be because of the suspicion, on the part of those who hold the power to loosen and bind, command and forbid, among the rulers of that time, that it was contradictory. So understand.

The scholars, in accordance with what the commentators of the hadith and others have mentioned, have derived from the story: the recommendation of travelling in search of knowledge and the excellence of seeking it; the recommendation of observing good manners with the scholar, respecting the shaykhs, not objecting to them, and interpreting what is not understood from their outward acts, movements, and sayings; fulfilling their covenants and offering apology when one differs from them. It also shows the permissibility of taking a servant on a journey and carrying provisions for it; that this does not contradict trust in Allah (tawakkul); and that attributing forgetfulness and the like, among disliked matters, to Satan is permissible metaphorically and out of courtesy, rather than attributing them to Allah, the Exalted. It shows that the scholar may excuse himself to one who wants to learn from him for not teaching him what his nature cannot bear; that the will (mashi'a) is put first in matters; and that the one followed may impose conditions on the follower. It indicates that forgetfulness is not held against a person, and that three (repetitions) carry weight in repetition and the like. It shows the permissibility of boarding a boat. It also shows that judgment is made by the outward until its opposite is clarified, as Musa (peace be upon him) denounced it. It shows that a person may ask for food when he needs it; that doing good is not abandoned even with the ungenerous; the permissibility of taking wages for work; that the destitute does not leave destitution by owning a tool with which he earns or by owning something that does not suffice him; that usurpation is forbidden; that it is permissible to bury money in the ground; and it contains the affirmation of the miracles (karamat) of the saints according to the view of those who say al-Khidr is a saint. And there are other things that appear to the one who investigates or contemplates. In sum, this story has included many benefits and lofty, weighty matters. So contemplate that deeply, and may Allah, glorified is He, guide you.

* * *

(Among the points of allusion in the verses) according to what some of the people of allusion (ahl al-ishara, the mystics who read hidden meanings) have mentioned: ﴿Then they found a servant from Our servants﴾. In it is an allusion that Allah, the Exalted, has chosen servants whom He attributed to Himself and separated from others. The most distinguished of His chosen is the one whom He attributed to the Glorious Name, which is the Name of the Essence that encompasses all attributes, or to the pronoun of absence referring back to Him, the Exalted. And none is that except His beloved, the most noble (ﷺ). ﴿We gave him mercy from Us﴾, which is the station of nearness to Him, the Glorious, the Majestic. ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Us﴾, which is the special knowledge that is known only from His side, the Exalted. Dhu al-Nun said: "Knowledge of the divine presence (al-'ilm al-ladunni) is that which judges creatures by the positions of success and failure."

Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: "It is the disclosure of secrets without suspicion or contrary conflict, but it is the unveiling of lights from the hidden unseen. It is attained by the servant when he guards his limbs from all acts of disobedience and extinguishes his movements from all desires, and becomes a shadow before the Real without wish or intent." It has been said: "It is a knowledge by which the Real, glorified is He, makes known to His friends what is in the good of His servants." Some have said: "It is an unseen knowledge that relates to the realm of acts, and more particular than that is standing on part of the secret of destiny before its occurrence, and more particular than that is the knowledge of the Names and the special qualities, and more particular than that is the knowledge of the Essence."

Some of the gnostics (al-'arifin) have mentioned that among the sciences there is what none makes known except the Prophet, and they cited as proof his (ﷺ) saying in the hadith of the Ascension, as al-Qastallani mentioned in his al-Mawahib and others: "My Lord asked me, and I could not answer Him, so He placed His hand between my shoulders, and I found its coolness. He then bequeathed to me the knowledge of the first and the last, and taught me various sciences. Then He took from me a covenant to conceal it, for He knew that none but me could bear it. And there is a knowledge with which He gave me the choice, and He taught me the Qur'an, and Jibril used to remind me of it. And there is a knowledge He commanded me to convey to the general and the particular of my community." End of quotation. And Allah, the Exalted, has a knowledge that He has kept to Himself, the Glorious, the Majestic, which He has not made known to any of His creatures. ﴿Musa said to him: "May I follow you so that you teach me of what you have been taught, as a guidance?"﴾ He said this from a divine trial, as we have previously stated.

Fars said, as in Asrar al-Qur'an: "Musa (peace be upon him) was more knowledgeable than al-Khidr in what he took from Allah, the Exalted, and al-Khidr was more knowledgeable than Musa in what came to Musa (peace be upon him)." He also said: "Musa was subsisting by the Real, and al-Khidr was annihilated in the Real." ﴿He said: "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me"﴾ ﴿"And how can you be patient with what you have not encompassed in knowledge?"﴾

[Page 23]

It was said: al-Khidr knew that Musa (peace be upon him) was the most honored of creation before Allah, the Exalted, in his time, and that he had great fervor. So he feared being in his company, lest there should occur from him with him what would not befit his station.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 82 (part 5 of 5):

Some of them said: He made him despair of himself, lest his companionship distract him from companionship with the Truth. He said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey any command of yours.﴾ Some of them said: Had he said, as the one to be sacrificed (al-Dhabih), peace be upon him, said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the patient﴾, he would have been granted success in patience, as the one to be sacrificed was granted it. The difference is that the speech of the one to be sacrificed is more manifest in seeking refuge (in God) and in breaking the self, since he made his finding himself one of a group characterized by patience dependent upon the will of God the Exalted. Moses' speech is not like this, peace be upon him: ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾. They took the path of asking, which involves giving oneself over to the way, and this does not contradict reliance upon God (tawakkul), and likewise earning (kasb). ﴿He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ It is as though he, peace be upon him, intended to remove what made them need to ask those miserly people. In this there is a regard for causes (al-nazar ila al-asbab), and it is one of the states of the perfected, as has passed in the account of al-Hasan al-Basri and Habib. In this there is an indication that he (Moses) was more perfect than al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. He said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you.﴾ That is: according to what I wished.

Al-Nasrabadi said: When al-Khidr knew that Moses had reached the limit of discipline (al-ta'dib) and that his knowledge fell short of his own, he said that lest Moses ask him afterwards about some knowledge or state, and be disgraced.

It was said: He feared that Moses would ask him about the secrets of the divine sciences, the attributive and essential ones, and he would be unable to answer, so he said what he said. ﴿As for the youth, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ It was said: He was exceedingly beautiful of face and was loved to the utmost by his parents, so he feared that they would be tempted by him. The verse is apparently problematic, for if God the Exalted had decreed disbelief upon them, then killing the child would not benefit them; and if God, glorified be He, had not decreed that, then his remaining would not harm them. It is answered that what was decreed was their remaining upon faith if he were killed, and his killing was so that they would remain upon that.

It was said: What was decreed may be changed, and this entails no more than a change in the relation of His attribute to the thing, not a change in the attribute itself, lest change be entailed in Him, may He be exalted and glorified. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾.

It is also raised as an objection that the feared harm would be removed by granting him faith, so what need was there for killing? It is answered that the apparent meaning is that he was not disposed to that, and so it contradicts wisdom. It seems that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, perceived in what Moses said a kind of contention, so he freed himself from that by his saying: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord.﴾ That is: rather, I did it by the command of God, may He be exalted and glorified, and He is not questioned about what He commands and does. Perhaps his saying to Moses, peace be upon him, what he said when he pecked the sparrow in the sea, was a closing of the door to contention regarding what God, may His majesty be exalted, commanded. And perhaps the knowledge of such matters belongs to the knowledge which God, glorified be He, has reserved for Himself: ﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.﴾

Some of them interpreted the meeting place of the two seas as the meeting of the sheikh's guardianship (wilaya) and the disciple's guardianship; the rock as the self (nafs); the fish as the heart (qalb) salted with the salt of love of this world and its adornment; the ship as the sacred law (shari'a); its breaking as the demolition of the namus (the established norm) outwardly together with righteousness inwardly; the drowning of its people as their being cast into the seas of error; the youth as the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara); his killing as his slaughter by the sword of spiritual discipline (riyada); the town as the body; its people as the human powers of the senses; their refusal to host them as their refusal to give the faculties what is proper to them, given their weariness and weakness; the wall as the attachment that stands between the rational soul and the world of the immaterial (al-mujarradat); the desire to fall as approaching the severing of ties; its setting up as strengthening the body and gently treating the powers and senses; the will to take a wage as the will to endure the patience of severe discipline in order to attain unveilings (kashf) and the outpouring of lights; the poor as the common people (al-awamm); the sea in which they work as the sea of this world; the king as Satan; the ships which he seizes as worship devoid of brokenness, humility and submissiveness; the believing parents as the heart and the spirit; the better replacement as the soul at peace and inspired; the treasure as the theoretical and cognitive perfections; and the righteous father as the separate intellect whose perfections are actual. Their attaining maturity (bulugh al-ashudd) is their arrival, through the training and guidance of the sheikh, at the perfect station. This is what al-Naysaburi chose, and others chose another interpretation which is more cunning than this. And God the Exalted is the Granter of success to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final destination.

[Page 24]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 83 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn.﴾ The question was posed as a test. The commonly held view is that the questioners were the Quraysh, prompted by the Jews. It is also said that the Jews themselves asked, and this is narrated from al-Suddi. Most of the reports indicate that the verse was revealed after they asked, so the expression is in the present tense (yas'aluna) to bring the past scene vividly to mind, because in asking in that manner, having witnessed from the Prophet (ﷺ) what they witnessed, there was a kind of strangeness. It is also said that the present tense indicates their continued questioning until the answer came. Some reports, however, indicate that the verse was revealed earlier. It is narrated from Uqba ibn Amir that he said: "A group of People of the Book came with scrolls, or books, and said to me: 'Ask permission for us to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' I went to him (ﷺ) and informed him of their presence. He (ﷺ) said: 'What have I to do with them? They ask me about what I do not know. I am only a servant who has no knowledge except what my Lord has taught me.' Then he said: 'Bring me water for ablution.' I brought it to him and he performed ablution, then he went to a place of prayer in his house and prayed two rakahs. Then he turned away until joy appeared on his face. Then he said: 'Go and bring them in, and whoever of my companions you find at the door.' I brought them in. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw them, he said: 'If you wish, I will tell you what you asked me about, and if you wish, [I will tell you] something other than that, do so.'" The majority hold the first view, and the soundness of this report has not been established.

It has been disputed concerning Dhul-Qarnayn. It is said that he was a king whom Allah the Exalted sent down to the earth, and to whom He gave a means to everything (sababan). This is narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr. In support of this, one cites what Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in his Kitab al-Adda', and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): that he heard a man calling out at Mina, "O Dhal-Qarnayn!" Umar said to him: "You have named yourselves after the names of the prophets; what have you to do with the names of the angels?" This is a strange view, indeed it hardly can be sound. Even if the report is sound, it is not explicit in this matter, for it is possible, though distantly, that the intended meaning is that this name is one of the names of the angels, peace be upon them, so do not name yourselves with it, even if some of the people before you named themselves with it.

It is also said that he was a righteous servant whom Allah the Exalted made ruler over the earth, gave knowledge and wisdom, and clothed in awe. We do not know who he was. Several explanations have been mentioned for his being called Dhul-Qarnayn:

The first: he called to the obedience of Allah the Exalted, so he was struck on his right horn and died. Then Allah the Exalted resurrected him. He called again, so he was struck on his left horn and died. Then Allah the Exalted resurrected him, and he was named Dhul-Qarnayn, and he ruled what he ruled. This is narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face.

The second: two generations of people passed away during his time.

The third: the two sides of his head were of copper. This is narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: he had two horns on his head like the cloven hooves [of an animal], and he was the first to wear a turban to cover them. This is narrated from Ubayd ibn Ya'la.

The fifth: his crown had two horns.

The sixth: he traversed the two horns of the world, that is, its east and its west. This is narrated as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)).

The seventh: he had two locks of hair. This is narrated from Qatada and Yunus ibn Ubayd.

The eighth: Allah subjected light and darkness to him, so when he travelled, light guided him from in front of him, and darkness extended behind him.

The ninth: he entered light and darkness.

The tenth: he saw in a dream as if he ascended to the sun and took hold of its two horns.

The eleventh: it is possible that he was given this title because of his bravery, as if he gored his peers like a bull (with its horns). Similarly, Ardashir Bahman was titled "Long-Handed" because his command was implemented wherever he wished. It is not hidden from you that it is remote that a man, to whom was granted what was granted in the earth, and who attained the fame that he attained in its length and breadth, should be unknown. As for the explanations mentioned regarding the reason for his name, some of them hardly can be sound, and perhaps this is not hidden from you.

Page 25

It is also said that he was Firidun ibn Athfiyan ibn Jamshid, the fifth of the kings of the Persians of the Fayshadhiyya dynasty, and he was a just king, obedient to Allah the Exalted. In the book Suwar al-Aqalim of Abu Zayd al-Balkhi, it is stated that he was supported by revelation. In most histories, it is stated that he ruled the earth and divided it among his three sons: Iraj, Salm, and Tur. He gave Iraq, India, and the Hijaz to Iraj and made him the possessor of the crown; he gave Salm Rome, the lands of Egypt, and the West; and he gave Tur China, the Turks, and the East. He established a law for each by which they would be governed, and the three laws were called siyasa, which is arabized from "si-aysa," meaning three laws. The reason for calling him Dhul-Qarnayn is that he ruled the two extremities of the world, or the length of the days of his reign, which, according to Rawdat al-Safa, was five hundred years, or the magnitude of his courage and his subjugating the kings. This is refuted by the fact that historians have unanimously agreed that he did not travel either east or west, but rather Kawah al-Isfahani the blacksmith subdued the lands for him, the one through whose hand Allah the Exalted tore apart the kingdom of al-Dahhak, and he remained commander of the armies until he died. This view also necessitates that Khidr, peace be upon him, was at his vanguard, based on what is well known that he, peace be upon him, was at the vanguard of Dhul-Qarnayn, but none of the historians mentioned that. It is answered that whoever says he is Alexander affirms all that is established for Alexander in the verses and reports, and does not concern himself with the historians' not mentioning that, and this is as you see. It is also said that he is Alexander the Greek, son of Philip (Faylaqus). It is also said: Qalfis. It is also said: Qulays.

Ibn Kathir said: He is the son of Filis ibn Misrim ibn Harmas ibn Maytun ibn Rumi ibn Liti ibn Yunan ibn Yafith ibn Nun ibn Sharkhun ibn Tawnat ibn Yufil ibn Rumi ibn al-Asghar ibn al-Aziz ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon him. The seat of his kingdom was Macedonia, a town in the lands of Rome, to the west of the abode of the exalted sultanate, the protected Constantinople; between them is a distance of about fifteen days or so, near the city of Shiraz. The statement of Ibn Zaydun that it is Egypt is an error. He is the one who defeated Dara the Younger (Dara al-Asghar) and took control of the kingdom of the Persians, and his birth was in the thirteenth year of the reign of Dara the Elder (Dara al-Akbar). Some claimed that he was his father, because he married the daughter of Philip (Faylaqus). When he approached her, he found in her an offensive odour, so he sent her back to her father, and she had become pregnant with Alexander. When she gave birth to him, he remained under the guardianship of her father, and so he was ascribed to him. It is also said that Dara the Elder married the daughter of the king of the Zanj, Halabi, and he disliked her smell, so he ordered that a stratagem be devised for that. She used to wash with water of sandarus, which removed much of her odour; then he rejected her and returned her to her people. She gave birth to Alexander, who was called Iskandarus. What indicates that he was his son is that when Dara the Younger, son of Dara the Elder, was overtaken, with a breath remaining in him, he placed his head in his lap and said to him: "O my brother, inform me of the one who did this to you, so that I may take revenge on him." This is a false claim. His saying "O my brother" is from the mode of honouring and addressing equals.

He was named Dhul-Qarnayn only because he possessed the two extremities of the earth, or for his bravery. He cited in support of this view that the Qur'an indicates that this man's dominion reached the farthest west, the farthest east, and the northern direction, and that is the whole of the inhabited earth. It was asked: "This king, it is necessary that his memory should remain immortal, and the king who became famous in the books of history as having reached this limit is none other than this Alexander. Because when his father died, he gathered the kings of Rome and the West and subdued them, and reached the Green Sea (the Mediterranean). Then he returned to Egypt and built Alexandria. Then he entered al-Sham and headed to the Children of Israel, and came to Bayt al-Maqdis, and slaughtered [animals] at its altar. Then he turned to Armenia and Bab al-Abwab. The Iraqis, the Copts, and the Berbers submitted to him, and he prevailed over Dara and headed for India and China, and raided distant nations. He returned to Khurasan and built many cities, and returned to Iraq. He fell ill in Shahrazur and died there. It is said that he died in Rumiyyat al-Mada'in, and they placed him in a golden coffin and carried him to Alexandria. He lived thirty-two years, and the duration of his reign was twelve years." It is also said that he lived thirty-six years, and the duration of his reign was sixteen years, and it is said other than that. Since it has been established by the Qur'an that Dhul-Qarnayn ruled most of the inhabited world, and it has been established by the histories that the one whose condition is this is Alexander, it becomes necessary to decide with certainty that the intended Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander. Thus al-Imam mentioned it. Then he said: "This view is the most evident because of the aforementioned evidence, except that it has a strong difficulty: he was a student of Aristotle the sage, who resided in the city of Athens, whom his father entrusted him to. He stayed with him for five years, learned philosophy from him, excelled in it, and was upon his doctrine. So Allah the Exalted's exaltation of him necessitates the judgement that the doctrine of Aristotle is true, and that is something for which there is no way." It is answered: We do not concede that he was upon his doctrine in everything he held, and discipleship to a person does not necessitate agreement with all of that person's views. Do you not see the great number of times the two Imams opposed their teacher, Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him? So it is possible that he opposed him in matters which would entail disbelief. And his slaughtering at the altar of Bayt al-Maqdis is evidence that he did not hold all that the philosophers held. It is not hidden that this is a remote possibility. The well-known view is that he held what the philosophers say, and the mentioned slaughter is not established, so the argument from it is weak. It is also said that his saying that and adopting the doctrine of Aristotle does not entail his disbelief at that time, for he was affirming the Creator, may He be exalted, and magnifying Him, not worshipping anything besides Him, whether an idol or other. This is indicated by what al-Shahrastani reported: that the philosophers consulted together about prostrating to him out of honour and veneration, and he said: "Prostration is not permissible to other than the Originator of all." He had not been sent a messenger, for he was about three hundred years before the mission of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the prophets, peace be upon them, at that time were from the Children of Israel and were sent to them, and he was not one of them, so his ruling was the ruling of the People of the Interval (ahl al-fatra). It was objected that even if this is conceded, it does not resolve the difficulty, because Allah the Exalted would hardly magnify one whose ruling is the ruling of the People of the Interval with such magnification as the verses and reports indicate. Also, the third point: in the histories it is stated that the aforementioned Alexander had Aristotle in the position of a vizier to him, and he used to consult him in important matters and act upon his opinion, and it is not mentioned in them that he met Khidr, peace be upon him, let alone taking him as a vizier, as is well known regarding Dhul-Qarnayn.

It was also objected that the mentioned Alexander did not, according to the reliable histories, undertake any journey toward the west, and the Ottoman writer Katib Jalabi, may Allah have mercy on him, drew attention to this. It is also said that he is Alexander the Roman, who is much earlier than the Greek, and he is called Dhul-Qarnayn the Elder. His name is said to be Marzuban ibn Mardaba, of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh, peace be upon him, and he was black. It is also said that his name was Abd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. It is also said: Mus'ab ibn Abd Allah ibn Qaynan ibn Mansur ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Azd ibn Awn ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan ibn Saba' ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. Some made this disagreement concerning the name of the Greek Dhul-Qarnayn after the view was mentioned that his name was Alexander ibn Philip (Fayluqus) was related, and what was mentioned concerning the name and lineage of the Roman was what was previously related from Ibn Kathir.

[Page 27 begins below]

Some of the verifying scholars held that the Greek Iskandar and the Roman Iskandar both refer to the same person, Dara the Younger (Dara al-Asghar). The history known as the Roman calendar, also called the Syriac or the Persian (ʿAjami) calendar, is commonly attributed to him. Its starting point, according to the well-known account, is the sunrise of Monday at the beginning of the first year of his reign, according to Ibn al-Banna'. Others say it begins from the beginning of the seventh year, the year of his departure to conquer the lands, as stated in the Zij (astronomical tables) of al-Sufi. Others say it begins from the beginning of the year in which he died, as stated in al-Mabadi wa al-Ghayat. Some of the verifying scholars attribute it to Seleucus, son of Tubukhus, who ordered the building of Antioch. Ibn Abi al-Shukr affirmed this view. Some scholars, such as Kalang Bik, refrained from attributing it to either of them because of the conflict among the evidences. Some scholars denied that there were two Iskandars among the earlier kings.

[Page 28 begins below]

Others claimed that there was only the Iskandar who defeated Dara and seized the kingdom of Persia. He said: Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an may be him, and may be someone else. What most scholars hold is that among the ancient kings there were two named Iskandar, about two thousand years apart, and that the first of them is the one meant by Dhu al-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned One). Some call him the Roman, and some call him the Greek. He is the one who lived a very long life. It was said that he lived one thousand six hundred years, and it was said two thousand years, and it was said three thousand years. Nothing reliable is reported about this.

Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, the astrologer, mentioned in his book called al-Athar al-Baqiyah ʿan al-Qurun al-Khaliyah (The Remaining Traces of Past Centuries) that Dhu al-Qarnayn is Abu Karb, named Ibn ʿUmayr ibn Afriqis al-Himyari. He is the one whom Tubbaʿ al-Yamani (the Tubba' of Yemen) took pride in, when he said:

*Dhu al-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim,*
*a king who rose high on earth, unrefuted.*
*He reached the west and the east, seeking*
*the means of kingship from a wise and guiding one.*
*He saw the sun setting at its sunset*
*in a spring of murky mud and black clay.*

Then he said: This view seems to be closer to the truth, because the rulers of Yemen were from the Himyarites, like Dhu al-Manar, Dhu Nuwas, Dhu Ruʿayn, Dhu Yazan and Dhu Judan. The writer Katib Jalabi chose this view, and he mentioned that Dhu al-Qarnayn lived in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that he met him in Mecca, the Honored, and they embraced each other. He also mentioned that the fame of the reign of the Greek Iskandar, the student of Aristotle, in the books of history is at its highest, as the Imam mentioned below. This is only because the time of the Greek is close to that of the one meant. Between them there are about two thousand years. The records of those ages were swept away by a great storm, and nothing remains to rely upon or to refer to in solving difficult questions. It may be said that the lack of widespread mention of him strengthens the view that he is the one asked about, since the purpose of the Jews in asking was testing, and testing is only good when the matter is hidden and not famous. Fame, especially when it is complete, is a sign of knowledge.

Many scholars held that Dhu al-Qarnayn lived in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him. Al-Azraqi mentioned that he became a Muslim at the hand of Abraham, peace be upon him, and circled the Kaʿba with him, and that Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, was the third of them. It is also narrated that he made the Hajj on foot. When Abraham, peace be upon him, heard of his arrival, he greeted him, prayed for him and gave him some advice. It was also said that a horse was brought for him to ride, but he said: I will not ride in a land where the Friend (Khalil, i.e., Abraham) is. At that moment, the clouds were made subject to him, and the means were extended to him. Abraham, peace be upon him, gave him good news of this. So a cloud would carry him, his troops and all their equipment whenever they wanted to attack a people. These scholars did not explicitly state that this Dhu al-Qarnayn is the Himyari one, but the implication of the words of Katib Jalabi is that he is.

It has been mentioned that Iskandar may be a title for the one mentioned, arabicized from *Alksandar*, and its meaning in the Greek language is "a good man." It may be said that the one who said: the name of Iskandar is Musʿab ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Qaynan ibn Mansur, and so on to the end of the previous lineage that ends at Qahtan, meant this Himyari man, not the Roman nor the Greek. But the transmitter made a mistake, because no one has said that the Romans are among the sons of Qahtan, and neither are the Greeks. True, Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi mentioned that Yunan was a brother of Qahtan. Abu al-'Abbas al-Nashi answered him in his poem, where he said:

*O Abu Yusuf, I have looked, and I have not found,*
*on close examination, an opinion from you that is sound, nor an agreement.*
*You have become wise among a people, whereas a man*
*who tested them all did not find among them a covenant.*
*Do you link heresy with the religion of Muhammad?*
*You have come with a monstrous thing, O brother of Kinda!*
*And you mix Yunan with Qahtan in error.*
*By my life, you have indeed placed a great distance between them.*

[Page 29 begins below]

It is mentioned in the books of history that the kings of Yemen, until Abyssinia overpowered them, were from the sons of Qahtan. An objection was raised against this view about Dhu al-Qarnayn: in the reliable history books, Sumayy ibn ʿUmayr ibn Afriqis is not found among the kings of Yemen. What is mentioned is Shamar, in the past-tense form from tashmir (exerting oneself), son of Afriqis. They did not mention between him and Afriqis any ʿUmayr. Some have said of him that he was Dhu al-Qarnayn, and they said: he is called Shamar Yarʿash, for a trembling that was in him. Perhaps Sumayy is a distortion of Shamar, and Ibn ʿUmayr is a distortion of Yarʿash. They also mentioned about his father Afriqis that he campaigned toward the west, into the land of the Berbers, until he reached Tangier, and moved the Berbers from the land of Palestine, Egypt and the coast to their present dwellings. He was the one who built Ifriqiya, and it was named after him. His reign lasted one hundred and sixty-four years. It is also said that he went toward Iraq and headed toward China, and that he uprooted the city now called Samarqand. They said: it is an arabicized form of Shamarkand. To this, Diʿbil al-Khuzaʿi alludes, in his words boasting of the kings of Yemen:

*They wrote the book at the gate of Marw,*
*and at the gate of al-Shash they were the scribes.*
*They named Samarqand after Shamar,*
*and there they planted the sprouting ones.*

It is said that he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn only because he had two braids (dhu'abatayn) that were his. According to Ibn Qutayba, his reign was one hundred and thirty-seven years. According to al-Masʿudi, it was fifty-three years. According to others, it was eighty-seven years. Furthermore, this (Shamar) was not Abu Karb. The one called by that kunya in some of the history books that we have seen is As'ad ibn Kalikarb, also called Tubbaʿ al-Awsat (the Middle Tubbaʿ). It is mentioned that he believed in our Prophet ﷺ before his mission, and he said about this:

*I testify concerning Ahmad that he*
*is a messenger from God, Creator of souls.*
*If my life were extended to his life,*
*I would have been his vizier and his cousin.*

They mentioned that he was harsh in oppression and frequent in campaigns, so his people grew weary of him, and they incited his son Hassan to kill him, and he killed him. It is not hidden that neither of these two persons can be the Dhu al-Qarnayn who is said to have met Abraham, peace be upon him. As for the first, they mentioned that he reigned after Yasir Yanʿum ibn ʿAmr, and Yasir reigned after Bilqis, the wife of Solomon, peace be upon him, who was his paternal uncle. How then can it be imagined that this one is that one, given the long time between Abraham and Solomon, peace be upon them both? As for the second, it is much later, and no one has called him Dhu al-Qarnayn, nor has any campaign in the east and west of the earth been attributed to him. I saw in some books that in the time of Manuchihr ibn Iraj ibn Afridun, Moses, peace be upon him, was sent, and the king of Yemen at that time was Shamar Abu al-Muluk, who was under his obedience. He ended. According to this too, it is not possible that this Shamar is the Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned earlier, and this is clear.

If you set aside all these views, on the basis that the reports about the kings of Yemen are confused, and one can hardly find two narrations that agree on them, and you take the view that there was a king among them in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, who was Dhu al-Qarnayn, out of good assumption toward the one who said so, then the matter becomes problematic from another angle. The books of history, all of them, state that Faridun lived in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that he divided the inhabited world among his three sons, as was mentioned earlier. How, then, can it be reconciled with this view that Dhu al-Qarnayn, a man from the kings of Yemen, was also in that time? The same problem arises if we say that Dhu al-Qarnayn is one of the two Iskandars, the Greek or the Roman, and we say that he too lived in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him. The summary is that the view that Faridun lived at that time and ruled the inhabited world, as in the general histories of the Persians, prevents the view that Dhu al-Qarnayn in that time was someone else. Rather, the view that one of the three, Faridun, Dhu al-Qarnayn of the Tubbaʿ line, or one of the two Iskandars, existed in that time, [and] his ruling of the inhabited world prevents the existence of any other of them in that time, and his ruling of the inhabited world as well.

It was objected that Dhu al-Qarnayn, whoever of these three he was, lived in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, because Nimrod was also in his time, and two believers and two unbelievers came to rule the world. The two believers are Solomon, peace be upon him, and Dhu al-Qarnayn. The two unbelievers are Nimrod and Bukhtnassar. There is no escape from this, if the report is correct, except by saying that the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, was long, and the rule of these two over the world occurred successively. But this, as you see, is far-fetched.

I saw in some books the view that Dhu al-Qarnayn ruled after Nimrod, and by this the problem is resolved. Someone said: What the history books require is that the report is not correct, or that it must be interpreted, for in none of them is there any mention of the universal rule of Solomon, peace be upon him, or of Nimrod or Bukhtnassar. The apparent reality is that it is not correct. It was also objected to his being in that time that he is not mentioned in the Torah, as the Jews today unanimously claim, and his existence, if he existed, would be extremely unlikely. So the apparent reason for his not being mentioned is that he did not exist. It was answered: We do not accept that he is not mentioned. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Muhammad, you mention Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the prophets only because you heard their mention from us. Tell us about a prophet whom God Most High did not mention in the Torah except in one place." He said: "Who is he?" They said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn." (The report continues.) Rather, the apparent meaning of their question is that he has a mention in their book. Their denial of it today is not to be considered. Moreover, what was mentioned as an objection is merely an expression of improbability, and it is not hidden that it is not a strong obstacle.

In sum, in the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn, hardly any of the views is free from "he said, and it was said." It seems to me that after you have become acquainted with the views, what supports them and what counts against them, you will choose that he is Iskandar son of Filaqus, the conqueror of Dara, and you will assert that he was called the Greek just as he was called the Roman, and that he was a believer in God Most High, who did not commit any act of unbelief, in belief, speech or deed. And you will say that his being a student of Aristotle does not prevent that:

*Moses, whom Gabriel raised, is an unbeliever,*
*and Moses, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger sent.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 83 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Ash'ari was a student of the Mu'tazilites, and the head of the Mu'tazilites was a student of al-Hasan (al-Basri). Aristotle (Arisṭū) differed with Plato (Aflaṭūn) on most questions, though he was his student. The claim that Aristotle was like a vizier to him, consulting him on important matters and acting on his opinion, does not indicate that he followed him in all his beliefs. For that, even if it is established, pertains to royal affairs and not to doctrinal questions. Moreover, Mulla Sadr al-Din al-Shirazi mentioned that Aristotle was a wise, devout monotheist who held that the world has a beginning and an end, alluded to by the words of the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when We will roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾. What has spread about him concerning the matter of the world is a delusion arising from a failure to understand his speech. The same applies to all the pillars of the philosophers. We do not concede that he did not travel toward the west, nor that al-Khidr was the vizier of Dhu'l-Qarnayn, although it is famous; and the absence of his being a vizier to him does not refute his being Dhu'l-Qarnayn. It has been said that he was a vizier to a king who was also called Dhu'l-Qarnayn, but he is other than this, and confusion arose in that. It has also been said: it is possible that he (peace be upon him) was among the wise men who were with him, and was like a vizier to him, and consulting others in some matters does not detract from that. He was then famous for wisdom rather than prophethood. In ancient eras, they used to call the prophet a wise man, and perhaps he was also known by another name. The historians' silence on any of this does not indicate non-existence. It has also been said: we do not concede the absence of mention; rather, their saying that al-Khidr was the vizier of Dhu'l-Qarnayn is a statement that he was the vizier of the aforementioned Alexander according to the one who says he is Dhu'l-Qarnayn. The fact that al-Khidr is, according to the more correct view, a prophet does not prevent this, and Alexander is not like that, as will come shortly, God willing, from the majority; because what is meant by his vizierate to him is managing his affairs and supporting him, and there is no harm in a prophet supporting and managing the affairs of a righteous king who is not a prophet, and this occurs among the Children of Israel, even if you do not choose what has been mentioned. If you choose that he is from the kings of Yemen or another Alexander, it will bind you either to saying that he was not in the time of Abraham (peace be upon him), or to saying that he was in his time after Nimrod, or with him but under his command, and Fareedun was not then (in that era). It will also bind you to setting aside the history books entirely, just as it binds you in the most complete manner if you choose that he is Fareedun.

And the closest view to me, for binding the adherents of the religions and sects who are astray, and for whom it is difficult to discard the history books and disregard what is in them entirely, given their abundance, their spread across the eastern and western lands, the diversity of their authors' religions, and the difference of their eras, is to choose that he is Alexander son of Philip, the conqueror of Darius:

"And what is upon me if I state my belief,
Leave the ignorant to think ignorance is enmity."

All the Jews are in agreement on this, but may God curse them: they attacked Alexander and attributed to him the most vile attribution, even though they mention that he honored them when he came to Bayt al-Maqdis and exalted their rabbis. And God knows best. Then, the question is not about the essence of Dhu'l-Qarnayn but about his affair. So it is as if it were said: "And they ask you about the affair of Dhu'l-Qarnayn." Say (to them) in reply: ﴿I will recite to you from him a remembrance﴾. The address is to the questioners, the pronoun ("him") refers to Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and "min" (from) is partitive, meaning from his news and stories. The prepositional phrase is an attribute of "dhikran" (a remembrance) which was placed before it, thus becoming a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). By "recitation" is meant "mention," and it was expressed in this way because it is a narration from the side of God, Mighty and Majestic; that is, "I will mention to you a reported news item from his news." It is also possible that the pronoun refers to Him, the Exalted, and "min" is initial (ibtidā'iyya), with no deletion, and "recitation" is in its literal sense: "I will recite to you from His side, glorified and exalted, concerning his affair, a remembrance," that is, a Qur'an. The "sin" is for emphasis and for indicating certainty, suitable given the prior affirmation of him (peace be upon him) and the confirmation of his promise's fulfilment: that is, I will not abandon recitation at all, as in his saying:

"I will thank 'Amr if my death is delayed,
For favours he did not bestow upon me, though they were great."

It is not for indicating that the recitation will occur in the future, as has been said, because this verse was not revealed by itself before the revelation of the whole story, but connected to what follows, for a while, when they asked him, upon him be prayers and peace.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, begins the recitation of the known reminder as it was promised. Here *tamkin* (establishment, empowerment) means enabling and preparing the means. One says *makkanahu* and *makkana lahu*, like *nasahtuhu* and *nasahtu lahu*, and *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*. Some distinguished between them: the first means making him capable, and the second means giving him capability and power. Because the two are linked in existence and close in meaning, each is used in place of the other. The same applies when *tamkin* is derived from *makan* (place), on the assumption that its *mim* is original. The meaning is: We gave him ability and power to act in the earth in terms of management, judgement, the large number of his soldiers, awe, and dignity. It was also said that his establishment in the earth means that God subjected the clouds to him, extended the means for him, and spread light for him, so that night and day were alike for him. There is a report about this, but I do not think it is sound. It was also said that his establishment was through prophethood and the performance of *mu'jizat* (miracles). Abu al-Shaykh, in *al-Azamah*, related the claim that he was a prophet from Abu al-Warqa', from Ali, may God honour his face. Muqatil held this view, and al-Dahhak agreed with him. It is opposed by what Ibn Abd al-Hakam included in *Futuh Misr*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, Ibn Abi Asim in *al-Sunnah*, and Ibn Mardawayh report by way of Abu al-Fadl: that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali, may God honour his face, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, "Was he a prophet or a king?" He said: "He was neither a prophet nor a king, but he was a righteous servant who loved God, so God loved him, and he advised God, so God advised him." Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from Ibn Zayd that he said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the two barriers, and he was a warner. I have not heard reliably that he was a prophet." Most scholars held that he was not a prophet, but some hesitated because of what Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim reported, and he judged it sound, from Abu Hurayrah who said: (The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was cursed or not, and I do not know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet or not, and I do not know whether the *hudud* (prescribed punishments) are expiations for their people or not.")

You know that this negation could not have remained for the Messenger of God ﷺ, so it is possible that he, peace and blessings be upon him, later came to know that he was not a prophet, as is indicated by what was reported from Ali, may God honour his face, for he would not say that except from hearing. This is supported by what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: "Ali, may God honour his face, was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn, 'Was he a prophet?' He said: 'I heard your Prophet ﷺ say: He was a righteous servant who advised God, so God advised him.'" ﴿And We gave him of every thing﴾: he was given of the important matters of his kingdom and of its aims connected to his rule. *Sababan* (a means) means a way that brings him to it, namely everything by which one reaches the goal, whether knowledge, power, or equipment, not knowledge alone, although some reports restrict it to knowledge. *Min* is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*), and what it explains is *sababan*. The sentence contains an implied genitive: "of the means of every thing." The meaning is the customary means. The objection that on this assumption each thing would have many means rather than one, while two means is not a thing, is answered. It was also permitted that *min* be causal (*ta'lilliyyah*), in which case there is no implied term. Some scholars chose this, so consider it. Some who held that he was a prophet argued from the verse for that view, but this is not correct, as is not hidden.

[p. 31]

The verse begins with ﴿so he followed﴾ read with a separate alif (أتْبَعَ, *atbaʿa*), and the fa' (فَ) is *faṣīḥah* (the "eloquent" fa', which marks an implied clause). The implied sense is: "so he intended to reach the place of sunset, and so he followed ﴿a way﴾ that would lead him to it." Perhaps he began by intending to reach the place of sunset because it was nearest to him. It was also said that he did so to observe the movement of the sun. This does not mean that the west is superior to the east, as some of the Maghribis (people of the Maghrib) claimed. As al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, there is no certainty that one of the two directions is preferred over the other, because the evidences conflict.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read ﴿fa-ittaba'a﴾ (فاتَّبَعَ) with a connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*, the hamza that is elided in continuous speech) and a doubled tā' (تَّ), and they did the same in the subsequent instances. Some scholars have inclined to the view that the two forms have the same meaning and both take one object. It was also said that *atbaʿa* with the separate alif takes two objects, and the sense here is: "he made a means to follow another means," or "he made a means follow his command," as in the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made a curse follow them in this world﴾. Abu Ubayd said: *ittaba'a* with the connecting hamza refers to travelling, while *atbaʿa* with the separate alif means "to overtake," as in the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Then a piercing flame pursued him﴾. Yunus said: *atbaʿa* with the separate alif is used for the diligent, swift, and eager pursuer, whereas *ittaba'a* with the connecting hamza only implies simple movement and tracing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 86 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun﴾, i.e., the furthest end of the earth towards the west, to the point that no one can pass beyond it, and he stood, as is apparent, on the shore of the Western Ocean, which is called Oceanus (Uqyanus), and in which are the islands called al-Khalidat (the Everlasting Isles), which, according to one opinion, are the starting point of longitudes. (He) found it, i.e., the sun, ﴿setting in a spring of black mud﴾, i.e., one containing ḥama'ah, which is black mud, from ḥamiat al-bi'r, meaning the well became full of mud when its mud increased.

ʿAbdullah, Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbaydullah, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and his son ʿAbdullah, Ibn ʿUmar, Muʿawiyah, al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read (ḥāmiyah) with a yā’, meaning hot. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, denied this reading when he first heard it. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through the route of ʿUthman ibn Abi Ḥāḍir, that Ibn ʿAbbas was told that Muʿawiyah recited (fī ʿaynin ḥāmiyah). He said to him: "We do not recite it except as (ḥamiah)." Muʿawiyah then asked ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr: "How do you recite it?"
He said: "As you recited it." I said: "The Qur'an was revealed in my house." So he sent for Kaʿb, and said to him: "Where do you find the sun setting in the Torah?" Kaʿb said: "Ask the people of the ʿazimah (the scholars), for they know it best. As for me, I have not found in the Torah that the sun sets in water and mud," and he pointed with his hand to the west. Ibn Abi Ḥāḍir said: "If I were with you both, I would support you with a statement that would increase your insight into (ḥamiah)." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And what is it?" I said: "The saying of Tubba' concerning Dhul-Qarnayn, mentioned in his longing for knowledge and his following of it: 'Dhul-Qarnayn had indeed...' up to the end of the three preceding verses, and the place of the evidence is his saying:
"He saw the sun's setting at its going down in a spring of a man of mud and black slime."
Ibn ʿAbbas said: "What is al-khalb?" Ibn Abi Ḥāḍir said: "Mud, in their language." He said: "And what is al-tha'ṭ?" He said: "Ḥama'ah (black mud)." He said: "And what is al-ḥarmad?" He said: "Black." Ibn ʿAbbas then called a boy and said: "Write down what this man says."

It is not hidden that there is no absolute contradiction between the two readings, since the spring may combine both descriptions, being full of black mud and having hot water; and since the reading with yā’ may originally derive from the hamzated form, its hamzah changed to yā’ because of the kasrah before it, although this only regularly occurs when the hamzah is quiescent. This is what was said. It has been objected that this is refuted by what took place between Ibn ʿAbbas and Muʿawiyah.

It is answered that, even if its authenticity is granted, its basis is transmission and arbitration in favour of preferring one of the two readings, and what you have heard apparently prefers the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father; and it seems that Muʿawiyah's return to the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, as al-Qurtubi mentioned, was for this reason.

Indeed, what Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ḥakim (who authenticated it) related "from Abu Dharr, who said: I was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a donkey, and he saw the sun when it set, and said: 'Do you know where it sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a spring that is hot, not with a hamzah,'" agrees with the reading of Muʿawiyah, and shows that ﴿fī ʿaynin﴾ is connected to "setting" (taghrubu), as is apparent. The statement of some over-strained interpreters that it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of (wajadahā) is not worthy of attention. What seems to have prompted them to say this is the difficulty that arises on the apparent meaning, for the body of the sun is greater than the body of the earth by many multiples, so how could it enter a spring of water in the earth? This is answered by saying that the meaning is that he found it so in the eye's perception, since there was nothing there but water, not that it is so in reality. This is like the rider of the sea, who sees it as though it rises from the sea and sets into it when he does not see the shore; and one who is in a wide smooth land likewise sees it as though it rises from the earth and sets into it. Nor is it objected to this that he expressed it with (wajada), and finding (wijdan) indicates existence, since (wajada) can mean "to see," as al-Raghib mentioned; so let it have this meaning here. Then, by "the spring of black mud" is meant either a spring in the sea, or the sea itself, and calling it a "spring" is not objectionable, especially since, relative to the greatness of Allah the Exalted, it is like a drop, however great it is in our sight.

Some of the Baghdadis claimed that (fī) here means ʿinda ("at"), i.e., it sets at a spring. Some people claimed that the verse is on its apparent meaning, and nothing is beyond Allah's power. We affirm the immensity of Allah's power, and we do not give heed to this view. Similar to it is what al-Ṭarṭūshī related, that a fish swallows it. Rather, this is a statement that only children and the like would accept, for it may remain rising in some regions for six months and setting likewise, as in a latitude of ninety degrees, and it may set within the span of an hour, and its light appears from the east in some latitudes, as in Bulgaria on some days of the year. So the sun, according to what is true, has never ceased moving, rising for some peoples and setting for others according to their horizons. Indeed, Imam al-Haramayn said: there is no disagreement on this.

What supports what has been mentioned is what Ibn Abi Hatim in his Tafsir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The sun is like a water-wheel that runs by day in the sky in its orbit; when it sets, it runs by night in its orbit beneath the earth until it rises from its east. And likewise the moon." Also what Ibn ʿAsakir related from al-Zuhri, that Khuzaymah ibn Hakim al-Sulami asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the warmth of water in winter and its coldness in summer. He said: "When the sun falls beneath the earth, it travels until it rises from its place. When the night is long, its stay beneath the earth increases, so the water becomes warm because of that. When it is summer, it passes swiftly, not lingering beneath the earth because the night is short, so the water remains cold as it was."

It is not hidden that this movement beneath the earth varies in the sun's being directly overhead of the feet according to horizons and times, so the feet are sometimes directly under it and sometimes not. What Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan supports this: he said: "When the sun sets, it turns in the orbit of the sky on the side behind the qiblah, until it returns to the east from which it rises, and it runs from there in the sky from its east to its west; then it returns to the horizon on the side behind the qiblah to its east. Thus it is subjected in its orbit, and likewise the moon." This hardly holds. What is problematic for what has been mentioned is what al-Bukhari related "from Abu Dharr, who said: I was with the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque at sunset, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where the sun sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and that is His saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾.'"

It is answered that the meaning is that it goes beneath the earth until it reaches the extreme of its descent, and when it arrives at the point directly opposite mid-day, at the zenith of the foot relative to the horizon of the people from whom it has set, that arrival is most like prostration. Indeed, there is no barrier to its prostrating there in a true prostration fitting for it. So "beneath the Throne" means a specific place directly opposite some parts of the Throne; otherwise it is at every time beneath the Throne and within it. This is based on the view that it is a spherical body encompassing all the spheres and celestial bodies, and by it directions are determined; this is the view of the philosophers. What relates to this will come, Allah willing, in Surah Ta-Ha. On what has been mentioned, the meaning of "its resting place" is the point at which its descent ends; it runs for each people toward that point, then begins to rise. Al-Khattabi said: It is possible that the meaning of its resting beneath the Throne is that it rests beneath it in a rest that we do not encompass, and there is nothing in its prostrating beneath the Throne each night that hinders its rotation in its course. End. The full discussion of this will come, Allah willing, in Surah Ya-Sin. In sum, this interpretation does not require the sun to leave its stipulated orbit, nor even its eccentric orbit, though its nearness and distance from the Throne differ relative to its motion in that eccentric.

Yes, some reports indicate that it leaves its place. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: when the sun sets, it is lifted up with it to the seventh heaven at the speed of the angels' flight, and it is held back beneath the Throne, and it asks permission from where it is commanded to rise. Then it is carried between the seventh heaven and the lowest of the degrees of the Gardens at the speed of the angels' flight, and it descends opposite the east, from heaven to heaven. When it reaches this heaven, that is when dawn breaks; when it reaches this aspect of the heaven, that is when the sun rises. Although our principles do not forbid it, since Allah's power extends to all possibilities and the splitting and rejoining of the sphere is not impossible in absolute terms, it cannot be squared with its setting being realised for some peoples and its rising for others, and its remaining risen for about six months in some latitudes, and other matters that are not hidden. So perhaps the report is not sound.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti has stated that Abu al-Shaykh related it through a weak chain. Moreover, the apparent sense of the narration of al-Bukhari and the narration of Ibn Abi Shaybah and those with him is that Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked twice; but in the second instance he referred the knowledge to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger ﷺ, seeking more benefit and out of extreme courtesy towards the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

﴿And he found near it﴾, i.e., near that spring on the shore of the sea, ﴿a people﴾, whose clothing, as is said, was the hides of beasts, and whose food was what the sea cast up. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They are a people called Nasak; none can count them for multitude except Allah the Exalted.

Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: They are a people of the offspring of Thamud, who used to dwell in Jabarsa, a great city with twelve gates, which in Syriac is called Jarjisa. Something similar is related from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn al-Sa'ib claimed that there were believers and disbelievers among them. What the majority hold is that they were disbelievers, so Allah the Exalted gave him the choice between punishing them by killing and calling them to faith. This is His saying: ﴿We said: O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish﴾ by killing from the outset, ﴿or you take among them goodness﴾, i.e., a course of goodness, by way of omitting an attribute or by the figurative use of the verbal noun for emphasis; that is, by calling them to the truth and guiding them to what brings success with the degrees (of the Garden). The position of "inna" with its clause is either in the nominative, as a subject or predicate, or in the accusative as object: either your punishing them occurs, or your command is to punish them, or you do or bring about their punishment; and likewise with "taking." Punishment is mentioned first because it is what they deserve at present for their disbelief. The expression "either you take among them goodness" rather than "either you call them," for example, is a hint toward preferring the second alternative. Those who hold that he was a prophet take the verse as evidence, and this view is, according to some, by means of an angel, and according to others, directly. Whoever does not hold that he was a prophet says: the address was through a prophet of that age, or it was inspiration (ilham) and not revelation (wahy), since that choice was in accordance with the law of that prophet. This is objected to on the ground that such a choice, involving the taking of lives, cannot be by inspiration without information, even if it agrees with a law. This is countered by the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, sacrificing his son in a dream, which is less than inspiration. But it is said: the dreams and inspirations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are revelation, as is explained in its proper place. The discussion here is on the assumption that he was not a prophet, and that is evident.

Ali ibn Isa said: The meaning is: "We said, O Muhammad," and "They said," that is, his soldiers who were with him, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn." So the verb "We said" was omitted, relying on the obviousness that he was not a prophet. This is a far-fetched interpretation. Close to it is the claim that the speakers were the scholars who were with him, who said it by their own ijtihad (independent reasoning) and after consulting him about it, and that God attributed it to him figuratively (majaz). The truth is that the verse is clear in indicating his prophethood. Perhaps it is even clearer in this than the indication of the words of God Most High, ﴿and I did it not on my own command﴾, for the prophethood of al-Khidr (peace be upon him). What seems to have prompted turning the verse away from its apparent meaning are the reports that indicate otherwise. Perhaps the better way of interpreting it is to say: the speech came through a prophet.

(Said) Dhu al-Qarnayn, to that prophet or to those among his close companions who were with him, after he had received the command of Allah, the Exalted, choosing the latter of the two options of choice, as he had been guided to: ﴿As for whoever wrongs himself﴾ by not accepting my call and persisting in the great wrongdoing he was upon, which is polytheism, ﴿we shall punish him﴾ with killing. The apparent meaning is that it was by the sword. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that he said: "His punishment was that he would place them in a bronze ox (baqar min safr), then fire would be lit beneath them until they were torn apart within it." This is far from soundness. He used the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), following the custom of kings. The attribution of punishment to himself is because he was the one who commanded it. The claim that this was done by him personally is very far-fetched. It has also been said that by the pronoun he meant Allah, the Exalted, and himself, and the attribution is by way of creation (khalq) and acquisition (kasb). This too is far-fetched, along with the association of Allah, the Exalted, with another in the pronoun, and there is the disagreement you know about. ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, (and He) ﴿will punish him with a terrible punishment﴾, meaning a severe, dreadful one, which is the punishment in the fire of Hell. "A punishment" (adhāban) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "yu'adhdhibuhu." It has also been said that it is governed by two verbs, it and "nu'adhdhibuhu." By "the terrible punishment" is meant, in view of the first, what was related from al-Suddi, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden. In His saying ﴿to his Lord﴾ rather than "to you" there is an indication that the preceding address was not by way of revelation to him, and that his dialogue was with the prophet or with his close companions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 88:

﴿As for him who believes﴾ in accordance with My call (and) does (ʿamalan) righteous deeds (ṣāliḥan) as faith requires (fa-lahu) in both abodes ﴿a reward, the best﴾, that is, for him is the best recompense, or the best deed, or the Garden. Jazaʾan (reward) is either a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence, placed before the subject (mubtadaʾ) for emphasis, or it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: he will be recompensed with it as a recompense. The sentence may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) or a parenthetical clause (muʿtariḍah) between the subject and the predicate preceding it. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: recompensed with it. Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) objected to this, saying that the Arabs hardly ever use the circumstantial accusative placed before its governing element except in poetry. Al-Farra' said: it is an accusative of specification (tamyīz).

Ibn ʿAbbas and Masruq read jazaʾan in the accusative without tanwin. Al-Mahdawi explained this as the dropping of the tanwin because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqaʾ al-sakinayn). Others explained it as the tanwin having been dropped because of the construct (idafah), with the subject omitted, its meaning being understood: for him is the recompense of the best reward.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq read it in the nominative with tanwin, as the subject (mubtadaʾ), with al-husna as its apposition (badal) and the prepositional phrase as the predicate.

Most of the Seven read it in the nominative without tanwin, explained as a subject in construct form (mubtadaʾ muḍaf). Abu ʿAli said: what is meant with the construct is the recompense for the good qualities he brought and performed, or what is meant by al-husna is the Garden, and the construct is like in "the abode of the Hereafter."

﴿And We shall say to him of Our command﴾, that is, of what We order, ﴿ease﴾, that is, easy, facilitated, not burdensome. Its estimated form is "one of ease," and the verbal noun is used for it as hyperbole. Abu Jaʿfar read yusran with two dammas wherever it occurs here. Al-Tabari said: what is meant by taking the good is the taking of captives, so he was given the choice between killing and capturing. The meaning is: either you punish with killing, or you treat them well by sparing their lives and taking them captive. What is related of the answer on this view is said to be of the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), since the apparent meaning is that God gave him a choice regarding killing them or capturing them, while they were disbelievers. So he said: as for the disbeliever, the strength of Islam is to be observed regarding him; as for the believer, one should not confront him except in what is required.

In al-Kashf it is said that on both views a subtle point is observed in placing what comes from God in the case of mercy, indicating that what comes from Him follows and completes, and placing what comes from Him in the case of punishment in keeping with the order of existence, with ascent, so that it may be more enraging. It seems he took "fa-lahu" etc. to mean "fa-lahu min Allah" etc., which is the apparent sense. He also permitted taking ﴿either you punish, or you take﴾ as distribution (tawzīʿ) rather than choice, the meaning, as is said: let your conduct toward them be either punishment or kindness; the first for one who remains in his state, the second for one who repents. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 89–90:

﴿Then he followed a way﴾, that is, a route returning from the west of the sun, leading to its east, ﴿until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾, meaning the place upon which the sun first rises from the inhabited part of the earth, that is, the furthest limit of the inhabited earth on the side of the east.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa and Ibn Muhaysin read (maṭlaʿa) with a fatḥah on the lām, and it is related from Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah. According to the muḥaqqiqun (verifying scholars), it is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), and the sentence is according to an elided genitive construction, meaning the place of the rising of the sun, and what is intended is a place upon which it rises. Al-Jawhari said that it is a noun of place, like (maksūr al-lām), so the two readings agree without any need to posit an elided word. Some masters of morphology (aʾimmat al-taṣrīf) have stated explicitly that (maṭlaʿ) occurs for place and time with both fatḥah and kasrah. The preference of the muḥaqqiqun is based on the fact that in the speech of the eloquent it is not attested with fatḥah except as a verbal noun, and there is no need to attribute the Qur'an to an anomalous form, since that may detract from eloquence. Abu Hayyan said: the kasrah is attested in a number of words and is contrary to analogy, for analogy requires that its present tense be (taṭliʿu) with a kasrah on the lām. Al-Kisa'i used to say: this is a dialect that has died out in many of the dialects of the Arabs, meaning that those Arabs who said (taṭliʿu) with a kasrah on the lām have gone, and (maṭliʿ) with kasrah remained as a noun of time and place on that analogy. End. So understand.

Then, the apparent state of Dhu al-Qarnayn, and that he had been given (a means) of everything, is that he reached the rising-place of the sun in a short period. It has been said that he reached it in twelve years, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, unless he stayed for a while during his journey, for the length of the inhabited earth can be traversed, by one travelling in a straight line, in a period much shorter than this, as is not hidden from one who knows surveying.

﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no screen against it.﴾ Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in (al-ʿAzama) related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I was told from al-Hasan, from Samura ibn Jundub, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the verse, 'for whom We had made no screen against it': a building that had never been built in, they would enter their burrows when the sun rose until the sun declined."

A group related from al-Hasan, and mentioned that it is the hadith of Samura, that their land does not bear building; when the sun rises they dive into the waters, and when it sets they come out grazing as livestock graze. It has been said: what is intended is that they have nothing to shield them of clothing or building. They are, as has been said, a people of the Zanj; it has been said they are of the Indians; and from Mujahid: those of the Sudanese who do not wear clothes at the rising of the sun are more numerous than the people of the earth. And from some of them: he went on until he passed China, and I asked about these people, and they said: between you and them is a journey of a day and a night. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 89–90:

﴿Then he followed a way﴾, that is, a route returning from the west of the sun, leading to its east, ﴿until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾, meaning the place upon which the sun first rises from the inhabited part of the earth, that is, the furthest limit of the inhabited earth on the side of the east.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa and Ibn Muhaysin read (maṭlaʿa) with a fatḥah on the lām, and it is related from Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah. According to the muḥaqqiqun (verifying scholars), it is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), and the sentence is according to an elided genitive construction, meaning the place of the rising of the sun, and what is intended is a place upon which it rises. Al-Jawhari said that it is a noun of place, like (maksūr al-lām), so the two readings agree without any need to posit an elided word. Some masters of morphology (aʾimmat al-taṣrīf) have stated explicitly that (maṭlaʿ) occurs for place and time with both fatḥah and kasrah. The preference of the muḥaqqiqun is based on the fact that in the speech of the eloquent it is not attested with fatḥah except as a verbal noun, and there is no need to attribute the Qur'an to an anomalous form, since that may detract from eloquence. Abu Hayyan said: the kasrah is attested in a number of words and is contrary to analogy, for analogy requires that its present tense be (taṭliʿu) with a kasrah on the lām. Al-Kisa'i used to say: this is a dialect that has died out in many of the dialects of the Arabs, meaning that those Arabs who said (taṭliʿu) with a kasrah on the lām have gone, and (maṭliʿ) with kasrah remained as a noun of time and place on that analogy. End. So understand.

It has been said that he reached it in twelve years, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, unless he stayed for a while during his journey, for the length of the inhabited earth can be traversed, by one travelling in a straight line, in a period much shorter than this, as is not hidden from one who knows surveying.

(كَذَلِكَ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn is such. The referent (ذَلِكَ) is what was described before, his reaching the west and the east and what he did. The purpose of this is to glorify him and to glorify his affair. Or it means: his authority over them is like his authority over the people of the west, in giving them choice and option. It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (مَصْدَر) of وَجَدَ, meaning: he found it rising in a manner of finding like his finding it setting in a muddy spring. Or it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun of لِنَجْعَلَ, meaning: We did not make for them a covering, a making like the making that is for you in what We have bestowed upon you of luxurious garments and lofty dwellings. This has the drawback that it does not come readily to understanding. Or it is an adjective of (سِتْرًا), and the meaning is as in the previous one, and there is in it what there is. Or it is an adjective of (قَوْمٍ), meaning: upon a people like that tribe over whom the sun sets, in disbelief and in judgment. Or it is an object (مَعْمُول) of (بَلَغَ), meaning: he reached its setting just as he reached its rising.

﴿And We had encompassed what was with him﴾ of the soldiers, the implements, and the means of sovereignty (خُبْرًا), meaning knowledge that related to its outward aspects and its hidden aspects. This, according to the first view, conveys further glorification of the matter, and that beyond what was described there is much that none can encompass except the All-Knowing, the Subtle, the All-Aware. According to the last view, it is an interpretation of what he endured in the journey until he reached, and the meaning becomes: We had encompassed what he met with and what came to him during his journey, as knowledge, or as glorification of the means that led him to it, in His saying, Exalted is He: "then he followed a way until, when he reached..." That is, We encompassed what was with him of the means that led to this remote place, which We had not given to anyone else. This, as in al-Kashshaf, is more evident than exaggeration. According to the second view, it is a completion that conveys the excellence of his choice, meaning: We encompassed what was with him of good reception and excellence of work, as knowledge. According to the third view, it is to show that it is so in visible appearance and in reality, and that none encompasses knowledge of it except God, Exalted is He. According to the fourth and fifth views, it is a concluding remark (تَذْيِيل) for the story, or for the two stories, so it does not contradict them, as it was supposed. According to the sixth view, it is a completion that confirms that he set among them his practice concerning whoever he found in the west of the sun.
