Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verses 92–93:

﴿Then he followed a way﴾, meaning a third route, cutting across between the east and the west and taking from the rising of the sun toward the north. ﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾, i.e., the two mountains. In al-Qamus he says: "al-sadd (sadd) is a mountain or a barrier." The use of sadd for it is because it blocks a gap (fajj) in the earth. It has been said that the application of this term to it here is by way of relation of proximity (ʿalaqat al-mujawara), but this is not the right view. Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub read al-suddayn with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (al-sudd, with *ḍamma*). According to what al-Kisa'i said, the meaning is one. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: al-sudd with *ḍamma* is the noun (ism), and with *fatḥa* it is the verbal noun (maṣdar). Ibn Abi Ishaq said: the first (with *ḍamma*) is what your eyes see, and the second (with *fatḥa*) is what your eyes do not see. ʿIkrima, Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and Abu ʿUbayda said: the first (with *ḍamma*) is what was created by God Most High without any human workmanship involved in it, and the second (with *fatḥa*) is what involved human workmanship. The way the *ḍamma*-form indicates this is that it has the sense of the passive participle (bi-maʿnā maf'ūl), and because its agent is not mentioned, it indicates that the matter is specific and that the mind does not turn to anything other than it; thus it implies that it is God Most High. As for the indication of the *fatḥa*-form that it is the work of servants, it is by way of inference from the indication of occurrence (ḥudūth), and portraying it as though one can see it being done right there, so let it be observed. This accords with what has human involvement, though it suffices in it that the grandeur of that (the *ḍamma*-form) is lost. You know that reading them both is evident in their agreement, and that the omission of the agent and the occurrence are two shared matters. Some reversed this and said: the *fatḥa*-form is what is from God's creation, since the maṣdar does not mention its agent, and the *ḍamma*-form is what is by the work of servants, since it has the sense of the passive participle; and what comes to mind from it is what servants did. Its weakness is evident. The accusative of (bayna) is as the object (maf'ūl) because it is the thing reached (maballūgh), and it is among the mutasarrifa adverbs (those that are inflected) so long as it is not compounded with another like itself. It has been said that it is an adverb of place (ẓarf), and the object is omitted, which is what he intended or something similar. These two barriers are in a place about ninety (degrees) in breadth toward the north, and this is what is meant by the word "end" (ākhir) with the *jarr* by the letter *yāʾ* in the Book of Ezekiel (Ḥizqiyal), peace be upon him. Some of the rabbis of the Jews have mentioned that Yajuj and Majuj are at the furthest north, where no one other than them can settle, and they are in a corner of it; but it was not established for them whether they are on the side of the north facing the east or on the side facing the west. This agrees with what we have mentioned regarding the location of the two barriers, and it is what Katib Jalabi inclined to. It has also been said: they are the two mountains of Armenia and Azerbaijan, and this has been attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Baydawi's approach tends toward it.

It has been objected that this is a delusion, and perhaps the attribution to the rabbi is not correct. Whoever holds this view also holds that the barrier of Dhu al-Qarnayn is the well-known barrier at Bab al-Abwab, and along with that it entails that Yajuj and Majuj are the Khazars and the Turks, contrary to what the historians say, for the builder of that barrier according to them is Kisra Anushirwan. It has also been said it was Isfandiyar, and that too no longer survives to this day, but was destroyed long before this. He claimed that the barrier and Yajuj and Majuj are there, and that all of them have become so subtle that they cannot be seen, as our contemporary the leader of the sect called the Kashfiyya, the Sayyid Kazim al-Rashti, sees it. This is a kind of raving and one of the signs of abandonment.

Ibn Sa'id said: that place, where the longitude is one hundred and sixty-three degrees and the latitude forty degrees, and in it, along this longitude and latitude, are the lands of the Khana and the Jinn, and there are no Yajuj and Majuj there. Yes, there is a great barrier there, about two hundred and fifty hours' journey in length, but it is not between the two barriers, nor is its builder Dhu al-Qarnayn, and what is said in describing his barrier can hardly be applied to it. What prevents saying this is also not hidden. It has been said: they are in a place on earth that we do not know, and how many unknown lands there are; perhaps great waters have come between us and that place. The claim of having surveyed all deserts and seas is not accepted, and it is possible by reason that there is in the ocean a land like America which has not been discovered until now, and the absence of finding does not entail the absence of existence.

[p. 38]

After the report of the Truthful (the Prophet) about the existence of these two barriers and what follows them, we are obliged to believe in that, like everything else he reported of possible things. Turning to the words of the deniers arises from weakness of religion.

﴿He found beside them﴾, i.e., beside the two barriers, ﴿a people﴾ (qawman), a nation of humankind. It has been said they were the Turks. Some claimed that the people were of the jinn, but this is a false claim, not far-fetched, as Abu Hayyan said.

﴿Who could scarcely understand any speech﴾ from the speeches of the followers of Dhu al-Qarnayn, or from the speeches of others than them, because of the strangeness of their language, its remoteness from the languages of others, and its lack of resemblance to them, together with their lack of quickness of understanding; for if it were close they would understand it, and if their quickness of understanding were great, they would have understood what was meant by the speech through the contextual clues and so would have learned it. The apparent meaning is to keep the word (qawl) on its obvious meaning.

Some claimed that al-Zamakhshari made it a metaphor for understanding in general, or for what is supposed to be said, so as to include signs and the like, where he said: that is, they can hardly understand it except with effort and hardship, through signs and the like. There is a point to consider in this. The apparent meaning is that understanding was inferred from the negation of "they can hardly" (la yakadūna), so that understanding is affirmed for them, but with difficulty. This rests on the view of some of them that the negation of *kāda* is an affirmation and its affirmation a negation, and this is not the preferred view.

In that case, Dhu al-Qarnayn's understanding of their speech and his making them understand him would be among the means that God Most High had given him. Some scholars said: "It is not far-fetched to say that the speakers were a people other than those who could not understand speech, and that they did not say this by way of translating for them. This is supported by what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud." In any case, there is no contradiction between this and ﴿they can hardly understand speech﴾.

And they said: ﴿O Dhu al-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog﴾ are two tribes from the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh (peace be upon him). Wahb ibn Munabbih and others affirmed this, and many later scholars relied upon it. Al-Kisa'i said in *al-'Ara'is*: Yafith travelled to the East, and five sons were born to him there: Jumar, Binrash, Ashar, Iskuwil and Miyashih. From Jumar come all the Slavs (*Saqaliba*), the Romans and their kinds. From Miyashih come all the types of non-Arabs ('Ajam). From Ashar come Gog and Magog and their kinds. From Iskuwil come all the Turks. From Binrash come the Fagjaq and the Greeks. It has also been said that both of them are from the Turks, and this was reported from al-Dahhak. In the words of some scholars, the Turks are among them, on the basis of what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through al-Suddi, from a strong report: "The Turks are a detachment (*sariyya*) from the detachments of Gog and Magog. They went out, then Dhu al-Qarnayn came and built the barrier, so they remained outside of it." In the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Qatadah, Gog and Magog are twenty-two tribes. Dhu al-Qarnayn built the barrier against twenty-one of them, and one of them was out on a raid, so it remained outside, and it was named the Turks for this reason.

It has also been said that Gog is from the Turks and Magog from the Daylam, and it has been said from the Jil. From Ka'b al-Ahbar it is reported that Gog and Magog are from the descendants of Adam (peace be upon him), without Eve. That is because he (peace be upon him) slept and had a wet dream, and his semen mixed with the dust, and Gog and Magog were created from it. Al-Nawawi, in his *Fatawa*, reported the view that they are the children of Adam (peace be upon him) without Eve from the majority of scholars.

The claim of the wet dream has been objected to on the ground that prophets (peace be upon them) do not have wet dreams. It is answered that what is negated is a wet dream about someone who is not lawful for them, so they may have wet dreams about their wives. Thus, perhaps the wet dream of Adam (peace be upon him) belonged to the permissible category. It is also possible that he (peace be upon him) had an emission without seeing himself having intercourse, as happens often to his children. It has also been objected that, according to this view, they would have existed before the Flood and would not have been destroyed by it. It is answered that the universality of the Flood is not agreed upon, so perhaps the one who says this is among those who do not hold to its universality. I myself consider this view to be a fable (*khurafa*). The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: This is not reported from anyone among the early scholars except Ka'b al-Ahbar, and it is refuted by the *marfu'* hadith that they are from the offspring of Nuh (peace be upon him), and Nuh is definitely from the offspring of Eve. It seems he meant by the hadith something other than what was reported from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Nuh had three sons: Sam, Ham and Yafith. From Sam came the Arabs, Persians and Romans. From Ham came the Copts, Berbers and Sudanese. From Yafith came Gog and Magog, the Turks and the Slavs." He stated that this (hadith) is weak. In the Torah, in the first book, in the tenth chapter, there is explicit mention that Gog is among the sons of Yafith. Some Jews claimed that Magog is the name of the land where Gog lived, and not the name of a tribe, but this is false according to the text. The apparent view is that they are two non-Arabic names, so their diptote status (*mana' al-sarf*) is due to being a proper noun and being non-Arabic. It has also been said that they are Arabic, from *ajja al-zalim*, meaning he ran quickly, and their original form has a hamza, as Asim, al-A'mash and Ya'qub in one narration recited, and this is the dialect of the Banu Asad. Their pattern is *maf'ul*, and the formation of *maf'ul* from that root, although it is intransitive, is [used] because it is transitive through a prepositional particle.

It has been said: if what was mentioned is a transferred (*manqul*) name, then it is for the transitivity; if it is an improvised (*murtajal*) name, then it is evident. Al-Akhfash said: If we take their *alif* to be original, then Yaʼjuj is *yafʻul* and Ma'juj is *maf'ul*, as if derived from *ajij al-nar* (the crackling of fire). Whoever does not hamza them takes the *alif* as an augment: Yajuj is from *yajajtu* and Majuj is from *majajtu*. Qutrub said: in the unhamzated form, Majuj is *fa'ul* from *al-majj*, and Yajuj is *fa'ul* from *al-yajj*. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Sakhawi said: the apparent view is that it is Arabic, its original form has a hamza, and omitting it is for lightness. It is either from *al-ajja*, which is disagreement, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging against one another﴾, or from *al-ajj*, which is rapid running, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and they will rush out from every elevation﴾, or from *al-ajja*, which is intense heat, or from *ajja al-ma'* when water becomes *ujuj*, that is, salty and bitter. End of quote. The reason for their diptote status on the view of their being Arabic is proper-noun status and feminine gender with regard to the tribe.

Al-'Ajjaj and his son Ru'ba recited *Ajuj* with a hamza in place of the *ya'*. It is sometimes said *Juj*, without hamza or *ya'*, outside the Qur'an. This form occurs in the book of Ezekiel (peace be upon him). ﴿Causing corruption in the land﴾, that is, in our land, by killing, destruction and all the other forms of corruption known from humans. It has also been said that it means taking and consuming the provisions. It is reported that they used to go out during the spring, leaving nothing green without eating it and nothing dry without carrying it away. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Habib al-Awsafi that he said: Their corruption was that they ate people. It has been argued from the attribution of *mufsidun* (corrupters) to Gog and Magog that the minimum of the plural is two, but this is nothing at all. ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute (*kharj*)﴾, that is, a payment from our wealth. The *fa'* is for deriving the offer from their corruption in the land. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talhah, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *kharajan* with an *alif* after the *ra'*. Both have the same meaning, like *nawl* and *nawal* (gift).

It has been said that *al-kharj* is the verbal noun, used for *al-kharaj* (tax). *Al-kharaj* is the term for what comes out. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-kharj* is levied on heads; one says: pay the *kharaj* of your land. Tha'lab said: *al-kharj* is more specific than *al-kharaj*. It has been said: *al-kharj* is the wealth that comes out once, and *al-kharaj* is repeated *kharj*. It has also been said: *al-kharj* is what one gives voluntarily, and *al-kharaj* is what it is obligatory for you to pay. ﴿On condition that you set up a barrier between us and them﴾, a barrier preventing them from reaching us.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr recited *saddan* with a *damma* on the *sin*.

[p. 39]

**(Page 40)**

He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better" (with *idghām*, assimilation of the two nuns). Ibn Kathir and Humayd recited it with *fakk* (disjoining the two nuns), so that the word is *makkananī*. The meaning is *alladhī makkananī*, "that which my Lord has established me in," and Allah, glorified is He, had made him *makīnan* (firmly established), able, possessing kingship, wealth and all other means. "Is better" means better than what you wish to give me as tribute (*kharj*), so I have no need of it. "So help me with strength" means help me with that which gives strength for the purpose: implements such as blocks of iron (*zubar al-ḥadīd*), or men, or both in general. The *fā'* (so) is to derive the command to help from the superiority of what Allah has established him in of their wealth, or from the non-acceptance of their tribute. "I will make" is the answer to the command. "Between you and them" puts the adverbial phrase's *muḍāf ilayhi* (the pronoun of the addressees, *you*) before its reference to the pronoun of Yājūj and Mājūj, to show complete concern for their interests, as they showed it in their saying: "Make between us and them a barrier" (*radman*), meaning a strong obstruction and a firm screen. It is greater than a *sadd* (dam or wall) and more secure. One says *thawbun murad-dam* ("a garment *murad-dam*"), meaning it has patches upon patches, and *saḥābun murad-dam*, meaning clouds thickly piled one upon another. It is mentioned that the original meaning of *radm* is to fill a breach with stones and the like. It is also said that it means to close any gap in general. From this is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Have the poets left any patched place (mutaraddam)?*

Then it was applied to what has been mentioned. It is also said that *radm* and *sadd* have the same meaning. The first view is supported by what Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "It is like the strongest barrier." On this view, he promised them relief in their request beyond what they hoped for, and this is what befits the status of kings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 96:

﴿Bring me blocks of iron.﴾ It is the plural of zubrah (زُبْرَة), like ghuraf (غُرَف) of ghurfah (غُرْفَة), and it means a great piece. The root meaning of zubar (زُبَر) is gathering together; from it comes zabartu al-kitab (زَبَرْتُ الكِتابَ), "I gathered its letters," and zubrat al-asad (زُبْرَةُ الأسَدِ), for the hair that gathers on the lion's shoulders. Al-Tasti (الطَّسْتِيُّ) reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq (نافِعَ بْنَ الأزْرَقِ) asked him about ﴿zubar al-hadid﴾, and he said: "A piece." He recited the verse of Ka'b ibn Malik (كَعْبِ بْنِ مالِكٍ):

They blazed upon them when their heat was kindled, with blocks of iron and stones, a fierce fire.

The request to be given the blocks does not contradict the fact that he did not accept anything from them, because the intended giving that was commanded is giving in exchange (for a price), or merely handing over and delivering. Even if what they gave him was not a gift of what belongs to them, it is a requested assistance. And even on the assumption that "ītā'" (إيتاء) means giving and not merely handing over, it is said: giving an instrument for work does not necessitate owning it, and even if one owned it, this would not count as a reward (ju'l), for it is the giving of wealth, not the giving of the like of this. What indicates that the intended meaning is not giving is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim (عاصِم): (ردما ائتوني) with the tanwin (تنوين) kasra and the hamza of waṣl (وصل الهمزة), from atahu bi-kadha (أتاهُ بِكَذا), meaning he came to him with such-and-such. In this reading, (زُبَرًا) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "bring me blocks of iron." The specification of blocks of iron in mention, rather than rocks, wood, and the like, is because the need for them is more pressing, since they are the strong pillar of the barrier, and their availability is rarer.

Al-Hasan (الحَسَنُ) read zubur (زُبُرَ) with a damma on the ba' like the zay. There is an ellipsis in the speech: that is, they brought it to him, and he began building it bit by bit, until, when he made the building between the two sides of the two mountains equal to them in height, the object of sawa (ساوى) and its subject include the pronoun of Dhu al-Qarnayn. It was also said that the subject is the pronoun of the barrier understood from the speech, meaning: they brought it to him, and he began to block with it until the barrier equalled the space between the two cliffs. From this is understood the equality of the barrier in height with the two mountains. The sadaf (صَدَف), as we have indicated, is the side of a mountain, and its origin is said to be inclination. It is related in al-Kashf (الكَشْف) that one does not call a single one sadaf until another meets it, and then he said: it is among the correlative nouns, like zawj (زَوْج, "pair") and similar. Abu 'Ubaydah (أبُو عُبَيْدَةَ) said: it is every great, elevated structure, but it is not hidden that this is not the intended meaning here.

Some claimed that what is intended here is the mountain, but this is contrary to what the majority hold. Qatadah (قَتادَةُ) read sawwa (سَوّى) from taswiyah (التَّسْوِيَةِ).

Ibn Abi Umayyah (ابْنُ أبِي أُمِّيَّةَ) reported from Abu Bakr from 'Asim (سُوُّوِيَ) in the passive voice. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and al-Hasan read al-sudufayn (الصُّدُفَيْنِ) with a damma on the sad and the dal, and this is the dialect of Himyar, just as opening both of them in the reading of the majority is the dialect of Tamim. Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin (ابْنُ مُحَيْصِنٍ), Abu Raja' (أبُو رَجاءٍ) and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman (أبُو عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ) read al-sudfayn (الصُّدْفَيْنِ) with a damma then sukun.

Ibn Jundab (ابْنُ جُنْدَبٍ) read it with a fatha then sukun, and this is related from Qatadah. In another narration from him, he read it with a damma then a fatha, which is the reading of Aban from 'Asim. al-Majshun (الماجِشُونُ) read it with a fatha then a damma.

(He said) to the workers (لِلْعَمَلَةِ): (Blow) — that is, with the bellows — upon the blocks of iron placed between the two cliffs, and they did so. ﴿Until, when he made it﴾ — that is, made what was blown upon into fire, meaning like fire in heat and appearance, so this is an eloquent metaphor. The attribution of the making to Dhu al-Qarnayn, though they performed the action, is to indicate that he is the foundation of this matter, and they are in the position of tools. (He said) — those who take charge of the copper, in melting and otherwise. It was also said that he said to those blowers, after they had blown on it until it became like fire and what he intended from them first was accomplished: (Bring me) — from those who take charge of the copper — ﴿pour upon it molten copper﴾ — that is: bring me molten copper, I will pour it upon it. So the first was elided because the second indicates it. The Basrans used this to argue that operating on the second in the case of tanazu' (تنازع) is preferable, for if qitran (قِطْرًا) were the object of ātūnī (آتُونِي), the object of ufrigh (أُفْرِغْ) would have to be pronounced and elided; and although that is permissible since it is a supplementary element (فَضْلَة), it causes ambiguity.

Qitr (القِطْر), as we have indicated, is melted copper, and this is the view of the majority. It was also said: melted lead; and it was said: melted iron, but this is not correct. al-A'mash (الأعْمَشُ), Talhah (طَلْحَةُ), Hamzah (حَمْزَةُ) and Abu Bakr, in a variant from him, read ātūnī (ائْتُونِي) with the hamza of waṣl, meaning "come to me," as if he were summoning them to help by hand at the time of pouring. The attribution of the pouring to himself is for the secret I have just paused over; and likewise the discussion of the word uj'al (اجْعَلْ) and his word sawa (ساوى) according to one of the two opinions.

The Qur'anic quotations are rendered in the translation with their ﴿ ﴾ markers, and the Arabic grammatical discussions are kept in Arabic script.

[p. 42]

﴿فَما اسْطاعُوا﴾ With the deletion of the ta' of the ifti'al form, for lightness and to avoid the meeting of two letters close in articulation point, namely the ṭā' and the tā'.

Ḥamzah and Ṭalḥah read it with the idghām (assimilation) of the tā' into the ṭā'. This involves joining two consonants at rest (jam' bayn al-sākinayn) contrary to its usual rule, and Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) did not permit it, though a group of scholars did permit it. Al-A'shā, on the authority of Abū Bakr, read فَما اصْطاعُوا (fa-mā iṣṭāʿū) with the sīn changed into ṣād because it is adjacent to the ṭā'. Al-A'mash read فَما اسْتَطاعُوا (fa-mā istaṭāʿū) with the tā' and without deletion. The fa' is a fa' faṣīḥah, meaning: so they did what they were commanded regarding bringing the molten copper or coming to it, and he poured it over it, so it mixed and its parts adhered to one another, and it became a solid mountain. Then Yājūj and Mājūj came and intended to climb over it and pierce it, but ﴿they could not scale it﴾, that is, they could not climb over it and ascend it because of its height and smoothness. It was said: its height was two hundred cubits, and it was said: one thousand eight hundred cubits. ﴿Nor could they make a breach in it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. It was said: its width was fifty cubits, its foundation had reached the water, and into it had been placed rock and molten copper, and the blocks of iron were used for building above the ground. It is not hidden that pouring molten copper upon them after the heat of the fire had affected them until they became like fire, together with what they mentioned that the extension of the barrier in the earth is one hundred farsakhs, cannot be completed except by a divine command outside the normal course, such as the turning aside of the effect of the great heat of the fire from the bodies of those who directly perform the work. Otherwise, such heat ordinarily is something no living creature can be near, and likewise blowing upon those great and numerous blocks until they become fire. It is possible that each of the two matters was by means of strange instruments or deeds which he or someone with him was given, which hardly anyone today knows. The ancient and even later philosophers (ḥukamāʾ) have wondrous works which they reach by strange instruments, nearly beyond the bounds of reason. This is beyond doubt, so let what happened to Dhū al-Qarnayn be of that kind. It was also said: its construction was of rocks linked together by hooks of iron and molten copper poured into their hollows, such that no gap at all remained there.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Bakrah al-Shaffī that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have seen the barrier of Yājūj and Mājūj." He said: "Describe it to me." He said: "Like a striped cloak, one stripe black and one stripe red." He said: "You have seen it." The apparent meaning is that the seeing was by sight, not in a dream, and it is a strange matter if the report is sound. As for what some have mentioned, that al-Wāthiq bi-Llāh al-ʿAbbāsī sent Sallām the interpreter (al-Turjumān) to investigate this barrier, and he went towards the north in a long story until he saw it and returned, and he related to him some of its matters, the reliable historians have weakened it. In my view, it is a lie, because of what it contains that the verse rejects, as will be clear to one who examines it in detail.

It is not hidden how subtle is the use of the tā' in istaṭāʿū here.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 98:

﴿He said﴾: that is, Dhu al-Qarnayn said to those near him from the people of that land and others, "This" refers to the barrier (sadd). It has also been said that it refers to his being empowered to build it, and the preference goes to the first reading, so that the referent of the later pronoun is unified; that is, "This is what appeared at my hands and came about through my effort, namely the barrier, whose nature is what has been mentioned of sturdiness and difficulty of access." ﴿A mercy﴾: that is, a result of a great mercy, and it was expressed by it for emphasis. ﴿From my Lord﴾ upon all of His servants, especially upon its neighbours. That the barrier is a mercy to the servants is evident. If you take the reference to be to the empowerment, then its being a mercy to them is that it is a means to that. Perhaps the former reading is also preferred, since the latter requires this interpretation, although the matter there is easy. In the reports about it with what has been mentioned there is a notification, according to what has been said, that it is not among the effects normally produced by the activity of creatures, but is rather pure divine beneficence, even though it appeared through human activity. In the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) there is an education in the meaning of mercy. Ibn Abi Abla recited ﴿this is a mercy﴾ with the demonstrative in the feminine form, and it is explained as observing the predicate, or as taking what is pointed to to be the power and strength to do that. ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes﴾: that is, the time of His promise, may He be exalted; the statement therefore elides a modifier, and the attribution to the promise is metaphorical, while the attribution to its time is literal. It is also permissible that "the promise" means "the promised thing," namely its time or its occurrence, in which case there is no elision and no metaphor in the attribution, but rather a metaphor in the temporal reference. What is meant by the time of that is the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that it is the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. This has been objected to, on the grounds that the noble composition does not support it. The meaning of its coming is what encompasses its coming and the coming of its precursors, such as their emergence, the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the like, not merely the imminence of its occurrence, as al-Zamakhshari and others said, since some of the matters that will be related occur after its coming, necessarily. ﴿He made it﴾: that is, the barrier referred to, together with its sturdiness and firmness, ﴿levelled﴾ (dakka'), with the feminine extended alif, and the qualified noun is a feminine implied, that is, a level ground. Some said: the statement is on the assumption of an elided modifier, that is, "like a levelled [thing]," which is a she-camel with no hump; and the assumption is necessary, because the barrier is masculine and is not described by a feminine. Other than the Kufans read ﴿dakkan﴾ as a verbal noun from "I levelled it," and it is in the sense of the passive participle, that is, "levelled, made even with the ground," or it is in its own sense, and the description with it is for emphasis. The accusative is on the basis that it is a second object of "made," which is in the sense of "rendered." Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that it is in the sense of "created," but this is nothing.

This making, at the time of the coming of the promise, is with the coming of some of its precursors. In it is a demonstration of the greatness of His power, may His majesty be exalted, after the demonstration of the breadth of His mercy, mighty and majestic is He. His knowledge of this making, according to what has been said, is among the consequences of His knowledge of the coming of the Hour, since among its precursors is the levelling of the lofty and firmly rooted mountains, for it cannot be completed without them. His gaining knowledge of its coming was from prophets who were in his era, peace be upon them. It is also permissible that knowledge of all of that was through hearing from the Prophet; likewise the knowledge of the coming of the time of their emergence, on the assumption that this is meant by the promise. It is permissible that it be from ijtihad, and it is permissible that it be from hearing.

In the Book of Ezekiel, peace be upon him, there is an announcement of their coming at the end of time from the end of the ... with a ya' in many nations which none can count except God Most High, and their corruption in the earth, and their intention toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and their destruction to the last of them in its wilderness by kinds of punishment. He, peace be upon him, was before Iskandar, the conqueror of Dara. If he is Dhu al-Qarnayn, then it is possible that he was informed of that and so gained knowledge of what has been mentioned; and God Most High knows best. Then, in the statement there is an elision, that is, it continues until the end of time; so when the promise of my Lord comes, He makes it levelled. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾: that is, His promise, glorified is He, the well-known one, or whatever He has promised, mighty and majestic is He, so that this enters primarily; ﴿true﴾, established without doubt, certainly to occur. This sentence is a concluding remark by Dhu al-Qarnayn on the conditional clause he mentioned, and an emphasis of its content. It is the last of what is related of his story.

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿And We left some of them﴾, is a sentence sent forth from His Presence, glory be to Him. According to some verifiers, the plural pronoun in the object refers to all creatures. The verb "left" (tark) here means "made" (ja'l), and it is one of the words with opposite meanings (addad). It is coordinated with His statement, ﴿made it level, crushed﴾, and it serves to confirm its content. That this is related from Dhul-Qarnayn does not harm this reading. The meaning is: We made some of the creatures on that day, that is, the day when the Promise came with the arrival of some of its beginnings, ﴿surging against one another﴾, that is, against others among them. "Surging" (mawj) is a metaphor for agitation, meaning they will be agitated like the agitation of the sea, so that humans and jinn will mingle from the intensity of the terror. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas. Perhaps this is because of great events that occur before the first blast.

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to people, and the meaning is: We made some people on the day the Promise came, with the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, surge against others out of their terror of them and their flight from them. However, this is remote. It has also been said that the pronoun likewise refers to people, and the meaning is: We made some people, on the day the barrier was completed, surge against some of them, to look at it and to marvel at it. It is not hidden that this is itself a matter to be marveled at.

Abu Hayyan said: The more apparent view is that the pronoun refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. That is: We left some of Ya'juj and Ma'juj surging against some other of them when they come out from the barrier, crowding into the lands. This will be after the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him). In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, after mentioning the Dajjal and his destruction at the gate of Lud at his hand (peace be upon him), it says: "Then 'Isa (peace be upon him) will come to a people whom Allah the Exalted has protected from the Dajjal. He will wipe their faces and tell them of their ranks in Paradise. While they are thus, Allah the Exalted reveals to 'Isa (peace be upon him): 'I have brought forth servants of Mine that no one has the power to fight. So lead My servants to Mount Tur.' Then Allah the Exalted sends Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and they come out upon the people. They drink up the water, and the people shelter from them in their fortresses. They gather their livestock into them, and they drink the waters of the earth, until some of them pass by a river and drink what is in it, until they leave it dry. Then whoever passes after them will pass by that river and say, 'There was water here once.' 'Isa, the Prophet of Allah, and his companions are besieged until the head of an ox, or the head of a donkey, is better for one of them than a hundred dinars."

In the narration of Muslim and others: "They will say, 'We have killed those on the earth. Come, let us kill those in the heavens.' So they shoot their arrows toward the sky, and Allah the Exalted returns them to them stained with blood, as a trial and a tribulation. The Prophet of Allah and his companions will then turn to Allah the Exalted, and He sends upon them the nagaf in their necks, and they become dead in the morning."

In the narration of Dawud: "like the nagaf in their necks, and they become dead like the death of one soul, with no sound heard from them. The Muslims will say, 'Is there not a man who will sell himself for us, to go and see what this enemy has done?' A man from among them will then go out, seeking reward and having prepared himself for being killed. He descends and finds them dead, some upon others. He calls out, 'O company of Muslims, rejoice! Allah the Mighty and Majestic has sufficed you against your enemy.' They then come out from their cities and fortresses and release their livestock to pasture, and their pasture is nothing but their flesh, and the animals give thanks as they have never given thanks for anything. The Prophet of Allah 'Isa (peace be upon him) and his companions descend to the earth, and they find no place a hand's breadth free except that it is filled by their stench and their decay. They cry out to Allah the Exalted, and Allah, glory be to Him, sends a yemeni wind, dusty, which becomes distress and smoke upon the people, and they are struck by a cold in the head. Allah removes what is upon them after three days, and the earth has cast their carcasses into the sea."

In another narration: "The Prophet of Allah 'Isa (peace be upon him) and his companions turn to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He sends birds like the necks of Bactrian camels, which carry them and throw them wherever Allah the Exalted wills." In another narration: "and they throw them into the sea," and in another: "into the Fire." There is no contradiction, as becomes apparent with minimal reflection. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic sends rain that leaves no house of clay or of wool, and it washes the earth until He leaves it like a slippery rock. Then it is said to the earth: "Bring forth your fruit and return your blessing." On that day a band will eat from a single pomegranate and shelter beneath its peel, and blessing will be placed in the milk; a single milch camel will suffice a large company of people. The Muslims will light fires with the bows, arrows and shields of Ya'juj and Ma'juj for seven years. Perhaps Allah the Exalted preserves that in the valleys and places of torrents as an increase in the joy of the Muslims, or He preserves it wherever they perished and does not cast it with them wherever He wills, for nothing can overpower Allah the Exalted.

The hadith indicates their great multitude. What confirms this is what Ibn Hibban included in his Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the least that any one of them leaves from his loins is a thousand offspring." Some have interpreted this as referring to long life.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said that there has been disagreement about their number and attributes, and nothing has been authentically established concerning that. The most astonishing thing related about this is the statement of Makhul: "The earth is a journey of a hundred years, eighty of which belong to Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and they are two nations, each nation being four hundred thousand nations, no nation resembling another." This is a false statement. Similar to it is what is related from Abu al-Shaykh, from Abu Umamah: "The world is seven climes, six of which belong to Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and the rest is one clime." This is the speech of one who knows neither the earth nor the climes.

Yes, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) related through al-Bakkali, from Ibn 'Umar, that Allah the Exalted divided mankind into ten parts, nine of which are Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and one part is the rest of humanity. However, I have not found its authentication by anyone other than al-Hakim, and his authentication is well known. From what has preceded and what will follow, if Allah the Exalted wills, it becomes known that the claim of some people, that they are the Tatars who caused much corruption in the lands and killed the righteous and the wicked, is false. By my life, that claim is among the greatest errors, even though there is a complete resemblance between Ya'juj and Ma'juj and those disbelievers, which is not hidden from those who are acquainted with the reports of what will be and what has been. The refutation of what some people claim, that they are the Tatars, is established.

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. The apparent meaning is that the intended blast is the second blast, because it is the one appropriate to what follows. Perhaps the first blast is not mentioned because it is a general calamity in which there is no state specific to the disbelievers. It has also been said: so that there is no separation between what occurs in the first creation of the states and terrors and what occurs in the last creation.

The Sur is a horn; reports concerning its description include what bewilders the intellects. It is authentically related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How can I be at ease, when the holder of the horn has put the horn to his mouth, bent his forehead, and inclined his ear, waiting to be commanded to blow?"

Abu 'Ubaydah claimed that it is the plural of ṣūrah (form) and ayd, and that in the reading of al-Hasan it is read as al-ṣuwar with the vowel fatha on the waw, so it would be like sūrah and sūr. The refutation of this is more apparent than to be hidden. Therefore Abu al-Haytham, as reported from him by the Imam al-Qurtubi, said: Whoever denies that the Sur is a horn is like one who denies the Throne, the Bridge and the Balance, and seeks interpretations for them. He mentioned that the nations are agreed that the one who blows into it is Israfil (peace be upon him).

﴿And We gathered them﴾, that is, the creatures, after their joints had been scattered and their bodies torn apart, into one plain for reckoning and recompense, ﴿a gathering﴾, that is, a wondrous gathering whose reality cannot be grasped.

"And We shall present Hell (ʿaradnā Jahannam) on that Day to the disbelievers (lil-kāfirīn) — presented openly and manifestly, (ʿardan), that is, a terrible, awesome presentation whose extent cannot be measured."

Wait, I should translate faithfully. Here is the translation:

**﴿And We shall present Hell﴾** — we made it apparent and manifest. **(On that Day)**, that is, the Day when We gather all creation together **(for the disbelievers)** from among them, in that We placed it in a position where they can see it and hear its roaring of rage and its groaning **(in presentation)**, that is, a dreadful, awesome presentation whose magnitude cannot be measured. The specification of the presentation to them, although it is in view of all the people of the gathering, is because it is for their sake specifically.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 101:

﴿Those whose eyes were﴾ (in this world) ﴿in a covering﴾ thick and a heavy veil, enveloped by it on all sides, ﴿from My remembrance﴾: from the signs which lead people of insight (ulu al-absar), who reflect upon them, to My remembrance through Tawhid (affirming God's oneness) and Tamjid (glorifying Him). Thus "remembrance" is a metaphor for the aforementioned signs, by way of mentioning the effect and intending the cause (itylaq al-musabbab wa iradat al-sabab). In this there is the implication that whoever does not look in a way that leads him to the remembrance of exaltation is as if he had no sight at all, and this is the purpose of the figurative usage.

It has been said: the speech contains an elision of a modifier, i.e. "from the signs of My remembrance," but this is not the right view. It is also permissible that "the eyes" means the inner insights of the heart, and the meaning would be: their insights were in a covering from remembering Me in a manner befitting My majesty, or from My remembrance which I sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also permissible that it be specified as the Noble Qur'an. (And they were) despite that ﴿unable to hear﴾: a negation of their hearing in the most complete form, and therefore he turned away from "and they were deaf," which is shorter, to it. The meaning is that they, despite that, were like those who have completely lost the faculty of hearing, and this is an exaggeration in depicting their aversion to hearing what would guide them to what benefits them, after depicting their blindness to the signs seen by the eyes. Therefore there is no need to posit an elision of "remembrance," intended to mean the Qur'an or all divine laws, for after the aforementioned remembrance in the noble structure was first specified to the visible signs, it does not become an indicator for this elision. Ibn Hisham said in al-Mughni: the verbal indicator must correspond in meaning to the elided item, so "Zayd darib wa 'Amr" (meaning "Zayd is a striker and 'Amr [is a striker]") is not valid, where the first darib has its well-known meaning and the second means "traveler." Positing that and intending from it the meaning of the signs figuratively, given that the signs are realized within the inimitable speech, its condition is not hidden, and so is the condition of intending the signs; then intending the inimitable speech from it figuratively after a figure is more evident. Some of the scholarly investigators said: the positing of that is only by the indicator of His statement, exalted is He, "hearing," and that the disbelievers are in this state, not by the indicator of mentioning "remembrance" before, so that Ibn Hisham's statement might come in. It is not hidden that there is no dispute over positing "remembrance" in the sense of the Qur'an or the divine laws when what is meant by the aforementioned remembrance is that.

The relative pronoun is an attribute of "the disbelievers," or a substitute for them, or an explanation, brought to censure them by what is within the scope of the relative clause, and to indicate its being the cause of what befell them of being presented to Hell.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 18, verse 102:

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾ that is, they disbelieved in Me, as His saying ﴿My servants﴾ indicates. Al-husban (reckoning, supposing) here means al-zann (thinking, supposing). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read it as ﴿Afa-zanna﴾ (Do they then think). The hamza is for censure and rebuke, in the sense of denying the reality and deeming it abhorrent. The fa' is coordinating with an implied element that the relative clause makes explicit, according to the way the denial and rebuke are directed, and to all the conjoined elements together, as preferred by Shaykh al-Islam. The meaning is: Did they disbelieve in Me despite My exalted station, and so reckon ﴿that they could take My servants﴾ from among the angels, ʿIsa and others of the near ones, peace be upon them, as is indicated by the idafa (possessive construction), since in such expressions the idafa is most often for honouring the annexed noun.

Qatadah limited what is meant by that to the angels. The apparent meaning, however, is that it includes them and others of those we have mentioned, and Abu Hayyan and others preferred this.
Page 46
It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that what is meant is the devils, but this is far-fetched, and perhaps the report is not sound. It is related from Muqatil that what is meant is the idols, and that is as you see. Some verifiers permitted that it may mean what includes those mentioned and the idols and all other false objects of worship, such as the stars and others, by way of taghlib (predominance of one group). Perhaps the context requires that the idafa here is not for honour, i.e., did they suppose they could take My servants, who are under My dominion and authority, ﴿besides Me﴾, that is, passing beyond Me, as ﴿awliya'﴾ (protectors), that is, as objects of worship, or as helpers to them against My might? What follows "an" is taken to fill the place of the two objects of "hasiba" (to think). That is, did they suppose that they would take them as protectors? The point of the denial was that they take them thus, but the reckoning was introduced for emphasis. It is also said that what is meant is what has been mentioned, in the sense that this is not taking at all, since taking happens only from both sides, and those who take them are far from their protection, as in their saying: "Glory be to You, You are our protector, not them" (25:18). It is also said that "an" and what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun as the first object of "hasiba", and the second object is omitted, i.e., did they suppose their taking them would be beneficial to them, or a cause for lifting the punishment from them, or something similar? This is based on permitting the omission of one of the two objects in the category of ʿalima (to know), which is the view of some grammarians, and it was objected that this grants the taking itself and counts it in some respect; the better course is what is free of that.

Moreover, in al-Kashshaf it is stated that the correct view is that His saying ﴿fa-hasiba﴾ is coordinated with ﴿kanat﴾ and ﴿kanu﴾, indicating that the reckoning arises from blindness and deafness. The hamza of denial is applied to it as censure upon censure, and cutting it off from what it is coordinated with, in form but not in meaning, to signal the emphasized independence of the censure, as though it were said: they do not remove what they have of the veils of blindness and deafness, and they add to these the reckoning that follows from them. His saying ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, for added censure. End of quotation. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, after citing what was mentioned up to the words "as though it were said", it is stated that this is refuted by the omission of the pronoun and the mention of an attribute other than blindness and deafness, since these two are presented as innate conditions of theirs and were not mentioned as their voluntary acts, such as their reckoning, so that it could be made a consequence of them. Also, it is an old trait of theirs that cannot be made to arise from their deafness to the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Restricting the denial to their later reckoning, apart from those two, is a forced interpretation that is not hidden. End of quotation. This is not free of scrutiny. Reflect.

ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Zayd ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, and al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, Nuʿaym ibn Maysarah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywah, Masʿud ibn Salih, Ibn Kathir, and Yaʿqub with a variant from them both read ﴿Afa-hsaba﴾ with sukun on the sin and damma on the ba', annexed to ﴿alladhina﴾. This is explained as: ḥasiba is a subject (mubtada'), meaning muhsib (sufficient), i.e., is it sufficient for them that their taking My servants besides Me as protectors ("an yattakhidhu") is their predicate. This indicates the utmost censure, because it makes that the total of their provision on the Day of Reckoning, and what suffices them in place of the other beliefs and virtues that are indispensable for one who succeeds on that Day. Al-Zamakhshari made the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb the agent of ḥasiba, because it relies on the hamza, and the active participle, when it relies, equals the verb in governing. Abu Hayyan objected that ḥasiba is interpreted as an active participle, and what was mentioned is specific to the explicit descriptive form. Then he pointed to its answer: Sibawayh permitted, in "I passed by a man better than his father," and "a man equal to him are good and evil," and "a man whose father is his companion," and "a man, indeed he is a man," and "a man, enough for you of a man," the nominative case by means of interpreted attributes. It is also mentioned that they permitted, in "I passed by a man, father of ten, whose father," the raising of "his father" by "father of ten," since it means "parent of ten." In that case there is no objection to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned.

﴿Indeed We have prepared Jahannam﴾, that is, We have readied it, which is clear that it is created today, ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ known, the speech turning away from the pronoun as censure of them, and indicating that this preparation is due to their disbelief, which includes their false reckoning, ﴿as a nuzul (provision)﴾, that is, something they enjoy upon arriving, namely what is prepared for a nazil (guest), that is, a visitor, of the food that is present. A group of exegetes chose this. According to what is said, in this there is a rebuke of them for their reckoning, and a mockery of it, since their taking them as protectors was of the kind of preparing equipment and provisions for the Day of Return. So it is as if it were said: We have prepared for them, in place of what they prepared for themselves of equipment and treasure, Jahannam as equipment. In the mention of nuzul there is a hint that for them, beyond Jahannam, is punishment of which it is a model. The verse "Their recompense is Jahannam" (98:6 and similar) does not contradict this, since what is meant there is that it is their recompense with what is in it. Reflect. Al-Zajjaj said: nuzul is the place of descending, and this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also said that it is the plural of nazil, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal).

Abu Haywah and Abu ʿAmr, with a variant from him, read ﴿nuzlan﴾ with the zay sukun.

(Say), O Muhammad: ﴿Shall We inform you﴾ is an address to the disbelievers. If the interrogative is taken as seeking permission, there is in it some of the mockery that it contains. The plural form of the speaker ("We inform") is said to be used to specify this from the outset, and to announce that the news is known to the believers as well. ﴿Of those most losers in deeds﴾ (bi-l-akhsarīna aʿmālan) is in the accusative as a *tamyīz* (specification, a noun that clarifies the item to which a comparative or a verb refers). It is in the plural, although the original rule for the *tamyīz* is that it be singular, and the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) is inclusive of both the few and the many, as the grammarians have mentioned. The plural is used to announce the variety of their deeds and to intend that the loss include all of them. It is also said to be a plural because what the grammarians have mentioned applies only when the verbal noun remains in its verbal-noun status. However, when it is construed as an active participle (*ism fāʿil*), it is treated in the manner of one, and here *aʿmāl* functions with the meaning of *āmil* (doers), so it is pluralized as *aʿmāl* and the intended sense is "doers," and an adjective may serve as a *tamyīz*, as in the saying: *lillāhi taʿālā darruhu fāris(an)* (may God the Exalted be praised for his horsemanship).

Some have claimed that *aʿmāl* is the plural of *āmil*, but this was objected to on the grounds that the plural of *fāʿil* on the pattern *afʿāl* is rare, and some grammarians have denied it except in specific words such as *ashhād*, the plural of *shāhid* (witness). It has also been said that it is the plural of *ʿamil*, on the pattern of *katif*, with the meaning of *dhū ʿamal* (one possessing deeds), as in the *Qamus* (Lexicon), but this is, as you see, weak.

Some later scholars claimed that if *aʿmāl* is taken to mean *āmilīn* (doers), then *al-akhsarīn* means *al-khāsirīn* (the losers), because when the *tamyīz* is an adjective, it is an expression of the thing it specifies, being identical with it in essence and predicated of it by identity. Indeed, the grammarians have explicitly stated that the *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) may also be so, and it is a predicate of its subject in meaning. It is clear that the comparative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*) cannot be identical with the active participle, because of the additional element of comparison. Therefore, wherever the active participle occurs as a *tamyīz* and is in the accusative governed by the comparative, it must have the sense of the active participle (*fāʿil*) so that the two are identical. But someone objected to this, saying that *afʿal* with the definite article is not free of the sense of comparison, just as it is not free of it when it is in a construct relation (*iḍāfa*). This happens only when it is followed by *min* (than), as Ibn Malik explicitly stated in *al-Tashīl* and al-Radi mentioned. You are not unaware of the problems in all of this.

The truth is that the plurality is only for what was mentioned first. Yes, Abu al-Baqa mentioned that it is plural because it is in the accusative as in the case of the active participles. This was interpreted by saying that he meant by the active participle the lexical meaning, and that he intended that it was pluralized to indicate distribution, in that it does not lack any of them.

Then, according to what is in *Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim* (Abu al-Suʿud's commentary), this is a statement of the state of the disbelievers with regard to the good deeds that proceeded from them, which are good in themselves and also in their own reckoning, since they were pleased with them, confident of receiving their reward, and seeing their effects. Following this is a statement of their state with regard to their evil deeds, which are evil in themselves while being good in their own reckoning.

[Page 48]

**Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world** (﴿الَّذِينَ ضَلَّ﴾): that is, they are wasted and utterly nullified in the sight of God, Mighty and Majestic, **(their effort)** in carrying out those deeds, **in the life of this world** (﴿فِي الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾). The phrase "in the life of this world" is connected to "effort" (sa'y), not to "lost" (ḍalla), because the nullification of their effort is not restricted to this world.

It has been said that the intended people are the People of the Two Books (Ahl al-Kitab), and this is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Mujahid. On this view, the deeds include what they performed of the rulings that were abrogated (al-ahkam al-mansukha, rulings that were superseded by later revelation, naskh) and that relate to acts of worship. It has also been said that they are the monks who confine themselves in cloisters and subject themselves to severe ascetic exercises. And it has been said that they are the Sabians (al-Sabi'a).

Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali, may God honour his face, about them, and he said: "Among them are the people of Harura," meaning the Kharijites (al-Khawarij, the seceding sect). It has been objected that the words of God Most High, ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("Those are the ones who disbelieved") etc., contradict this, because they (the Kharijites) do not deny the Resurrection and are not unbelievers. It is answered that "min" (among) here is connective (ittisaliyya), so it does not require that they be connected to them in every respect; it is enough that they share in the error. Moreover, it is possible that Ali, may God honour his face, believed them to be unbelievers. It has been regarded as good that this is an allusion to them by way of severe censure, not an explanation of the verse.

What is mentioned in Majma' al-Bayan (Majma' al-Bayan, the commentary of al-Tabarsi) is that al-Ayyashi narrated with his chain that Ibn al-Kawwa asked the Commander of the Faithful, may God honour his face, about the people of this verse. He said: "Those are the People of the Book. They disbelieved in their Lord and innovated in their religion, so their deeds came to nothing. And the People of the River are not far from being among them." This supports the first answer, and it indicates that the intended meaning is broader, covering all unbelievers.

The place (maḥall) of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is nominative, as it is the predicate (khabar, the second part of the nominal sentence) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), because it is an answer to a question. It is as if it were said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "Those whose..." It is also permitted that it be in the genitive position as an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to "the greatest losers" (al-akhsarin). It is also permitted that it be a qualifier (na't) or a substitute (badal), and that it be accusative by way of censure (nasb 'ala al-dhamm), with the answer being what will come, if God wills, in His words, Glory be to Him: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ﴾ ("Those are the ones who...") etc.

It has been objected that this is refuted, because the beginning of the verse does not announce the loss of deeds and the straying of effort, as the context of an answer requires. The first consequence (tafri' al-awwal), though it indicates their deeds being brought down, is silent about the most important thing in establishing the meaning of loss: the certainty of obtaining profit and the belief that what they did is beneficial. Furthermore, the second consequence (tafri' al-thani) definitively excludes that possibility, since there is no room for including it under the command, by virtue of the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama). The answer to this does not hold except with some strain, so reflect.

﴿وهم يَحْسَبُونَ أنَّهم يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعًا﴾ ("while they think that they are doing good work"). Ihsan (excellence) means performing deeds in the manner that is fitting, and this is its descriptive goodness (husn wasfi), which entails its essential goodness (husn dhati). That is, they believe that they are performing those deeds in the fitting manner, because they are pleased with their deeds, for which they strove to establish and toiled to achieve. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "lost" (ḍalla), meaning: their aforementioned effort was lost while they were doing good in that and benefiting from its effects. Or it relates to the genitive noun (mudaf ilayhi) in "their effort" (sa'yuhum), since it is in the nominative position: their effort was lost, and they were (in the state that) they... The difference between the two readings is that what coincides with the state of their thinking mentioned in the first reading is the straying of their effort, while in the second it is their effort itself. It has been said that the first is more apt for explaining their error. And the paronomasia (tajnis al-tasif, a pun formed by letters differing only in dots) between "yahsabuna" (they think) and "yuhsinuna" (they do good) is evident. A similar example is the verse of al-Buhturi:

"The one deceived by God was not the one who set out at night to fail, / nor was the one made mighty by God the one who sought him."

(Ula'ika) is a new sentence from Him, the Exalted, brought to complete the definition of "the greatest losers" and to clarify their loss and the misguidance of their striving, and to specify them so that the description applies to those addressed without being included under the command, as has been said. That is: "Those are the ones described with what has been mentioned of the misguidance of effort and the reckoning mentioned," ﴿who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾ — His proofs that call to monotheism, comprising both the revealed (sam'iyyah) and the rational (aqliyyah). It has been said: "with the Qur'an," but the first is better. The mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyyah) serves to increase the reprehensibility of their state in the disbelief mentioned. ﴿And His meeting﴾ (liqa'ihi) is literally in the sense of encountering a thing and coming upon it, and this is not what is intended. Most scholars hold that it is a metonym for the resurrection, the gathering, and what follows of the matters of the Hereafter, i.e., they did not believe in that as it truly is. It has been said that the speech contains an elided noun, i.e., "the meeting of His punishment," but this is not the right view.

(Fa-habitat) — with a kasra on the ba' — and Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha. The fa' indicates a consequence: so their deeds (a'maluhum), the known ones, became void entirely (habaṭan kulliyyan). ﴿So We shall not assign for them﴾, i.e., for those described with the voiding of deeds mentioned, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾, i.e., We shall disdain them and hold them in contempt, and We shall not give them any measure or consideration, because the basis of consideration and concern is good deeds, and these have been utterly voided. Since this disdain and contempt is among the consequences of the voiding of deeds, it is joined to it by way of consequence. As for what is among the requitals of disbelief, it will come after this, God willing. Some have claimed that, on this reading, it should be joined with waw, as the conjunction of one of two consequences to the other, since the source of their being despised is disbelief, not the voiding; and this has been objected to on that basis, and that claim arises from extreme inattention, as is not hidden. Or the meaning is: We shall not set up a scale for the weighing of their deeds, because they have been voided and have become scattered dust. This negation, after the report of their voiding, is in the manner of emphasis, unlike the negation on the first meaning; for this reason it is preferred, and it has nothing to do with Mu'tazilism.

Mujahid and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read ﴿fa-la yuqimu﴾ with the yeh, because of the preceding phrase ﴿the signs of their Lord﴾. And from 'Ubayd also: ﴿fa-la yaqimu﴾ with a fatha on the yeh of the present tense, as if he made qama transitive. And from Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub, with a variant from them: ﴿fa-la yaqumu lahum yawma al-qiyamati wazn﴾, on the basis that yaqumu is the present of the intransitive qama, and wazn is its subject.

(ذَلِكَ) That (Dhalika) is an explanation of the outcome of their disbelief and of all their other sins, following the explanation of their deeds that were made void by it; it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter and the affair is that."

As for the statement of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Their recompense is Hell﴾, it is a sentence explaining it, so it has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case analysis).

It is also permitted that (ذَلِكَ) be the subject, with (وجَزاؤُهُمْ) (their recompense) as a substitute for it, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) or a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull), if the reference is to the recompense that is in mind, with (وجَهَنَّمُ) (Jahannam) as its predicate. The masculine form (al-tadhkir) is used even though the predicate is feminine, because the one referred to is the recompense, and because the predicate is in reality for the substitute.

It is also permitted that (ذَلِكَ) be the subject, (وجَزاؤُهم) its predicate, and (وجَهَنَّمُ) an appositive (atf bayan) to the predicate, with the reference being to Jahannam, which is present in mind.

It is also permitted that the subject be (ذَلِكَ) and the sentence (جَزاؤُهم جَهَنَّمُ), a subject and predicate, be its predicate, with the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) omitted; the reference is to their disbelief and their deeds, and the masculine form is used in accordance with what was mentioned, i.e., "that is their recompense by it, Hell." This has been criticized on the grounds that the omission of a returning pronoun governed by a preposition is common in such cases only when it is governed by a partitive or locative preposition, or when a preceding returning pronoun is governed by the same kind of preposition as in his saying:

"So the one you claim to be successful by..."

i.e., by it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (ذَلِكَ) be the subject, (وجَزاؤُهُمْ) a substitute or appositive, and (وجَهَنَّمُ) a substitute for "recompense," or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is Jahannam." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because they disbelieved﴾ is the predicate of (ذَلِكَ). After mentioning the aspects of i'rab that he mentioned, he said: it is not permissible for the prepositional phrase to be connected to (جَزاؤُهم) because of the separation between them by (جَهَنَّمَ). It was said: the apparent view is that it is connected to it, and separation does no harm in such a case.

This is an explicit statement that what was mentioned is the recompense for their disbelief, which includes all the other vices indicated by His saying, may He be exalted, which is conjoined to "they disbelieved": ﴿and they took My signs and My messengers in mockery﴾, i.e., mocked at by them. For they were not content with mere disbelief in the signs and the messengers, peace be upon them, but also committed a similarly great offense.

It is also permitted that the sentence be independent (mustanifa), though this is contrary to the apparent meaning. As for the signs, it has been said that they are the manifest miracles upon the hands of the messengers, peace be upon them, and the divine scriptures revealed to them, prayers and peace be upon them.

[p. 49 continues]

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ is a statement, by way of promise, of the final destiny of those who possess the opposites of the qualities of the disbelievers, following the statement of the destiny of the latter by way of threat. That is: indeed, those who believe in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, glory be to Him, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ of the deeds, ﴿for them shall be﴾ in accordance with what preceded of God Most High's decree and promise. Thus the past tense is used in view of what has been mentioned. In this, according to what Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam, a title for a leading scholar) said, there is an indication that the effect of mercy reaches them in accordance with the eternal compassion, unlike what passed concerning the making of Jahannam (Hell) a ﴿nuzul﴾ (lodging, hospitality) for the disbelievers, for that is in accordance with what occurred from their evil choice. It has also been said: it is possible that what they were promised, because of its certainty, was treated as if it had already occurred, so the verb ﴿kānat﴾ (was) was used to indicate this. He did not say "We have prepared (a''tadnā) for them," as was said in what passed, in order to indicate that the matter of the Gardens is not nearly complete, but rather what is in them continues to increase, for the preparation (i'tād) of a thing and readying it require its completion and perfection. It has come in the reports that for the believer, a tree is planted in Paradise for every glorification (tasbīḥah) he utters. It has also been said: the expression with what was mentioned is more evident in the certainty of the matter than the expression with i'tād. Do you not see that a house may be readied for a person and he does not dwell in it, and yet it is not devoid of kindness? So understand.

﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾: Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid that al-Firdaws is the orchard in Roman (Greek) speech. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi that it is the vineyard in Nabataean speech, and its origin is firdasa. Ibn Abi Shaybah and others reported from Abdullah ibn al-Harith that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b about al-Firdaws, and he said: the garden of grapes in Syriac. Ikrimah said: it is the garden in Ethiopic. al-Qaffal said: it is the garden thickly covered with trees. al-Zajjaj related that it is the valleys which produce various kinds of plants. al-Mubarrad said: as far as I have heard from the Arabs, it is the thick-set trees, most of which are grapevines. al-Farra' stated that it is also Arabic, and its meaning is the orchard in which there is a vineyard, and it is of those words that are used both masculine and feminine. Some claimed that it was not heard in the speech of the Arabs except in the verse of Hassan:

"Indeed the reward of Allah for every monotheist
is gardens of Firdaws, wherein he will abide forever."

But this is not sound, for Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Their dwellings at that time were manifest,
wherein were the farādīs, then garlic and onions."

It also occurs in the poetry of Jarir, in verses in which he praises Khalid ibn Abdullah al-Qasri, where he says:

"Indeed we hope to accompany a company
who will be the first to arrive at Firdaws."

And among what the people of Makkah heard before the conversion of Sa'd is the saying of a unseen caller:

"Respond to the caller of guidance and wish
upon Allah, in Firdaws, the death of one who knows."

The truth is that its mention is frequent in the poetry of the Islamic-era poets and rare in the poetry of the pre-Islamic era. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you ask Allah Most High, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise and the highest of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth."

And from Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Paradise has one hundred levels, between each two levels is what is between the heaven and the earth, and al-Firdaws is the highest of Paradise. So when you ask Allah Most High, ask Him for al-Firdaws."

It is related from Ka'b: "There is nothing higher in Paradise than the Garden of al-Firdaws, and in it are those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong."

It is established that the people of al-Firdaws hear the creaking (aṭīṭ) of the Throne.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "al-Firdaws is the enclosure of the Most Merciful." All of this does not contradict the fact that al-Firdaws in the lexicon means the orchard, as is imagined, since there is no obstacle to the highest part of Paradise being an orchard; but because it is of the utmost vastness, every piece of it was called a garden, so it is said "gardens of al-Firdaws." Thus it has been said. It has been objected that the verse, in that case, indicates that all the believers are in al-Firdaws, which includes gardens, and this is not valid if al-Firdaws is the highest of the ranks, since there is no doubt that their ranks differ. And to say that those who believed and did righteous deeds refers to a specific group out of the general believers, although it is set against the disbelievers, is not valid.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that "gardens of al-Firdaws" means orchards around al-Firdaws, and for this reason the gardens were attributed to al-Firdaws. But you know that this does not satisfy the thirst, since the verse would then indicate that all the believers are in the gardens of al-Firdaws, and it is well known that some of them are in al-Firdaws itself. It has been said: the matter is as Abu Hayyan mentioned, except that it requires an istikhdām (a figure in which one word is used in two senses) in the verse, by which is meant the general gardens in what follows. And with this, besides being contrary to the apparent meaning, there is what is not hidden.

It has also been said that what is meant by the gardens of al-Firdaws is all the gardens, and the attribution to al-Firdaws, which is the highest of them, is based on its including them, and this relation suffices for the attribution. Perhaps you will choose that al-Firdaws in the reports has one meaning and in the verse another meaning, and you will choose from its meanings what is made to fit the attribution, such as the thickly covered trees and the like. The apparent meaning of the verse of Hassan and the verse of Umayyah is evidence that al-Firdaws has a meaning other than what came in the reports, so reflect upon it.

Know also that there is an objection regarding the command to the one who asks to ask Allah for al-Firdaws for himself, given that it is the highest of Paradise, according to the report of Ahmad from Abu Hurairah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When you send blessings upon me, ask Allah Most High for me the wasīlah (intercession station), which is the highest rank in Paradise, which no one will attain except one man, and I hope that I am he."

It is answered that there is no obstacle to one rank being divided into ranks some of which are higher than others, and the wasīlah would be an expression for the highest ranks of al-Firdaws, which are the highest ranks of the gardens. A parallel to this is what has been said about the definition of i'jāz (inimitability), so remember it. It has also been said that what is meant by "rank" (darajah) in the hadith of the wasīlah is the rank of status, not a place, unlike what preceded, so there is no objection.

The prepositional phrase and what it governs are connected to an omitted element, either as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of the words of God Most High ﴿nuzulan﴾ (as lodging/hospitality), or as an explanation, as in ﴿su'iyyan laka﴾ (striving for you), and the predicate of kāna is in both cases ﴿nuzulan﴾. Or it is that the predicate is ﴿nuzulan﴾, and ﴿nuzulan﴾ is a ḥāl from ﴿jannāt﴾ (gardens). If it is taken in the sense of what is prepared for the one who lodges, then the meaning is: for them the fruits of the gardens of al-Firdaws were a lodging; or the gardens themselves were made a lodging, as hyperbole in honoring them. In this there is an indication that what Allah Most High has prepared for them through the tongue of prophethood, in His words (as in the hadith qudsī): "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has it occurred to the heart of any human being," is like the lodging in relation to hospitality. And if it is taken in the sense of the place of lodging (munzal), then the meaning is evident.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 18, verse 108:**

﴿Abiding therein﴾ is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). According to some, it is a *ḥāl muqaddara* (a circumstantial clause whose state is anticipated rather than simultaneous). It has been verified that it is a *ḥāl muqārina* (a coinciding circumstantial clause), and what is considered in coincidence is the time of the judgement, which is their being in Paradise. After they have entered it, they are coinciding with it, since it has no end. So reflect on this and do not be heedless. ﴿They desire no change from it﴾: it is, as Ibn ʿĪsā and others said, a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) like *ʿiwaj*, *ṣighar* and *ʿiwad* in the line:

*ʿādanī ḥubbuhā ʿiwadan*

That is, they do not seek any transition from it, since it is inconceivable that anything could be more precious or more elevated in their estimation than it, such that their souls would long for it and their eyes would aspire to it, even though their ranks differ. The essential point is that the meaning of not seeking a change from it is that it is the most excellent and highest of abodes.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it seems to be an *ism jamʿ* (collective noun), and its singular seems to be *ḥawāla*, but its remoteness is not hidden. Al-Zajjāj said, on the authority of a people, that it means the *ḥīla* (ability, means) of moving about, but this is weak and forced.

It is also permitted that the meaning is the negation of transition and movement, as an emphasis of abiding (*khulūd*), because not seeking movement entails abiding, so it emphasizes it. Or because the speech is in the manner of the saying: "and the lizard is not seen entering its hole," meaning they do not transfer from it so that they would seek it. It has also been said regarding the form of emphasis: when they do not wish to move, they do not move, because there is no compulsion in it and no desire to depart from it, so nothing remains but abiding, since there is no intermediary between the two, as has been said.

The sentence is a *ḥāl* from the subject of *khālidīn* or from its pronoun within it, and so it is a *ḥāl mutadākhila* (an interlocking circumstantial clause). In it is an indication that abiding does not bring them boredom.

[p. 52]

﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾, i.e., the sea in its entirety, (*midad*), which in origin is a term for whatever a thing is replenished with, and which in common usage is restricted to the ink with which the inkwell is replenished. ﴿...for the writing of the words of my Lord﴾, i.e., prepared for writing down His words, may He be exalted.
